washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/10/08/out.headline: Mamdani defends Oct. 7 message that angered Jewish leaders, unnerved some Democrats
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/10/08/out.author: Tim Craig, Michelle Boorstein, Teo Armus

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday stood by a social media post about the 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel that enraged segments of the Jewish community and unnerved some Democrats ahead of the midterm elections.

Mamdani, a high-profile democratic socialist leader, touched off the uproar on Wednesday when he commemorated the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks with written remarks that devoted more space to Israel’s response against Palestinians than it did to acknowledge the losses suffered by the Jewish people on that day. The post on X accused Israel of committing “ongoing genocide” and “war crimes” and highlighted the plight of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

“That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing,” Mamdani wrote. “Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.”

Mamdani’s statement was met with strong criticism from a cross-section of Jewish leaders, who accused him of downplaying the pain felt within their community over the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, the deadliest day for Jews since World War II. They accused Mamdani of inflaming divisions that have led to a surge in antisemitic hate crimes in New York and nationally.

“The Mayor’s role is to bring people together for the good of all New Yorkers, and he continues to fall short of that goal,” said Mark Treyger, the chief executive of the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York. “None of this is normal and we refuse to accept it.”
The unease comes as some Democrats nationally are worried that the rise of candidates opposed to Israel is alienating some Jewish voters from the party.

Since Mamdani was elected in November, democratic socialists have unseated several incumbents in Democratic primaries for congressional and state legislative seats. Many of the winning candidates campaigned on messages that included rebukes of Israeli policy or questioned the legitimacy of the Jewish state.
Several Republican leaders, including House Speaker Mike Johnson (Louisiana), lambasted Mamdani for his social media post on Wednesday.

Most high-profile Democratic leaders in New York steered clear of the controversy, but several Democratic members of Congress from other parts of the country spoke up to say they were offended by the mayor’s statements.
“He basically said ‘The Jews that died, sad, but it’s their fault,’” Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Florida) wrote on X. “Just an atrocious statement.”

At a news conference Thursday, Mamdani said he believes his comments a day earlier appropriately balanced the more than 1,100 lives lost in Israel during the Hamas attacks with the more than 74,000 Palestinians who have died in the subsequent Israeli military operation in the Gaza Strip.
Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, said he is trying to balance the agony that both Jews and Arabs feel about the conflict.

“I believe there must be room to mourn every single life,” said Mamdani, who later added, “We know that [Oct. 7] brings back the most horrific memories for so many people in this city, and also for others it’s a day continuing in the Israeli government’s use and it’s justification for a genocide.”

Mamdani attempted throughout Wednesday’s anniversary to balance the emotions felt by both Jewish and Muslim New Yorkers. In the evening, he attended a vigil that honored Israeli and Palestinian lives lost during the conflict.

Underscoring the challenges he faces in unifying the city, Mamdani was heckled at the event by supporters of the Israeli government and pro-Palestinian protesters who feel he has not followed up on some of his campaign promises, including a more recent previous pledge to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if he visited New York.
Mamdani ended Wednesday by meeting with Palestinian activists, and he dined at a Palestinian restaurant in Manhattan’s Upper Westside.
“I think the statement, the attendance [at the vigil], the meeting, it all speaks to a reckoning with horror,” Mamdani said Thursday.

Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, who has worked with the Mamdani administration, said his policies in her view have “done really important things.” She praised the coexistence event he attended Wednesday but said she feels at times that his rhetoric leaves Jewish supporters feeling unseen.

“Some will argue he shouldn’t talk about Israeli war crimes but that’s not my perspective,” she said. “First of all, he will always talk about that and that’s okay. We need to carve out space for people to hold multiple truths.”
Mamdani has repeatedly taken actions that anger segments of the Jewish community.

He signed two executive orders that were viewed as weakening ties between his city and Israel. He also vetoed a bill that would have allowed police to create buffer zones to keep protesters away from schools — a policy Jewish organizations lobbied for in response to recent campus protests.

In May, Mamdani posted a social media video marking Nakba Day, a commemoration of the mass displacement and expulsion of Palestinians that accompanied the birth of the state of Israel in 1948. The word nakba is Arabic for catastrophe.
The same month, Mamdani, a self-described “anti-Zionist,” skipped the annual Israel Day Parade. Jewish leaders said they could not recall another mayor who declined to attend the event.

In recent weeks, Mamdani has attempted to soothe relations between his administration and his critics in the Jewish community. He announced in September a citywide initiative to combat antisemitism, which includes about $7.5 million to counter hate crimes and enhance security at Jewish institutions.
But Jewish leaders in New York and elsewhere said Mamdani’s social media post this week has renewed tensions.

“To be honest, I think yesterday was the worst day of his tenure as mayor,” said Joel Rubin, a former deputy assistant of state and former Jewish campaign adviser to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont). “He completely exacerbated tensions.”
In his campaign for mayor last year, Mamdani won about a third of the Jewish vote, according to exit polls. He also maintains close ties with liberal and secular Jewish institutions.
Yet some Democratic leaders worry that the rise of Mamdani and other democratic-socialist-aligned candidates could hinder the party’s ability to retain Jewish voters.
In Michigan, the Democratic candidate for Senate, Abdul El-Sayed, is locked in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers that could decide control of the chamber.

El-Sayed does not identify as a democratic socialist, but he has received strong support from its members, and he recently held a fundraiser in New York that was attended by several close Mamdani allies. He would be the first Muslim U.S. senator and, like Mamdani, is an outspoken critic of Israel.

Retired Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman, a moderate Democratic who lost his primary contest for a U.S. Senate seat in Florida this past summer, said Wednesday that Mamdani’s social media post hurt the party.
“He ignited controversy in the exact moment Dems are making their appeals to moderates and independents,” Vindman said on X.

Megan Romer, national co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, cast aside the idea that Mamdani’s comments might hurt Democrats in competitive midterm races, saying he was entitled to approach the Israeli-Palestinian issue as he sees fit.
“He’s extraordinarily popular. He can say whatever he wants,” she said. “That’s part of the deal — he’s not going to please everybody.”

Scott Stringer, a former New York City comptroller who unsuccessfully ran in last year’s Democratic mayoral primary, said voters are smart enough to distinguish between Mamdani and more moderate candidates.
“I do not for the most part believe that anyone gives a s--- about Mamdani’s anti-Jewish rants,” he said.
Yet he warned that Mamdani needed to focus on trying to bring disparate groups of voters together.

“Going forward, we’re going to have to deliberate and figure this out as a party or we will end up electing a Republican,” said Stringer, who is Jewish. “It’s not working for us nationally and it’s not going to work for us in 2028.”

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Jonathan Barrett

paragraphs.text: Firmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.
A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.
“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.
“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”
Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.
But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.

Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.
The lack of demand means Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.
Frantic discussions

The polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.
This prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.
The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.

Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going to use retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.
The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.

The anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, who has spent time in prison for insider trading, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.

paragraphs.text: Riley Griffin and Alexandra S. Levine
Thu, October 8, 2026 at 6:00 PM CDT 3 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc. banned advertisements in the US from ByteDance Ltd., the former controlling owner of TikTok, intensifying the competition with the popular social video site.
Most Read from Bloomberg

On Thursday, Meta began implementing a complete restriction on ads and paid marketing messages placed on its platforms by ByteDance, the Chinese company that remains in charge of key parts of TikTok in the US. The ban will take effect in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to Meta, and also extend to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries.

"We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro said in an emailed statement. "Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience."

Meta and TikTok have competed neck-and-neck for years, even with a key imbalance in that rivalry: TikTok has been able to operate in Meta's most important market, the US, while Meta has been unable to do so in TikTok's most crucial market, China. But that competition took a more heated turn in August after Meta agreed to an historic $18 billion settlement with US states requiring it to implement new safety features for minors across its Instagram and Facebook apps.

Since then, Meta has been pressuring TikTok and Google's YouTube to commit to making similar changes, suggesting it cannot solve industrywide child safety problems on its own. TikTok has remained publicly silent on the matter, ratcheting up the tension between the companies as Meta grapples with what it sees as yet another competitive disadvantage.

Last month, TikTok enacted a number of measures to make it harder to shift from its app to other social platforms, including by eliminating dedicated Instagram links from its users' profiles. It also rejected ads from Meta demanding that TikTok commit to comparable concessions on child safety.

Soon after the settlement with the state attorneys general, Meta ran ads in top newspapers upping its pressure campaign. Meta executives have also called out TikTok publicly for failing to show up at a recent Office of the Surgeon General event on the harms of excessive screen use, and for dropping out of a national security meeting with the House Select Committee on China to avoid broader scrutiny amid its child safety litigation.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: AI Debt Spree Hammers Tech Debt as Traders Rush to Reprice Risk
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Caleb Mutua, Preeti Singh and Laura Benitez

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The rush to finance AI is rattling investors in the more than $10 trillion US corporate market, sparking a repricing of risks around some of the biggest technology companies that's showing up in spiking prices for credit insurance, heightened volatility and weakening preformance.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Heavyweights including Oracle Corp., Broadcom Inc. and SpaceX are among the borrowers that priced nearly half a trillion dollars of new debt this year to pay for the infrastructure powering artificial intelligence, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The tally is widely expected to rise by orders of magnitude in the months and years ahead. Broadcom alone may raise about $600 billion to finance computing power in the coming years, according to Bloomberg calculations.

The pace and sheer scale of the borrowings, combined with unknowns around the technology and rising interest rates, is put growing pressure on the sector. Tech has been among the worst-performing sectors across credit in recent months, leaving investors nursing losses, while average daily trading volumes for tech names in the bond and credit derivatives markets have soared.

In recent days, news of a wave of potential fresh financings from SpaceX and Broadcom, possibly topping $100 billion, sent credit derivatives linked to hyperscalers and chipmakers climbing to prices that suggest traders see a growing risk of a default over the next five years. For Oracle, it's now above 20%, for SpaceX it's about 16% — and even Nvidia Corp., the world's most valuable company, is given a more than 7% risk of default in that time.

"Every new financing announcement feels like another entrant in an auction for investor balance sheet, and that's creating a level of spread volatility that would have seemed hard to imagine a year ago," said Mark Clegg, senior fixed-income trader at Allspring Global Investments. "Some days it feels like the market is holding an emergency meeting every few hours to reprice the size of the AI buildout."

So-called mega transactions in the tens of billions of dollars used to be few and far between and syndicate banks would spend months telegraphing the deals ahead of launch, plus most of the huge deals were earmarked for mergers and acquisitions. This year, there have been nine US high-grade deals that are $25 billion or above in size, the most ever, most of them in tech.

The US high-yield market, meanwhile, is poised for one of its busiest year on record. And while debt markets have absorbed the record supply relatively well, investors are starting to demand higher compensation to lend to the sector, particularly as financing needs expand beyond the so-called hyperscalers into chip financing, data centers, and other structures, according to Steven Kohlenstein, fixed-income portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price.

"One concern is the growing concentration of exposure to a relatively small group of companies and ultimately the same underlying AI investment cycle, even as that risk gets distributed across different issuers, sectors, and financing structures," said Kohlenstein. "That creates the potential for correlated risks that may not be fully reflected in current valuations."

For now the issue is less about actual deterioration in credit quality than about market saturation. Most of these big borrowers are profitable, with steady cash flow and earnings momentum. And their weaker performance hasn't spilled over into the broader market, which has held up relatively well.

These borrowers are also tapping as many corners of demand as they can, borrowing in global markets and exploring various debt structures to help mitigate risks. But even so, the crush of debt in such a relatively short span of time gives investors at least some bargaining power to demand more compensation for taking on the debt. And there are unknowns about the AI rollout, the potential payoff and the risks around the technology, all of which could upend valuations.

Among expected borrowings that have recently come to light, Broadcom is sketching out plans for its next blockbuster deal just days after it launched a $60 billion debt financing to help fund Anthropic PBC's artificial intelligence buildout, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. Broadcom's five-year CDS widened by 3 basis points to a record 136 basis points on Thursday, according to ICE Data Services.

Oracle, widely considered a key barometer for gauging AI-credit risk, is in talks with Apollo and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to arrange money for a big purchase of chips, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday. That could potentially involve a structure where outside investors fund a separate special purpose vehicle that purchases chips and leases them to Oracle instead of Oracle funding a large chip purchase upfront with unsecured debt, according to some market participants.

The structure would likely reduce Oracle's other near term borrowing needs and ease pressure on its credit rating. Still, the uncertainty is unnerving investors. The cost of guaranteeing Oracle debt against default about 10.5 basis points Thursday to a record close of 261 basis points.

Meanwhile, a measure of SpaceX's credit risk is trading at a record for a second straight day after reports the company is in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to buy chips from Nvidia Corp.

In many ways, the repricings reflect a market that is at a crossroads. Companies have immense and growing funding needs to pay for the computing capacity required to keep scaling up the technology. But revenue growth is at risk of becoming less extraordinary as competition and potentially regulation grow, according to Andrew Dassori, chief investment officer at Wavelength Capital Management. The potential market swings that result can create opportunities for traders, he said.
"Markets are adapting to these conditions and you see this in how spreads move and through the lens of volatility," said Dassori.
--With assistance from Davide Barbuscia, Brian Smith and James Crombie.

washingtonpost.com/immigration/2026/10/0.headline: ICE officer shoots, wounds man in car on crowded New York street
washingtonpost.com/immigration/2026/10/0.author: Silvia Foster-Frau, Tim Craig

paragraphs.text: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fired at least seven rounds into a car on a crowded New York street Thursday afternoon, city officials said, wounding a man while a 5-year-old boy sat unharmed in the back seat.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that an ICE officer had fired during a “targeted enforcement operation.” The agency said it was attempting to apprehend a “criminal illegal alien” from the Dominican Republic with a criminal record that includes a conviction for grand larceny and multiple past arrests.

According to local authorities, around 4 p.m. Thursday, the man parallel parked in front of a fire hydrant. One of the ICE officers, in plain clothes and with a gun drawn, approached the driver-side window of the gray Honda CRV, said New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, citing residential police cameras.

Another officer approached the driver-side headlight. The driver started to pull away and moved out of view of the camera, Tisch said. Soon after, the ICE officer opened fire, striking the driver in the neck under his left ear, Tisch said.

Both Tisch and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani noted that the officers were not wearing clothing that indicated they were law enforcement personnel and said at least one officer was carrying a long gun.

“They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There was no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents,” Mamdani said at a late-night news conference. “School had just gotten out. The street was crowded with families and children.”

When the New York City police arrived on the scene after the shooting, the wounded man was handcuffed and sitting on the ground. Police officers placed him in their vehicle and offered medical aid, Tisch said.
He was taken to a nearby hospital and was “conscious and receiving medical attention,” the New York Police Department said in a statement after the shooting.
Mamdani said he spent two hours on the phone Thursday night with President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin negotiating for the release of the wounded man.
Instead, ICE “put the man in an unmarked vehicle and whisked him away,” Mamdani said.

DHS did not release the name of the immigrant it was targeting or explain why the officer fired his weapon. Tisch said the man had two previous arrests in New York City: one for robbery in 2023 and one for the criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025.

Tisch also said that although the police investigation is preliminary, they believe the 5-year-old boy is the wounded man’s son. Police confirmed that the boy is staying with a family member, she said.

The wounded man’s vehicle had ballistic damage to the front windshield, the back window was shattered, and the car was perpendicular to the road, Tisch said. A gray, four-door Sedan belonging to ICE was also found at the scene with damage to a front panel and a disconnected lower panel.

Federal immigration officers have killed two immigrants and injured a third in shootings during enforcement operations since July. All three of those incidents involved officers firing at people who were inside their vehicles. Those and previous shootings have ignited outrage from Democrats, immigration advocates and family members of the deceased, who say that ICE is using excessive force against people who do not represent a threat.

In its statement, DHS emphasized that the man shot Thursday night had been released by New York officials after his earlier arrests. “When dangerous illegal aliens are released back onto the streets by radical sanctuary politicians, our officers are forced to make arrests at large in the community,” the statement said.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) called ICE a “rogue agency” and said “New Yorkers are outraged, immigrant communities are terrified,” and residents are “demanding answers.”

“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire, let alone wonder if they’ll make it home safe,” Hochul said in a statement. “Federal authorities need to provide answers, and they must do so immediately.”

Hochul later posted on social media that she had spoken with Trump and Mullin about the shooting. “I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York.”
She also said she had asked that any body-camera footage of the incident be released to the public.
Marble Hill is part of the borough of Manhattan and bordered by the Bronx. According to a 2020 New York City demographics study, the area is 71 percent Latino.

Although Mamdani campaigned on a promise to protect New Yorkers from ICE, federal immigration operations have continued in city neighborhoods over the past year. The operations, which frustrate immigrant rights advocates, often appear focused on targeted individuals as opposed to broad sweeps similar to those ICE has deployed in other cities, including Minneapolis.

In early September, Mullin traveled to New York to announce that 2,197 undocumented immigrants had been arrested in the region in August. Mullin said the actions, dubbed Operation Rotten Apple, included arrests of individuals who had committed violent crimes.

Immigration rights advocates have been increasingly frustrated that New York City police officers, who are barred by law from cooperating with ICE, have been spotted near federal agents during arrests. Police officials have stressed that they are there to maintain public order and safety, and do not assist in federal immigration enforcement.

On Thursday night, immigrant rights demonstrators gathered outside the hospital where the victim of the ICE shooting was being treated. Videos from the scene showed demonstrators trying to push past police barricades and clashing with officers.
Craig reported from New York. N. Kirkpatrick contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Sydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal case
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Nino Bucci

paragraphs.text: A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.
The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.
Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop.

They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”.
Graham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week.
He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia.
He provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment.
Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied.

Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”.
Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place.

Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this.

He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas.

Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable.

The company was not swayed and on 2 December last year sent him a termination letter that stated it had carefully reviewed his written submissions and found that he had not provided flight screenshots with his name, medical evidence that showed his partner was unable to travel, an adequate explanation for not telling his manager he was in Singapore, and had previously complied with “absence and approval processes”, demonstrating that he was familiar with them and had instead made “a conscious choice not to follow” them.
“Your conduct represents a serious breach of company policy, a failure to follow lawful and reasonable instructions, and an irreparable breakdown of trust and confidence,” it said in the letter.
Graham told the commission he worked remotely twice before November 2025: the previous year from Townsville and in April and May 2025 from Bali. He had been employed by Xe for 20 months.
But his manager said she had not been aware he had ever worked remotely from overseas.

A Microsoft Teams message from Graham to his manager was included in evidence before the commission that detailed his claim he was working from home as he had a plumbing issue during one of the days he also told the commission he worked from Bali.
Matheson found that she was satisfied that the dismissal of Graham was unreasonable because while there was a valid reason for his dismissal, the process followed was procedurally unfair.
This was because Xe failed to fully raise the matters it was relying on in making the decision to dismiss Graham, Matheson said.
She found that reinstatement was inappropriate but also decided against awarding compensation.
This was, she said, in part because his misconduct contributed to the decision to dismiss him, and he was paid four weeks in lieu of notice.

theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.headline: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.
One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.
“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.
In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.
Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.
For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-5996396/hurrica.headline: Isaias strengthens into Category 2 hurricane on collision course with the Gulf Coast
npr.org/2026/10/09/nx-s1-5996396/hurrica.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: MIAMI — Isaias strengthened into a Category 2 hurricane as it barreled toward the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday, prompting orders for tourists to abandon beaches for safer spots inland, sending locals scurrying for gas and groceries and leading fishing crews to secure their boats before the potentially destructive storm's arrival.

The first hurricane of the Atlantic season was forecast to intensify rapidly and cause dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Heavy rain and flooding were possible into the weekend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina.
"We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall," said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
He added: "Today is the day to prepare and get ready and be in your safe place by tomorrow as conditions will rapidly deteriorate along the northern Gulf Coast as Isaias approaches."
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph), according to the hurricane center, surpassing the 96 mph (154 kph) threshold for a Category 2 storm.
Isaias was headed northeast at 14 mph (22 kph) and was centered about 260 miles (415 kilometers) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.

A hurricane warning was in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida, the hurricane center said. A storm surge warning was in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River.
Preparations underway

Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.

At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, while several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida's Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.

On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.

Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, "but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst."

Water from the storm surge and high tide could reach heights of 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters) in parts of Alabama and Mississippi, forecasters said. Isaias also could dump up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain on coastal areas and spawn tornadoes overnight Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore.
The National Weather Service warned of possible "long-duration power outages."
The hurricane formed late in the season

Isaias developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season and was one day short of tying a 121-year-old record for the area's latest-forming hurricane. That record dates to 1905, when the year's first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.

The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane. Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, Mexico, and Southern California this weekend.
Isaias is expected to strike a swath of coastline that's familiar with major hurricanes.

One of the 20th century's worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism are already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.

As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.

With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday's college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump planned to attend.

In Loxley, a small Alabama community where county officials urged voluntary evacuations, Nichole Eubanks and her husband prepared to ride out the storm on their farm, which is home to dozens of animals, including pigs, donkeys and about 20 rescued cats.
They planned to put contact information on the hooves of their goats, donkeys and pigs in case they got loose.
"It's definitely scary, and you never really know where these storms are going to go and how bad it's going to be until it gets there," said Eubanks, 35.

In the Alabama fishing village of Bayou La Batre, Tony Rice and Lance Connor installed doors on their fishing boat Thursday to protect the vessel. The boat was one of many moored there, and Rice said they planned to move it to a less-crowded spot to decrease the chances of it bumping into others.
In Pensacola, Florida, officials said the airport will close to commercial flights Friday morning. Mayor D.C. Reeves urged residents to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
"Obviously no need to panic at this point," Reeves told a news conference. "This is really about preparation."

theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/.headline: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/.author: Pippa Neill

paragraphs.text: A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.
But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.

Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.

Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.

Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.
However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.

He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.
Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.

They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.

“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.
“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”

The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.
Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.
“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.

Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”
The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.

Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”
The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.

Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/riyadh.headline: Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport as airlines suspend flights to Saudi capital
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/riyadh.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh ⁠airport with a ballistic missile, badly damaging a plane and leading some airlines to suspend flights to the capital.
The group provided no evidence, and Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the claim.

However, three people briefed on the matter told Reuters that shrapnel from an interception or another projectile left a Saudia Airlines commercial plane heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at a terminal on Thursday.
They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the ⁠time but they could not rule out any injuries.

Witnesses heard explosions in Riyadh, including a large blast at the King Khalid international airport. One witness told the Associated Press that fire and ambulance crews were deployed. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from the airport in a video verified by Reuters.
The witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that outgoing flights were halted, and that passengers were instructed to evacuate the airport.

Lufthansa and Air India confirmed they were ⁠suspending flights to Riyadh. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from the airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT on Thursday, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports.
It comes after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the country’s southwest.

The Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and warning workers to stay away from ⁠energy plants, which would be targeted.
Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis.
The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the country’s south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.

Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.
Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: Plans for Sydney’s controversial new public square in doubt after NSW government intervention
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Penry Buckley

paragraphs.text: Plans for a grand new public square in the centre of Sydney are in doubt after the New South Wales planning minister declared the project “state significant”, wresting the approval process away from the City of Sydney.

The lord mayor, Clover Moore, released renders in August for the plaza opposite Sydney’s town hall. The design for the space, which the council had expected to be completed by 2031, include a semi-circular clearing projecting eastwards towards Hyde park, with a fountain and a grove of native trees.

The plans have been the source of a battle between Moore and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, who has said he does not support the project, describing it as “too expensive, majorly disruptive for Sydney”, and said it would close down businesses in the area.

It had also become a flashpoint in a culture war, ridiculed in the Sydney tabloid The Daily Telegraph, which published AI-generated images of the new square heaving with protesters. The council led by Moore, who’s been the city’s progressive independent mayor since 2004, has previously received negative coverage from the publication for other proposals, including an Oxford Street cycleway first formally raised by the council in 2020.
The council has now acquired the last of seven buildings needed to be bulldozed for the square. The demolition and construction was expected to cost $150m.

But on Friday, the planning minister, Paul Scully announced he had declared the project a state significant development (SSD), after seeking advice from the NSW Independent Planning Commission, taking the decision for approval away from the council.

“This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application,” he said.

The project has also been opposed by Woolworths, whose town hall store occupies one of the buildings that would be demolished under the plan. At a press conference outside the store on Friday, the Australian Retail Council’s chief executive, Chris Rodwell, welcomed Scully’s decision.
“Look at this building. This is not a building that needs to be bulldozed … it’s home to Australia’s single busiest supermarket.”

Scully said the IPC would make the determination on any proposal submitted by the City of Sydney. Under the SSD pathway, the planning minister himself is the consent authority, unless the IPC is delegated to take on that role.
In a surprise statement on Friday, Moore, also welcomed the decision to declare the project state significant, saying, “I could not agree more”.
“Regardless of who assesses it, we remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported.

“The city owns the buildings, has responsibly saved the money over a 40-year period to deliver the project debt free, and has had some of the world’s leading designers and architects work on the plans.”

She said the government had recently approved the acquisition of the final property required for the square. But she said the timing of Scully’s intervention “raises questions” and it would be “deeply disappointing” progress was delayed until after the March state election.
Moore called on the minister to commit to “a transparent, genuine, fair and impartial assessment” that did not delay the project.
Scully declined to comment.

In its advice, the IPC noted the project involved “complex interfaces with state-owned transport infrastructure and requires coordinated assessment of engineering, construction, operational and stakeholder issues”.

But it said the proposal would “deliver public benefits through the provision of significant civic and social infrastructure”, and had “the potential to generate significant economic benefits through increased tourism, events, cultural activity and visitation to Sydney’s CBD”.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/eu-ass.headline: EU to Assess Windfall Tax on Energy Firms to Soften Price Shock
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/eu-ass.author: John Ainger and Jorge Valero

paragraphs.text: John Ainger and Jorge Valero
Fri, October 9, 2026 at 6:55 AM EDT 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- The European Commission will analyze the potential impacts of imposing a bloc-wide tax on windfall profits made by energy companies, as governments grapple with how best to cushion a price shock going into winter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The European Union's executive branch told a meeting of finance ministers in Luxembourg Friday that it would look into the feasibility of using a regional windfall tax to provide relief to citizens, according to people familiar with the matter. That follows calls from several member states, including Germany, to examine such an initiative.

During the energy crisis that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the EU introduced a revenue cap on so-called inframarginal electricity producers, like wind and solar. But the measure fell well short of a €50 billion ($56 billion) collection estimate, and triggered court cases that the EU is still dealing with, according to EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra.

"You always need to look at the full solution space," Hoekstra told reporters when he arrived for Friday's meeting. "It is not without complications," he said, adding that a number of member states were opposed to such a tax.

The Iran war has disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz, leading to a sharp increase in the price of products like diesel. Governments across the 27-member bloc are grappling with how to cushion the blow to consumers and businesses at a time when many countries are already facing fiscal constraints.

In a letter earlier this year, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Austria, Italy and Poland called on the EU to put forward a windfall tax to ease the shock. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil also said that France wasn't opposed.

"We can see how refineries and oil companies are profiting from this crisis, while consumers are ultimately the ones bearing the burden," Klingbeil said on Thursday. "I have a clear expectation that the commission will now put proposals on the table."

Lowering energy prices is set to be a key discussion among EU leaders at a summit in Brussels next week. Yet there are few obvious solutions given that the bloc is reliant on third countries for the vast majority of its fossil fuel supplies. The commission has already said that member states could implement a windfall profit cap at a national level.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Nobel Peace Prize Goes to International Jurist Navi Pillay
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Ott Ummelas

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
Most Read from Bloomberg

"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack," Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, told reporters. "We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice."
The laureate will receive 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) in prize money, the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo said in a statement on Friday.

"Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law," Watne Frydnes said. Her "commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world."

Pillay, 85, has served as a judge in South Africa, at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014 and later chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988.

"A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.

Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children's rights activist.
In 2025, a leak of Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado's name triggered an unusual betting surge on the Polymarket platform hours before she was unveiled as the award recipient.

Arguably the most prestigious prize in global diplomacy, the Nobel Peace Prize can also stir controversy. Last year, Donald Trump campaigned aggressively, and ultimately unsuccessfully, to obtain the award, which he has long coveted. Earlier this year Machado gifted her medal to the US president, stunning Norway.

The annual prizes for achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace were established in the will of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite, who died in 1896. A prize in economic sciences was added by Sweden's central bank in 1968.
The laureates are announced through Oct. 12 in Stockholm, with the exception of the Nobel Peace Prize.

The deal is split between a three-year tranche and a nine-year tranche, each fixed at a size of €500 million. finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Wall Street Sees an Ominous Sign in Bond Market’s Latest Selloff
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Greg Ritchie

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- It's one of the least understood signals in the fixed-income world, but lately, everyone on Wall Street is abuzz about what it means as it reasserts itself in the market.
Most Read from Bloomberg

It's known as the term premium, or the extra payout that investors demand in return for the risks of owning 10-year Treasuries instead of just rolling over short-dated securities for the same amount of time. How exactly to measure it varies. So do the explanations for its moves.

What's not in question is that during the past few weeks it spiked to levels not seen in over a decade and drove the latest leg of the bond selloff that's sent US Treasury yields to a 24-year high. And that, in turn, is fanning fears of a potential shift that will heap pressure on an already battered market and keep borrowing costs elevated across the economy.
That term premium is essentially protection against unpredictable turns, ranging from geopolitical shocks to government fiscal crises, that could hit the market before long-term bonds come due.

It's distinct from the current outlook for inflation and the direction of monetary policy, both of which are also reflected in yields. Because the premium isn't directly observable and must be inferred, Neel Kashkari, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, once likened it to dark matter, the invisible substance physicists say explains some cosmic mysteries.

"There's multiple ways to calculate it, but they're all going higher," said Frank Rybinski, head of macro strategy at Aegon Asset Management. "And what that tells me is that this move has staying power."
What Bloomberg's Strategists Say...

"The sharp repricing of term premium embedded in Treasuries — with 10-year term premium breaking out to a 12-year high — suggests investors are demanding greater compensation for holding duration amid mounting fiscal and geopolitical uncertainty."
— Frank Monkam, Macro Markets Strategist
Click here for more

There was no clear-cut catalyst. Barclays researchers led by Demi Hu said macroeconomic uncertainty, breakdowns in the usual correlations between stock and bond moves, the rising supply of debt and worries about fiscal policy are all things that figure into the term premium and could be playing a role.

Neil Shearing, the group chief economist at Capital Economics, said the recent move could reflect technical factors, like portfolio adjustments at the end of last month, or the side effects of mounting concern in Europe about France's debt load. Stephen Douglass, chief economist at NISA Investment Advisors, pointed to some indications of stress in credit markets, as well as broader doubts among investors over the benefits of holding fixed-income assets when inflationary shocks are becoming more frequent.
"It's not a simple story," said Douglass, who warned against reading too much into short-term moves. "But I would say that I think we are in a rising term-premium environment."
That's a worry for bond bulls. A structurally higher term premium could keep long-term interest rates elevated, preventing the market from rebounding from its slump.

The metric came down steadily in the 1990s, when increasing globalization was exerting a deflationary force, and fell further still during the 2010s as central banks' quantitative-easing programs distorted global bond markets by flooding them with cash. It dropped as low as negative 1.7% in March 2020, when investors were rushing for the safety of bonds, before rising consistently into positive territory after late 2024, according to a model created by economists working for the New York Fed.
It had remained relatively steady during most of the selloff that started after the US launched its war against Iran in late February.

Then, in mid-September, it started surging. The New York Fed model shows it climbed around 40 basis points to about 0.98%, the highest since 2014 and more than enough to account for the nearly 30 basis-point rise in 10-year Treasury yields over that time. Bloomberg Economics' estimate shows a similar increase. Another, which incorporates economists' forecasts for Fed policy into the calculation, has climbed to 1.08%, the most since 2010.

That break higher came as other drivers of prices were little changed. Inflation expectations have been stable. The Fed's unanimous decision to raise rates last month quelled some concerns about its commitment to reining in consumer prices. And oil, while elevated at over $100 a barrel, has been holding in a narrow range.

A sustained term-premium increase would add to the pressure on the market from elevated inflation, robust economic growth, plus a flood of borrowing from companies investing in artificial intelligence and from deficit-running governments around the globe. Fed Bank of Dallas President Lorie Logan last week said a rising term premium, by pushing up borrowing costs, may slow the economy and reduce the need for the central bank to hike rates.

"The bond market is no longer waiting for the Fed to tighten financial conditions," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro at Lombard Odier Investment Managers. "High term premia, inflation uncertainty and government borrowing needs can keep longer-dated yields restrictive even when the expected path of short rates becomes less aggressive."

One reason behind the latest moves may be spillover effects from the disorderly selloff in French bonds. Some also point to hedging activity by holders of mortgage-backed securities that can temporarily exaggerate market moves.

Yet behind it may be lurking longer-term risks that have been building up in the global economy. One is that shocks to the supply of energy and other commodities — like those that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the US war on Iran — may become more frequent as geopolitical divisions widen.

Then there's the federal government's $2 trillion budget deficit — the equivalent of about 6% of the nation's gross domestic product, an historically high level of stimulus at a time of low unemployment and solid economic growth. While the Trump administration has repeatedly vowed to rein in spending, there's little expectation that will happen anytime soon.

"The macro picture is full of risk which should translate into a healthy term premium," said Mark Malek, the chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. "Any time we have a headline flair up, investors are reminded of that risk."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.headline: Dollar’s Longest Winning Streak Since Early 2025 Keeps Going
finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.author: Anya Andrianova and Melos Ambaye

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The dollar rally is forging ahead as soaring oil prices weigh on currencies of energy importing nations and global inflation fears persist.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is extending its advance into a fourth week to notch a nearly 3% gain in the period — its longest winning streak since early 2025. Brent oil jumped Thursday amid fresh attacks from Iran threatening energy flows in the Middle East and pushing investors into the safety currency.

"Risk off, fiscal concerns in Europe and fears of supply disruptions out of the Strait of Hormuz continue to push investors into the dollar given little alternative," said Sarah Ying, head of FX strategy at CIBC Capital Markets. "Until oil prices come back down we see a period of sustained dollar strength."

Further buoying the greenback is the US' ability to withstand more interest-rate increases than other major economies. Fiscal concerns in France and high energy prices have put pressure on the euro, which touched the lowest level since May 2025 earlier this week.
"Part of the bull case for the dollar I think is the strong case for higher rates on a relative basis," said Robert Tipp, chief investment strategist and head of global bonds at PGIM Fixed Income.

Last month, the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in three years, and central bank officials continue to signal more needs to be done to battle inflation. On Thursday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said further hikes will likely be necessary, though officials have some flexibility on timing. Similarly, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President Alberto Musalem said rates should be lifted over the next six-to-nine months, but stopped short of endorsing a move at this month's policy meeting.

The dollar's run, however, could be derailed by concerns over artificial intelligence spending and the US midterm elections in November. The greenback pared recent gains on Friday, with the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index down 0.1%.

So far, the dollar has benefited from the AI boom and subsequent record-setting rally in US stocks that have lured foreign investment. On Thursday, stocks sold off after OpenAI reported revenue that was lower than recent estimates.

Investors also worry about election results, which will establish the composition of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Polls show the Democratic Party may take at least one chamber of Congress, getting the control to propose legislation. Some Wall Street strategists are positioning for a push from Democrats for tighter AI regulation, which could trigger a market selloff.

"The risk going into midterms, however, is that the dollar starts to lose a bit of shine," said Dominic Bunning, head of G10 FX strategy at Nomura. "There is a risk Trump looks to de-escalate on Iran in the weeks ahead of the vote, get a bit of respite on energy prices to help boost Republicans' chances."
Trump said Thursday the US would not attack Iran ahead of the November elections, after earlier this month saying a ramp-up of military strikes against Iran were "possible" following the elections.

For now, speculative traders have added to their bullish stance on the dollar in the week through Sept. 29, turning more positive on the currency for a second week, Commodity Futures Trading Commission data show.

"I'm bullish, at least in the short term, as money still flowing into the US because of the AI capex story being so strong, and that's leading to higher inflation and higher nominal growth," said Brent Donnelly, president of Spectra Markets.

livemint.com/global/scrapped-ipo-of-nvid.headline: Scrapped IPO of Nvidia-backed company points to limits of AI Boom

paragraphs.text: SYDNEY—Nvidia-backed cloud-computing company Firmus Grid scrapped plans for Australia’s largest initial public offering in almost 30 years, a new sign that investors are growing leery of lofty valuations for companies exposed to artificial-intelligence demand.

Firmus, which sells Nvidia-powered computing capacity to large technology companies such as OpenAI and Meta Platforms, pulled plans to raise $5 billion after investors balked at its proposed $30 billion valuation. Firmus said it would instead pursue further private investment.
The retreat comes about a month ahead of Anthropic’s planned blockbuster IPO as investors take a more critical look at companies seeking to ride the AI wave via a public listing.

The AI boom has sent global stock markets soaring this year, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both hitting records earlier this month. However, investor enthusiasm for AI’s ability to deliver productivity gains has run up against challenges such as the popularity of cheaper AI systems made in China, safety fears after some agents went rogue and a growing backlash to data-center construction across the U.S. and elsewhere.

Firmus and Nasdaq-listed CoreWeave are among a cohort of “neocloud” providers that supply computing power to AI firms. Market participants remain bullish that demand will keep rising but aren’t sure whether the neoclouds can attract enough revenue to support the huge investments needed to build out capacity.

Firmus had been targeting a market capitalization of 43.7 billion Australian dollars, equivalent to US$30.4 billion. That was up from US$10.5 billion just two months ago, when institutional investors Blackstone and Coatue participated in raising US$2 billion for Firmus.
To many analysts and investors, the latest valuation looked too high for a company with just two operational data centers and a further five in development across Australia, Malaysia and Indonesia.

“It all comes down to valuation: We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn’t have a compelling valuation,” said John Pearce, chief investment officer at Australian superannuation fund Unisuper. Unisuper had chosen not to buy Firmus stock in the IPO, Pearce said.
CoreWeave, which operates 51 facilities, has a market capitalization of $37 billion. Its shares fell nearly 8% Thursday on worries over the profitability of AI-related companies.
With bond yields having surged, many analysts had flagged worries about Firmus’s cost of debt.

“In a higher-yield environment, investors are clearly demanding greater compensation for risk, including in equities, which places a cap on lofty valuations,” said My Bui, an economist at Australian wealth manager AMP.

Investors are still struggling to figure out the value of companies that own chips with an uncertain lifespan. With newer, more powerful chips continually being developed, operators of data centers have to keep updating chips while depreciating the value of older assets.

The IPO would have been Australia’s largest since the partial privatization of telecommunications provider Telstra, which raised about US$10 billion in 1997. The Firmus bookbuild was jointly led by Bank of America, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley and local broker Morgans.
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, holds a direct equity stake in Firmus, and it is also a customer and hardware supplier to the Australian firm.
Many analysts still lean bullish on AI infrastructure, pointing to the hundreds of billions of dollars in spending planned globally.

“The demand for compute still far outstrips supply. As long as the AI data center build-out continues, neoclouds should keep filling the gap the hyperscalers can’t build fast enough to cover,” said Toby Hearst, associate investment strategist at Yardeni Research.

technologyreview.com/2026/10/09/1146250/.headline: The Download: AI’s refusal problem and weight-loss drug side effects
technologyreview.com/2026/10/09/1146250/.author: Thomas Macaulay

paragraphs.text: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no

Today’s AI models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts. If you ask your chatbot how to poison a colleague or how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down. But refusal fails, sometimes horrifically.

Some people are attempting to use AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms. Sooner or later, failed refusals may result in global calamity. What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey.

Governments will also get to draw their own lines, potentially restricting free speech. At the same time, the capabilities that make AI useful could also make it dangerous. If we want it to help cure cancer, AI needs genetics expertise that could also produce bioweapons.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/judy-shelton-scott-b.headline: Treasury's Bessent hires Trump's controversial former Fed board pick, Judy Shelton, as advisor
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/judy-shelton-scott-b.author: Steve Liesman

paragraphs.text: Judy Shelton, whose controversial economic ideas led the Senate to block her nomination to the Federal Reserve, has been appointed a counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The Treasury said Shelton will advise Bessent on currency policy, "with a particular focus on evaluating financial conditions in China."

Shelton is not known as a China expert. She authored "The Coming Soviet Crash" in 1989, followed by "Money Meltdown," about the need for a unified international monetary regime, in 1994. Before joining Treasury, Shelton was a senior fellow at the Independent Institute, a free market think tank, and, before that, at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University. She holds a Ph.D. in business administration from the University of Utah.

"Throughout her career, she has specialized in analyzing the internal monetary and financial conditions of nations and their impact on exchange rates," The Treasury said in its announcement, which will be released later Friday.

A bipartisan group of senators, including all Democrats and a handful of Republicans, rejected President Donald Trump's 2019 nomination of Shelton as a Fed governor over her views on Fed independence, her support for the gold standard and her questioning whether the U.S. needed a central bank.

Her appointment comes at what looks to be a time of turmoil at the Treasury regarding high-level personnel. A recent Wall Street Journal story cataloged seven Senate-confirmed officials who have left the department through the end of August. Only one position has been filled.
Bessent recently named David Zervos, former chief market strategist at Jefferies, as a counselor — the same job title as Shelton. Neither Shelton nor Zervos require Senate approval.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261007.headline: Only one workout helped older adults lose fat and keep muscle

paragraphs.text: Losing body fat is one thing. Losing fat while keeping the muscle that helps you stay strong and active is another, especially as you get older. Research suggests that one particular type of exercise may have an advantage when it comes to achieving both goals.

High-intensity interval training (HIIT), which involves alternating short bursts of demanding exercise with easier recovery periods, may be especially helpful for older adults who want to reduce fat without sacrificing lean muscle.

In a study published in Maturitas, researchers from the University of the Sunshine Coast compared three different exercise intensities. Although participants across the groups experienced modest fat loss, HIIT stood out for its ability to reduce fat while maintaining lean tissue.

"We found that high, medium and low intensity exercises all led to modest fat loss but only HIIT retained lean muscle," said lead author and exercise physiologist Dr. Grace Rose of the University of the Sunshine Coast.
The results highlight an important distinction in healthy aging: losing weight is not necessarily the same as improving body composition.
Six Months of Exercise Revealed a Key Difference
The Australian research team investigated how workout intensity affects body composition, meaning the proportions of fat, muscle and other tissues that make up the body.

A total of 123 healthy older adults from the Greater Brisbane region participated in the trial. Their average age was 72, and their average body mass index was approximately 26kg/m2, which the researchers described as normal for adults over 65.

Participants completed three supervised gym sessions each week for six months. Each session lasted 45 minutes, and participants were assigned to high-intensity intervals, moderate-intensity exercise, or a low-intensity comparison group.

To track changes, researchers measured body composition at the beginning of the study, after three months, and again at six months. They used a specialized scanning technique that estimates fat and lean tissue throughout the body.
The findings revealed that exercise intensity made a difference.

Both high- and moderate-intensity training significantly reduced fat mass, with larger improvements than those seen in the low-intensity group. However, the two more demanding approaches differed in their effects on lean tissue.
"While moderate training reduced fat mass, it also caused a small decline in lean muscle," Rose said.
Participants performing HIIT, meanwhile, reduced fat without experiencing the same decline in lean mass.

This could be particularly valuable later in life, when maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important for physical independence. Strong muscles help people climb stairs, get out of chairs, maintain balance, and carry out everyday activities.

One important distinction is that the scans measured lean tissue rather than muscle strength directly. Lean mass includes muscle but also other tissues and water, so changes in these measurements do not necessarily translate into equivalent changes in strength.
High-Intensity Exercise Also Reduced Abdominal Fat
The researchers found another potentially important benefit involving fat stored around the middle of the body.
"Both high and moderate intensities improved the composition of weight carried around the middle. Further analysis is needed of the low intensity results."
The original study found improvements in visceral adipose tissue among both the high and moderate intensity groups.
Visceral fat is different from the fat that sits directly beneath the skin. It accumulates deeper in the abdomen, surrounding internal organs such as the liver and intestines.
Excessive amounts of this fat have been linked to insulin resistance, cardiovascular disease, and other metabolic problems.
According to Rose, these findings matter because body composition can influence the development and progression of chronic diseases as people age.
While body weight and body mass index provide useful general information, they do not reveal how much fat or muscle a person carries, or where that fat is stored.
Someone who loses fat while maintaining muscle may experience a more favorable change in body composition than someone who loses a similar amount of weight along with valuable lean tissue.

Still, the original researchers emphasized that the improvements were relatively small. They cautioned that the differences were not clearly clinically meaningful when compared with lower intensity exercise, particularly after accounting for measurement uncertainty.
Why HIIT May Help Aging Muscles Stay Strong
