White House spokesperson Davis Ingle pointed to the Trump administration’s efforts to lower prescription drug costs, cut taxes, secure the border and grow job numbers: “No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the president understands how to communicate with them. President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”
Politicians touting their independence from Washington is nothing new. But as the poll reveals, it’s notable
that so many who voted for Trump, who has been the GOP's dominant force for a decade, are ready for candidates to take that leap.

Much of the fracture is driven by the non-MAGA wing of his coalition, the people who voted for Trump in 2024 but do not identify as part of his most loyal base, the survey found. When asked about specific issues such as the economy, trade and tariffs, data centers, immigration and the Iran war, non-MAGA Trump voters were roughly twice as likely as MAGA Trump voters to say their GOP candidate should break from the president.
But Trump still retains an intense hold over the base. More than two-thirds of MAGA voters said GOP candidates should continue to align with Trump across all of those issues.

That creates a no-win situation for many Republican candidates: Tie yourself to Trump and his policies too tightly and you lose independents and non-MAGA Republicans. Break too far, and you risk leaving MAGA disenchanted.
Candidates trying to thread that needle are quick to praise the president but blame his advisers, as Salazar did, or avoid mentioning Trump by name at all.

Roe said each candidate has to measure the “downstream effects” of a decision to distance themselves from the president, adding that it’s a balance between “alienating your base with appealing to voters that are looking for some independence.”

On the campaign trail, many Republicans acknowledge that the president remains an asset in shoring up base voters crucial to November. It’s part of the reason Trump has aggressively traveled to red states — including Alabama, Alaska, Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio and Texas — bastions of conservatism that need his star power to coax die-hard supporters to the polls. The White House official pointed to the president’s rally with South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham ahead of her run-off as an example of Trump’s ability to juice turnout.
RNC press secretary Natalie Baldassarre insisted that Republicans “remain united behind the president’s agenda” and are “laser focused on winning.”
“Our candidates will run the races necessary to best represent their districts and prevent Democrats from taking control,” she said.

The president is telling voters to “pretend” he is on the ballot, and he has insisted the party is already in a better place as he blitzes states across the country, touting his economy and arguing that higher prices are a small price to pay for national security amid the lingering war with Iran.

But some candidates are still nervous that if they campaign beside the president, they could alienate undecided voters. Some Republicans have encouraged Trump’s team not to send the president to a blue-leaning Omaha district and other key districts where his approval rating is underwater ahead of Election Day.

“I don’t think there are that many candidates who are clamoring for Trump to come to their state. But to the extent they do, it’s a gamble that they’ve already lost the voters who are gonna vote against them, and they need to light a fire under the voters who are sitting it out, and he’s the torch,” said Democratic strategist David Axelrod, who was chief strategist for Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign. “The problem is the torch can burn the whole house down.”

The damned-if-you-do, damned-if-you-don’t dilemma is perhaps best captured with Paxton’s campaign in Texas. On Wednesday, Trump took the stage in San Antonio, bringing up Paxton, the same day his latest closed-door comments complaining about the Iran war and high prices dragging down his campaign went public.
But standing on stage with Trump, he struck a much different tune.

“Wow, what is it like to be up on stage with the president of the United States? Pretty amazing,” he said. “Mr. President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us and for coming for Texas.”

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/margin-debt-stock-ma.headline: Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/margin-debt-stock-ma.author: Sean Conlon

paragraphs.text: HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.
It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.
That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.
"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.
Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.
"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."
Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.
'Gambling with an asterisk'

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.
Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.
To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.
Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.
"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."
"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.
"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.
Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"
Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.
In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.
"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."
For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.
Affecting equities
Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.
In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."
Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.
A new hobby

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.
Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."
It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."
Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."
"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.
But Luu's mother has faith in him.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.
Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.
She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."
— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

technologyreview.com/2026/10/09/1145737/.headline: Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
technologyreview.com/2026/10/09/1145737/.author: Eamon Whalen

paragraphs.text: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexa­copter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius. Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing. Here’s what it takes to land the gig.
Aviation experience

When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot. The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be. Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors.
A collaborative mindset

At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-­aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says. The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight. Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest.
Ability to stay calm under pressure

At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says. Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather. Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene. He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk.
Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261008.headline: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space

paragraphs.text: After spending more than seven months aboard the International Space Station, NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have safely returned to Earth. Their spacecraft splashed down Thursday in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles, bringing an extraordinary mission to a close.

The four astronauts spent 237 days in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, and completed thousands of trips around Earth while carrying out scientific experiments that could help shape future missions to the Moon and Mars.
NASA will host a news conference at 3:30 p.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct. 15, at Johnson Space Center in Houston, where returning crew members will discuss their experiences and research accomplishments.

"Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey spent 237 days living and working in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, advanced important science, and returned safely home because of the extraordinary expertise and competence of thousands across NASA, SpaceX, and our international partners," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Building the capability, experience, and confidence to do this repeatedly is exactly what will allow us to go farther, and I am grateful to Crew-12 and their families for their service to humanity's greatest adventure."
NASA Astronauts Return After 237 Days and 100 Million Miles
The returning crew included NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
Their spacecraft touched down in the Pacific at 8:34 a.m. PDT. SpaceX recovery teams aboard specialized vessels reached the capsule shortly afterward and brought the astronauts and spacecraft aboard.
Following routine medical evaluations, the crew members will be transported to shore before traveling to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.

"NASA's activities supporting the International Space Station -- transporting crew, conducting impactful research, and maintaining critical national assets -- enable the science, engineering, and risk‑reduction needed for future missions across the solar system," said Dana Weigel, manager of NASA's Low Earth Orbit Program at the agency's Johnson Space Center. "We're grateful for the dedication across the human spaceflight team that makes this possible, and we're thrilled to welcome Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey home."
Over the course of their 237-day stay, the astronauts circled Earth more than 3,792 times, accumulating over 100 million miles of travel.
For Meir and Fedyaev, Crew-12 marked their second journey into space. Hathaway and Adenot, meanwhile, completed their first space missions.
The crew launched on Feb. 13 at 5:15 a.m. EST, reaching and docking with the International Space Station the following day.
Space Station Experiments Could Help Future Moon and Mars Missions
Beyond the remarkable distance traveled, Crew-12 devoted hundreds of hours to scientific investigations designed to support future human exploration and improve life on Earth.

One research project explored ways to produce stem cells in space for potential use in cell-based medical treatments. Another demonstrated technology capable of producing IV fluids on demand, an ability that could become especially valuable during long-duration missions far from Earth.
The astronauts also investigated how pneumonia-causing bacteria may contribute to lasting heart damage. Understanding this relationship could offer new insights into cardiovascular health.

Other experiments focused on nutrition in space and how individual physical characteristics may influence blood flow during spaceflight. These studies could help researchers better understand the health risks astronauts face during extended stays in microgravity.
Together, the investigations provide valuable information about keeping humans healthy beyond Earth while testing technologies that may eventually support crewed expeditions to the Moon and Mars.
Historic Spacewalks Mark Crew-12 Mission
The mission also included significant milestones outside the space station.

Meir carried out four spacewalks during Crew-12, raising her career total to seven. That achievement places her third among NASA women for the most career spacewalks, behind former astronauts Peggy Whitson and Suni Williams.
Adenot also reached a historic milestone by completing three spacewalks. In doing so, she became the first French woman to venture outside the International Space Station.

With Crew-12 safely back on Earth, NASA has completed another extended mission that combined scientific research, international cooperation, and human spaceflight experience. The knowledge gained will contribute to preparations for more ambitious journeys beyond Earth's orbit.

politico.com/news/2026/10/09/house-gop-p.headline: House Republicans are bracing for catastrophe in once safe red seats
politico.com/news/2026/10/09/house-gop-p.author: Andrew Howard, Meredith Lee Hill and Mia McCarthy

paragraphs.text: In late September, top Republicans across House GOP leadership, leading political operations and individual campaigns received a trove of internal polling. It sparked a new level of panic.

The polling didn’t just reveal a harsh environment for the party in power on par with typical midterms, but rather some close-to-catastrophic scenarios in a slew of formerly safe red seats across the country, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss private information.

Key seats in Kentucky, North Carolina, Nevada and other areas that President Donald Trump won by 10 points or more in 2024 were competitive. All three vulnerable GOP-held seats in Iowa looked doomed. And most ominously, a crop of Republican incumbents who haven’t had to run serious races in years were vulnerable, from Oklahoma to Wisconsin and beyond.
Now, less than four weeks before Election Day, the concerns are running so deep and the atmosphere is so uncertain that Republicans are beginning to brace for some of the worst-case scenarios.

"Polls aren't looking good,” retiring Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.) said in an interview. “But we've also seen in the past couple of cycles, polls are really hard to predict. I think there's just a lot of things in play, and of course, what do we have three weeks out — that's light years in political time.”

One senior House Republican involved in the conversations added: “I think the scary part is we don’t know where the bottom is.” They, like others in this report, were granted anonymity to discuss the political climate honestly.

Their worst fear — according to conversations with more than two dozen Republican lawmakers and senior operatives — is that white working class voters in some states who have become central to the GOP coalition won’t just stay home next month, but instead they’ll be so angry or disillusioned by high fuel prices and the war in Iran that enough of them will vote for Democrats.
“The environment has a lot people scared to death,” said one GOP operative working on a red-leaning House race that is competitive.
“Where is the surge in Dem votes coming from?” that operative asked. “Is it truly no turnout among white working class? It's such an open question and we just don't know the answer. It's impossible.”
Spokespeople for the National Republican Congressional Committee and the Republican National Committee brushed off the concerns.
"Anonymous strategists who spend more time bed-wetting to media than working in the trenches to win races have no idea what they're talking about,” RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said.

NRCC spokesperson Mike Marinella agreed: “House Republicans have a more favorable map, a stronger ground game, a historic fundraising and spending advantages, and battle-tested incumbents while Democrats are stuck dragging their unelectable socialist nominees across the finish line.”

Still, top Republicans’ travel schedule reveals the extent of their concerns: Johnson is heading to deep-red Kentucky on Friday for a fundraiser to boost Republican Ralph Alvarado in the 6th District, which Trump won by 15 points in 2024. Johnson and Trump are also both planning trips to Montana where Republicans are working to fend off a Democratic challenger in a district the president won by more than 11 points.

“Speaker Johnson is leaving it all on the field and leaving no stone unturned as he campaigns in more than 40 districts and over 20 states in the month leading up to the election,” Johnson’s spokesperson Greg Steele said. And, pointing to Johnson’s record-setting third quarter funding, Steele added that: “Johnson is not slowing down and helping to get resources to every district that will decide the majority.”

Trump is holding a rally in deep-red Tennessee on Saturday, in GOP Rep. Matt Van Epps’ district. That seat — which is still considered generally safe — and several others in the state have not been on Republicans’ radar at all, but the current drag of the war and other factors are just too big for them to be comfortable.
“I’m worried about all three in the area,” one Tennessee Republican said of the red-leaning districts Democrats are targeting. “Too many unknowns.”

Even as internal GOP data shows a series of troubles, Republicans argue the polls are overemphasizing Democrats’ advantage. “I think there’s no question there is some undersampling,” said one RNC official, granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

“I’m not surprised any of these are close. I’m not surprised that Democrats are trying to make it seem like we’re on defense everywhere,” they said. “These are never [races] that we assumed were overall slam dunks, but I very much like where we sit in all of them.”
Still, the person added that RNC officials don’t have their “heads in the sand” about the challenges, even as they have a more optimistic view of the map.
Loudermilk pointed to Republicans’ lack of cohesive messaging on high gas prices and other goods: “I don’t know if we’re doing a good enough job doing that.”

“It’s not the best of environments,” Rep. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.) told reporters in late September, though he still maintained the GOP will keep House control. “I liked it a lot better when I first got elected in 2010, when the environment was much better for Republicans.”

Top Republicans are most worried about staunching the bleeding in key Midwest districts. Senior Republicans believe their internal polling, if it holds, shows likely losses across all three at-risk GOP seats in Iowa: Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks and the race to replace now-Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, according to four people with direct knowledge of the private information.

A White House official, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the races, said the “doom and gloom notion” among the Iowa seats isn’t a new phenomenon. “But I do think that they’re probably performing better than most think that they are. And I think that folks will be pleasantly surprised [when] we go into November 3.”

But benchmarks they’re watching across the larger region are deteriorating as well. Wisconsin Rep. Bryan Steil, the House Administration chair, is in a tighter than comfortable race after winning by 11 points in 2024 — as is Rep. Brad Finstad across the border in Minnesota, who won his district by 12 points 2024.

In Michigan, the party has a host of problems in battleground districts, but now feels that once-safer seat Republicans — like Bill Huizenga, who Johnson campaigned with Wednesday, and the race to replace Rep. John James, who is running for governor — are in jeopardy.

Similarly, after top GOP outside groups cut bait on the blue-leaning Nebraska district held by retiring Rep. Don Bacon, Republicans in the state turned their attention to Rep. Mike Flood’s seat, which Trump carried by 12 points.
One silver lining for Republicans in safer red seats is many are digging in now to shore up their races, and aren’t sleepwalking to November.

The White House official said it’s Trump’s “coalition of voters” that Republicans need to turn out in the midterms, and “the president is on the road almost every night this month … communicating with those individuals.”
But Democrats continue to stretch further into red territory while forecasting big wins.

“We feel confident that we will get to 218,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee political director Brooke Butler said in an interview earlier this week, saying the party could win as many as 240 seats. “The question that I’ve told people from the beginning cycle is ‘How much?’”

But while Democrats are increasingly bullish, they are navigating their own tough decisions because of Republicans’ massive cash advantage, leaving the GOP optimistic they can hold a few seats where Democrats don’t have the resources to compete. Top GOP House operatives remain confident about a number of core battleground districts — including where candidates have already put some distance between themselves and Trump.

One national party operative remained hopeful that as Election Day nears, the races will get closer than polling currently suggests, as has been the case in past cycles. That would help them hold some of these redder seats that are competitive.

Even as Republicans hope some red seats fall off the board as Election Day nears, many operatives told POLITICO they’re worried that outside groups will have to start siphoning resources into red areas to shore them up, moving important dollars out of the battlegrounds.

“People that are in R+10 districts are showing [polling that] they’re tied and they're saying, ‘I need help,’” said a GOP operative working on a battleground House race. “There's real opportunity for Democrats in a lot of these.”

Rep. French Hill, the chair of the Financial Services Committee from deep-red Arkansas whose opponent was just added to the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” list, said in a recent interview with POLITICO that he considers “the atmosphere a very tough political environment right now because of President [Donald] Trump’s lack of favorability at the top, and you know people are concerned about, as I say, what it’s like to live under an inflated economy the last four years.”
Johnson, an eternal optimist, made clear during a campaign stop in Pennsylvania this week that he believes “this will be a close election.”

He’s ramping up his warnings across the campaign trail of what Democrats winning power would mean: “They would try to impeach the president, of course, immediately …They’d spend every waking hour investigating the president, his family, and the cabinet, and leaders of business and industry. That would roil the markets. Just ask yourself, if you're a hardworking family, how would that be for your family? That Democrats turned Congress into lawfare on steroids.”
Samuel Benson contributed to this report.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-09/.headline: Companies are buying up L.A. County’s $4-billion sex abuse settlement
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-09/.author: Rebecca Ellis

paragraphs.text: The man was sure only his lawyers and family knew about his lawsuit against Los Angeles County over sexual abuse he says he endured inside a juvenile hall as a teenager.

The case, filed under a pseudonym, was one of thousands resolved by county officials last year in a historic $4-billion sex abuse settlement. He asked to remain anonymous to discuss the abuse, which he said was among his most closely held secrets.
So he was bewildered this fall to receive a phone call from a company in Florida that seemed to know all about it.
The unwanted cold caller offered a deal: In exchange for a lump sum of cash up front, the company would collect his future payouts, which are set to come in installments over the next five years.

“I’m really curious, like, how you got my number?” said the man, according to a recording of the call reviewed by The Times. “This is a very confidential matter. There is no way that you should know my name, let alone my phone number.”
He says he never got an answer. Instead, the salesperson offered him a $200 referral fee if he could find others to sell their payouts, too.

Offers like these, victims suing L.A. County say, have become inescapable. Over Facebook messages and cold calls, private companies are offering lump sums to victims who are willing to sign over the rights to their anticipated settlement money, sometimes sacrificing a significant chunk of the payout in the process.
“They’re circling like sharks in the water,” said James Turpin, another claimant in the settlement, who said a representative from a funding company messaged him on Facebook.

Many involved say they’re desperate to get whatever money they can and move ahead with their lives as the case has gotten bogged down by delays and fraud allegations. While some victims are getting their first payments this fall, two law firms behind the bulk of the claims in the settlement have had their payouts paused pending probes, leaving thousands in limbo.

“It’s been too long and I’m tired of reliving that over and over again,” said Deborah Isom Smith, who sold her payout stemming from her claim related to MacLaren Hall, a former county-run children’s shelter notorious for abuse. “I just want to go live my life.”
The funding companies are standing by to assist.

“Hi all, I know waiting on your LA settlement money is tough,” wrote a representative from Liberty Settlement Funding on a Facebook group for victims of MacLaren Hall. “No pressure at all — just here to help.”

Over the last few months, more than 180 victims across the country have moved to sell their payouts to about a dozen different companies, according to Ray Boucher, one of the lead plaintiff attorneys coordinating the cases.

Frederick Love, chief legal officer for LA Settlement Funding, which has bought many of the payouts, said their transactions were “priced as tightly as possible to provide the maximum benefit to the sellers.” He said the discount rates range from 9% to 11%.
Most victims will get a lump sum equivalent to about 80% of the amount they’re selling, according to court filings, while some are poised to fare far worse.

One Gardena man signed a contract to sell $90,400 of his payout for $25,000, according to court filings. An attorney representing the funding company, Datura Capital, said the rate was a mistake, and the man will get about 72% of his payout at the corrected rate.

“I am not doing this lightly and there is an urgent need for doing so,” the man wrote in an Aug. 26 declaration. “I was told by the doctors that I have chronic kidney disease and need treatment right away. I don’t have the funds for this otherwise.”

In California, a judge needs to approve the sale of a settlement payout after finding it in the best interest of the claimant. The filings typically detail various reasons the victims need the money now: looming homelessness, college tuition, a down payment on a house.
Boris Treyzon, a partner at ACTS Law, which represents about 1,700 plaintiffs, said he’s appeared in court recently to urge a judge to reject a sale.
“The interest rates are insane,” Treyzon said.

Lawyers representing plaintiffs in these cases say the contracts leave critical questions unanswered, including who is responsible for paying attorney fees — which typically gobble up about 40% of the payouts in these cases — and what happens if a victim ends up getting more money than anticipated in the initial deal.
Love, of LA Settlement Funding, said his company is only buying the victims’ portion of the settlement and said “any payments that are in excess of that being assigned” will go back to the plaintiff.

A spokesperson for L.A. County said in a statement that the the loan companies are the latest example of third parties chipping away at funds set aside to compensate victims of sexual abuse. The county faced the deluge of lawsuits after a change in state law, known as AB 218, allowed people to sue over abuse that took place decades ago.

“Aggressive finance firms exploiting vulnerable AB 218 victims for a payday now scheme is yet another failure of the system to put appropriate guardrails on the ever-ballooning problem facing California public entities,” the county said in a statement. “The ongoing siphoning of taxpayer dollars for profit, whether from plaintiff attorneys who are taking up to 50% of a victim’s settlement or settlement firms offering fast payment for a fee, is fundamentally against the original intent of AB 218.”

Neffertashia Burroughs, who said she was abused in a juvenile hall as a teenager, said she isn’t happy with the deal, but doesn’t see another option. Like many victims, she said the case has opened up old wounds and she’s tired of the timeline for payment shifting seemingly every month.
She’s on the brink of eviction, she said, and sometimes does not have enough to feed her children.
“I am struggling to heal myself while remaining trapped in a system that seems to consist of delays, uncertainty, and repeated excuses,” she wrote in an email. “I am exhausted.”

Others say they feel the rates are decent, but are perturbed by the flood of calls from companies who won’t explain how they got their contact information. Nearly all the sex abuse lawsuits are filed under pseudonyms.

“So help me understand how you guys got my information,” Krista Hubbard texted a salesperson with a funding company based in Miami Lakes, Fla. “If I need to, I will have your company audited if I cannot get an answer.”
“Have a nice day,” the salesperson responded.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/09/w.headline: As pro-Trump rulings boost Justice Alito’s stature, retirement speculation swirls
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/09/w.author: Justin Jouvenal

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump has had no shortage of sharp words for the Supreme Court, including his own three picks. But he’s offered effusive praise for a justice he had no role in elevating: Samuel A. Alito Jr.

Trump recently fumed that the justices he nominated were “a shell of their original selves” after Brett M. Kavanaugh, Neil M. Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett appeared to side with the majority in blocking the administration’s sweeping restrictions on mail ballots for November’s midterm elections.
In the same message, he called Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas “legends” for dissenting. Weeks earlier, Trump gushed that Alito was “one of the Greatest of All Time.”
Alito, 76, has achieved new prominence on the court in the Trump era, after spending years in the shadow of conservative colleagues with more star power like Thomas and Antonin Scalia.

As the president’s agenda has come to dominate the court’s docket, Alito has boosted his profile as its most unwavering supporter. His unabashed conservative voice on race, transgender rights and other culture war issues resonates with Trump and his base.

The growing spotlight was underscored by the intense speculation that has swirled around whether he will retire and a series of media appearances with the recent release of his first book, “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country.”
If Alito decided to retire soon, it would open a window for what would be Trump’s best chance to pick a conservative successor. But the justice has said that, at least for now, he intends to stay.
“I’ve been bemused by the retirement speculation; it’s not too pleasant to look up and see the vultures circling,” Alito said in an interview with “Fox News Sunday.”

And after more than two decades on the bench, Alito’s seniority has given him the opportunity to write some of the court’s most consequential — and controversial — opinions. The court’s rightward shift has also given him more influence.
Peter Canellos, who has written a book about Alito called “Revenge for the Sixties,” said “this is his moment.”

“He is at the peak of his powers,” Canellos said. “Many of the battles on the court are among conservatives between a more traditionalist approach with Chief Justice Roberts, and Alito’s approach, which is to move the law in a more conservative direction. Alito feels like he can win a lot of those battles.”
Last spring, Alito wrote a major opinion that sharply weakened a key provision of the landmark Voting Rights Act, a ruling that limits the consideration of race in drawing voting maps.

In 2022, he wrote for the majority in the seismic Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which ended nearly 50 years of federally protected access to abortion for women and returned the question of how to regulate the procedure to the states.

Alito was nominated by George W. Bush in 2005 and had served in the Reagan administration. As Trump’s three appointees joined the court, he became part of a new and powerful conservative supermajority.

Alito has backed the Trump administration in every major case it has brought before the high court during the president’s second term. That included breaking with the majority when the court blocked Trump’s sweeping tariffs and his proposed ban on birthright citizenship.
That staunch support also was on particular display in Alito’s dissent in the recent mail-in ballot case.

The Trump administration in September asked the high court to temporarily allow an executive order requiring states to send mail ballots in envelopes with barcodes to prevent fraud and to submit lists of eligible mail voters to the federal government. The policy would have gone forward while litigation over it played out in the courts.
The executive order barred the U.S. Postal Service from delivering ballots in states that didn’t hand over lists.

A number of Democratic and Republican election administrators said it would be challenging — even impossible — to implement the rules so close to the election without major disruptions. A federal whistleblower warned that large numbers of Americans could be disenfranchised. Those assertions went largely unchallenged by the Trump administration.

In weighing whether to uphold a stay on the order, the court considers who is most likely to win the case, as well as which side would face greater harm by allowing the order to go forward while litigation continues.

Alito, joined by Thomas, found it would be the Trump administration that would suffer the greater harm from having its policy blocked rather than states and voting groups. He quickly dispatched the issues raised by administrators and the whistleblower.
“I take that problem very seriously, but it is not enough to convince me to deny the application,” Alito wrote.

For liberal critics, the dissent demonstrated Alito’s willingness to embrace Trump’s policies at virtually any cost. Jay Willis, the editor of the legal publication Balls and Strikes, said Alito has become a “mouthpiece for Trump.”
“Alito is emblematic of this tranche of Republicans that whatever being a Republican once meant to them, it now means doing what Donald Trump wants,” Willis said.

But Leonard Leo, the conservative legal leader who helped push Alito’s nomination, said it’s simplistic to view the justice as blindly backing Trump. Leo said Alito is making decisions in keeping with his legal philosophy and has long been a supporter of a strong executive, a theme of many of Trump’s actions in his second term that have come before the court.
“He’s someone that seeks the right answers to legal questions,” Leo said. “Sometimes it’s going to align with the goals of a presidential administration, sometimes it will not.”
Alito, who declined to comment, made a similar point in a recent interview with the Wall Street Journal.

“I vote in every case the way I think the case should be decided,” Alito said. “If that means a high correlation with what Trump wants, fine. If it means zero correlation with what Trump wants, fine as well.”

In his new book, Alito describes himself as a “working judicial originalist,” which he describes as a “judge who tries to achieve originalist aims while working within the framework of our judicial system.”
Originalism is the method of judicial interpretation that holds the Constitution and laws should be understood by their meaning at the time they were adopted.
Some originalists advocate for judicial restraint, and Alito’s mentor, Scalia, who pioneered originalism, said the theory should sometimes lead to results that cut against a judge’s personal beliefs.

Alito calls for a different type of originalism that “sometimes calls for bold action” in his book. He also counsels that originalist judges shed “this insecure mind set” about arriving at preferred policy outcomes.

In the book, which is a collection of speeches over the course of his career as a justice, Alito also offers his views on the emergency docket, Gettysburg Address, baseball and the Catholic intellectual tradition. Alito is a Catholic. He mentions Trump only in passing.

Richard Lazarus, a law professor at Harvard University, said Alito has evolved in a way that has brought him more in concert with the Trump wing of the Republican Party, adding “he is a very different Alito than he was a few decades ago.”

Lazarus said Alito had a reputation as unassuming and not overly ideological during his years as U.S. attorney for New Jersey and then as a judge on U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit before his nomination to the high court.
Alito was always reliably conservative, but in a Reagan mold, Lazarus said.
“Alito has, in my view, moved far to the right and with a very different personality,” Lazarus said. “His voice, his opinions and his votes are now loud, they’re mocking and they’re contentious.”
In one example from 2020 that drew condemnation from gay rights advocates, Alito took aim at same-sex marriage, which the Supreme Court sanctioned in a 2015 decision called Obergefell v. Hodges.

“You can’t say that marriage is a union between one man and one woman. Until recently, that’s what the vast majority of Americans thought. Now, it’s considered bigotry,” Alito said in a speech to the Federalist Society. “That this would happen after our decision in Obergefell should not have come as a surprise.”

Alito returned to the theme in the book in a reprint of a 2018 speech at Catholic University that was not open to the public. He called the gay marriage decision the “decisive point in our nation’s turn against religious liberty.” He also suggested he was right to predict it would “drive believers out of public life.”

In a Wall Street Journal podcast, Alito said he is wrongly caricatured as ill-tempered in the media. “I think that’s very unfair. … Nothing similar is written about some of my colleagues who have issued blistering dissents,” he said.

Legal experts said Alito’s sentiments, which are sometimes couched in grievance, share a similar style with Trump. As does the sense that an older America is slipping away. In his book, Alito portrays traditional values as under siege.

“Many of the central ideas of what was regarded as the counterculture in the 1960s and 1970s are now mainstream — for example, the change in sexual mores, use of at least some type of drugs, and the repudiation of much of our country’s past and what used to be called Western civilization,” Alito writes.
Alito’s rising stature is also due to the length of time he has spent on the court, since justices typically get to write more important opinions as they gain seniority, legal experts said.

Trump’s reordering of the court with three conservative appointees is also a factor, they said. Trump’s picks gave conservatives a 6-3 majority, shifting the court’s center of gravity rightward toward the flank occupied by Alito and Thomas. It has also given him more originalist compatriots.
J. Joel Alicea, a Catholic University law professor and former Alito clerk, said Alito has become adept at writing opinions that are extremely conservative while still bringing along other justices.

“[Alito] doesn’t produce opinions that get five votes that kind of feel like a political compromise,” Alicea said. “He writes opinions that get five votes, and each justice feels their own originalist and conservative principles are respected.”

If the Democrats take the Senate in November, it could put fresh pressure on Alito to resign. The lame-duck period between November and January would be Trump’s last chance to get a nominee through a Republican-controlled Senate.

Alito said in a CBS News interview that he thinks about retiring every term given his age but still has more to contribute to the court. He also recently told Bloomberg he doesn’t plan to retire during the lame-duck period.
“I intend to stick around through this term,” Alito told Bloomberg before the Supreme Court’s new term began Monday. “I made that decision many months ago.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navane.headline: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navane.author: Julian Borger, Rachel Savage

paragraphs.text: The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/delta-air-lines-dal-.headline: Delta Air Lines cuts 2026 forecast on fuel surge, but CEO says demand is still strong
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/delta-air-lines-dal-.author: Leslie Josephs

paragraphs.text: Delta Air Lines slashed its 2026 profit outlook as high fuel prices persist, but CEO Ed Bastian said higher fares aren't turning off travelers.

Delta on Friday forecast full-year earnings per share of between $5.10 and $5.60 on an adjusted basis, compared with its outlook in July, when fuel prices were lower, of $6.50 to $7.50 a share. The company's fourth-quarter guidance was below analyst estimates, too.
Delta cut its free cash flow outlook for the year to $2.5 billion, from as much as $4 billion it expected in July.

Still, Bastian said in an interview that fares have continued to tick up as the airline passes along much of a $6 billion increase in fuel costs this year, and that travelers keep booking. Jet fuel prices in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico region have almost doubled to $4.34 on Thursday from $2.19 a year earlier, according to FactSet.
"The consumer response continues to be quite strong. We're seeing it across all channels, all cabins of service, all geographies, business, leisure," he said.

Delta forecast a 20% increase in revenue for the fourth quarter over the same period last year, more than the 16% rise in the third quarter, when adjusting for the airline's benefit from its refinery in Trainer, Pennsylvania, where it refines crude oil into jet fuel and other products, giving it an advantage over other carriers.
"Obviously the fuel pricing, the volatility of fuel prices have something to do with that," Bastian said.
Delta is the country's most profitable airline and the first to report results from the third quarter, which encompasses the busy summer season.

Costs continued to weigh on the bottom line. The fuel price surge since the Iran war began in February has put a damper on airline profits even as carriers flex pricing power. The latest inflation read in September showed airfare up more than 23% from a year earlier.
Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on consensus estimates from LSEG:
• Earnings per share: $1.72 adjusted vs. $1.75 expected
• Adjusted revenue: $17.59 billion adjusted vs. $17.67 billion expected
It was the first time in two years that Delta missed estimates.
Delta reported net income of $756 million, or $1.15 a share, down 47% from $1.42 billion, or $2.17 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, Delta posted earnings of $1.76 per share.

Adjusting for sales from its refinery, maintenance business and profit-sharing, revenue rose 16% from the previous year to $17.59 billion. Operating revenue jumped 21% in the third quarter to $20.19 billion.
Delta's premium revenue, which has become a larger portion of its total sales, grew 18% in the third quarter to $6.82 billion, while main cabin sales rose only 12% to $6.8 billion.
Musk dispute

Delta, which announced free Wi-Fi across its fleet almost four years ago, recently said it would add Amazon Leo satellite internet to its airplanes as carriers race to improve service on board to living-room-quality speeds.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk criticized Bastian on X last week, saying the Delta CEO would "lose his job over this" after the View from the Wing travel blog said Bastian told staff at an internal event "We do not want to be with Elon Musk. Trust me."

SpaceX's Starlink Wi-Fi has become the main supplier of satellite Wi-Fi, with airline partnerships that include United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Airlines, as well as others around the world.
Delta's Bastian brushed off the idea of a personal spat with Musk on Friday and told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview that "everyone's entitled to their opinion."
"There's no tit-for-tat as far as I'm concerned," Bastian said. He said Delta had talks with SpaceX six years ago, but they "weren't ready to scale."

theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/.headline: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/10/09/hea.headline: A headmaster’s challenge to his male students: Speak up about rape
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/10/09/hea.author: Casey Parks

paragraphs.text: Usually, Stephen Beatty opens the Monday morning assemblies with a dad joke or two. He’s the headmaster of Royal St. George’s College, an all-boys school in Toronto, and he likes to start the school week with a bit of fun.

But as news broke that a former Cornell University student had accused seven fraternity members of sexually assaulting her while she was incapacitated, Beatty told his faculty he needed to hold a different kind of assembly this week.

Maybe the boys could tell, as Beatty held the door open, that this assembly would be different. They kept their phones in their pockets. They found seats in the 136-year-old Anglican chapel without so much as a snicker.

Beatty had known most of them since they were young enough to cry over lost pets and dying grandparents. He’d celebrated when they earned their yellow belts in judo. He’d read to them every Friday in his office when they were 8. But they were teenagers now, and it was his job to help usher them into adulthood.
“Gentlemen,” he said, “I want to talk with you today about something difficult.”

Beatty knew how badly his students wanted to blend in. They all wore the same blue blazers with the school’s crest embroidered on the front. They kept their ties loose at the neck. Most had the same fuzzy haircut that reminded Beatty of an alpaca. They were good boys, he thought. He couldn’t imagine any of them committing the kinds of sexual acts that might get them arrested. But he wanted — he needed — to ask more from them.

As he stood at the pulpit, Beatty thought of a comment he’d seen online. People had been calling the accused fraternity brothers “the Cornell 7.” One woman noted on Instagram that allegedly 50 other young men had been in a Snapchat group where a man invited them to participate in the assault. She called them “the Cornell 57.”
“Not one had the courage to stop this,” Beatty said. “They stayed silent.”

Beatty scanned the crowd. The boys had their eyes locked on him. They didn’t fidget. They were listening. Beatty told his boys he wanted to talk about that silence. “School is about learning. And perhaps the most important thing you are learning is about yourself,” he said, then asked: “What kind of man do you want to be?”
BEATTY HAD GIVEN a version of this speech twice before.

He’d first talked to his students about rape more than a decade ago after two football players in Steubenville, Ohio, were convicted of sexually assaulting a high school girl, while others videoed the acts and posted clips to social media. Beatty gave a second version of the speech in 2024 after a woman said she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of Hockey Canada’s junior championship team. The players were found not guilty last year, but Beatty remained troubled by the circumstances — multiple men were involved, and the woman was intoxicated.

When Beatty read about the Cornell case, he felt the same outrage. He wasn’t sure if he had anything new to say, though. Then a few of his female colleagues told him they hoped he would speak up again.
He couldn’t live with himself, he decided, if he didn’t take every opportunity to teach the 350 boys in his charge how to be.

Beatty is 59 — “An old man,” he calls himself — but he remembered how hard it was to be a teenage guy. He’d attended Royal St. George’s in the 1970s and ‘80s, and he’d yearned then for guidance. Once, after his best friend died in an amusement park accident, Beatty had walked, grief-stricken, to a teacher’s home to ask how to survive the loss.

That teacher had helped Beatty navigate the hardest times of his life. Beatty wanted to be that kind of mentor, but as he considered what to say about Cornell, he worried his students would feel labeled as bad just because they’re boys. Beatty didn’t want them to feel painted into the corner of toxic masculinity. Shame would not inspire them.

All weekend, Beatty fretted over what to say. He talked to his 92-year-old father and his college-aged sons, then, Sunday night, he carried his laptop down to his basement, turned on the Buffalo Bills football game, muted it, and began to write.
I am horrified.

He took his hands off the keyboard. Earlier that semester, he’d watched one of his boys, a giant baseball player, embroider flowers in art class. He’d watched other boys recite poetry. He’d traveled to the woods with them, and he’d listened as they talked about their parents, their fears, the secret struggles they rarely revealed.
I know your kindness, your sense of fairness, and the care you show for one another. I believe in you.

Beatty knew good people could falter in terrible situations. As a teenager, he’d watched without protest as his peers bullied an overweight boy. He knew decent people could remain silent even when they knew something wasn’t right. He knew how safe silence could feel.
I know. Boys, please believe me, I know.

BEATTY WROTE LATE into the night. He read the speech again and again, and he canceled his early morning appointments. He was nervous, but as he stood at the pulpit Monday morning and looked out at his boys, that anxiety disappeared. They were listening.

Beatty thought often of the overweight boy he grew up with. He’d known as a young man that his silence hurt that boy, but Beatty had thought he was protecting himself. In the decades since, he’d realized that silence had corroded him, too. Silence numbed young men, he knew now. It stopped them from asking for help. It left them feeling alone.
“Silence can be framed as some manly quality. The strong silent type. Don’t believe that,” he told the boys. “It is not strong.”
“What is truly masculine and strong is breaking silence,” he continued. “We need to be brave. Not silent. Decide that the man you are and the man you will be will not be silent.”

In his years as headmaster, Beatty had learned that you can’t just tell a boy what not to do. You have to give him clear instructions. And so he told the students to think of his speech as a fire drill — practice for a real emergency. If someone makes a degrading joke about a girl, the boys should say, “That’s enough.” If a boy shares a private photograph of a girl, the recipient should reply, “Don’t send me that. Delete it.”

“What would you do when a group chat turns cruel, or a friend starts talking about someone as though she is a prize to be won or a possession to be had?” he asked his audience. “Do you join in? Do you stay quiet because you don’t want to make things awkward?”

Beatty encouraged the boys to make things awkward. If they witnessed an assault, they needed to do everything in their power to stop it. They needed to be loud. They could break a window, pull a fire alarm. They could call their parents, or they could call him.

He told them to pull out their cellphones, then he gave them his number. Use it, he told them. Use it when you don’t know what to do. Use it when you need someone to help without judgment or consequence. He told them that he loved them.
”I know you,” he told them. “I know that’s the kind of man you want to be and the kind of man you will be.”

Beatty sometimes joked that there’s nothing profound in boys. They could be deep and substantive, but they weren’t usually complex in their expression. A few grunted “Nice speech, sir” as they filed out of the chapel. Others thanked him in the cafeteria that afternoon.

When he got back to his office, he saw most had already texted him. They were short messages. More than one had written only, “Hey, Mr. Beatty, it’s me.” Still, Beatty felt emotional. His boys were saying something. For now, that was enough.

theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/0.headline: You have a higher chance of getting cancer at a younger age than your parents. So what went wrong?
theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/0.author: Devi Sridhar

paragraphs.text: In the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.

Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50, often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.

While there were slight variations among the three countries, larger patterns are clear. Among women who are under 50 in England, breast, bowel, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreatic and stomach cancers have increased. For men under 50 in England, there were increases in bowel, kidney, liver, pancreatic and prostate cancers. This is the opposite of what we would hope to achieve in public health – and no, it isn’t only because we have better diagnostic tools, or are doing more testing. While this explains some of the increase, it doesn’t account for it all. The data indicates that younger generations are experiencing a higher incidence of some cancers than previous generations at the same age. Put more simply: you have a higher chance of cancer at a younger age than your parents.

Scientists are now working to unpick what has changed between generations that might be driving this uptick, especially trying to find things people may have been exposed to during childhood or adolescence in the 1990s that they wouldn’t have been in the 1950s.

Here are some potential explanations: what we eat has changed significantly over the past 50 years, with the rise in ultra-processed and fast foods as well as sugary drinks. We also are more sedentary as a population. These changes are linked to rising levels of excess weight and obesity. Body fat, especially around the vital organs and waist, is a risk factor for chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction, all of which are linked to higher cancer incidence. Globally, obesity rates have more than doubled among adults and quadrupled among adolescents since 1990. Data collected in 2024 found that about 66% of adults in England were either overweight or living with obesity.

But diet, physical activity and excess body weight doesn’t fully explain the rise of certain cancers – such as breast cancer – in young people. Studies have shown that for women before menopause, a higher BMI is, in fact, linked to a slightly lower risk of cancer (which is in contrast to older women, where a higher BMI significantly increases risk of developing breast cancer.) Going further, scientists are looking at the health impact of sustained exposure to environmental toxins like air and water pollution, chemicals and plastics that have become widespread and almost impossible to avoid over the past 50 years.

It has been scientifically challenging to identify one toxin that explains the global increase in cancers. Cancer can develop long after exposure to a toxic chemical, and over our lives we encounter a range of chemicals and pollutants. Saying which one, or whether it was during childhood, in utero, or adulthood, is difficult to pin down.

On the positive side, one area that we have made progress with in young people is lung cancer, largely driven by anti-smoking campaigns and widespread awareness of the links between smoking and lung cancer. So not everything is getting worse.

None of the continuing research into risk factors for early onset cancer should mean attaching blame to patients. One of the first human impulses when getting a diagnosis is to think “what caused this?”, and even further, “what have I done?” – and this isn’t helpful. In addition, scientists estimate that only 40% of cancers at a population level are because of an “individually modifiable” behaviour like smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity, or weight. The other 60% is a mix of ageing, genetic susceptibility, infection, possible environmental factors, and sometimes just bad luck.
With the research and investment continuing into scientific research, we will eventually learn what’s driving the rise in cancer in younger people. But for now, that mystery is still to be uncovered.
• Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/adi.headline: Adidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe branding
theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/adi.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark.
Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design.
White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims.
During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months.
He pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers.
“There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said.
Adidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013.
It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted.
“This is a pretty simple matter,” he said.
White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.
He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.
“Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said.
“Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.”
The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled.
