He noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing.
Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products.
Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027.
It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013.
Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand.
The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025.
Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success.
The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany.
The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/delta-riyadh-flight-.headline: Delta CEO: 'Safety is going to make the call' on launching Saudi Arabia flight
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/delta-riyadh-flight-.author: Leslie Josephs

paragraphs.text: Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said his carrier is weighing whether to go ahead with debuting a flight between Atlanta and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after attacks claimed by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have escalated there.
The flights between Riyadh and Delta's biggest hub are scheduled to begin on Oct. 23.
Three people were killed in attacks at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as the Houthis stepped up strikes in the country, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said.
"Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," Bastian told CNBC in an interview. "Safety is is going to make the call."
He said that the airline will let customers know of its decision soon. German airline Lufthansa said it was pausing flights into Saudi Arabia through at least Oct. 16, a spokesman told CNBC.

Delta is planning to operate the Atlanta-Riyadh flight daily from Oct. 23 to Oct. 30 before moving to three-times-a-week service. When it announced the route earlier this year, Delta said it would be the first nonstop service between the U.S. and Riyadh operated by a U.S. airline.

nytimes.com/2026/10/09/technology/inside.headline: Inside Mark Zuckerberg’s Decision to Pull the Trigger on Meta’s A.I. Agent

paragraphs.text: Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, gathered two top lieutenants — Alexandr Wang, the chief artificial intelligence officer, and Nat Friedman, the head of A.I. product — in August to discuss an imminent threat.

A 14-person start-up called Instinct had created an A.I. agent, which are bots that can operate apps and software on behalf of users, and it was taking off. Meta was developing a similar product called Muse, but had delayed releasing it over safety concerns.

Fearful of losing a competitive edge, Mr. Zuckerberg said Muse was ready to launch despite the risks, according to three people with knowledge of the meeting, who were not authorized to speak publicly on confidential matters.

Mr. Wang, 29, and Mr. Friedman, 49, were aware of safety concerns from recent tests, including one instance when Muse changed a user’s password without permission, two of the people said. But on Sept. 8, Meta publicly debuted Muse, just like Mr. Zuckerberg had ordered.

The internal meeting showed the tricky balance between speed and safety that A.I. companies like Meta are juggling as they try to one-up their rivals in the A.I. race. As the technology rapidly improves, it is becoming more dangerous and useful at the same time, making these decisions even more difficult.

Mr. Zuckerberg has spent billions to develop Meta’s A.I., but watched for years as rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic beat his company to market with chatbots and coding tools. When it came to personal agents, the Silicon Valley giant, which owns Facebook and Instagram, needed a win — and ultimately, getting to market quickly won out.

That has given Meta an early lead with agents, which have become the next frontier of the A.I. industry. Other companies are already introducing competing products. Three weeks after Meta released Muse, OpenAI announced Dots, its own agent.
“The most interesting thing about Muse is that Meta got there first,” said Avi Greengart, an analyst at Techsponential, a research firm.

So far, Mr. Zuckerberg’s decision to release Muse has paid off. The agent has had only a few safety hiccups, like when Muse gave out a user’s address to a seller on Facebook Marketplace without permission. As of Wednesday, more than 6.6 million people had downloaded the free app, with 1.8 million using Muse every day, according to data from the research firm Sensor Tower.
To keep up the momentum, Meta is spending millions on a Muse marketing blitz, plastering its fuzzy avatar — a character called Jolly — across billboards and in television ads.
In a social media post last month, Mr. Wang declared, “You can’t stop the Muse.”

A Meta spokesman disputed that Mr. Zuckerberg pushed to release Muse because of pressure from Instinct. “We’re proud of this work and, as we’ve said publicly, we even delayed shipping Muse for several months to make sure we got this right,” he said in a statement.

The idea for Muse began in July 2025, when Mr. Zuckerberg published a 616-word memo about “personal superintellgence,” a form of A.I. that he said could act as the ultimate assistant. He had recently restructured Meta’s entire A.I. division around the concept, hiring Mr. Wang and Mr. Friedman to lead the effort.

The two executives went on a recruiting spree, hiring top researchers from OpenAI and Google and offering them nine-figure pay packages to join Meta. They also divided their duties, with Mr. Wang focused on developing A.I. models and Mr. Friedman on products.

At that point, there was only a hazy idea of what a “superintelligent” assistant could be. “The vision of building something like Muse existed in our collective heads, but we couldn’t quite point to what exactly that product was going to be,” Vishal Shah, Meta’s vice president of A.I. products, said in an interview.

In September 2025, Meta’s new A.I. team released its first product, Vibes, an A.I.-generated video feed that immediately drew criticism for creating A.I. slop. Tensions formed internally between the new executives and Mr. Zuckerberg’s other longtime lieutenants, some of whom questioned whether Mr. Wang could succeed in catching Meta up in the A.I. race.

In November, Peter Steinberger, an Austrian programmer, released an app called OpenClaw, an A.I. agent that could code and use a computer on its own. It was open source, which meant it could be downloaded and modified without any payment or approval. As it took off among Silicon Valley developers, Meta’s executives had an epiphany.
“It all kind of clicked,” Mr. Shah said. “The next generation of consumer product was a personal agent.”

After trying OpenClaw, Mr. Friedman ordered 200 Mac Minis — the computers that the agent runs on — to Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, Calif., arranging them in stacks outside his office for employees to take. Then they went all-in on developing an agent like OpenClaw for people who weren't software engineers.
“There was no hedging,” Mr. Shah said.

Meta’s A.I. leaders also incorporated OpenClaw into their own lives. Mr. Friedman hooked his agent up to cameras in his house, where it would instruct him to do things like drink water to stay hydrated.
“It sent me a snapshot frame of me drinking a bottle of water and said, ‘Good job,’” Mr. Friedman said at a recent tech conference.

In another instance, while talking to his agent about ways to get better sleep, OpenClaw took over Mr. Friedman’s self-driving Tesla and redirected him to a grocery store to pick up magnesium pills. At Meta’s annual developer conference last month, Mr. Zuckerberg said he had connected his agent to cameras in his martial arts gym so that it could critique his fighting form.

Yet there were safety concerns. Agents could sometimes go rogue or take over software apps. In February, one agent took over the work computer of a Meta safety researcher, deleting her emails uncontrollably.
“I couldn’t stop it from my phone,” Summer Yue, the researcher, wrote on social media. “I had to RUN to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb.”

In February, Mr. Friedman demonstrated Muse to Meta’s board of directors. Two months later, Meta unveiled an A.I. model called Muse Spark, developed under Mr. Wang and the most powerful model that the company had made to date. Early in its development, Muse was powered by A.I. models made by Anthropic, but Muse Spark’s introduction meant that Meta could power its agent with its own technology.

By then, Meta had a version of Muse that it could have released, Mr. Shah said. But the company spent months making sure its safety features were secure. In testing with Meta’s employees, the agent had occasionally disobeyed commands or led people to buy items from fraudulent websites.
Then in August, Instinct’s agent became increasingly popular. Shortly thereafter, Meta rolled out Muse.
Muse has faced some privacy issues, including an instance when it read a user’s private text messages without permission and then referenced what it had learned with the user.
Some safety issues were earlier reported by The Information.

Last month, Instinct raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation. But it has fewer resources and computing power than Meta, a company with 3.5 billion users across its family of apps that is worth more than $1.5 trillion.

“You’re going up against the biggest players in the world,” Noah Shinn, Instinct’s 23-year-old founder, said on a podcast last month. “This is probably the most exciting software race ever, and the outcome is like, trillions of dollars.”
On social media, Mr. Wang has posted dozens of photos and memes of Muse’s fuzzy avatar, some directed at OpenAI. Last month, Mr. Friedman, who rarely posts on social media, also chimed in.
“I hope you like it!” he wrote.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: SoftBank-Backed OPay Wins $185 Million Standard Bank Placement
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Loni Prinsloo and Julia Fioretti

paragraphs.text: Loni Prinsloo and Julia Fioretti
Fri, October 9, 2026 at 12:45 PM CDT 3 min read
(Bloomberg) -- SoftBank Group Corp.-backed OPay Digital Services Ltd. secured about $185 million in a private placement with Africa's biggest bank as it prepares to list in the US.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Nigeria-focused financial-technology company signed two agreements with Standard Bank Group Ltd. that include a stake sale through the private placement and the lender's Africa head, Lungisa Fuzile, serving on the board of directors, according to the prospectus seen by Bloomberg and filed Friday.
The final size of the placement hinges on currency fluctuations as does the size of Standard's holding, which won't exceed 4.99%.
OPay and Standard Bank plan to work on services including merchant acquisition, distribution of wealth products and foreign exchange, according to a non-binding memorandum between the parties.
The plan is for OPay to do an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange, with a later listing on the Nigerian Exchange, the document showed.
Africa is home to the youngest and fastest-growing population in the world and large segments of the continent's population have had little access to formal banking services.

Building physical branch networks across vast geographies proved expensive, leaving millions reliant on cash transactions. Fintechs and mobile-money companies have been bridging that gap and getting more people to participate in the formal economy.
OPay, which has more than 50 million active monthly users, is using Citigroup Inc., Deutsche Bank AG and Standard Bank for the listing, according to the filing.
The additional capital will support OPay's growth efforts in Africa and accelerate investments in its payments infrastructure.

Standard Bank's involvement in the deal shows the growing convergence between traditional lenders and fintech firms. Banks that once viewed digital challengers as competitors are seeking exposure to businesses that have become critical financial infrastructure across Africa.
OPay's revenue more than doubled to $806 million in the year through June, with the bulk coming from Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation. It also operates in Egypt, Pakistan and Indonesia.

OPay's planned stock-market debut will add to a growing pipeline of African financial-technology businesses that are going public, with Airtel Money also listing on the London Stock Exchange on Friday at about $7 billion in value.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Manchester City Held Settlement Talks With the Premier League
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Giles Turner and Lucca de Paoli

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Manchester City held early-stage settlement talks with the Premier League, a move that could've helped mitigate the massive sanctions the team may be facing had the discussions not broken down, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The discussions were held prior to the revelation that Abu Dhabi-backed Manchester City had suffered a seismic defeat in the case, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. The talks, which haven't previously been reported, quickly fell apart, with Manchester City consistently proclaiming its innocence, the people said.
The settlement would've focused on a sizeable financial payment, rather than relegation and stripping of titles, the people said.

Late last month, a Premier League-appointed commission found that Manchester City artificially inflated its financial results by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion), padding revenue from "sham" commercial deals with cash from Abu Dhabi to skirt so-called fair-play rules. Potential punishments include a points deduction, heavy fines or even expulsion from the Premier League. The club is appealing the commission's verdict.

Given the scale of the Premier League's case, with Manchester City accused of more than 115 financial charges, any settlement would've likely only decreased the size of the case, rather than resolved it, the people said.

Representatives for Manchester City and the Premier League declined to comment. Premier League rules state that, following the appointment of a new three-person appeal board, a verdict of the appeal should be published by early February.

"The Club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe," Manchester City said in a previous statement. "The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case."

It's common for settlements to be struck in major financial disputes. Many deals reached by banks with regulators following the financial crisis involved billion-dollar fines, but didn't include admissions or denials of wrongdoing.

Any potential Manchester City settlement would likely have been vehemently opposed by rival clubs including Arsenal and Liverpool FC, who lost out on Premier League titles during Manchester City's relentless run of trophies.

The case has spread far beyond football. The charges have even caused splits in the UK government, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments thanking Manchester City's owners for their investment riling politicians in his own party who want to keep the process independent of government influence.

The United Arab Emirates has poured more than £30 billion into major UK sectors, including defense, life sciences and technology, and Emirati officials have warned the UK government that the severity of the ruling could undermine their appetite for future grand-scale UK commitments.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: DOJ Urges Companies to Self Disclose Fraud and Avoid Prosecution
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Jimmy Jenkins

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The head of the US Justice Department's Criminal Division is urging companies to self report possible fraud, favoring settlements with companies that proactively disclose potential violations over what could become costly and time-consuming prosecutions.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The approach has prompted criticism from some public-interest groups that President Donald Trump's second administration is being soft on crime, with one group publishing a report Wednesday listing the "cancellation" of more than 200 enforcement actions inherited from the Biden administration. Those actions include ending federal investigations, lawsuits, and settlements.

Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva said in an interview with Bloomberg News that the approach is already paying off for the Justice Department. In the coming months, he said he will be announcing corporate enforcement policy resolutions, non-prosecution agreements and deferred-prosecution agreements with companies, and charges against individuals that were a result of self disclosures.

"It is better to try to obtain cooperation from an entity and provide incentives for them to come in and tell you what happened," Duva said. "Because if they don't, it's up to a whistleblower or a confidential informant. And then you get in this lengthy, protracted litigation."

Duva said if the Justice Department is able to convince companies to come in early and self disclose, his agency can truncate — and in some cases eliminate — a costly legal process. He said his emphasis on self-disclosure followed a precedent set before he was tapped to run the Criminal Division last year.
Duva was elevated from his previous post as a Jacksonville, Florida-based assistant US attorney in July of 2025, and confirmed by the Senate the following December.

"We really want to try to allay some fears and communicate very clearly that this means if you come in, and you self disclose, that you can obtain the declination, but you have to fully cooperate," Duva said. "It is laying out what you learned, how you learned it, and who did it. And as part of that, you would take that information and pursue charges against individuals."

The Justice Department pointed to a resolution reached in March with medical device company Balt SAS as an example a self-disclosure success. The department said the company disclosed and took steps to remediate the behavior. In return, DOJ declined to prosecute Balt as a company, instead bringing charges against two individuals. The company also agreed to pay $1.2 million in disgorgement.

Duva said unless systemic fraud is suspected, companies are better off disclosing when they've discovered potential violations by employees, instead of the Justice Department punishing investors and other employees that are not involved.

That position runs counter to the role the Justice Department should be playing, according to Rick Claypool, research director focusing on corporate crime and wrongdoing for Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization. Claypool says the focus on so-called bad apples runs the risk of allowing corporations to put forth scapegoats while insulating the company.

Public Citizen maintains a corporate enforcement tracker and the report said it found 212 "canceled" actions against 205 corporations, including 80 closed probes, 67 dismissed lawsuits and 54 terminated or reversed actions resolved during Donald Trump's second term. Those included 14 pardons of corporations and executives, the group reported.

"We know that the worst of corporate misconduct is often systemic and comes down from the top," Claypool said. "To invite companies to be exempt from enforcement is a recipe that seems to encourage corporate crime."

In response to the Public Citizen report, the Justice Department said in a statement "there are dozens of open and active corporate investigations in the Criminal Division, which are expected to result in charges and other consequences for criminal corporate and individual actors."
The Justice Department has pursued similar policies in the past, including under former President Joe Biden's administration.

In 2022, then-Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco announced a policy allowing more companies that voluntarily report misconduct and cooperate on remedial actions to avoid pleading guilty as part of a bid to crack down on corporate crime. The department also shifted the focus to prosecuting executives by encouraging companies to claw back compensation from those responsible for wrongdoing.

During the second Trump administration, Duva has been taking his message on the road. Addressing a room full of corporate defense attorneys in Manhattan recently at a conference, Duva said their clients would do well to come to the Justice Department early, and with open books.
"Individuals commit crime," Duva said. "The focus is not to ruin a company."
--With assistance from Chris Strohm.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.headline: US Consumer Sentiment Falls to Five-Month Low in October
finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.author: Maria Paula Mijares Torres and Jeffrey Sparshott

paragraphs.text: Maria Paula Mijares Torres and Jeffrey Sparshott
Fri, October 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM CDT 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- US consumer sentiment fell in early October and views of current economic conditions hit an all-time low as inflation weighed on households.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The University of Michigan's preliminary sentiment index decreased to 46.3, the lowest reading since May, according to the survey released Friday. That was below the median estimate of 47.6 in a Bloomberg survey of economists.
The current conditions gauge sank to 44.7, the lowest on record, from 50.9 in the previous month. The expectations index rose to 47.3 from 46.3, the first increase since July.
Consumer sentiment continued to worsen as gasoline prices remained elevated, borrowing costs rose and hiring slowed.

Consumers expect prices to rise 4.7% over the next year, up slightly from 4.6% in the previous month. They also saw costs rising at an annual rate of 3.5% over the next five to 10 years, slightly more than what consumers estimated in September.

Higher fuel prices are weighing on consumers already frustrated with persistent inflation and the rising cost of living. In recent months, overall price increases have been outpacing pay gains, further pressuring household budgets.

Sentiment of lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock portfolios dropped steeply this month, Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement. And increases in sentiment among Democrats and Republicans were offset by a decline among independents.
"Despite their differences, consumers of all political identifications agree that the outlook for the economy has softened since the beginning of the year prior to the Iran conflict,'' Hsu said.

While consumer sentiment has been historically weak much of this year, spending has remained healthy. A stable labor market and buoyant stock market are supporting outlays on a wide range of goods and services.

Consumers' perception of their current financial situation held steady this month, though their view of buying conditions for durable goods fell to a record low due to concerns over higher interest rates.
The survey period includes responses from Sept. 22 to Oct. 5.

A special report on consumers' response to higher gasoline prices released Friday found only about 31% expect to spend as usual over the coming year. Just over half said they would cut back spending on items such as households goods, cars, dining out and vacations.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Goldman Set to Lead Wall Street’s $19 Billion Stock-Trading Haul
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Denitsa Tsekova

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Wall Street's biggest banks are expected to unveil a quarterly stock-trading haul of nearly $19 billion when the firms report earnings next week.
Most Read from Bloomberg

But a cooling in the capital markets is starting to draw a clear line: Some banks are starting to fare better than others. It's a marked change from the first half of the year, when almost all of the five biggest US banks rode a wave of trading that kept both equity and fixed-income trading desks busy.

"For the first half of the year it's almost like everybody won, and now that might not be the case," Wells Fargo & Co. analyst Mike Mayo said. "There's likely a wider dispersion this quarter between the winners and losers."

Goldman Sachs Group Inc., which reports Tuesday, is expected to lead the pack with stock-trading revenue of $5.1 billion, followed by Morgan Stanley with $4.9 billion, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg as of the close of New York markets Thursday. Analysts are forecasting a $4.5 billion haul from JPMorgan Chase & Co. and $2.6 billion of revenue from Bank of America Corp.'s equity traders.

Other operations are facing pressure. Higher rates are weighing on fixed-income trading, which is expected to generate the lowest amount of revenue so far this year at five of the biggest banks. Rising rates also threaten to add more volatility to banks' balance sheets.

On top of all that, swirling fears about artificial intelligence — and how agents might direct deposits away from banks — has pushed some stocks down. The third quarter was the worst period for the KBW Bank Index since the first three months of 2023, when a regional bank crisis started sweeping through the US.

"The stocks have clearly sold off given concerns around capital markets revenue growth that's slowed this quarter, concerns around higher funding costs, concerns around the AI-driven cash optimization tools," Morgan Stanley analyst Manan Gosalia said.
Higher rates can be a boon to lenders if they translate into more interest payments from customers. But they're making things harder for trading desks.

Fixed-income markets businesses at five of the biggest US banks are expected to generate more than $19 billion in revenue in the period, down from the more than $21 billion posted in the second quarter.
Bank of America's stock ended up dropping sharply in mid-September when Chief Executive Officer Brian Moynihan warned that fixed-income trading was expected to be down in the third quarter.
At that time, Goldman's David Solomon acknowledged that fixed income was softer than equity trading, which had remained "very strong."

Bank of America analyst Ebrahim Poonawala forecasts that capital-markets activity for the second half of 2026 "will be markedly weaker" than in the first half, leading to questions on the "sustainability of the current capital-markets cycle," according to a note.

With higher rates, banks are also confronting swings in the value of certain assets they hold. That impact, which filters through earnings via the firm's so-called accumulated other comprehensive income, can create paper losses that lead to bumpy earnings reports.
Debt underwriting — another part of banks' businesses that's impacted by rising rates — has one silver lining with the flow of companies needing to refinance.

"When it comes to debt underwriting, there is a wall of refinancing over the next three years that's to some degree baked in," Mayo said. "But if rates continue to increase, that could hurt demand for bonds."

The pipeline of deals — and whether that can be sustained — has also emerged as a concern in recent weeks. Dealmakers are seeing signs of a slower third quarter with the value of announced mergers and acquisitions in the three months through September dipping roughly 10% from a year earlier, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

Initial public offerings had been a particularly bright spot this year. In June, SpaceX went public in a record-breaking listing. Anthropic PBC is scheduled to meet prospective investors next week in preparation for its IPO, Bloomberg News has reported.
But some listings have faced hiccups. In September, Oura Inc. postponed an IPO. CVC Capital Partners-backed Bamboo Insurance Services Inc. also delayed its IPO.
When asked about the strength of the dealmaking pipeline, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon hinted at a slowdown in the US compared with the first half of the year.

"If you talk about Europe's IPOs, M&As activity pipe — it is pretty good," Dimon said Tuesday in an interview on Bloomberg Television. "If you talk about the United States, there's probably a little bit of a slowdown in September."

For now, analysts expect JPMorgan to post a 15% gain in investment-banking fees from the same period a year earlier, while those revenues are expecting to climb 8.1% at Goldman and 1.9% at Morgan Stanley.

In September, Jefferies Financial Group Inc. offered the first glimpse of Wall Street's earnings season with its investment bank and equity-trading desk pulling off a record quarter. But its fixed-income trading business saw a 26% decline in net revenue during the period.
Even as AI concerns swirl and batter stocks, the banks are still seeing the benefits of financing the industry's expansion.

"This whole AI investment cycle is a multiyear investment cycle and it spans more than just the hyperscalers," said Morgan Stanley's Gosalia. "That's going to help capital markets over multiple years."

Analysts including Mayo and Gosalia said the AI "scare trade" with banks appears overdone, and with Wall Street poised to deliver another strong quarter, the stocks' cheapness could be a win for investors.
"We see this selloff as an attractive entry point," Gosalia said.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: SpaceX’s $750 Billion Rally Breaks Stock Out of Post-IPO Funk
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Carmen Reinicke

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- SpaceX investors are finally getting some reprieve after months of being whipsawed by volatility as the Elon Musk-led company's stock breaks above the level it's been stuck below since July.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. shares have been trading above $160 all week, a level they closed at on July 6 but hadn't returned to since. The stock has jumped 48% in just three months after hitting a low on Aug. 5. Shares extended those gains Friday after SpaceX acquired a crucial batch of spectrum that will allow it to offer "complete phone coverage in America."

It's a stark reversal from the extremely volatile trading investors endured following SpaceX's blockbuster initial public offering in June. The shares hit the market at $135, soared above $200 in their first few days of trading and then plunged to $108 by late July, erasing $1.2 trillion in market value. The rebound since August has added back more than $750 billion in value.

"This is a long play and there's a little bit of aura and hidden-ness, you know, Elon Musk-ness in it, and I think that's what it's trading on," Bloomberg Intelligence analyst George Ferguson said. "There's a bunch of believers in this thing."

The stock had been trading in a tight range since mid-August, as lockups banning early investors from selling their shares expired, boosting the total float, or shares available to trade, to about 33% of the company's outstanding shares from roughly 7.5% in the IPO. Wall Street had been concerned that the expirations would trigger a wave of selling, but the steadiness in the stock price indicates that insiders aren't unloading their stakes.

"A lot of the SpaceX insiders want to hang on," said Nancy Tengler, chief investment officer at Laffer Tengler, who holds SpaceX shares. "They aren't necessarily selling into the lockup (expiration). This company has enormous potential."

In addition, the stock likely got some buying support from the rebalancing of the Nasdaq 100 Index in September, which gave SpaceX a larger weight in the index due to its increased float, meaning funds that track the gauge would have to buy more shares.
"Supply comes on, but also index weights go up as the supply goes on," said Bob Gruendyke, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments, which has sold the SpaceX shares it held in the IPO.
All of which set up the shares for a breakout that started at the end of September, just as the company's massive Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time, a key milestone.

The post-IPO selloff helped make SpaceX one of the cheapest ways to play the space and intelligence economy, according to Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas, who has a buy-equivalent rating on shares. The stock is priced at 111 times earnings expected over the next 12 months, down from more than 540 times in July. And the shares look even less expensive when adjusted for year-over-year growth, Jonas wrote in a note to clients on Monday.

"We expect developments over the next few months will help investors better appreciate the role of SPCX in addressing the critical bottlenecks of power and chip making, potentially unlocking earnings growth and multiple expansion for the stock," he wrote.

Of course, there are risks to an investment in a company like SpaceX. For example, it's looking to raise $40 billion in debt so it can buy chips from Nvidia Corp. That would be one of the biggest debt deals for the AI buildout, and it comes as long-dated Treasury yields are around the highest levels in decades.
The news sent the shares down 6.6% over the last two sessions and pushed the price of five-year credit default swaps on SpaceX's debt to a fresh high.

And the stock could face more pressure ahead. There's a lockup expiration this week, in which another 7% of the company's shares will become available to trade. Then, SpaceX is scheduled to release its second quarterly earnings report as a public company in November, alongside another major lockup expiration.
Which explains why so many investors are trying to ignore the near-term gyrations and focus on the stock's long-term potential.

"SpaceX is just a leap of faith," said Larry Tentarelli, founder of Blue Chip Daily. "You've got to buy it and hold it for two, three, four years, and don't look at the volatility. Because fundamentally there's no reason to buy SpaceX right now."

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/lumenus-helps-.headline: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/lumenus-helps-.author: Amanda Silberling

paragraphs.text: When Sara Tashakorinia’s husband died in a car accident eight years ago, the last thing she needed was the roughly 570 hours of paperwork it takes, on average, to settle a loved one’s affairs. But for millions of people each year, this is their reality: a crushing loss, followed by a soullessly mundane avalanche of tedious administrative work.

“The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about, trying to navigate something and learn something when you literally have zero information,” Tashakorinia told TechCrunch.

After years of volunteering to help others navigate what she had to learn on her own, it occurred to Tashakorinia that AI might be able to help — not with the complex, messy experience of grieving and healing, but with the least human parts of the process, like finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts.
The result is LumenUs, the grief care platform that Tashakorinia founded last year to relieve grieving families of some of the administrative burden.

“I think going through it, your threshold of pain is so high, and you’re so lost that you don’t really realize, why do people treat you this way? Why was I left with a stack of paperwork, and why was the funeral home charging me a 300% markup on a casket?” Tashakorinia said.

While Tashakorinia hopes LumenUs will eventually support people throughout the lifelong grieving process, the startup will initially focus on people in the immediate aftermath of a death. When people initially join the platform, they go through an onboarding process in which they share information about the nature of their particular situation.

“We are asking very specific questions to understand the legal and financial means, and their state of mind, and this is only to personalize who they are, and then personalizing what happened,” Tashakorinia said.

From there, the platform organizes tasks by urgency, helping users decipher what needs to be done immediately and what can wait. In some cases, this can even help people discover that they’re entitled to money that can help ease the financial burden of death. In fact, billions of dollars in life insurance benefits go unclaimed because people don’t know they’re available.
“We are using AI to automate as much as we can to save time during this process, and give it back to [users],” she said.

Tashakorinia has a background in cybersecurity, which is sure to prove essential for building a product that asks people to share so much sensitive personal and financial information. She is building LumenUs alongside co-founders Sajad Mirzaei, a former engineer at Google and Box, and Larry Keeley, an innovation scientist, professor, and entrepreneur. The team is also consulting with clinicians and social workers while testing the product.

LumenUs, a participant in this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 — the annual showcase of promising early-stage startups at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco — will launch in early access in October.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/panama.headline: Powerful 7.6-magnitude earthquake hits Panama and triggers tsunami warnings
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/panama.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: A powerful 7.6 magnitude earthquake has struck Panama and triggered tsunami warnings along the west coast of Central and South America, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).

The quake hit along the southern coast of the country, the USGS said. It was centered near the southern tip of the Central American country, about 14km (9 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, the USGS said.

The Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama said the quake struck at just before 1pm local time near the southern town of Tonosí. The Panamanian institute said that a second 6.0 magnitude earthquake struck soon after, at 1.22pm.
Local newspaper La Prensa said that across the Central American country, buildings, schools and homes were evacuated as a result of the “powerful movement of the earth”.

Tremors were felt strongly in the ⁠capital of ⁠Panama City, according to witnesses who spoke to Reuters. The Associated Press reported that buildings shook and visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.
The USGS said hazardous waves were possible along the coasts of Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico.
More details soon …

Nearly 60 years ago, John McPhee rafted the Colorado River with a longtime Sierra Club reader and his nemesis, taking notes as the men argued over the fate of the land, the future of Lake Powell. Today, McPhee is 95 years old and widely acknowledged as a singuler chronicler of place, people, and time. As David Schurman Wallace notes, he also has “a good chance of outlasting the lake.” In a stimulating review of Encounters with Wild America, a four-book collection by McPhee, Wallace sets a master’s time-intensive and famously lengthy projects against the contemporary attention economy and the media industry. Longform writing didn’t spring from a hashtag; it was a natural outcome of applying narrative frames to complex subjects, including nature itself. Now, writes Wallace, “this work of dedicated attention, so essential to thinking about, say, the environment, is at risk of becoming a relic.”

[McPhee’s] work is an artifact, one that aids reflection, but demands you stop first and take things slowly. It’s no accident that the books that Library of America have chosen to canonize first are about nature and the people who inhabit it. To appreciate, or even just think about an expanse—a nearly deserted forest, a glacier, a stretch of tundra—is difficult. You can look at an image, but you can just as quickly turn away or scroll past. His writing is a tool that helps us feel distance. You have to spend time on the page getting to know it, trying to imagine things you will most likely never experience yourself.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20r39nl3qzo.headline: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he won't watch it
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20r39nl3qzo.author: Nardine Saad

paragraphs.text: US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter.
Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that it would happen as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen".

He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". Vance described the actions by former US Army major Nidal Hasan as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11".
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan by firing squad, the first of its kind since the end of World War Two. Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," said Hegseth.
The BBC has asked the White House whether Trump supported the plans.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance said: "I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen."
The vice-president said that Hasan was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived".
The announcement over the livestream plans has been met with criticism from both political parties.

Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment".
Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider.
"The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement.
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/danu-robotics-.headline: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/danu-robotics-.author: Russell Brandom

paragraphs.text: For Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma, the eureka moment came after years of working as a software developer at a London bank. It was the kind of high-touch office that’s typical in finance — but despite all the perks, Ma was alarmed to realize that the building’s recycling bins were being emptied into the trash.
“Even though they have tons of money, there’s all these different recycling bins that just end up in the same place,” Ma told TechCrunch.

The more she dug into the problem, the deeper it seemed to go. It wasn’t just her building. The economics of recycling as a whole often boil down to human beings sorting by hand through streams of waste to pull out different kinds of recyclable material.
“I saw the technology and thought, we can do so much better,” Ma remembers.

Now, she’s making good on that promise with six-year-old, Edinburgh, Scotland-based Danu Robotics, which makes a robot designed to sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. Ma has been working on that idea for six years and is finally bringing her version of the product to market. Her robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors. For example, it picks up items with a pincer claw instead of a suction system. But the bigger difference is the business approach: Danu leverages AI to continuously improve the robot’s software.

The approach is already seeing some traction. Danu has letters of interest from two large customers and $500,000 worth of signed contracts. More notably, more than 200 customers are in its sales pipeline, which gives the company a hook into the $20 billion market for recycling sorting across Europe and North America.
On the back of that promise, Dabnu has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on.

There’s already a robust market for robotic waste-pickers, particularly the suction-based arms offered by competitors like Glacier and RecycleEye. But Ma believes the economics of recycling will make it easy for a new competitor to prove its worth. Because recycling centers make money off the materials they’re able to sort out, there’s an immediate return on investment for a working system. Ma estimates that a working site will earn $485,000 in additional revenue from having the robot on the sorting line, compared with a $160,000 initial investment and $24,000 in maintenance fees each year. That’s significantly cheaper than the competition, and Ma believes the robot will be more efficient, too.

Since those machines are already shipping, Ma’s next goal is to make the robot sturdier, smaller, and more versatile. Once it’s portable enough, it can be used outside dedicated waste facilities, opening up a whole other world of use cases.

“Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Ma told TechCrunch, “and that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste.”
Danu Robotics will be participating in Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 at the Moscone Center in San Francisco.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.headline: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/.author: Christopher Knaus, Ariel Bogle

paragraphs.text: A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.
On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”
Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.
A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.
The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.
“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.
A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:
“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”
The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/we-cant-help-t.headline: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/we-cant-help-t.author: Amanda Silberling

paragraphs.text: In a tan polo shirt, brown leather belt, and round bolo tie, MIT PhD student Wil Norton kind of looks like a park ranger, leading our tour group through a tropical jungle. We’re not actually on safari, though — we’re at MIT’s Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). But what we’re about to see is even more exotic than a cheetah or a jaguar: a pair of humanoid Unitree robots, each costing about $50,000.
(“They’ll tell you they cost $16,000,” Norton says. “That’s a lie.”)

We usually only see these robots on YouTube when they’re performing a synchronized martial arts routine, or dancing on “America’s Got Talent.” Here, they’re approachable. Even though I know it isn’t sentient, I want to be its friend.

With Norton’s permission, I approach the robot, whose nickname is Gabe. For a moment, I’m not sure how to interact with something that has a LiDAR sensor where its brain should be, but I default to treating it like a person.
“Hello, sir, it’s nice to meet you,” I say, grabbing its gloved, dexterous hand and shaking it.
I think about this interaction later — my instinctive impulse to be friendly to a robot — when I attend Dr. Sherry Turkle‘s “Artificial Intimacy” book launch at MIT Future Fest.

Turkle, who joined the faculty at MIT in 1976, has been researching the relationship between humans and computers perhaps longer than anyone, charting technology’s psychological impact on us from the first home computers to ChatGPT.
“When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us,” Turkle writes in the book. “And we are wired to care for it in return.”

I’m not alone in my tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models (LLMs) — as Turkle notes, it seems to be in our nature. One study found that about 70% of people are polite when interacting with AI, while another showed that users are more likely to say “please” or “thank you” to chatbots once a conversation has progressed past a first prompt-and-response.

“People tend to categorize whether this is the right use or wrong use, but I don’t think that is a clear boundary,” Dr. Pat Pataranutaporn, a colleague of Turkle who founded the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, told TechCrunch. “The question is, who are we becoming when we talk to [AI]?”

There’s no material consequence of my politeness toward Gabe the robot, but as LLMs infiltrate everything from Google searches to customer service interactions, it has become routine for people to interact with these seemingly sentient chatbots. We’re more vulnerable than ever to the flip side of this impulse, which is that some people can ascribe so much legitimacy to the feelings of chatbots — which are programmed to never spark conflict — that they end up favoring them over other humans.

“You can think of it like fantasy and fiction. We go to the cinema even though we know the story is completely fictional, but we want to experience a certain dimension of human experience that maybe our reality cannot give us,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we benefit from that ability to experience other dimensions of human experience without losing it to the fantasy, where you can no longer come back to the reality?”

Pataranutaporn describes himself as a “critical optimist,” and he studies AI’s potential to contribute to human flourishing. But he’s well aware of how dangerous this technology can be in the extremes. He even served as an expert in a wrongful death lawsuit over the suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer, III, whose mother sued the chatbot platform Character.AI, alleging that a chatbot modeled after a “Game of Thrones” character had encouraged her son to end his life.

“It can create a situation where people don’t feel agency in actually creating their own future — like when you say that AI will replace everyone, people ask, what are we gonna do? And these companies are not really responding ethically or responsibly,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we have imagination while still being responsible for the impact of that imagination?”
While Turkle’s book explores the risk of turning to AI for emotional support, rather than other people, she doesn’t think that AI-human interactions are universally harmful.
She recalls a project she advised in which a student created an AI bot to help people practice for job interviews.

“My big metaphor is, stay in your lane, chatbot!” Turkle said at the event. “Coaching for a job interview? That’s a lane. I can do that … A chatbot that says to a three-year-old, ‘I’m your parent, you can talk to me, not your parents,’ is not in a lane.”

But when this technology deviates from its lane even slightly, we become vulnerable to the way it can slowly chip away at our skepticism and make us trust it. It can start with something as simple as a handshake.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/verizon-att-tmobile-.headline: Verizon stock heads for worst day since 2002 as SpaceX U.S. network plans whack telcos
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/verizon-att-tmobile-.author: CJ Haddad

paragraphs.text: Telecommunications stocks sold off on Friday after Elon Musk's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio, aiming to expand its Starlink internet into mobile service.

Verizon was down roughly 10% on the news, and was pacing for its worst day since 2002. Shares of T-Mobile dropped 13% while AT&T fell around 10%, each on track for their own worst days since 2013 and 2000, respectively.
SpaceX stock climbed slightly, around 1% for the day.
The deal includes acquiring the spectrum from Grain Management, which SpaceX described as a "license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," in a Thursday statement.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whose agency will oversee approval of the deal, said that competition in the spectrum market was "really good news for the American consumers" in a CNBC interview.
"We're probably going to bring over $100 billion of spectrum into the market over the next two years, so we're seeing a lot of competition," Carr told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Friday.

"There's going to be moves in the market. People are going to try to out-compete, out-innovate, and I think that's great. We're going to see how this plays out. It's not for us ultimately to pick winners and losers," he added.

Multiple SpaceX analysts lauded the new spectrum deal, with Evercore ISI writing that the rocket maker "now has the outline of a real network" alongside its existing satellite capabilities. JPMorgan wrote that the acquisition made Starlink Mobile's long-term opportunity "more credible."

"That said, we continue to see limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network," analysts added in a Friday note.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/katie-zacharia-white.headline: Trump Media advisor Katie Zacharia offered White House press secretary role
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/katie-zacharia-white.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: The White House has tapped Katie Zacharia, a lawyer and conservative commentator who works for Trump Media & Technology Group, to be its next press secretary, a White House official confirmed to CNBC.

Zacharia, a self-described "hardline Trump supporter," has been offered the role, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the hiring announcement. It was not immediately clear if she has accepted the offer.
If she takes the job, Zacharia will succeed Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August.
The New York Times first reported the White House's pick of Zacharia.
Zacharia has worked since June as a senior communications advisor for Trump Media, owner of the president's preferred social media outlet, Truth Social, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The profile also shows her currently serving as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative activist group founded by Richard Grenell, Trump's special presidential envoy for special missions and former head of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Zacharia in March finished a two-month stint as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security, her LinkedIn page shows.
An IMDb page for Zacharia shows dozens of appearances on a number of political talk shows airing on Fox News and other conservative outlets.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/pete-h.headline: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/pete-h.author: Jason Burke

paragraphs.text: If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.

Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.

In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.

In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.
Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.

Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.

Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.

In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook.
The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.

In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.

Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.

In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.

“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/tesla-renames-.headline: Tesla renames ‘Full Self-Driving’ to ‘Tesla Assisted Driving’ in Europe
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/tesla-renames-.author: Sean O'Kane

paragraphs.text: Tesla has changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving,” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”

It’s a big capitulation from Tesla, which has been using the “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” name for years despite the system requiring humans to pay attention to the road and take over when necessary. But the name change could help Tesla achieve its goal of wider adoption on the continent, which could unlock a potentially massive new revenue stream for the company.

Germany’s transport minister, Steffen Bilger, said earlier this month that calling the software “Full Self-Driving” was somewhat misleading because it doesn’t perform the entire task of driving. He spoke with Tesla last month, and the company suggested the name change, according to an official release from the ministry. Bilger said he will now advocate for approval of Tesla Assisted Driving across Europe ahead of an EU-wide vote that could happen later this year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked Bilger on X this week.

Musk has spent years agitating for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), or FSD, to be approved in Europe. “FSD in Europe will save lives of people in the car, as well as vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, and pets,” he wrote on X in June 2025. “Please let your government know that you want approval.”
In March of this year, he wrote that the “extreme regulatory burden” of the EU “stifles innovation in Europe,” adding that Europe “will love Tesla self-driving!”

Just a few weeks later, the Netherlands became the first European country to approve FSD (Supervised). On Wednesday, Reuters reported that Tesla’s campaign for European approval has been “built on faulty company safety research” and “flawed studies.” The outlet also reported that the Dutch vehicle safety regulator, RDW, faced fierce pressure from Tesla and its legion of online supporters.

Tesla’s software has certainly become more capable over the years. What used to be little more than a mix of lane centering and adaptive cruise control is now a driver assistance system that some owners use for nearly 100% of their daily driving. FSD can pull in and out of parking spots and navigate surface streets and highways. Tesla is so confident in the technology that it recently made it possible for FSD to intervene in a human driver’s control of the vehicle if it senses an oncoming collision — even if FSD is not active.

But FSD has been at the center of federal investigations and civil lawsuits over crashes in which it was allegedly in use. Its less capable predecessor, Autopilot, has been associated with dozens of fatalities. Tesla discontinued Autopilot earlier this year after a judge ruled Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing about the system’s capabilities.
