cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-lisa-cook-fed-.headline: Trump created a committee to dig into the Fed's Lisa Cook. What is it and what comes next?
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-lisa-cook-fed-.author: Matt Peterson, Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump on Friday announced an unusual legal step: He created a committee to help him decide whether to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook.

Trump has accused Cook of mortgage fraud, and in 2025 ordered her to be fired. The Supreme Court blocked that effort on procedural grounds but said he could try again. Trump in August informed Cook that he was considering another attempt to fire her. Her attorneys responded later that month, denying the allegations of fraud and saying Trump had no cause to remove her.
The decision to form what Trump is calling a "committee of inquiry" raises a number of questions about the path forward for Trump and Cook.
How will the committee work?

According to the president's memo, Cook is expected to attend a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5. She can bring an attorney. The committee will weigh the evidence against her and her response. She will have until Nov. 10 to follow up after the proceedings.

Then the committee will make a recommendation to the president as to whether there is cause to fire her from the Fed. The final call is up to the president. There is no set deadline for that final decision.
Who is on the committee?

Trump appointed three people to hear the evidence against Cook: Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council; Keith Sonderling, acting director of the Office of Government Ethics and Labor secretary; and Andrea R. Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. All three are Trump appointees.
Has a president used a committee like this before?
Yes, at least once. The Supreme Court's majority opinion in Trump v. Cook, written by Chief Justice John Roberts, mentions a precedent.

President William Howard Taft in 1912 convened a similar "committee of inquiry" to consider the removal of two members of the Board of General Appraisers, a precursor to what is now the U.S. Court of International Trade. The committee ultimately recommended their removal. Roberts describes the committee as "a prime example of the view that Taft was our 'most judicial president,' as he was our most 'presidential chief justice.' "

But notably, the Supreme Court didn't require Trump or other presidents to follow that example. The court says Cook was entitled to notice of the president's decision, an explanation of the evidence, and an opportunity to present her defense. That process could take place entirely in writing, Roberts notes.
A Fed governor is not "entitled to an audience with the President or a full-blown judicial trial," Roberts writes.
Will Cook cooperate with the committee hearing?

Her attorneys Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement she "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her." Still, they said they "have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law." They have said repeatedly that Cook did not commit mortgage fraud.
Will the committee be independent from the president?

No, the committee is made up of executive branch appointees who report to the president. They are tasked with weighing the evidence, and are required to hear Cook's point of view. But they are not impartial members of the judicial branch.
Does the committee need to find that Cook committed a crime?

No, it only needs to show that the president has cause to fire her. The Supreme Court didn't make a detailed determination of what constitutes cause, and that question will almost certainly be the subject of future litigation should Trump ultimately decide to remove her.

Roberts wrote in Trump v. Cook that a finding of cause depends "at least in part, on the seriousness of the alleged misconduct, and the extent of any nexus that may exist to the Governor's professional duties."
Could Cook's testimony expose her to criminal jeopardy?
Potentially. The order requires Cook to appear and allows Justice Department officials to question her, but it does not say whether her answers would be protected from use in a later criminal case.

The Fifth Amendment generally protects government employees from having statements that are compelled under threat of losing their jobs used against them in a criminal prosecution. But it is not yet clear whether Cook's testimony in this proceeding would qualify as legally compelled.

Her attorneys could therefore seek assurances about how her testimony would be used before she answers questions that could expose her to criminal liability. Invoking the Fifth Amendment or seeking immunity would not legally amount to an admission of guilt, though Trump could seek to portray it politically that way.
Will the committee have the final word on Cook's employment?

Almost certainly not. The committee will make a recommendation to Trump, but his decision may not be final either. The Supreme Court's ruling establishes that it is entitled to review the president's determination of cause. Should Trump proceed with firing Cook after the hearing, the decision will likely end up in front of the justices again, a process that could take months.
Will interest rates change as a result of the committee?
Not immediately, or possibly ever.

Cook is expected to participate in the Fed's upcoming vote on interest rates scheduled for Oct. 28. After the Supreme Court blocked Trump's earlier attempt to fire Cook, she remains as a member in good standing of the Fed.

Trump has not yet made another attempt to fire her, though the committee is tasked with making a recommendation on that question. She would likely continue to serve on the Fed during any court challenges after the committee process concludes.
What does the committee's creation mean for former Chair Jerome Powell or other Fed members?

Trump's decision to establish the committee has no immediate bearing on Powell's standing at the Fed. Powell ended his term as Fed chairman in May but can remain on as a voting member of the Fed's Board of Governors through January 2028.

Past Fed chairs have resigned their governorships once their term as the Fed's leader expired, but Powell said in March he wanted to stay on in order to see the end of a separate investigation against him "with transparency and finality."

That investigation concluded two weeks ago without any criminal charges, and the Department of Justice said it would not pursue the matter further. Powell hasn't spoken about the Cook matter since the Supreme Court's ruling.

The White House criticized a third Fed governor, Michael Barr, over his involvement as the Fed's top bank regulator in the failure of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. But the White House stopped short of calling for his resignation.
What has the Fed said about the committee?
The Fed referred questions about the committee to Cook's attorneys. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has previously said the Fed would follow the Supreme Court's ruling.
– CNBC's Angela Greiling Keane, Kevin Breuninger, Erik Holm and Steve Liesman contributed to this report.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68xzqqn4ekro.headline: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68xzqqn4ekro.author: Tinshui Yeung

paragraphs.text: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.

Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.

The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".

Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/remember-orkut.headline: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/remember-orkut.author: Jagmeet Singh

paragraphs.text: Orkut, the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection.

In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join.

Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube.

In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote.
“I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added.

This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users.

In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch.

Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch.
An email sent to Orkut seeking comment from Büyükkökten did not elicit a response.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/fed-lisa-cook-trump..headline: Trump appoints committee to investigate statements by the Fed's Lisa Cook
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/fed-lisa-cook-trump..author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump formally established a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements related to "one or more mortgage instruments," the White House announced Friday.

The extraordinary announcement is the latest development in Trump's long-running effort to fire Cook, a nominee of former President Joe Biden, from the central bank's board. Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, recently said the failure to do so by his handpicked chair, Kevin Warsh, is the fault of a "hostile" board.

The committee comprises three executive branch officials, including Kevin Hassett, Trump's top economic aide and a chief defender of the administration's economic record, according to a presidential memorandum posted on the White House website and shared Friday on social media.

The other two members are Keith Sonderling, Labor secretary and acting head of the Office of Government Ethics, and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Chair Andrea Lucas, according to the notice, which is dated Wednesday. No outside, independent arbiters are mentioned.

The highly unusual move, which hasn't been used in nearly a century, is bound to fuel new accusations that Trump and his aides are eroding the Fed's long-maintained independence while once again wielding government power against the president's enemies. Congressional Democrats quickly slammed the announcement, while Cook's lawyers expressed deep skepticism about the panel's validity.

There is no modern precedent for such a committee, though past presidents have convened similar panels. President William Taft in 1912 appointed a committee to investigate the Board of United States General Appraisers, and President Herbert Hoover did the same in 1931 to probe statements by the president of the Navy League.
The Supreme Court, in its June ruling temporarily blocking Trump from his first attempt to fire Cook, cited Taft's committee.

Trump's panel and Cook are scheduled to appear for an in-person hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm election, the memo states. Its members can consult with the Department of Justice and other agencies "to aid in its inquiry," the notice says.

Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, sharply questioned the legitimacy of the inquiry, but nevertheless said the governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."

"In light of the President's repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook – regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law," the lawyers told CNBC in a statement.
"But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," they said.

"We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise. Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her," Lowell and Eisen said.
Trump first tried to fire Cook last year, after administration officials raised allegations that she made false statements on at least one mortgage-related document.
Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing and filed a lawsuit to block her dismissal. A federal court temporarily barred Trump from firing her, and the Supreme Court in June narrowly upheld that ruling.

But the high court did not stop Trump from trying again for Cook's removal. Rather, it rejected Trump's first bid because Cook was not given proper legal due process, and said any new attempt to fire her would require additional steps. Under the Federal Reserve Act, a president can remove a Fed governor only "for cause."
In August, White House aide Dan Scavino told Cook in a letter that Trump was once again "considering" firing her in connection with the mortgage allegations.

"As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump states in the memo establishing the committee of inquiry, which is addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

"To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal" within the meaning identified by the Supreme Court, it says.
The Fed did not provide a comment and referred CNBC to Cook's lawyers.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in a statement later Friday morning accused Trump of "convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation's central bank."

"Instead of playing judge in a kangaroo court of his own making, Trump should end the war in Iran and cancel his chaotic tariffs," said Warren, the top-ranking Democrat on the Senate's Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Trump "is escalating his smear campaign against Lisa Cook while turning the presidency into a personal ATM: crypto schemes, taxpayer-funded propaganda ads, cash for his family — the list could go on forever."

"This has nothing to do with 'ethical concerns.' It's about Trump trying to seize control of the Fed, something that would mean even more economic chaos for American families," Schumer said in an X post.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/a16zs-olivia-m.headline: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/a16zs-olivia-m.author: Russell Brandom

paragraphs.text: I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.

Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.

Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?

I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.

How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?

I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.

I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.

The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?

Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.

The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.
It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?

I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.

Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.

There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.
So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?
It’s definitely very early.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/the-used-car-market-.headline: The used car market is stagnant. Here's how to profit anyway
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/the-used-car-market-.author: Michael Khouw

paragraphs.text: There's an old but useful expression used for buying cars: Kick the tires and light the fires. The phrase, which started in aviation but bled its way into automobiles, is a reminder to look under the hood and poke around before purchasing a car. The same advice would work for shares of CarMax.

On the surface, the stock looks fairly priced. CarMax is trading at roughly 17x fiscal-year expected earnings of $3.16/share. That's roughly in line with its 10-year historical forward multiple. While that valuation may not look stretched, the underlying fundamentals reflect a sharp squeeze on used-car affordability. Middle-market consumers, already pressured by high new and used car prices, see that compounded (literally) by severe financing headwinds. St. Louis Federal Reserve data puts average used auto loan APRs at 15.9% with an average loan term of 68 months. Even with used vehicle prices softening slightly, high borrowing costs keep monthly payments out of reach for many prospective buyers.

Operational metrics used to evaluate a car dealership's performance show the impact. The cash conversion cycle has lengthened, inventory turnover has slowed, and average days on the lot have crept higher.

Because borrowing rates are unlikely to drop precipitously in the near term, a catalyst for an auto sales boom remains elusive. However, given the fair multiple and stable cash generation, an abrupt collapse is also not the base case. The setup favors a range-bound stock with a capped upside ceiling.
The strategy: November (hedged) short strangle
Investors expecting KMX to stay within a defined channel can sell a wide strangle and buy an out-of-the-money call to neutralize upside tail risk.
• Sell the November 50 Put at $1.50
• Sell the November 60 Call at $1.00
• Buy the November 67.50 Call for $0.20 (Upside Hedge)
Key trade metrics & risk parameters

As a package, this three-legged structure collects a net credit of roughly $2.30/share ($230 per spread, since each contract represents 100 shares), or about 4.3% of the current share price, over 6 weeks (42 calendar days), or more than 37% annualized.
• Downside breakeven: $47.70, 12% below current price.
• Upside breakeven $62.30, 16.5% above current price.
• Maximum upside risk is $5.20/share ($520 per spread); that risk is capped above $67.50 ($7.50 spread width – $2.30 credit).
• Ideal Target Profit Zone: between the short strikes of $50.00 to $60.00, in which case you retain the full $2.30 credit if held to expiration.
Positioning rationale

The sweet spot is between $50 and $60 at November expiration, where all three options expire worthless, and you keep the full $2.30 credit. On the downside, the structure provides a nearly 11% buffer. If KMX breaches $47.70, the position carries standard put-assignment risk, allowing an investor who doesn't mind owning the shares to acquire them at an effective net basis of $47.70 (roughly 15x forward earnings).On the upside, standard short strangles leave the trader exposed to unlimited risk associated with a short stock position. By buying the November 67.50 call for a small portion of the premium received, upside risk is capped at $5.20 above $67.50, guarding against short-covering spikes or a sudden, unanticipated macro easing/rate decline, while still maintaining attractive yields.

washingtonpost.com/immigration/2026/10/0.headline: ICE didn’t know 5-year-old boy was in car when officer fired, Mullin says
washingtonpost.com/immigration/2026/10/0.author: Tim Craig, David Nakamura, Silvia Foster-Frau, Ted Hesson

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — Federal authorities on Friday strongly denounced the reaction of New York officials to the shooting of a Dominican man by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, casting the man as the aggressor who used his car to ram two government vehicles and accelerate toward officers despite having a 5-year-old in the back seat.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the ICE officers did not know the boy was in the vehicle driven by Oscar Belgal, 28, who was struck in the neck during the shooting Thursday afternoon in New York City. Belgal was treated at the scene and taken to a hospital before being moved to a detention facility outside the state, authorities said.
Mullin said Belgal, the boy’s father, would face criminal prosecution and be placed in deportation proceedings.

“He knew he had a child in the car and chose to accelerate at a high-rate of speed,” Mullin said at a news conference in Washington, flanked by senior ICE officials. “He’s a criminal, a thug, a gang banger. The outrage should be with him endangering a 5-year-old.”

New York officials, including Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), have denounced the agency and demanded that ICE pause enforcement operations in the state. Mamdani called on federal officials to “abolish ICE.”
“No, we’re not putting a pause on enforcement,” Mullin said. “I’m sorry, we’re not. In fact, I’m not sorry.”
Mullin accused New York officials of failing to cooperate with immigration enforcement efforts to take custody of undocumented immigrants who are arrested for state and local offenses.

New York City has policies that limit local law enforcement from sharing certain information with federal officers or honoring detainer requests unless immigrants have been convicted of violent crimes. The state also has policies to prevent federal authorities from accessing motor vehicle and drivers’ license records of immigrants without a court order or search warrant.

Mullin said ICE had issued 14,766 detainers in New York since President Donald Trump took office last year to take custody of people in New York jails. But, he said, the state has failed to cooperate. “Silence is what we got from the state of New York,” he said.

Mullin said he spoke with Mamdani on Thursday night and the mayor asked him to release Belgal, prompting Trump to tell Mamdani that the administration would transfer custody to local police if they are willing to pursue criminal charges against Belgal.
“The mayor said, ‘We are not detaining him,’” Mullin said.
Mamdani did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have faced widespread public outrage over aggressive enforcement tactics. Earlier this year, federal officers fatally shot two U.S. citizens during a surge in operations in Minneapolis in January. Since July, two immigrants have been shot and killed by ICE officers who fired into their vehicles.
Democrats, immigration advocates and family members of the deceased say that ICE is using excessive force against people who do not represent a threat.

Mullin, a former U.S. senator from Oklahoma, took over DHS in late April, promising to take a quieter approach than his predecessor, Kristi L. Noem. The agency has backed off from conducting large-scale raids that previously led to broad community protests and a drop in support for the president’s deportation agenda. Still, under Mullin’s watch, ICE has significantly increased detentions, arresting over 50,000 immigrants in August, which DHS said was a record.

Trump officials have consistently stated that their goal is to keep Americans safe by targeting enforcement against “the worst of the worst” — undocumented immigrants who have committed violent crimes or repeated offenses. But arrest data shows that many of those being arrested have only civil immigration violations. More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July did not have a criminal record, according to a Post analysis.

New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch and Mamdani told reporters late Thursday that the ICE officers were not wearing clothing that indicated they were law enforcement personnel and said at least one officer was carrying a long gun.

“They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There was no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents,” Mamdani said. “School had just gotten out. The street was crowded with families and children.”

Mullin said the officers were conducting a standard undercover operation against Belgal, who officers had unsuccessfully attempted to arrest in September before he fled. Belgal has lived in the United States for three years and been accused of crimes including grand larceny, robbery and theft armed with a dangerous weapon, authorities said.

ICE officers “identified themselves and gave lawful orders when they approached the vehicle,” Mullin said. “Not to mention he knew he was wanted. He had fled once ... I know he knew his day was coming.”
Mullin said authorities believe Belgal is connected to a gang that was involved in the shooting of a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer last year.
“It’s shameful we’re giving this case so much attention when this was a thug — the worst of the worst,” Mullin said of Belgal.

Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-New York) said he visited with Belgal’s 5-year-old son and his mother last night. He said the family told him Belgal picked up his son from school, put him in a car seat in the back and then went to visit family members in the area when he was shot.
The child is physically unharmed, but Espaillat said the family told him he is “traumatized by this whole experience.”

The lawmaker said he was not aware of Belgal’s alleged criminal history, but that regardless, the decision to fire at his vehicle in the middle of the day in a residential area put many people at risk.
“Any neighborhood in the country will be appalled of this kind of stuff happening right in the middle of it,” Espaillat said. “If anything, they were the ones that put our community in danger.”

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/automattic-los.headline: Automattic interim CFO resigns just weeks after boardroom shakeup
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/automattic-los.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.

The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”
Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit.

He was meant to replace the former CFO, Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean.

Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.

A source at Automattic told TechCrunch that Klaperman was upset the board was considering external candidates for the CFO role. Though he was announced internally as interim CFO, the board never legally approved his title, the source said. In addition, there was a disagreement with Mullenweg over a work project related to employee performance reviews, which led to Mullenweg’s demotion of Klaperman back to his former position at VIP. Klaperman resigned shortly thereafter.
Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure. The company is still performing an external search for a qualified CFO candidate, we understand.
After publication, the company issued a statement via X post, which implies that Klaperman was offended by the board’s search for external CFO candidates.

It read, “At Automattic, we consider it best practice to evaluate external candidates for critical roles alongside internal people stepping up. We are always talking to and recruiting the best talent. Sometimes people are offended or surprised by this and they resign, sometimes it has led to amazing mentoring or advising situations. We won’t comment on any specific person, but as a company we’re always trying to optimize and redefine ourselves to serve our customers better and promote the ideals we aspire to around Open Source, freedom, liberty, autonomy, and hackers.”

When the company originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO internally on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.
Updated after publication with more information about Klaperman’s departure.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/tesla-full-self-driv.headline: Tesla drops 'Full Self-Driving' brand name in Europe after regulator pushback
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/tesla-full-self-driv.author: Lora Kolodny

paragraphs.text: Elon Musk's automaker Tesla has changed the brand name of its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, system in Europe to "Assisted Driving" after German regulators called the branding "somewhat misleading."
The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners.

Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year.

On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport, known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla's brand name "FSD" was "somewhat misleading," adding that "It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times."

Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla's "browbeating" pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company's technology.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla's FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions.

In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that "false advertiser" label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing.
In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.
Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/hurricane-isaias-gul.headline: Hurricane Isaias disrupts U.S. oil production in Gulf of Mexico, threatens refineries
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/hurricane-isaias-gul.author: Spencer Kimball

paragraphs.text: Hurricane Isaias is disrupting U.S. crude oil production in the Gulf of Mexico and could limit about 2% of the country's refining capacity, at a time when fuel markets are already tight around the world.

Isaias is churning toward Mississippi, Alabama and the Florida panhandle as a Category 3 storm with maximum sustained winds of 120 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center, and is expected to make landfall Friday night or early Saturday.
As of Thursday, oil companies had shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or roughly 63% of total U.S. production in the Gulf, according to the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement.
The hurricane appeared to be veering away from the dense refining region in southern Louisiana near New Orleans and Baton Rouge.

But the storm could affect Chevron's refinery in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and a Vertex Energy refinery in Saraland, Alabama. Both areas are under hurricane warnings. The facilities there can produce a combined 466,000 bpd, or 2.4% of U.S. refining capacity, said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.

"Of course, losing any refinery capacity when diesel supplies are at their lowest level for this time of year since the EIA began reporting in 1982 is not a good thing," Lipow wrote in a Friday note, referring to the Energy Information Administration.
Chevron's refinery at Pascagoula remains operational, spokesperson Ross Allen said Thursday. Vertex officials weren't immediately available for comment about its Saraland refinery.

"The biggest risk to these two refineries are a loss of electricity or flooding damage," Lipow wrote in a note Friday. If the refineries do shut down, it would take one to two weeks to restart them if they did not sustain damage, he said.
Refineries on the Gulf Coast are running at 95% of their capacity, so there is no slack in the system to make up for lost production, Lipow said.

Diesel prices have soared as the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East knock out refining capacity. Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to ban diesel exports. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East.
U.S. refiners have stepped in to take advantage of wide profit margins to export diesel around the world, particularly to Europe.

In the past, fuel prices rose while crude prices fell during outages at Gulf refineries, said Kevin Book, managing director at ClearView Energy Partners. That's a result of those refineries not demanding crude and not producing fuel for consumers, Book told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday.
Lipow warned that tanker traffic will also be disrupted.

"Tankers will be delayed delivering crude oil to the refineries while other tankers are delayed loading gasoline, jet fuel and diesel out of the refineries," the analyst said. "Florida will experience delays in receiving gasoline, jet fuel and diesel."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdxwn9dr42yo.headline: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmdxwn9dr42yo.author: Maia Davies

paragraphs.text: A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.
The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.
Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes.
Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.
Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.
He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.

That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.
Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018.
He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".

A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/american-debt-delinq.headline: Americans' debt problems are flashing a warning not seen since the Great Recession
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/american-debt-delinq.author: Jeff Cox

paragraphs.text: The ability of U.S. families to stay current on their debts worsened over the past three years, hitting levels not seen since the aftermath of the global financial crisis, the Federal Reserve reported Friday.
In the central bank's Survey of Consumer Finances, researchers found that while wealth disparities narrowed somewhat, the ability to meet debt payments deteriorated significantly.

"Families were more likely to be behind on their financial obligations than at any point since the 2010 survey," stated the survey, a data-rich document the Fed releases every three years to chronicle the nation's financial health.

The country in 2010 was just emerging from what became known as the Great Recession, a period that ran from December 2007 to June 2009. A collapse in the subprime mortgage market resulted in contagion across the largest financial institutions in the U.S. and the world, sending unemployment at one point to 10%.

According to the new findings, the portion of families behind on loan payments at the end of 2025 soared from about 12% in the prior survey to nearly 20%, a gain of some 67%. Those behind by two months or more also accelerated considerably, moving to more than 8% from 5% in 2022.

While the report covered the period through 2025, Americans' concerns over their finances have persisted. A New York Fed survey released earlier this week showed that households reported their financial situations had worsened from a year ago and were likely to be weaker in the year ahead.

Friday's Fed report showed the share of debt to income also posted a large gain. Families with payment-to-income ratios of greater than 40% jumped to 8.6%, up from 6.5% in 2022 and the highest level since 2013.
At the same time, the net worth of higher earners soared, with those in the top income group seeing their median net worth rise 31%.
The report covers a period where the economy continued to grow but with inflation rates not seen since the early 1980s.
Amid that climate, the Fed found that real median, or midpoint, family income increased 7% but average income dropped 6%.

"Families in the lower ends of the income and net worth distributions saw modest increases in median and mean income, while families in the upper ends saw declines," the report stated. "These patterns indicate that income inequality decreased slightly between surveys."

The report noted that income gains were particularly strong with families aged 75 or older while tumbling 25% for those aged 35 to 44, which the Fed attributed to declines in capital gains income for that group.

"The exceptions to the general pattern of a rise in median income were for Black non-Hispanic families, Asian families, and families toward the top of the usual income and net worth distributions," the report stated. "For these families, both median and mean income fell."
Overall, net worth generally increased.

Inflation-adjusted average net worth rose 7% to $1.24 million, though median net worth climbed just 2% to $215,900, reflecting gains among those at the higher end. The report noted that net worth was "much slower" than the prior report that covered the 2019-22 period.

There were considerable disparities among education groups. Those with a college degree had 1.9 times the median income level than those with "some college" and nearly three times the median net worth. Lower-income families "saw some declines" in wealth while those with higher incomes saw gains. Families in the bottom one-fourth of income median net worth declined 6% while average net worth fell 4%.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-08/wh.headline: White House targets Stanford, Caltech and tech giants in visa crackdown
latimes.com/business/story/2026-10-08/wh.author: Nilesh Christopher, Jaweed Kaleem, Ana Ceballos

paragraphs.text: On Thursday, the Trump administration announced a probe into whether Stanford, Caltech, UC Davis and other universities across the country have been abusing a special visa used by international scholars and students to do research and work in the U.S. It is also suspending Microsoft, Adobe and six other tech companies from how they sponsor employees who are in the country under a highly skilled worker visa program.

The White House’s concern is that schools and companies are too quick to bring in people from outside the U.S. The moves rattled Silicon Valley executives and California educators who see easy access to the smartest, hardest-working people in the world as one of America’s greatest competitive advantages.

Vice President JD Vance said the universities being investigated are overusing J-1 visas to bring in students and researchers from abroad. The international scholars then take jobs and grants that could go to Americans.
“They are using these visas way too much,” he said. “They are using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”
Harvard, Yale, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, Arizona State and MIT will also be investigated.

Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas have been served and “nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building.” Many universities have buildings named for foreign donors.
While most of the companies targeted for the tech visa restriction were Indian, Vance called out Microsoft.
“There’s been no company, unfortunately, in the United States that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance told reporters at a White House news conference.
Vance said the company has abused the permanent labor certification program, which he argued has enabled Microsoft to hire international talent that is then paid less to replace American workers.
The new development suspends Microsoft from applying for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. on H-1B visas and later apply to become permanent residents.

American technology giants have relied on the H-1B visa program for decades to bring in thousands of skilled foreign workers they cannot find locally. Critics have accused the program of being riddled with fraud and abuse.

The administration’s power move came the same day President Trump awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to two prime examples of international talent who came to the U.S. on student and work visas: Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella and Tesla’s Elon Musk.

Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini were also on the list of companies that will no longer be able to apply for permanent residence status for their H-1B employees.

Microsoft defended the use of H-1B and said in a statement that it looked forward to sharing additional information with the administration. In a post, it said that of the thousands of H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.

“They equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said. “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category.”

There’s a limit of 85,000 H-1B visas issued in a fiscal year, and they are selected through a lottery system. Last year, Microsoft was the third-largest beneficiary of the program, with 6,258 H-1B visas, according to data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon led the list, employing more than 13,000 H-1 B visa holders; Adobe had 777 approved applications.

The Thursday announcement has sparked confusion among technology workers and companies. Immigration lawyers point out that the action is not a blanket suspension of green card applications for all employers, but a targeted enforcement freeze on the Permanent Labor Certification program for the eight named corporations.
Proponents of H-1B note that Silicon Valley’s biggest tech companies are founded or run by immigrants, and the efforts to thwart H-1B have already started stifling talent flow and startup creation.

“It’s only going to probably hurt some companies and hurt the best and the brightest that are coming here,” said Devashish Mitra, professor of economics at Syracuse University. “It’s like throwing the baby with the bathwater.”

The J-1 investigations follow other actions, making it more difficult for international students to come to U.S. campuses. This year, the Department of Homeland Security said it wanted to end a “duration of status” visa policy that lets students stay in the U.S. through the completion of their programs and limit stays to four years. A federal judge blocked the change, and the government is appealing.

The Trump administration has also proposed charging colleges $70,000 per student for Optional Practical Training, which lets international students work in their fields of study for a limited number of years after graduation. Students now pay about $500.
In a statement, a Stanford spokesperson said the campus “complies with all applicable visa laws, including those relating to J-1 visas. We will cooperate with the investigation.”
A UC Davis spokesperson said the university “carefully complies with all federal laws and regulations for visas and looks forward to working with our federal partners to confirm compliance.”
A Caltech spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

About 275,000 people started J-1 programs in 2025, down from 301,694 in 2024, according to State Department data. Trainees and temporary summer workers, such as au pairs and summer camp counselors, also use the visa to enter the U.S.
Most were not at universities, with a majority working summer jobs.
The Trump administration’s crackdown has started to dissuade students from coming to the U.S., with experts expecting a drop in their registration when data for 2025 are released next month.
New research scholars fell 27% from 2024 to 17,622, about half the 2015 total. Most new research scholars in 2025 came from China, followed by South Korea and India.
California drew the most research scholars, 3,211. It ranked second behind New York for all new J-1s in 2025, with 23,167.
The State Department vets applicants and approves sponsors. Research scholars can stay up to five years

Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, said she had found little information about what the new probes would cover. But she said the federal government already has tools “to identify fraud, both in the granting of the visa and then also tracking the person through the Department of Homeland Security.”

“I think that all of these things are focused on bringing fewer international students into the United States, and we have been seeing that impact,” she said, expecting “a huge drop in our international enrollment this year, given everything going on.”

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/ice-bronx-shooting-m.headline: ICE won't pause enforcement in NY after Bronx shooting, DHS' Mullin says
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/ice-bronx-shooting-m.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will not pause its activities in New York after ICE agents in the Bronx shot and wounded a man while he was in a car with a 5-year-old child, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday.

The shooting Thursday afternoon prompted furious rebukes of ICE from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who said she asked Mullin and President Donald Trump to immediately halt operations in her state.
"We're not putting a pause on enforcement," Mullin said at a news conference Friday morning, which was intended to push back on the growing criticism over the latest ICE shooting.

"I'm sorry, we're not," Mullin said. "In fact, I'm not sorry. Our job is to enforce the nation's laws and go after the worst of the worst, and our men and women do a dang good job at it every single day, and we will not stop doing our job."

A man identified as Oscar Belgal, 28, was shot in the neck after two plainclothes ICE officers approached his vehicle as it backed into a parking spot in the Marble Hill neighborhood, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference Thursday evening.
This is breaking news. Please check back for updates.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/nba-commissioner-ada.headline: NBA Commissioner Adam Silver says he still intends to get a deal done with EuroLeague as he plans launch of NBA Europe
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/nba-commissioner-ada.author: Alex Sherman

paragraphs.text: NBA Commissioner Adam Silver expressed confidence on Friday that he will get a deal done with EuroLeague to launch NBA Europe, a new European basketball league.
"We're going to get something worked out," Silver said in an exclusive CNBC interview. "It's like any negotiation – it's ongoing."
Silver spoke with CNBC's Contessa Brewer from Macao, China, where the NBA is playing two preseason games between the Dallas Mavericks and the Houston Rockets.

Earlier this week, EuroLeague basketball owners rejected a formal offer from the NBA to form a merged league that would become NBA Europe. EuroLeague has 13 shareholder clubs, including Barcelona, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, and Olympiakos, Milan.
Silver brushed off this week's rejection as a bump in the road.

"I think it's too extreme to say it's a rough patch," Silver said. "I mean, we've been going back and forth in EuroLeague. They're the existing pan-regional league right now in Europe. On top of that, there's leagues in every country. It's hard to believe there are 1,200 professional clubs in Europe. So EuroLeague is the top-tier competition right now. We're going forward with what we're what we're calling NBA Europe, and we're hoping we'll work something out with the EuroLeague. I think we will."

Silver confirmed the league has received bids for "many hundreds of millions of dollars" from existing European basketball clubs, "some of the big soccer brands in Europe," and wealthy individuals that are interested in buying the 12 new permanent NBA Europe teams coming to markets including London, Paris, Rome, Munich, Barcelona, Athens, Madrid and others.
"It's a sort of once and forever opportunity to be the NBA team in London, Paris, Madrid," Silver said.
The NBA continues to target an October 2027 launch date for NBA Europe.
WNBA to Macao

The NBA is also working on plans to send two WNBA teams to Macao as soon as next season, Silver confirmed. The two teams would play a preseason game or two, similar to how the NBA does it now, according to a person familiar with the matter.

"We are interested in having the women come here," Silver said. "I think I know there's many WNBA teams that would love to play internationally, and this is a beautiful arena. It's a great opportunity here, so we hope to make that happen."

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/china-europe-hybrid-.headline: China and Europe agree to cut Chinese hybrid vehicle exports by half
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/china-europe-hybrid-.author: Evelyn Cheng

paragraphs.text: BEIJING — European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday that China has agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc.
Europe has called on China to voluntarily reduce hybrid car exports into the continent, but authorities in Beijing had reportedly slapped down the request, according to the Financial Times.

The widening trade surplus between the EU and China has been a point of contention, with Germany and France previously having called on Brussels to develop a "last-resort" trade instrument to address imbalances.

Sefčovič said Friday that the final decision would still need Brussels' approval. Overall, he cast the two days of talks with China's Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing as a positive first step, following a summer of rising tensions between China and the EU.
China's Commerce Ministry on Friday released a list of 16 "'consensus outcomes."
They included licenses for rare earth and permanent magnet export licenses to the EU. Sefcovic did not elaborate on a timeline for the rare earth exports.
Earlier this year, on June 29 for the first meeting of the EU-China Trade and Investment Consultations.
The two sides agreed to next meet in March, with a video conference in January, according to the Chinese readout.

nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/trump-li.headline: Trump Announces White House Inquiry Into Fed Governor Lisa Cook

paragraphs.text: President Trump on Friday said the White House had formed a committee to investigate Lisa D. Cook, a Federal Reserve governor, and would hold a hearing to consider whether to fire her over unproven accusations that she committed mortgage fraud.

The “committee of inquiry” will look into claims that Ms. Cook made “false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments,” the White House said in a statement. The hearing, which called for Ms. Cook’s attendance, was scheduled for Nov. 5.

Mr. Trump asked the committee to report back on whether there were grounds for “Governor Cook’s removal” from office. While Ms. Cook was first accused by the White House of mortgage fraud more than a year ago, she has not been charged with any crime.
In a statement on Friday, lawyers for Ms. Cook said they had “grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law.”

“But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board,” the lawyers said, adding that they had been in touch with the White House to assess whether the process “has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise.”
They said Ms. Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”

Friday’s announcement marked the latest escalation in Mr. Trump’s efforts to fire Ms. Cook from the central bank, something a president can pursue legally only if there is “cause.” That has typically meant malfeasance or a dereliction of duty while on the job.

It came just four months after the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in favor of Ms. Cook remaining in the job, which she can technically hold until 2038. The justices argued that Ms. Cook had not been given adequate due process before Mr. Trump announced her removal in August 2025, but they left unresolved a number of key issues, including what constitutes “cause.”

Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly sought to pressure the Fed and its members into lowering interest rates, quickly billed the ruling as a procedural setback. That paved the way for further attacks. In August, the administration then restarted the process to try to fire her, claiming that Ms. Cook was “unfit for the office in which you serve as a controlling member of the Federal Reserve.”
At the heart of the matter are allegations that Ms. Cook misled lenders in order to obtain favorable terms on a mortgage.

In 2021, Ms. Cook purchased a condominium in Atlanta, and in at least one document, referred to it as a “primary” residence despite not living there. She also maintained another home in Ann Arbor, Mich., which was also treated as a “primary” residence.

In a formal rebuttal filed to the administration in August, Ms. Cook’s lawyers described the designation on the Atlanta condo as an “entirely inadvertent oversight,” not fraud. The letter also maintained that Ms. Cook had accurately identified it as a vacation home in other records. And, in the process, Ms. Cook’s lawyers argued that Mr. Trump and his other advisers had made similar mortgage errors, pointing to a series of news reports.

The White House’s statement, which was dated Oct. 7, stipulated that Ms. Cook would be “examined by the Committee, its representatives, and her legal counsel, if any.” It would provide the opportunity for her to present her argument and any supporting evidence, and left open the possibility that Department of Justice personnel may conduct questioning.

The committee that will hear Ms. Cook’s case is composed of Mr. Trump’s aides and appointees including Kevin Hassett, his top economic adviser; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics; and Andrea Lucas, the head of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Absent from the announced roster was Bill Pulte, the federal housing director, who has repeatedly attacked the Fed and originally investigated Ms. Cook over her mortgage activity. Mr. Pulte later referred his findings to the Justice Department.

Ms. Cook is not the only Fed official that Mr. Trump has targeted. The president repeatedly attacked Jerome H. Powell, whose term as chair of the central bank ended in May. At one point, the Justice Department pursued a criminal investigation into Mr. Powell and his handling of costly renovations at the Fed’s headquarters in Washington.

The probe was dropped after a number of legal setbacks and widespread opposition by Republican senators, one of whom blocked the advancement of Mr. Trump’s pick to become the next head of the Fed. Kevin M. Warsh eventually took over in May, but Mr. Powell, instead of departing as most chairs do, opted to stay on as a governor. That term does not end until January 2028.

The Fed’s internal watchdog late last month cleared Mr. Powell of any wrongdoing associated with the nearly $2.5 billion project, even as it concluded that the renovations were poorly managed and lacked sufficient budget constraints. Still, Mr. Trump has maintained that Mr. Powell should be “forced to resign” from the board in the wake of the inspector general’s findings.

nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/elon-mus.headline: Airlines Are Upgrading Wi-Fi. Not All Are Using Elon Musk’s Service.

paragraphs.text: Airplane Wi-Fi has long been slow and balky. But airlines are racing to change that.

Hoping that faster, more reliable internet access will help them attract and retain customers, many carriers are upgrading their planes to use Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. On Thursday, American Airlines said it would outfit more than 1,000 planes with Starlink.
But Delta Air Lines has chosen not to go with Starlink, which has upset Mr. Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.

Mr. Musk said last month that Delta’s chief executive would “lose his job” for choosing Amazon’s satellite service, and he earlier attacked the top executive of Ryanair, the European carrier, for snubbing Starlink, too. This week, he said Indian oligarchs were blocking Starlink there, which he called a “a crime against the people of India.”
From fee to free.
Lufthansa was the first commercial airline to offer in-flight internet access in 2004, using a service developed by Boeing. But Boeing shut down the project just two years later.

Other providers filled the void, and U.S. airlines started to offer Wi-Fi in the late 2000s. But few passengers used those services, which were often expensive, slow and unreliable. Over the years, the costs started to fall.
In 2023, Delta eliminated Wi-Fi fees for members of the company’s loyalty program. JetBlue Airways had been offering free internet access for years — but Delta kicked off an industry shift.
Why is Wi-Fi so important?

Many airlines offer free internet service to passengers who sign up for frequent flier programs. The programs allow the companies to collect more information about travelers and to encourage them to buy more tickets and sign up for credit cards.

At an industry conference last month, Robert Isom, the chief executive of American, said the airline was expanding its loyalty program at record rates. “A lot of that is driven by the free Wi-Fi,” he said.

Executives also say they are switching to Starlink because the earlier internet services they offered were subpar. This summer, executives at Alaska Airlines said customer satisfaction was about 20 percent higher on flights with Starlink.
But some industry experts say that most travelers pick airlines for many reasons and that Wi-Fi is not the most important one.

“People who are going to fly a lot in the future are going to self-select and gradually find the right program that fits best for them,” said Jay Sorensen, who runs IdeaWorksCompany, an aviation industry consulting firm. “You can’t really create that.”
That doesn’t mean Wi-Fi is irrelevant. Like soft drinks and snacks, internet access has become an expectation among passengers, Mr. Sorensen said.
Why is Mr. Musk feuding with Delta?
Most major U.S. airlines upgrading to high-speed Wi-Fi are going with Starlink, whose satellites orbit closer to Earth than older satellites.
American, Alaska, United and Southwest Airlines have selected Starlink. But Delta, the most profitable U.S. airline, and JetBlue have chosen Amazon Leo, a satellite service that is not yet available.

After Delta announced the partnership this year, Mr. Musk said the airline “wanted to make it painful, difficult and expensive for their customers.” Last week, he said Delta’s chief, Ed Bastian, had made an error that could cost him his position. Mr. Musk was responding to an unverified report that Mr. Bastian had said it was not wise to work with Mr. Musk.
In an interview with The New York Times, Mr. Bastian disputed that report.
“I wouldn’t say that in a public setting or a private setting,” he said. “What we said is that we’re not working with Starlink because we decided to go a different direction.”
On Friday, Delta reported $20.2 billion in revenue for the third quarter of the year, during the three months ending in September, a company record.
SpaceX and Amazon did not respond to requests for comment.

This isn’t the first time Mr. Musk has criticized executives, politicians and others he disagrees with. In addition to Mr. Bastian, his targets have included Jeff Bezos, the executive chair of Amazon, and the chief executive of Ryanair, Michael O’Leary.
Delta’s decision to use Leo could be risky. While other airlines have already begun offering Starlink service on some flights, Delta won’t begin installing Amazon’s service until 2028.

That doesn’t mean Delta isn’t making upgrades, Mr. Bastian said. One of the airline’s current internet providers, Viasat, recently launched two new satellites that will “change the game for our customers,” he said.

Mr. Bastian has said Delta chose Amazon because it will cost the airline less than Starlink and because the airline hopes to provide customers other perks from Amazon. Delta has been profitable in recent years partly because customers like its credit cards, lounges and partnerships with other companies. For example, Delta’s customers can earn miles by buying coffee at Starbucks and hailing rides on Uber.
“We’ll be working very closely with them to bring new experiences to customers,” he said of Amazon. “It’s not just about the Wi-Fi; it’s what you do with the Wi-Fi.”

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/iran-p.headline: Iran Protects Capacity to Build Missiles as Trump Pauses Strikes
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/iran-p.author: Gerry Doyle, Alberto Nardelli and Alex Wickham

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Iran has managed to preserve its missile and drone factories despite months of US and Israeli bombing, officials familiar with the matter said, allowing it to replenish its arsenals while President Donald Trump holds off on strikes ahead of the midterm elections.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Tehran still has the capacity to manufacture weapons to rebuild its arsenal, according to the Western officials, who asked not to be identified discussing private assessments. One official said Iran remains well-stocked with ballistic missiles and some anti-ship weapons, and can quickly add more.
The Western official said Russia was providing missiles as well, echoing a separate assessment in June. Russia's Ministry of Defense did not respond to a request for comment.

The assessment of Iran's capability runs counter to repeated claims from Trump and his team that eight months of airstrikes have decimated Iran's ability to threaten US bases in the region and American allies. Trump said earlier this year that Iran's military is "totally destroyed" and in a speech on Sept. 30 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the US had destroyed Iran's "military industrial capacity" and "their entire defense base."

That ability raises the likelihood that Iran could reconstitute its missile forces if Trump makes good on a vow, delivered via social media on Thursday, not to attack Iran before November's midterm elections. In addition, Tehran has escalated attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz, hitting at least 10 vessels in the last week, according to the UK Navy.
The White House and the Pentagon didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Trump had earlier floated the possibility of ramping up military strikes after the elections, amid a flurry of attacks on shipping. The later time frame would allow him to avoid further fanning oil prices just before the ballot.

Assessments from Western officials signal the Islamic Republic still has enough firepower to retaliate if Washington resumes airstrikes. With its economy withering behind a US Navy blockade of its oil exports and the war stuck in limbo, Tehran may lean deeper into asymmetric warfare, seeking to inflict as much pain as possible on its much bigger opponent.

The US-Israeli air campaign most likely severely degraded much of Iran's prewar missile manufacturing capacity over the long term, according to a report by Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who is a visiting research fellow at King's College London.

Israel estimated that Iran had about 2,500 ballistic missiles before the war, and it's not known exactly how many remain. Western intelligence assessments as recently as June said Iran held about three-quarters of the munitions it had before the war.

Iran has launched more than 4,000 Shahed propeller-driven cruise missiles, and at least 2,000 ballistic missiles since the conflict began on Feb. 28, according to a Bloomberg Economics analysis of public data.

The lull in major US attacks has given Iran time to recoup and rebuild as it prepares for a next round of fighting, which it knows is coming, said Becca Wasser, defense lead at Bloomberg Economics. The cycle seems likely to create a protracted conflict in which neither side has a clear advantage.

"There is probably less high-end stuff available, but they've been stockpiling cruise missiles for themselves and the Houthis for years, and hiding them," said William Alberque, a Europe-based senior fellow at the Pacific Forum. "I'd guess with a fair bit of confidence that we haven't seen the tip of the iceberg in terms of anti-ship attacks."

Oil prices, now trading above $100 a barrel, remain under pressure and sensitive to the outlook for supply. Even though transit through the Strait of Hormuz has increased, the cost of hiring a tanker rose to about $1.2 million a day, compared with less than $50,000 a day before the war.

And a conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militants is raising concerns over the kingdom's ability to rely on an export bypass through the Red Sea. On Thursday night, Houthi ballistic missiles struck two airports in Saudi Arabia, killing at least three people and wounding dozens.
The biggest challenge to attacking commercial vessels is most likely getting targeting data, said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute.

"The actual anti-ship missile stockpiles likely remain large, both because they are comparatively easy to make, and Iran has in-housed much of the production of older Chinese ASCMs, and Iran's southern mountains provide natural shelters against air attack," he said, referring to anti-ship cruise missiles.
