theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/flydub.headline: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/flydub.author: Jason Burke

paragraphs.text: The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.

Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.
Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.

The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.

“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree.
New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.

Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.

“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.
Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.
The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/batteries-are-.headline: Batteries are now cheaper than natural gas turbines used at many data centers
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/batteries-are-.author: Tim De Chant

paragraphs.text: Battery storage is now cheaper than a type of natural gas power plant favored by many data center developers, according to a new report from Wood Mackenzie.

On every continent and in each of the 43 markets that Wood Mackenzie surveyed, four-hour duration batteries were less expensive than open-cycle gas turbines. The consultancy predicts that the cost of electricity from batteries will continue to decline while electrons from gas turbines will only grow more expensive in the coming decades.

The report lands as energy prices in the U.S. and elsewhere continue to rise, fueling inflation as data centers push electricity demand to new heights. Prices for gas turbines have been driven up by AI data center developers, which have been buying any model they can get their hands on. The effects have been more acute for open-cycle gas turbines, which are more readily available but less efficient and more expensive to operate.

Those turbines are often used by utilities as peaking power plants, which step in to generate electricity in periods of high demand. As prices for those turbines rise, it can raise costs for utilities, too.

Open-cycle turbines are simpler to make than closed-cycle turbines, but even they now take two to four years to procure. Waitlists for closed-cycle turbines now extend into the early 2030s. Both backlogs have been spiking prices for all new natural gas power plants.
That’s not the case for every generating technology. Solar is now the cheapest form of new power in every market in Wood Mackenzie’s survey.

While solar remains cheapest even in North America, the situation remains complicated there. Solar prices are “under pressure” from tariffs and import restrictions, according to Wood Mackenzie, though utility-scale solar is expected to fare better. There, 168 gigawatts is largely protected from those near-term price shocks thanks to safe-harbor provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill, which kept tax credits for projects that have begun construction or are completed before the end of 2027.

The market for U.S. natural gas will narrow in the coming decade. In the Middle East and Africa, four-hour batteries will be 33% cheaper by 2035, “displacing gas peaking on cost across every gas market in the region.” In China, energy storage costs are 55% below its neighbors’.
“This economic shift is decisive and widening,” Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie, said in a press release.

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. nytimes.com/2026/10/09/world/africa/erik.headline: Inside Erik Prince’s Mercenary Deal in Congo

paragraphs.text: The hasty evacuation of a former Green Beret who was badly wounded during a firefight in the Democratic Republic of Congo last month has opened a window into the latest mercenary deployment by Erik Prince, the high-profile American military contractor.

The former Green Beret, Tim Kennedy, who is also known for his career in mixed martial arts and frequent appearances on Fox News, was shot several times during intense fighting in Congo’s eastern highlands, where government forces have been battling a powerful, Rwanda-backed rebel group.

An elite ex-soldier from New Zealand who previously served with his country’s Special Air Service unit was killed. Six people briefed on different aspects of the ambush and subsequent evacuation spoke to The New York Times on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the operation.

What brought both men to Congo was their employment by Mr. Prince, the founder of Blackwater Worldwide, a company notorious for a civilian massacre in Iraq in 2007. For years, Mr. Prince has sought opportunities in resource-rich countries plagued by conflict, mostly in Africa. Now his interests are expanding in Congo, where the government has hired foreign help to fend off the rebel advance in the east, while also trying to curry favor with the Trump administration.
To advance its goals, Kinshasa has turned to Mr. Prince, a prominent supporter of President Trump, giving him a central role in one of Africa’s most intractable conflicts.

Details of Mr. Prince’s operations in Congo were provided to The Times by a dozen current and former officials from the United States, Congo, Europe and other African countries, as well as U.N. officials, military contractors and some of Mr. Prince’s own employees. All spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss military casualties or confidential business arrangements.
Mr. Prince declined to comment for this article, as did a spokesman for Vectus Global, the company that leads his operations in Congo.

Mr. Prince’s growing influence in Congo comes as the Trump administration seeks a new toehold for American companies in the country’s lucrative mining industry, where China’s dominance over critical minerals like cobalt is a source of growing concern in Washington. Last December the United States and Congo signed an agreement granting preferential access to American mining interests in Congo, which many Congolese officials privately called a “peace for minerals” deal.

In late 2024, Mr. Prince signed a wide-ranging contract to provide security and mining services to President Félix Tshisekedi’s government. The contract was worth hundreds of millions of dollars over five years, although it is unclear how much has been paid out, said a former U.S. official who worked on regional diplomacy.

Since then, Mr. Prince has supplied drones and mercenaries to help Congo fight the M23, the rebel group backed by Rwanda, and has even moved into taxation. His company in Congo employs about 100 people in a drive to recoup some of the estimated $3 billion in taxes that Congo loses every year from fraud in the mining sector.

The tax effort is led by a former French Foreign Legion soldier who works from a gleaming new financial center in the capital, Kinshasa. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, an employee of Mr. Prince described plans to digitize mining records, tackle widespread fraud and curb what he called the “blatant looting” of Congolese resources by criminal syndicates that include Chinese mining companies.
Mr. Prince’s employee likened the anticorruption drive to that of Eliot Ness, the Prohibition-era law enforcement officer who aggressively went after the crime boss Al Capone’s bootlegging empire.

The employee said the tax effort is going well. But in the rugged highlands 1,000 miles to the east, where Congo’s war is being fought, Mr. Prince’s other mission has been stymied by setbacks and casualties — not for the first time, say his critics.

“Among mercenaries, especially in Africa, Prince is derided because he has zero successful missions,” said Sean McFate, a former private military contractor who is currently a fellow at The Atlantic Council.

For the past year, mercenaries employed by Mr. Prince have been based at an airfield in Kalemie, a town on the western shore of Lake Tanganyika in eastern Congo, several of the current and former officials said. Drone pilots from Colombia and Ukraine, contracted by Mr. Prince, carried out strikes against the M23, the most powerful of more than 100 armed groups operating in Congo. Last January, Mr. Prince’s forces helped the Congolese recapture the key city of Uvira.

But as fighting intensified recently in the nearby Minembwe Highlands, where remote villages nestle amid steep slopes, Mr. Prince’s employees were drawn into a vicious fight. One battle early last month led to the deaths of several Colombian contractors, according to a person briefed on the incident and a report seen by The Times.
Then on Sept. 17, a second group of mercenaries accompanying Congolese soldiers, this time including Mr. Kennedy, was caught in the deadly ambush.

What exactly happened is unclear. One person close to Mr. Prince, briefed on the incident, would only say that it was a “long ordeal,” which was exacerbated by a lack of support from Congolese forces.

When it was over, Mr. Kennedy had been shot multiple times and several others were dead, including Justin Conaglen, a former special operations soldier from New Zealand. Asked about Mr. Conaglen’s death, a spokesman for New Zealand’s foreign ministry said it was “providing support in this case” but declined to provide further information.

After the ambush, Mr. Prince’s officials began to search for air transport options to evacuate the dead and wounded, the people briefed on the incident said. Mr. Kennedy was rushed to Burundi and then South Africa for treatment at the private Milpark hospital in Johannesburg.

Mr. Kennedy has since been flown back to the United States, where he is recovering at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, a flagship facility that primarily treats active-duty troops, friends and officials said.
The Pentagon declined to comment, and Mr. Kennedy did not respond to questions.

Known for his dual career in the military and professional sports, Mr. Kennedy served as a Green Beret and competed in the Ultimate Fighting Championship until he retired from professional fighting in 2017. He has hosted shows for the History and Discovery channels, published an autobiography, “Scars and Stripes,” and has drawn criticism for making provocative statements about the nature of war on podcasts and TV.

Accusations last year that Mr. Kennedy had exaggerated his military awards prompted the Maryland National Guard to investigate. He publicly apologized for having “unintentionally misstated aspects of my military service.”
Mr. Conaglen took unpaid leave from the New Zealand military in March, before formally leaving the service in August, a spokesman for his country’s military said in an email.

Originally from New Zealand’s North Island, he competed in endurance sports and high-altitude mountaineering, and was part-owner of a holiday rental business in Raglan, a surfing town known for its black-sand beaches.
His remains were returned to New Zealand, where they were cremated on Oct. 1 after a memorial at a rugby club in the small town of Taipa.

Western mercenaries have long been a sensitive subject in Congo, where hundreds of European fighters joined an effort by the Katanga region to secede in the 1960s. Many Congolese also remember the C.I.A.’s role in the overthrow of their country’s first prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, who was later executed by a firing squad led by Belgian contract officers.

But Mr. Tshisekedi put aside those misgivings as the M23 began to resurge across eastern Congo in 2023. As Congo’s notoriously weak national army struggled to respond, he outsourced crucial parts of the fight to foreigners.

Romanians were tasked with defending Goma, the region’s biggest city, until they were routed in January 2025. Algerian drone pilots flew Chinese drones from Kisangani until their base was hit by a suspected Rwandan drone strike in May, current and former officials in the region said.
Those losses have left Mr. Prince as the pre-eminent military contractor in Congo — one who has embraced the language of colonialism.
In a podcast interview in 2024, he called on the United States to “put the imperial hat back on” in African countries that he said were “incapable of governing themselves.”
Asked if he was promoting a new form of colonialism, Mr. Prince replied, “Absolutely, yes.”

In interviews, Mr. Prince often plays up his tough-guy image, presenting himself as a hard-nosed pragmatist who is willing to harness the power of private military action. But in Africa, his ventures have often gone wrong.

In Libya, his mercenaries had to flee on a speedboat in 2019 after a dispute with the warlord who hired them. In Somalia, U.N. investigators accused his forces of violating an international arms embargo on Somalia in 2012.

In Congo, some fear more of the same chaos. Hiring Mr. Prince is a sign of the government’s desperation against the M23, but “it’s creating more problems than solutions,” said Zobel Behalal, author of a recent report on mercenaries in Congo. “It’s a sign that the army is very weak. And while others are making money, in the end it’s the population that suffers.”

Last month, Mr. Prince spent time promoting his new company, Vectus Air Defense Systems, which sells an anti-drone system that he says can protect oil fields, data centers and other sensitive sites. He also began negotiating with Congolese officials over a possible $200 million contract to protect the country’s air force assets, an adviser to the Congolese president said.

American officials say that Mr. Prince’s ventures in countries like Congo are entirely private and that he enjoys no U.S. government support. Still, Mr. Prince, who once donated $250,000 to a Trump campaign, uses his political connections to support his military operations. Mr. Prince’s sister, Betsy DeVos, also served as secretary of education during Mr. Trump’s first term.

Last January Mr. Prince traveled to Belgium for a meeting at the residence of the U.S. ambassador Bill White. In the meeting, Mr. Prince outlined his views on Congo to Belgium’s top Africa diplomat, Marc Pecsteen de Buytswerve, according to two European officials.
Then Mr. Prince asked for help.

His drones had been impounded at customs in the Netherlands and he needed to get them out. He also asked if Belgium would authorize the export of guns and ammunition from a Belgian manufacturer to Congo.

The State Department and Belgian foreign ministry declined to comment on the meeting, which State described as a “private diplomatic engagement.” But the answer to both of Mr. Prince’s requests, the officials said, was “No.”
Reporting was contributed by Eric Schmitt in Washington, Emanuel Stoakes in Christchurch, New Zealand, and John Eligon in Johannesburg.

washingtonpost.com/education/2026/10/09/.headline: Judge seals documents in Cornell case, citing doxing of unrelated people
washingtonpost.com/education/2026/10/09/.author: Todd Wallack

paragraphs.text: A New York judge on Friday sealed several of the documents in the case brought by a woman who said she was gang-raped at a fraternity house at Cornell University two years ago, citing the doxing of a U.S. Marine and his family.

Judge Phaedra F. Perry-Bond in New York’s Supreme Court in New York County said the address of a Marine who shares the same name as one of the defendants in the suit was mistakenly listed in the case files. While the woman’s lawyer has since filed a list of defendants with corrected addresses, the original filing with the mistaken address remained part of the public online court file.

“Certain ‘vigilantes’ have used an erroneous address to inundate a former Marine and his family with threats, simply because of a name shared with a defendant in the case,” Perry-Bond wrote in her ruling on Friday. “That behavior must cease immediately, is completely unacceptable, and provides more than ample cause to seal certain documents on this court’s docket.”

The sealed documents include the initial complaint brought by the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, who was 20 years old in 2024 when she alleges seven men sexually assaulted her. The judge asked Doe’s lawyer to refile redacted versions of the documents without the addresses to help deter doxing — the act of publishing someone’s personal information to harass or hurt them.
The judge said the court is mindful that the information is “highly likely” to already be on the internet elsewhere, but said the court must do its part to reduce any harm.

John Manly, an attorney representing the Marine’s sister and parents, told The Post Thursday that both the 23-year-old Marine and his family have received threats, even though the man was in the Marine Corps in 2024 when the incident allegedly happened at Cornell.
He said the family wanted the address removed from the court documents, but is also considering legal action against people who threaten and harass them, including seeking criminal charges.
“If you are sending threatening messages, we will find you and go after you,” Manly said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/09/science/nikon-mic.headline: Big Controversy Upends a Contest About Microscopic Videos

paragraphs.text: After weeks of controversy, Nikon announced on Friday that it had rescinded the first-place award it gave in its annual Small World in Motion contest after determining the winning video broke its rule against generative artificial intelligence use in submissions.

The Nikon Small World in Motion is an annual video contest that awards the best footage captured through the lens of a microscope. The competition began in 1975, originally accepting only photo submissions, and a separate contest was created for videos in 2011.

“After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative A.I.,” the company wrote in a statement posted on its website.
The New York Times was one of many media organizations that featured the winning video, among others, in its coverage of the competition’s results, which were announced on Sept. 16.
The competition’s rules and guidelines explicitly state that “A.I. generated videos are not permitted and Sponsor holds the right to request the original video for verification.”

“This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition,” Nikon’s statement said. “It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent.”
The competition rankings have been updated on the Nikon website, making Nguyen Nam Nhat, a microbiologist based in Vietnam, the new first-place winner.

The original winner, Ning Xu, an optical engineer at the National University of Singapore, submitted a video that purported to show the cilia of a child with primary ciliary dyskinesia, a respiratory disorder. Cilia are microscopic, hairlike structures that sweep mucus out of airways like the lungs, nostril and throat. Dr. Xu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dr. Xu previously claimed that his use of A.I. fell within the regulations of the contest, which allow for “enhancement of microscopy-generated source data, not for image generation from scratch,” Nikon wrote in an email to The Times before the prize was rescinded.
Doubts and concerns surrounding the video started simmering on the social media platform Bluesky after one poster questioned if the video was real.

“What in the world am I looking at here? @Nikon?” the post read. Dozens of replies, many of them from biologists themselves, expressed doubt that the video didn’t contain A.I.-generated components, if not completely fabricated by A.I.
Commenters shared concerns that the microscopy shown wasn’t physically plausible, pointing out inconsistencies with the sizing of the cilia.

In the weeks leading up to the disqualification, an increasingly vociferous campaign arose against Dr. Xu’s video. More than 100 comments accumulated under a LinkedIn post from Nikon announcing the winner, many of them questioning the authenticity of the video and demanding explanations from Nikon.
Scientists pointed out that organelles like the nuclei and mitochondria of the cell disappeared and reappeared randomly, which could be a telltale sign of A.I. use.

A.I. use in scientific imaging is not new, said Aydogan Ozcan, an expert in computational imaging and microscopy at the University of California, Los Angeles. “It helps scientists, including in my own lab, to improve the resolution and contrast of microscopic images,” he said. “But the rule is very simple: You need to disclose it.”
Problems can also arise when A.I. hallucinates structures that aren’t actually there.
While the controversy is upsetting to some, Dr. Ozcan says that this could be an opportunity for scientists and the public alike to standardize ethical A.I. use in scientific imaging.
“I consider this a wonderful way to bring people together and discuss this openly,” he said. “It’s great education.”

npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-5994972/margare.headline: Margaret Hamilton, whose software sent humans to the moon, dies at 90
npr.org/2026/10/08/nx-s1-5994972/margare.author: Rachel Treisman

paragraphs.text: Margaret Hamilton, the computing pioneer whose software put the first NASA astronauts on the moon, has died at age 90.
Hamilton's death — of unspecified causes, on Sept. 30 — was announced Wednesday by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she worked from 1959 until the mid-1970s.

"To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement," said Olivier de Weck, interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. "She not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved."

Hamilton, who grew up in Indiana, earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy from Earlham College in 1958. She moved to Boston the following year — so her husband could pursue his law degree — and took a job in the meteorology department at MIT, working with the professor who discovered chaos theory.

It was her first foray into software engineering. Hamilton then got a programming job in another lab, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system.

"She had so much foresight in thinking through the ways that humans would use computers, and to create reliable systems that could be used even in the highest-risk, life and death kind of environments," said Teasel Muir-Harmony, curator of the Apollo Collection at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.

In 1961, MIT's Instrumentation Lab won the NASA contract to develop software for the Apollo project. Hamilton saw a newspaper advertisement seeking people to develop the software to "send man to the moon," and applied. She was the first female programmer hired for the Apollo missions, starting with uncrewed flights and moving to onboard software.

By 1968, she had worked her way up to assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, leading a crew of over 100 engineers. Hamilton was in her early 30s, as were many of her colleagues in the nascent field of software engineering — a term she herself is credited with coining.

"In this period where she was working, this is a brand new field, and she really helped to define it," Muir-Harmony said. "Margaret Hamilton, like many of the people who worked on the Apollo program, helped really develop computing as we know it today."
Hamilton made an impression with her problem-solving and leadership skills. She often brought her daughter, Lauren, then 4, to the lab — resulting in an infamous "Lauren error."

"Her daughter overloaded a system during some kind of a test. And she thought, 'Oh my gosh, this is something that could actually happen in outer space. So I better account for this,'" said Dean Robbins, an author who published a book about Hamilton in 2017. "So her daughter actually played a part in her technical achievements."
Hamilton was known for her focus on "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate and solve errors on its own.
"Her goal wasn't simply to build a system that worked when everything went right," Muir-Harmony said. "It was to build a system that could continue working when things went wrong."

Perhaps the most famous example of that is the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. Just three minutes before the first humans were supposed to touch down on the moon, alarms went off on board, signifying computer overload. Fortunately, Hamilton's team had built a system that could shut down unnecessary background tasks at that moment.

"Mission Control was able to recognize what was happening, able to trust the computer … to prioritize tasks, to know that the astronauts could continue … with the first lunar landing," Muir-Harmony said.

After leaving MIT, Hamilton founded two software engineering companies. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Barack Obama in 2016, and the following year was immortalized in miniature as part of a "women of NASA" Lego set.

Hamilton is also the subject of a black-and-white photo from 1969 that often makes the rounds on social media, showing a young woman with long hair and glasses, smiling as she stands beside a towering stack of notebooks — filled with the code that sent humans to the moon.

But despite public recognition in her later years, Robbins said Hamilton was "not one to toot her own horn." In fact, she initially shied away from the idea of a biography and only agreed because she thought it would be fun to read with her great-grandchildren. (She is survived by four great-grandchildren, two grandsons, her daughter and son-in-law and three siblings.)

"She really warmed up to explaining what she had done, developing the software," he recalled. "She got very excited about telling me all about the technical aspects of developing this. And she was sending me photos and actual code that she had written, and pictures of the primitive machinery that they'd had to use back in the 1960s."

The entire process was painstaking. Muir-Harmony explained that programs were stored on the Apollo guidance computer by hand-weaving copper wire through magnetized cores ("which basically looked like little donuts"). As the overseer of that process, Hamilton earned the nickname "rope mother" in the lab.
Robbins struggled to simplify all of that for his grade-school audience, until he realized: Hamilton's story was all about problem-solving. And she broke barriers for women in the process.

"There was no playbook for how to use computers to get astronauts to the moon," he said. "She had to come up with it on the fly and under tremendous pressure. And I think she was proud of that in her own modest way."
Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 that from her perspective, the software experience was "at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission."
"Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world," she said. "There was no choice but to be pioneers."

wsj.com/business/energy-oil/oil-prices-r.headline: Oil Prices Steady After Trump Appears to Rule Out Iran Strikes Before Midterms — 2nd Update

paragraphs.text: Oil prices recovered from early losses and settled slightly higher Friday as traders weighed President Trump's pledge not to attack Iran before the U.S. midterm elections against persistent shipping risks in the Persian Gulf and extensive offshore production shut-ins in the Gulf of Mexico.
December Brent crude futures edged up 0.4%, to $104.72 a barrel, for a 2.4% weekly gain. West Texas Intermediate crude for November delivery rose 0.4%, to $91.85 a barrel, up 0.8% on the week.

Trump said Thursday that the U.S. wouldn't attack Iran before the November midterm elections, citing what he called "productive discussions" with Tehran. The U.S. naval blockade of Iran remains in place, with roughly a dozen Navy ships in the region, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Oil prices are likely to remain elevated in the short term as risks to Middle East shipping routes persist and U.S. offshore production remains disrupted, said Hani Abuagla, a senior market analyst at XTB MENA.
Analysts at MUFG said geopolitical risks remain high amid fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, while shipping through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to face threats.

Brent's spread between the first two futures months remains in backwardation at around $3 a barrel, indicating continued tightness in the near-term market, they said. Backwardation is when near-term oil futures trade at a premium to contracts for later delivery, typically indicating tighter supplies in the immediate market.

Goldman Sachs estimated that Brent's geopolitical risk premium reached $22 a barrel in September, the second-highest monthly level on record and above the peak of $16 during the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022. The bank also estimated that a 100 million-barrel decline in commercial inventories across OECD countries raised Brent's fair value by nearly $8 a barrel.

Tensions elsewhere in the region also remain high. Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen carried out another series of attacks Wednesday night and Thursday, including strikes targeting shipping in the Persian Gulf and Saudi Arabia, the Journal reported.

The U.S. also increased economic pressure on Tehran on Thursday. The Treasury Department sanctioned 17 vessels it said were part of Iran's remaining shadow fleet and had transported millions of barrels of Iranian crude, petroleum and petrochemical products to markets in South and East Asia.

Meanwhile, Hurricane Isaias increased disruptions to U.S. Gulf production. The storm reached Category 3 with winds of 120 mph as it approached the U.S. coast, and was expected to make landfall in Alabama "at or near major hurricane strength" Friday evening, according to the National Hurricane Center.

The Marine Minerals Administration said nearly 1.5 million barrels a day of oil and 1.3 billion cubic feet a day of natural gas had been shut in as of midday Friday, equivalent to 71.5% of current Gulf oil output and 58.8% of natural gas output.

The threat to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries has narrowed despite the offshore shutdowns. Less than 500,000 barrels a day of refining capacity in Alabama and Mississippi were at risk of a direct hit, down from 2.5 million barrels a day expected earlier in the week, S&P Global Energy said. Port closures and shipping delays could still disrupt refined-product exports, with U.S. Gulf Coast diesel exports averaging 1.4 million barrels a day so far this week, down from 2.1 million barrels a day the previous week, S&P said.
U.S. refineries appeared to have dodged a threat from the storm, Robert Yawger, a commodity specialist at Mizuho Securities USA, said in a note.

With production at record levels near 14 million barrels a day, "the U.S. can afford to take a few barrels of offshore production offline," he said. "But it can't afford to lose refining capacity with winter heating oil season on the horizon and distillate storage testing many-year lows."

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-09/.headline: Newport Beach, other coastal spots hit by flooding prepare for more damage
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-09/.author: Hannah Fry

paragraphs.text: Newport Beach expected intense surf Friday, but the high tide turned out to be much worse than the estimates.

Water from a massive swell — double the size that was initially predicted — blasted through 20-foot berms erected at the Wedge and washed out roads from about 21st Street to 6th Street, officials said. City crews responded quickly to pump out water as residents surveyed the damage.
“This is the worst I’ve seen it in my 20 years on the Peninsula,” said Newport Beach City Councilman Joe Stapleton.
The city was one of several coastal communities to see flooding Friday as residents braced for Tropical Storm Rachel, which is expected to cause more issues over the weekend.
• Flooding: No injuries were reported, but some houses were damaged in Long Beach and Newport Beach, where several streets flooded.

• Forecast: Rachel’s arrival will bring the potential for strong winds, rain and more damaging coastal flooding. If the current storm trajectory holds, the bulk of Rachel’s effects will be felt in San Diego County on Sunday morning. However, Orange and Los Angeles counties are still forecast to see widespread rain and coastal flooding as a result of the system, according to the National Weather Service. For more on the timeline, click here.

• Exceptionally high tides: At around 9 a.m. Friday, the high tide in San Diego and La Jolla was 17 inches higher than the official prediction, which doesn’t account for hotter-than-normal ocean waters or swells from tropical storms, according to forecasts from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Tides were coming in 16 inches higher than the official prediction in Santa Monica and 14 inches higher in San Francisco as of Friday morning.
Here is a round up along the coast:
Newport Beach

Streets on the Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach were flooded with at least a foot of water during high tides, with the police department advising residents and motorists to avoid the area. The flooding was remarkable even in a neighborhood that has been prone to regular inundations in the past, particularly during El Niño.
Officials are still trying to determine how many homes were damaged.

“This swell was very unprecedented coming up that high,” Georgia Rios, a spokesperson for the city of Newport Beach, told The Times. “We knew we were going to have a high swell due to Tropical Storm Rachel, but along with El Niño it really has been a combination force here in Newport.”

The city declared a local emergency on Friday and urged residents to pick up sandbags to protect their homes over the weekend. City crews are pumping out water on the streets, rebuilding beach berms and opening tide valves to help mitigate water intrusion.
“This is not even the worst that is expected,” Rios said. “It’s forecast to get even worse on Sunday with rain.”

Newport Beach Utilities Director Mark Vukojevic told ABC7 that the morning tide came in 20 inches higher than what had been predicted. “It’s significant. We’ve seen it be 12 inches higher, but this is, you know, kind of record-breaking for us,” he told the outlet.
Laguna Beach

The intersection of Coast Highway and Broadway was inundated with water from big waves and high tides. The typically sandy sections of Main Beach — where locals often gather to walk along the sand and play beach volleyball — were transformed into a sea of water.
Huntington Beach
High surf battered parts of Huntington Beach, resulting in localized flooding on streets in the Sunset Beach area. That stretch is prone to flooding during high tides and storm surges.
There were no reports of any property damage.
City officials said they have activated the Emergency Operations Center in preparation for the weekend and are making sand and sandbags available to residents.
Long Beach

Powerful waves crumbled large sections of the boardwalk on the Long Beach Peninsula and left several homes with severe structural damage. Video showed waves slamming against the bulkhead that protects beachfront homes.
The city has already been besieged by an unusually active, El Niño-fueled hurricane season, taking damage from Hurricane Marie over Labor Day weekend and Hurricane Polo last month.
“We’ve had three storms back pretty much back to back to back,” said Laath Martin, a spokesperson for the city. “This is definitely not something that we see very often.”
Officials have red-tagged two properties, including a duplex with three units. Three buildings have also been yellow-tagged ahead of Rachel’s arrival after sustaining damage from Hurricane Marie.
Long Beach has already distributed more than 7,500 sandbags as residents prepare for what could be a very trying weekend.
“It’s hard to predict exactly what will happen, but just based on forecasts, we’re preparing for more damage,” Martin said.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/09/u.headline: UAW leader reviled by Trump declares victory in reelection
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/09/u.author: Lauren Kaori Gurley

paragraphs.text: United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain, an adversary of President Donald Trump, said he won in his reelection bid Friday, notching him another four-year term leading one of the country’s most powerful unions, which plays a critical role in Michigan politics.

The official results of the election are still unavailable, but an unofficial tally posted on Fain’s campaign website showed Fain sailing to victory with about 68 percent of the vote, to his top challenger Rich Boyer’s 13 percent.
“The membership has spoken,” Fain said in a written statement. “These results are about taking on Corporate America and reversing the worst out of control wealth inequality in America’s history.”

The UAW, a major force for the Democratic Party in Michigan, has been a target of Trump as the union’s political influence has grown in national politics under Fain’s leadership. Fain has been approached about running for president in 2028, Politico reported in August.

Fain, a former rank-and-file electrician, catapulted to the top of the union as an outsider in 2023, following a corruption scandal that resulted in the convictions of more than a dozen UAW officials and the appointment of a third-party monitor to conduct oversight of the union.

Under Fain’s leadership, the union made big strides: negotiating hefty pay increases for workers at the Big 3 automakers after a historic strike and expanding membership into new worksites across the country. But he has also faced challenges as the union remains under the watch of a monitor. The Justice Department launched a federal investigation this summer into accusations stemming from the monitor that Fain had abused his power to seek special benefits for his fiancée and her sister.
Fain has denied the allegations and said that he believes accusations stemming from the court monitor are part of a politically motivated attack related to the UAW’s support for a ceasefire in Gaza.

For years, Fain and Trump have exchanged harsh words. At the Republican National Convention in 2024, Trump called for Fain’s firing. He has also called him “a stupid person” and told Michigan voters that Fain “sold you out.” Fain donned a shirt during his prime-time address at the Democratic National Convention in 2024 that read: “Trump is a scab,” referring to someone who crosses a picket line.
This summer, at a rally at General Motors facility in Michigan, Trump called Fain “bad news,” in a nod to union’s endorsement of Biden and later Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
“He thought that Biden or Kamala would be wonderful,” Trump said. “You wouldn’t have an auto industry right now if they got elected.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/09/technology/anthro.headline: Anthropic Says Its A.I. Agents Attempted to Access a Range of Government Sites

paragraphs.text: Anthropic said on Friday that its artificial intelligence agents, acting on their own, attempted to gain access to several federal, state and local government websites. The company did not name the agencies, but said it had briefed the White House on the incidents.

The San Francisco company said in a blog post that an A.I. model it was testing took several unauthorized actions, including using a flaw in a university website to download data and sending a form to a government agency that it was told not to submit.

Anthropic said it discovered the incidents after beginning a review of actions taken by its A.I. in July. At the time, OpenAI had disclosed that its technology attacked an A.I. start-up, Hugging Face, and Anthropic and other labs had discovered that their technology had escaped from testing environments and conducted hacks.
A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment beyond the company’s blog post.

The Philadelphia Police Department said earlier on Friday that it had been notified by Anthropic that its technology had submitted a false homicide tip to the agency’s website. The tip was dated July 18 and claimed that the submitter had information about an unsolved case, the department said.
The tip was flagged as spam and never investigated, the department said, but Anthropic notified the police this week about the incident and said that the company would publicly disclose it on Friday.

“An unreleased, non-frontier research model was meant to fill out a practice copy of a government form,” Anthropic said in its blog post. “When the copy failed to load or the model closed it by mistake, the model instead navigated to the website where the real form is normally hosted and submitted the form there.”
(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trum.headline: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trum.author: Robert Tait

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.

In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.
“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”

He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”

Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exception to its provisions.
But the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to an “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal” which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other.” he said.

Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone component and ammunition.

techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthropic-cant.headline: Anthropic can’t reliably control its AI agents. It’s cutting off its internal evals from the live internet instead
techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthropic-cant.author: Tim Fernholz

paragraphs.text: Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.

The incidents, disclosed in a blog post, involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, avoided paywalls and anti-bot restrictions, used URL shortening services to smuggle information pass restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police.
Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, underscoring the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior.

Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools.

The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government.

Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before.
However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents.

It’s not clear what that means, but Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers to use, and for the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access.
“You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.”

Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.”

The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations.

Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents.

cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-putin-diesel-r.headline: Trump's diesel agreement with Putin accused of contradicting Russia sanctions law
cnbc.com/2026/10/09/trump-putin-diesel-r.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump's Friday announcement that Russia will supply diesel fuel to the global market marked an apparent pivot from recent efforts to pressure Moscow to end the Ukraine war by targeting Russian energy exports.
Trump claimed the move, unveiled with less than a month left in an affordability-focused midterm election, would swiftly bring down record-high diesel prices.
But commentators and critics were quick to highlight contradictions between the new policy and prior efforts by the U.S. to clamp down on Russian oil sales.

Those efforts most recently included the enactment of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, empowering Trump to impose tariffs up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas, among other restrictions. Trump signed the bill into law just three weeks ago.

"Congress just passed a law giving Trump the power to impose new tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil & gas," Scott Lincicome, vice president of the libertarian Cato Institute, said on X after Trump's Friday announcement.
"Can America tariff America?" he quipped.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, accused Trump's latest move of being "directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill."

Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown University Law Center's Institute of International Economic Law, in an X post said that the relaxation of Russian diesel restrictions "pretty much proves the point that the Graham Russia Bill was not going to force the Trump Administration to increase economic pressure on Moscow."
Some of the criticism crossed party lines.

"Through the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, we gave the president significant authorities and leverage against China and Russia to bring Putin's war to an end with a negotiated settlement," Rep. Michael McFaul, R-Texas, said in an X post. "Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," McFaul said.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's questions about the diesel agreement with Russia.

Less than a year earlier, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on multiple Russian oil companies in response to what it called "Russia's lack of serious commitment to a peace process to end the war in Ukraine."

Trump also had previously slammed NATO allies for continuing to buy Russian oil. In a September 2025 Truth Social post, he wrote, "the purchase of Russian Oil, by some, has been shocking! It greatly weakens your negotiating position, and bargaining power, over Russia."
Later that month, Trump again harangued world leaders for doing business with Russia.

"They're funding the war against themselves. Who the hell ever heard of that one?" he said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. "They can't be doing what they're doing. They're buying oil and gas from Russia while they're fighting Russia."
Trump announced the diesel deal in a Truth Social post Friday afternoon after what he described as a "highly successful discussion" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Under the agreement, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then another 500,000 tons in November, followed by 1 million tons "immediately thereafter" and 3 million more depending on refinery conditions, Trump wrote.

The Treasury Department soon after said that Trump directed the Office of Foreign Assets Control to immediately issue a "temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market." OFAC specified that the sanctioned transactions will be authorized for about six months, until April 7.

Russia seemed to celebrate the move. "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world," an X account associated with Putin's economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev said in response to the announcement.

But Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whose military has started targeting Russian oil refineries, said in a searing statement that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said. "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
"We count on America's fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia," he said.
"A strong one, not a weak one," he added.
Trump thanked Putin later Friday afternoon for enabling "massive amounts of oil" to come to the U.S.
"We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it," Trump told reporters before heading to Syracuse, New York.
The Trump administration has previously eased some Russian energy sanctions temporarily, though more narrowly than Friday's announcement.

Earlier this year, in an attempt to stabilize markets after the start of the Iran war, the Trump administration issued limited, 30-day waivers allowing countries to buy sanctioned Russian oil that was already in transit.
But some interpreted the latest move as a more significant step.
"It looks like Trump cut a deal with the devil," Jeremy Siegel, professor emeritus of finance at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC's "Closing Bell" Friday afternoon.

"It's not a permanent solution at all. It's sort of a short-term Band Aid," Siegel said. "And cutting back on or eliminating sanctions on Russia for the invasion in Ukraine, I think, is a very unfortunate consequence."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5nlqnn184o.headline: France's school protests are about more than broken classrooms
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crq5nlqnn184o.author: Nick Beake

paragraphs.text: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
Europe correspondent
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.

Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.

The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.

But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.

Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.

"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.

But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.

Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.

He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.
"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.
Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.
She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.
The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.
The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.

This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.
Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.
And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.
What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.

The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.
Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.
She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.
For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.
But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.
"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.
"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."
As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.
But not for long.
A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.
"The canteen is still open."
The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.
Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5lye9z4xw4yo.headline: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5lye9z4xw4yo.author: Anthony Zurcher

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.
It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.
It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.
The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.
Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

paragraphs.text: What to know about the Iran war today:

• Three Saudi citizens were killed Thursday in an attack by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Riyadh's main airport. Fighting between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen has escalated this week in what appears to be the new epicenter of the wider war in the Middle East.

• Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Tehran had revised its proposals to initiate peace talks with the U.S. and stood ready to finalize them through mediators. President Trump rejected a "7-day plan" offered by Iran in late September to get both sides back around the negotiating table.

• The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, eased Friday to around $103 a barrel after Mr. Trump promised the U.S. would not resume attacks on Iran before the U.S. midterm elections early next month. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he offered no specifics.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed more than 100 Houthi targets
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Saturday it destroyed more than 100 military targets in a "large-scale operation" against the Iran-backed group.
"We are carrying out a large-scale operation targeting the personnel and capabilities of the Houthi terrorist militia," Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi coalition, wrote on X.
"We destroyed 136 military targets in areas controlled by the Houthi terrorist militia," he said in a separate post.
The Houthi's Almasirah TV channel reported that Saudi missiles targeted areas in the northwestern Yemeni governorate of Saada.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government — which Saudi Arabia supports — reignited in July, and has since spilled over into the neighboring kingdom.

In addition to seizing territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have attacked transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter with drones and missiles.

Trump says Russia will release millions of tons of diesel
President Trump said Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.

In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
Mr. Trump had earlier Friday teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks at a Columbus Day celebration.
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.

Trump teases "big announcement" on diesel fuel

President Trump teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."

"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "It's gonna — we're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."

Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

Sri Lanka has no plans to help 19 Iranian tankers stuck due to blockade, foreign ministry says
Sri Lanka's government says it has no immediate plans to help 19 Iranian ships that have been anchored in the international waters near the island nation facing food, water and fuel shortages.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States.
He said, however, there hasn't been any communication from the U.S. warning of repercussions should Sri Lanka decide to help.
Rodrigo said the ships are stationed 24 nautical miles from Sri Lanka's coast and have reported shortages of food, water and fuel.

Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told local Sunday Times newspaper the ships are Iranian oil tankers and they have been anchored off Sri Lanka for the past several months after the U.S. resumed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving dozens of Iranian vessels stranded and unable to return home.
