President Donald Trump dodged the question of whether he'd tune in himself - but confirmed he approved the decision to livestream Hasan's death.
"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5ynwnye009o.headline: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj5ynwnye009o.author: Will Grant

paragraphs.text: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.

The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison.
Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".
During the trial in the northern Baja California state, the court heard that the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area.
Their bodies were later found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.
Debra Robinson and her husband Martin have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial, and delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin said.
Family members of Carter Rhoad joined the trial by video link.

Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".
During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.
At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to honour the men by paddling out at a popular surfing spot and throwing flowers into the sea.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.
Amid the demands for action, state Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence.
"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.
"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8gknl1njjo.headline: Kenya's first Ebola case: Questions remain after man travelled across three nations undetected
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8gknl1njjo.author: Wycliffe Muia

paragraphs.text: A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.

The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.

That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo

The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.

Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.

The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.

Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya

Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.

The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.

The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.
Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

livemint.com/news/houthis-bombard-saudi-.headline: Houthis bombard Saudi air links in effort to cut kingdom off from rest of world
livemint.com/news/houthis-bombard-saudi-.author: Georgi Kantchev

paragraphs.text: DUBAI—Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militants are taking aim at Saudi Arabia’s air links to the world, rattling travelers and squeezing another key sector of the kingdom’s economy while its crucial oil industry remains under fire.

The missile attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and several southern Saudi cities threaten to choke off business travel and tourism just as the busy conference and travel season gets under way. The overlapping instability stemming from the conflicts involving the Houthis and Iran could also frustrate Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s efforts to renew a push to boost foreign investment.

A major test will come with the kingdom’s flagship Future Investment Initiative summit, which is expected to draw thousands of global executives and investors to Riyadh at the end of this month. The Saudi leadership isn’t planning to cancel the event but is growing more worried about the conflict’s impact on the economy and about tight supplies of missile interceptors needed to fend off attacks, people familiar with the matter said.

The kingdom has pressed the U.S. to intervene directly in the conflict, but the Trump administration has declined. Some Saudi advisers are pressing the country’s leaders, who escalated the fight in Yemen this week, to keep the door open to diplomacy with the Houthis, the people said.

Thursday’s attacks on Riyadh’s airport—which left three dead, including a pilot for flagship carrier Saudia, and destroyed a passenger jet—are already disrupting air travel. Flight tracker Flightradar24 said the airport closed again Friday afternoon after disruptions the day before, and cancellations were again piling up. A number of airlines have halted flights to Riyadh, and Singapore Airlines postponed the launch of its flights to the capital until March.

Many foreign consultants and other businesspeople found themselves stuck in Saudi Arabia as the weekend in the kingdom began on Friday. Some of their companies told them not to go to the airport after Thursday’s strike.
One medical-sector worker who had boarded a flight home at the time of the attack said he was kept in the plane for an hour as explosions went off outside.

An American defense executive who lives in Riyadh had been waiting in the airport lounge for his flight on Tuesday when Houthi attacks caused delays that would cause him to miss his connecting flight. He said he was back in the lounge Wednesday, when new explosions rattled the glass and caused everyone to jump with fright. He caught his flights but said he was worried about being able to get back on Sunday after the Thursday attack.

“The latest attacks certainly risk setting back the economic recovery,” said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. “Any firms considering investing in the kingdom will certainly want some clarity over whether these attacks will continue.”
Some international companies are evaluating evacuation options and looking for backup transportation for employees as the Houthi attacks disrupt flights and prompt tougher government travel warnings.

Hussein Nasser Eddin, chief executive of global security firm Crownox, said his company has been fielding inquiries from Fortune 500 clients operating in Saudi Arabia, including energy and aviation companies. Inquiries surged following Thursday’s attacks, he said.

Companies had already gone through a round of evacuations to get stranded employees out when the war with Iran began in February and shut down airspace around the region. They are now looking to reserve reliable vehicles and security coordinators so they can move staff out by road to neighboring countries like the United Arab Emirates if airports shut down, he said.
“Everyone is on their toes, because it is a serious red flag of a potential shift or escalation,” he said.

A new State Department warning Thursday says U.S. government officials now need special authorization to use the Riyadh airport. The U.K. warned against all but essential travel to areas of Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh.
Nasser Eddin said the next few days would be crucial in determining whether companies press ahead with planned trips and events or scale back their participation.

The uncertainty adds to the challenges facing Saudi efforts that were already hit hard by the war with Iran. The kingdom weathered those disruptions relatively well, thanks to a pipeline that allowed it to reroute oil across the desert to the Red Sea.

But renewed hostilities with the Houthis changed the equation. The militant group began shooting at Saudi tankers. Then a drone attack in September forced the shutdown of the pipeline. It has since partially resumed operations, and exports have recovered, but renewed Houthi attacks have now disrupted air travel.

“Saudi Arabian airspace constitutes a theater of operations for our missile forces,” the Houthis warned early Friday. Humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh would be allowed with prior authorization, the militants said.

The threats raise new challenges for Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to expand international tourism under the crown prince’s economic diversification plan. Religious tourism to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina is more resilient, but the kingdom has invested heavily to expand into resorts, conferences and sports.
Saudi Arabia’s travel and tourism sector grew by 7.4% last year, nearly twice the global rate, and contributed $178 billion to the country’s GDP, the World Travel & Tourism Council said in April.

Geopolitical risk firm Dragonfly, which like The Wall Street Journal is owned by Dow Jones, said Thursday’s strike was at least the fifth against a Saudi airport since early this month. The kingdom appears to be struggling to intercept the attacks, which are likely to continue, it said.
Opsgroup, an aviation industry network for pilots and flight controllers, warned after Thursday’s fatal strike in Riyadh that airlines should avoid Saudi airspace entirely.

Founder Mark Zee said there is a risk a plane could be hit by air defense fire, as in the case of Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 over Iran in 2020. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency raised similar concerns.

“The Houthis keep saying, ‘Listen, we’re going to target civil aviation infrastructure in some way or another,’ ” Zee said. “My fear in this is that they are seeing that playing with civil aviation is quite effective for their goals, and I don’t know where that goes from here.”

Canada already had advised airlines not enter Saudi airspace, while France issued a warning to avoid much of it. Germany has urged pilots to weigh the risks of flying, particularly south of Jeddah closer to the border with Yemen.

npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-147603/india-cra.headline: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-147603/india-cra.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.

Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.
The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators.

Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.
Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site

Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"
The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.
India's voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns

The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
India's youth movement broadens campaign against Modi
For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.

For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/10/saud.headline: Saudi Arabia faces new level of peril in Houthi attacks, amid wider Iran war
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/10/saud.author: Rachel Chason, Suzan Haidamous, Mohamad El Chamaa

paragraphs.text: Smoke billowed above the airport and explosions sounded in Saudi Arabia’s capital this week, as the Persian Gulf nation faced some of the biggest attacks it had seen in years by Iranian-backed Houthi militants.

While the U.S. push for a deal to end its war with Iran remains stalled, the escalating conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia is further rattling energy markets and threatening to draw in still more countries, in a region already beset by overlapping wars.

Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, the expansion of the violence represents a challenge to the Trump administration, which “already has enough putting pressure on oil prices,” said April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute, a think tank.
“The Trump administration wanted to limit the conflict as much as possible, and to keep the lid on it,” she said. “But the lid is popping off already.”

The Houthis, who receive training and support from Iran, and Yemen’s government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, were embroiled for years in an active civil war that left hundreds of thousands of Yemenis dead. Saudi Arabia, focused on improving its international perception, agreed to a 2022 truce that left the Houthis in control of much of Yemen’s north and the Saudi-backed government in control of the south.
But the Houthis have grown frustrated in recent years by what they say is a Saudi blockade on their territory.

Last month, the Houthis launched a stunning ground offensive to take control of Yemen’s western Red Sea coast along the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital waterway for global shipping, including as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthi offensive prompted a change in Saudi policy, Prince Turki al-Faisal, the former Saudi intelligence chief, said in an interview with Arab News last week.
“Restraint has always been a hallmark of Saudi policy and action, historically, from the days of King Abdulaziz,” he said. “That restraint is no longer operable.”

Days later, the Saudi Arabian-backed Yemeni forces went on the counteroffensive, announcing on Sunday an operation to oust the Houthis from Yemen, which began with barrages of airstrikes. The Houthis have in return struck airports and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including refineries.

As Iran steps up attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, reducing the amount of oil getting out, Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and continued efforts to blockade Saudi ports — some of which had been used as alternatives to Hormuz — are increasingly important, Alley said.

“The Houthis can and are striking deeply into Saudi and hitting critical energy infrastructure,” said Brett Erickson, a risk advisory consultant who closely monitors oil and gas markets. “And the Houthis have less valuable infrastructure … so they are going to continue to wreak havoc on the market.”
The Houthis have claimed strikes, he said, on refineries in Rabigh, Riyadh and Yanbu — vital in producing diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, which are still seeing severely elevated prices.

Houthi spokesman Nasruddin Amer told The Washington Post that Saudi Arabia had “brought this escalation upon itself” by refusing to respond to Houthi demands — including lifting what the Houthis describe as the Saudi-led blockade on Yemen.

Saudi Arabia is receiving help in terms of intelligence from the United States, analysts and U.S. officials say. But the Trump administration has stopped short of providing the level of support that officials in Saudi and its allies in Yemen’s internationally recognized government have sought.

Saudi Arabia is relying on other partners — including Pakistan and Turkey, with which it formed a defense pact in August — for help. But Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that the alliance is “defensive in nature” and that his country will not conduct military operations in Yemen.

Pakistan will stand “shoulder to shoulder” in defending Saudi Arabia, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in a statement Friday. Pakistan has said that its military support is defensive, but it has not specified the full extent of its assistance.

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi author and commentator familiar with Saudi government thinking, said that Saudi Arabia is appreciative of the help the U.S. is providing — especially live targeting information for strikes on the Houthis — but wishes there was more the U.S. would do.
“An armed, non-state actor controls a major international waterway,” he said, referring to Bab al-Mandab. “It is inconceivable that the U.S. would have allowed this to happen in the past.”
But Shihabi also said that Saudi Arabia is not waiting for help from the U.S. and is looking to work more closely with members of the Mecca alliance.
“We understand that each country has to carry its own water,” he said.

The Saudi-backed coalition made initial progress this week in retaking newly Houthi-captured territory along Yemen’s western coast. But in recent days, the balance of power appears to have shifted again — with the Houthis threatening to take the strategic town of Taiz in Yemen and repeatedly striking the airport in Riyadh, leading to three deaths, according to Saudi officials.

For Saudi Arabia, watching the Houthi momentum in September, it became clear that the moment became “do or die,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a Washington-based think tank. “They felt like they had to accept a Houthi takeover of Yemen or go forward with an offensive. So they went forward.”
Now, he said, both sides are “on the escalation ladder.”

While the Trump administration is focused on Iran, the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is spiraling — “and poses an existential threat to Saudi Arabia and also beyond,” said Tim Lenderking, who was a U.S. envoy to Yemen under President Joe Biden.

“The Houthis are unpredictable and very well equipped and heavily armed,” he said. “They are messianic in that they believe this is a divine mission to assert their authority in Yemen and beyond, including in Saudi Arabia.”
The recent attacks are likely to affect the kingdom’s tourism sector, a key part of its diversification strategy.

“Saudi Arabia has opened up so much, and so many more people went there in the last few years that if the attacks persist it will be a big problem,” said Toby Matthiesen, a professor and Gulf expert at the University of Bristol.

Part of that plan aims to turn the kingdom into a global travel destination beyond pilgrimages to Islam’s holiest sites. But so far, Middle East wars have led to the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s star-studded Red Sea International Film Festival and Formula 1 race.

One American living in Riyadh, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of strict Saudi rules about sharing sensitive information, said that he had woken up at some point for each of the past five nights because of the sounds of explosions or interceptions.
Information about the strikes is not announced to the public, and Saudi laws prohibit taking photos of impact sites.
“Then you go to work and pretend like nothing happened,” he said. “It’s almost worse because no one has any idea what is going on.”
Dan Lamothe and Shaiq Hussain contributed to this report.

For years, the crystallographer and biochemist Ada Yonath had to contend with the disdain and sometimes derision of many of her contemporaries after she set herself the challenge of mapping the molecular structure of the ribosome.

Ribosomes are found in all living cells. Effectively they are tiny factories that synthesise proteins, complex molecules that are vital for building and repairing the tissues and organs of animals and plants. Many scientists believed hers was a fruitless endeavour because ribosomes are so small – sometimes only 20 nanometres in diameter – irregular in shape and lacking internal symmetry. James Watson, one of the Nobel prizewinning discoverers of the double-helix structure of DNA, had tried and failed. But Yonath, who has died aged 87, proved her doubters wrong, and was rewarded with the 2009 Nobel prize in chemistry, only the fourth woman to receive it, which she shared with the biologist Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and biochemist Thomas Steitz.

“I was met with disbelief, even ridicule in the international scientific community,” she said later. “I was called a dreamer, a fantasist, even the village idiot. But when I succeeded, it created an overwhelming internal joy and those who once called me crazy or stupid became supporters.”

It was in the late 1970s, while being laid up following a bicycle accident, and indulging in some “easier” reading, that Yonath, then a young scientist based at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, chanced upon the article that would lead to her eventual breakthrough. Reading about the biology of polar bears, she learned that the bears pack their ribosomes in an orderly way in their cells prior to hibernating. “These stay intact and functional for months. So, if polar bears knew how to do it, we could too,” she reasoned.

Yonath surmised that, if she could crystallise an organism, and hence its ribosomes, she would be able to study their internal structure using X-rays and electron microscopy. However, ribosomes are fragile. Unlike other cell parts, they have no outer protective membrane and are easily damaged. Figuring that ribosomes of organisms that live in harsh conditions were likely to be hardier and more able to survive crystallisation, she attempted to crystallise the thermophile bacteria Geobacillus stearothermophilus, found in austere environments around thermal vents and in desert sands.

It took more than 25,000 attempts, but in the mid-80s, Yonath succeeded. She then froze the bacteria at –185°C, to stabilise its internal structure and to protect it from the X-rays, a technique she was an early successful pioneer of, now known as cryo bio-crystallography. Finally, in 2001 and 2002, after almost two decades of research, Yonath’s team succeeded in mapping, in three dimensions, the bacteria’s ribosome.

The significance of this discovery extended beyond pure science. Many antibiotics work by binding to sites on a bacterium’s ribosome, stopping it from reproducing. Previously, making antibiotics was a hit-and-miss process because often they would attack human ribosomes as well as those of the bacteria. But, armed with knowledge of the structure of different ribosomes, scientists could now deduce where on a ribosome an antibiotic would bind and so make the necessary structural alterations to the drug.

Yonath demonstrated how more than 20 antibiotics function, paving the way for new products, and also studied how antibiotic resistance might be overcome. The Nobel committee specifically noted this work in its citation, highlighting the “fundamental and medically important aspects of ribosome function” leading to “the development of novel antibiotic drugs in the ongoing medical struggle against ever emerging drug resistance among bacterial pathogens”.

Born in Jerusalem, into an Orthodox Jewish family, Ada was the elder daughter of parents who had emigrated from Poland to what was then British-mandated Palestine in 1933. Her father, Hillel Lifshitz, a rabbi and grocer, died when she was 11. Her mother, Esther, then moved with her two daughters to Tel Aviv, where she became a clerk. Despite her modest income, she recognised her daughter’s keen intellect and obtained her a place at the fee-paying Tichon Hadash high school, where Ada taught maths lessons in lieu of school fees.

In 1959, after two years of mandatory military service, she returned to Jerusalem to take a degree in chemistry at the Hebrew University, graduating in 1962, then a master’s in biochemistry (1964). Four years later she received a PhD from the Weizmann Institute for studies into the structure of collagen using X-ray crystallography.

She accepted postdoctoral positions in the US, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Carnegie Mellon University, in Pittsburgh, before returning to the Weizmann Institute, where, in 1970, she began her research into ribosomes and where she remained for the rest of her career. Despite the scepticism of many of her peers, she did receive long-term support and funding from Heinz-Günter Wittman at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in Berlin, frequently travelling to Germany to exchange data and compare notes.

In addition to her Nobel prize, Yonath received numerous awards, including the 2007 Wolf prize in chemistry, second only in importance to the Nobel, and was elected as a foreign member of the UK’s Royal Society.

Outside her work, Yonath was politically outspoken and critical of the Israeli government. Most recently, she criticised Israeli judicial reforms as a “genuine peril to democracy” and to Israeli scientific enterprise.
In 2018, when asked what qualities made a good scientist, she said: “Curiosity, first. Second, curiosity. And third, curiosity. Also, one has to love, and not be afraid of, a challenge.”
Her marriage to Moshe Yonath, a schoolteacher, ended in divorce. Her daughter, Hagith, and a granddaughter, Noa, survive her.

washingtonpost.com/entertainment/movies/.headline: What to know about ‘NAZA,’ a documentary that looks at Israeli war technology
washingtonpost.com/entertainment/movies/.author: Ethan Beck

paragraphs.text: In 2023, shortly after Israel began its military campaign in Gaza, Israeli filmmakers and journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor started conducting interviews with soldiers and intelligence officers in Tel Aviv.

The resulting documentary, “NAZA,” takes a look at the technology used by Israel in Gaza to identify military targets. Anonymous sources in the film said the technology also has been used to kill Palestinian civilians.

The war, a response to the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 Israelis, has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants. Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have condemned the film and threatened to revoke the citizenship of Abraham and Szor.

After a September debut at the Venice Film Festival, where the film received a 25-minute standing ovation, “NAZA” arrived in U.S. theaters, ahead of Israeli elections at the end of the month. It follows Abraham and Szor’s Oscar-winning documentary “No Other Land,” which looked at villages in the West Bank that Israel’s Supreme Court said could be demolished.

For much of “NAZA,” Abraham sits on rooftops in Tel Aviv, posing direct questions to 24 soldiers — whose identities remain secret — who had roles in the war in Gaza. The first public screening in the United States, which took place at the New York Film Festival, was protested by a small group with the Israeli-American Council.

“Different people have different reasons to speak,” Abraham said in New York. “For some of them, they felt a need to talk — especially in Hebrew — to penetrate walls of denial, of justification, of silence in Israeli society.”

Many of the findings in the film, related to Israel’s artificial intelligence technology and how it was used in Gaza, were published in the Guardian, which produced “NAZA,” along with the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine and the Hebrew-language publication Local Call.

Three years after the Oct. 7 attack, and a year into President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan, the people of Gaza face bleak conditions, The Post reported. Hundreds of thousands live in tents, plagued by infectious diseases, while hospitals remain overwhelmed. “NAZA” includes phone footage from Gaza captured in October and November 2023 as Palestinians looked for family members under rumble.

“You don’t need to hear from Israeli soldiers to understand the horrors of what is happening in Gaza,” Abraham said. “Part of the reason they persist is, still, a lot of people are denying them. Part of our hope is, by making this film, we are making that denial a little bit harder.”
Here’s what to know.
What does NAZA mean?

“NAZA” is an acronym for “nezek agavi,” which means “collateral damage.” The figures in the film use “NAZA” to describe the number of civilian casualties calculated before a strike. One subject in the documentary said the NAZA metric doesn’t distinguish between a child and an adult.

Another soldier said that targets resulting in fewer than 20 civilian deaths didn’t require special authorization. One interviewee said they once received approval for an operation targeting one Hamas militant even though 500 civilian deaths were anticipated. The military denied that this strike, “or anything close to that number,” took place.
“At the start of the war, we bombed everything,” one soldier said. “NAZA wasn’t an issue.”
Why are the interview subjects anonymous?

In “NAZA,” a soldier said that if they were visible in the film, the Israeli government would retaliate against them. The subjects wouldn’t speak unless anonymity was granted, Abraham said. Granting anonymity to protect sources is common in investigative journalism.

“This film would not have been made in any other way,” Abraham said in September. “Because the crimes are ongoing, we felt that it was important to make it. And we understand there is a complexity there.”
The Israeli military criticized the film’s anonymous testimonies, describing the claims as “general and unverifiable.” Abraham and Szor said the testimonies were vetted.
What military technology does the film focus on?

The interviewees in “NAZA” contend that Israel used advanced systems, often involving artificial intelligence, to kill suspected Hamas militants. One subject recalled working on and using an AI tool to create a database of Palestinians in Gaza that suggests targets connected to Hamas. Another system, described by a source in “NAZA,” recommended buildings to target.
(“An algorithm has never decided on a strike,” the Israel Defense Forces said a statement about the film.)
Palestinians were surveilled, an interviewee said, by hacking into the cameras and microphones on their cellphones: “You feel a bit like God because you hear everything they say.”

One said they did this to determine when a targeted individual arrived home. Intelligence officers used the phrase “Where’s Daddy?” to refer to hacking the phone of a child, before launching an airstrike on the family. “You hack her phone, and then you kill her,” one subject said.
What do the interviewees think about the war?

When prompted by Abraham, one interviewee said the war has resulted in a genocide, the same conclusion as that reached by a United Nations commission last year. “We have to describe these things as they really are,” they added.

Several described a sense of importance around “completing the mission,” with one adding that they don’t hate Arabic people. Many said they didn’t believe they were supposed to speak up. “I’m just a small cog,” one said.

Toward the end of “NAZA,” one interviewee contrasted what’s happening in Gaza with the Holocaust. The film draws out this comparison by noting a retrospective on documentarian Claude Lanzmann — who directed “Shoah,” the 1985 film that contains over nine hours of interviews with Holocaust survivors — taking place in Tel Aviv at the time. “I still see the Nazis as evil,” one interviewee said, “but what does that mean I am?”
How do Israelis feel about the film?
The Israeli military issued a lengthy rebuttal to “NAZA,” claiming the documentary “presents a distorted, misleading, and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process.”
Netanyahu described the film as part of “global antisemitic incitement” and said he intended to seek legislation to revoke the filmmakers’ Israeli citizenship.

More than 2,000 people, including Israeli filmmakers Ari Folman and Nadav Lapid, signed a petition in support of Abraham and Szor. (Another petition, by the International Documentary Association, which called for the Israeli government to withdraw its “threats against [the] filmmakers,” has been signed by actors Mark Ruffalo and Javier Bardem.)

Dozens of right-wing protesters gathered around the home of Szor’s parents in central Israel last month after “NAZA” premiered. Abraham fears he won’t be able to return home. After “No Other Land” premiered in 2024, Abraham’s family home was attacked. But he told the Guardian that the targeting of his family doesn’t compare to what the Palestinians experience.
“Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials,” Abraham said. “There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/09/w.headline: Why you shouldn’t count on inheriting money for your retirement
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/09/w.author: Maurie Backman

paragraphs.text: Over the coming decades, baby boomers and older generations are expected to transfer more than $100 trillion in assets to their heirs, according to some estimates. If your parents or grandparents are well off, you might assume that at least a portion of their money will become yours, and that might mean you choose to save less today.
Financial experts caution, however, against relying on an inheritance to fund your retirement. Here’s why that’s risky and what to do instead.
Your inheritance could arrive later than planned

Pushing yourself to save aggressively for retirement may seem unnecessary if you’re expecting a generous inheritance once your parents die. The reality, though, is you don’t know how long your parents will live and when that money might arrive. Americans, especially those with means, are living longer, and GLP1 drugs and other new treatments could prolong life further.

The Social Security Administration reports that life expectancy has increased from 18.1 years for men born in 1930 to 20.9 years for men born in 1960. For women, it’s gone from 21.4 years for those born in 1930 to 23.7 years among those born in 1960.

“Counting on money that is not yet yours is inherently a risky retirement strategy,” says Aaron Bosch, financial adviser at Moneta Group Investment Advisors in St. Louis. “Advances in modern medicine mean people in the U.S. are living longer than ever. For many people, an inheritance may not arrive until they are already well into retirement themselves.”
Your inheritance could be surprisingly small

Not only might an inheritance land too late to fund your retirement fully, but the cost of long-term care could erode that windfall. CareScout, a company that helps families navigate long-term care, puts the average annual cost of assisted living at $74,400 as of 2025. For a shared nursing home room, that figure jumps to $114,975.
“If your parents live longer than expected and some of those years are spent in a nursing facility, the number you were picturing could end up significantly smaller,” Bosch says.

The Washington Post found that elder care costs are whittling down older Americans’ savings. The share of people left with nothing left to pass on rose from 6 percent for those who died between 2006 and 2010 to almost 11 percent among those who died between 2017 and 2022.
Plus, even if you do receive a sizable inheritance, the IRS might take a chunk of it if it comes from a taxable source, like an inherited traditional IRA.
Not all inherited assets are created equal

There are different types of assets that can be part of an estate plan. Trent Von Ahsen, managing partner at Cedar Point Capital Partners in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, says not all assets may be equally useful for actually paying near-term retirement expenses.

“A share of a family business, for instance, or a piece of land is very different than cash,” Von Ahsen explains. Even if you inherit an asset that could be worth a lot in theory, that doesn’t mean it automatically becomes an asset you can liquidate on the spot.
Use an inheritance as bonus retirement money

Ultimately, the amount of money you inherit may be different from the amount you expect, and it may arrive later than anticipated. Prioritize retirement plan contributions so you’re saving on a consistent basis.

“I would build a retirement plan that covers essential spending from your own savings and retirement income. Then model an inheritance separately,” Von Ahsen says. “I would be very cautious about reducing retirement contributions or making an irreversible decision based on money you don’t yet control. If the inheritance arrives, you can revisit that plan then.”

Or, as Bosch says, “think of an inheritance as more of a bonus.” If it comes through, you may be able to retire sooner than planned or live differently. Until then, work with an adviser to figure out how much you can afford to contribute toward retirement while balancing other goals, and set up automatic recurring transfers into a 401(k) or IRA to ensure your savings are funded consistently.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/10/p.headline: Trump showers voters with checks and tax relief in final sprint to midterms
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/10/p.author: Riley Beggin

paragraphs.text: With less than one month until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump keeps trying to find ways to directly benefit voters to ease affordability concerns at the heart of the midterm elections.

Last week, Trump began sending $500 checks to nearly 1 million Americans in 30 states as a refund for Affordable Care Act fees he said were overcharged under President Joe Biden, along with a letter touting his record.

Two days later, he announced plans to send $90 payments to more than 20 million seniors. The checks were intended to offset October Medicare premiums, Trump wrote in an email accompanying the payments that listed the administration’s other health care policies.

But the proposals haven’t been limited to checks. On Monday, Trump signed an executive order onstage at a rally in Nebraska that expanded the availability of tax-free dyed diesel, which is typically limited to off-road use on farms and construction sites. The average cost of diesel in the United States is now $6.27 per gallon, according to AAA, nearly twice the cost of a year ago, driven up by fuel disruptions due to the Iran war.

“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said after signing the order, referring to Sen. Pete Ricketts (Nebraska) and Gov. Jim Pillen, both Republican incumbents running for reelection.

Trump also floated the idea of banning diesel exports as another way to bring down prices, but backed off of the idea after pushback from Energy Secretary Chris Wright and an announcement from the Group of Seven countries that they would release 100 million barrels of diesel reserves. On Friday, Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel fuel this month and another 500,000 tons next month, with more to follow.

The economy has consistently ranked as the top issue for voters in the midterm elections as Democratic motivation to vote remains relatively high and Trump’s popularity remains low, according to recent polling from the Pew Research Center.
“The president wants to win, and he’s trying to, step by step, fix the problems that have caused Republicans problems,” said former House speaker Newt Gingrich.

The moves appealing to voters seem like an attempt to distract from Trump’s dismissal of cost concerns and to “try to buy votes,” said Tim Burga, president of the Ohio AFL-CIO. “It reeks of desperation.”

Now Republicans are asking for voters to give them two more years of control of Congress. “It doesn’t work when you’ve broken the trust of the American people and you have completely discounted the fact that the affordability crisis is even a thing,” Burga said.

Trump has a long track record of backing efforts to send direct payments to voters, from first-term covid-19 pandemic stimulus checks to proposed DOGE and tariff dividends and a $1,776 “warrior dividend” bonus for service members. In September, Trump floated the idea of cutting $5,000 checks to every adult if they vote in Republicans, but few lawmakers have mentioned the idea on the campaign trail.

“When you talk about generic tax cuts, voters don’t always know how it’s going to impact them,” said Alex Conant, a national Republican political strategist. “When you make concrete promises about checks in the mail, it’s easier to imagine how it could help your situation.”
Trump’s recent efforts create something for his base “to grab on to,” Conant added, as Trump embarks on a tour of Republican strongholds to turn out conservative voters.
But it’s unclear whether it will be enough to ease frustrations with price pressures that haven’t abated under Trump, said Barrett Marson, a GOP strategist in Arizona.

“MAGA people are disenchanted, independents are furious, and middle Republicans are wondering when the tariffs and the war will be over so that we can have interest rates below 6 percent and gas at $3 and the price of everyday items coming down,” Marson said, adding that voters in Arizona are feeling like “Trump pulled a bit of a bait and switch.”
Trump’s policies have improved the economy and will continue to do so over the next two years, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

“The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: he signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, distributed $90 Medicare checks and $500 Obamacare refund checks, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first, and sent 401(k)s to record highs,” Rogers said, adding that Democrats support socialist candidates who would drive up costs and deficits.

The president’s economic advisers have also suggested he should suspend the federal gas tax writ large, which would strip off 18 cents per gallon for gasoline and 24 cents per gallon for diesel fuel and would typically require an act of Congress.
“It would be a good way of providing some relief at the pump, said Stephen Moore, a conservative economist who has advised Trump.

Moore said he’s urged the president to suspend the gas tax until prices return to less than $3.75 per gallon. He added that he believes it could be possible without help from Congress — which is out of Washington campaigning throughout October — by asserting a temporary emergency.

Another option, Moore added, would be to suspend refinery requirements to incorporate certain levels of biofuel like ethanol into gasoline, which refiners argue increases gas prices by driving up operating costs. He noted that it would take a few weeks for consumers to feel the effects — perhaps too tight of a turnaround with only 24 days until the midterms.

Last month, Trump also pledged $5,000 checks to American adults if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate. Even some of the president’s allies have acknowledged that is unlikely, given pushback from Republicans in Congress concerned about the deficit.
On Wednesday, Trump was asked to respond to people who are suggesting he is “throwing money at people” ahead of the election to entice Republican voters.

“What we’re doing is we have tremendous growth,” Trump responded while speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, arguing that tariffs have spurred economic growth, though experts say tariffs will have a negative impact on long-run gross domestic product. “We’re able to do things that the Democrats can’t.”

livescience.com/technology/communication.headline: Does written language speed up or slow down cultural change?
livescience.com/technology/communication.author: Ashley Hamer Pritchard

paragraphs.text: The written word is one of humanity's most important information technologies. Without it, mathematical and scientific discoveries would be lost to history. But it can also lock ideas in place long after they've stopped making sense.
So does writing speed up cultural change or slow it down?

Russell Gray, a professor in the Department of Linguistic and Cultural Evolution at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, heads a research project investigating how writing affects the way languages change. His team uses methods borrowed from evolutionary biology to trace languages through family trees — similar to the way biologists trace species.
Language is one element of culture that researchers can measure to determine whether writing speeds up or slows down cultural change.

"The obvious answer," Gray said, is that writing slows culture down because writing "is all codified and specified and people get trained in it." Gray doesn’t think the obvious answer is necessarily the right one. But other researchers agree that writing can lock in ways of thinking.

"Writing can lead to what learning psychologists sometimes call 'canalization,'" Charles Perreault, an associate professor in the School of Human Evolution and Social Change at Arizona State University, told Live Science in an email. "It can narrow the range of ways people think about a problem. When a rule, method, or story is written down, people may come to see it as the correct version … and may not even consider that a better or different way could exist."

Religious texts and legal codes are good examples. In both cases, the interpretation of rules written hundreds ‪—‬ or even thousands ‪—‬ of years ago shapes the way things are done, long after the circumstances that produced them have changed.

This idea shows up in artistic expression, too: A 2017 analysis by ethnomusicologist Patrick Savage looked at more than 4,000 British-American ballads from the 16th through 20th centuries and found that written melodies changed less than those shared through oral tradition.
But there are also ways that writing may speed up cultural change.
"Before writing, much cultural knowledge had to be stored in people's brains," Perreault said. "That has obvious limits."

People forget things they don't study routinely, and when people die, their knowledge often dies with them. Because writing moves information storage beyond the human brain, it can reduce those losses, Perreault said.

"If writing prevents knowledge from being lost, and if it also helps information spread through a society, as with the printing press, then it could accelerate the ratchet effect of cumulative cultural evolution," Perreault said. "But this remains, to some extent, a hypothesis."
By the book
One reason the question of whether written language speeds or slows cultural evolution is that writing is hard to separate from everything that comes with it.

Writing has been separately invented only around four times in human history — although "some people argue there's a fifth in India," Gray said — which means nearly every writing system on Earth descends from that handful. Those systems spread through contact; trade, war, religion and the other ways humans intermingle had their own effects on cultural change that are hard to untangle from the effects of writing.
Related mysteries
Also, "mass literacy is quite recent," Gray said. "If you've got these written varieties that are just used by, often, religious elites, that's potentially going to have much less impact."
So which force wins? Both experts think writing speeds up cultural change, though neither can prove it yet.
"I would say that writing probably speeds up cultural change overall," Perreault said. Gray agreed, though he acknowledged that most people would guess the opposite.
Still, Perreault cautioned, "these are empirical questions that have yet to be answered empirically."

npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5991897/democra.headline: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5991897/democra.author: Claudia Grisales

paragraphs.text: Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.
That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.
This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.

One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.

"We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.

That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.
She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.
"My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.

Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.
BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event.

Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.
"So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."

Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.
Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them.
"One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.

In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center.
It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election.
This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies.

Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging.
"Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said.

Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration.
So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional.
"Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said.
So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them.
"My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said.
Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.
"The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said.

npr.org/sections/the-picture-show/2026/1.headline: A year of ceasefire in Gaza through the lens of NPR's reporter
npr.org/sections/the-picture-show/2026/1.author: Anas Baba

paragraphs.text: Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.

GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.

A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.

Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.

That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/10/10/pop.headline: The White Sox’s season needs saving. Luckily, they know a guy.
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/10/10/pop.author: Stephanie Apstein

paragraphs.text: For a few minutes in August, the Bishop of Rome, Vicar of Christ, Successor of the Prince of the Apostles, Supreme Pontiff of the Universal Church, Sovereign of Vatican City and Servant of the Servants of God was just a 13-year-old boy named Bobby, holding up a baseball and gazing at it.

The 2026 White Sox had signed the ball for their most famous fan and sent it to him in Father Tom McCarthy’s carry-on luggage, along with a handful of jerseys, pennants, bobbleheads and Sox-themed miters (better known among laymen as pope hats). Now Pope Leo XIV, the clergyman born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, was pawing through the box and exclaiming every time he pulled out another piece of merchandise.
“He was,” McCarthy recalled last week, “like a kid on Christmas morning.”

As they opened the gifts, McCarthy recounted the recent Pope Night the White Sox had held at Rate Field: the pope hat giveaway, the sign of peace in the stands, the $14,000 check for the Midwest Augustinian Province in honor of the 14th Pope Leo. (“Why didn’t you take the name John?” McCarthy quipped. “You would’ve been the 24th. We would’ve gotten an extra $10,000!”)
It was a great night, McCarthy finished.
“Yeah,” the pope said. “Too bad we didn’t win.”

The Vatican did not respond to a message seeking details of how Leo has been following his White Sox in their quest for the American League pennant, but his friends and colleagues say he certainly keeps up on their progress.

It feels right that America’s pope should be a fan of America’s pastime. And somehow it feels even more right that he should root for the Chicago White Sox, a team that has perhaps required more divine intervention than any other in recent years.
The 2024 White Sox lost 121 games, the most in the 125 years of MLB’s modern era. They were eliminated from playoff contention on Aug. 17 that season and finished 41 games back — of fourth place.
Then they slashed payroll, to $74 million from $123 million. They went 10–28, a dismal .263 winning percentage, to start 2025.

But then here came the white smoke, and somehow, here came the White Sox. They went 50–74 (.403) the rest of the year, as the newly elected Leo donned a White Sox cap in St. Peter’s Square. The resurrection has continued this season: The White Sox finished 84–78, good for second in the American League Central, swept the Houston Astros in the wild-card series and have split their first four games of the AL Division Series with the Cleveland Guardians. The teams will play a decisive Game 5 on Saturday night in Cleveland as the White Sox look to advance to their first AL Championship Series since they won the World Series in 2005.

Aboard the papal flight to Paris from Rome earlier this month, Leo refused to confirm or deny divine intervention for the team’s improvement. He grinned mischievously and said, “No comment.” Then he commented anyway: “Great things happen in Chicago,” he said.
People close to the pope report that sports fit neatly into his belief system.

“As someone who’s kind of grounded in Augustinian roots, he really values community, and I think that that’s what sports does,” said Father Robert Hagan, who was mentored by Prevost when Hagan was a novice. “I think that’s what Chicago is experiencing with the White Sox — it brings people together.”

But they also report that he really just loves the White Sox. Leo is a classic Chicago sports fan: He yelled “Da Bears” from the popemobile, he has talked trash about the Cubs in at least two languages, and friends, said Sister Thérèse DelGenio in an interview, have noticed that he sometimes logs on to video calls in a Bears T-shirt.
“It humanizes him,” said Cardinal Blase Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago. “I think that people really do find that endearing.”

Elise Ann Allen, the pope’s Rome-based biographer, said in an interview that the young Bobby learned to navigate a home life in which his mother, Mildred, was a die-hard Cubs fan and his father, Louis, cheered for the St. Louis Cardinals.
“He said you had to be accepting of others and maintain an open mind, because if not, you wouldn’t get dinner,” Allen said.
Cupich tries to straddle a similar line, declining to choose between the Sox and the Cubs. “Living in Chicago, I have to be a Chicago fan,” he said. “It’s safer.”
This is something of a cop-out, he admitted. So does Leo get credit for picking a side?
Cupich laughed. No way, he said: “He doesn’t have to live here!”

Still, it was always the White Sox for young Bobby. He grew up in Dolton, Illinois, 15 miles south of Comiskey Park, when Luis Aparicio was starring on the South Side. On summer breaks from St. Augustine Seminary High School near Saugatuck, Michigan, and later from Villanova University, he would catch Sox games in the cheap seats with friends. He usually served as the designated driver.

When Prevost worked as a missionary in Peru in the 1990s, his then-roommate Father John Lydon recalled, their rabbit-ear televisions lacked access to American sports, so Prevost became a passionate fan of the local soccer team, Club Alianza Lima.

“It was the team of the people,” Lydon said, contrasting it with Club Universitario de Deportes, which was considered the squad of the elites. The priests watched games in their living room, and Prevost “got into it,” Lydon recalled, jumping up from the couch and yelling to celebrate goals.

Later, when Prevost was prior general of the Augustinians, NPR’s Scott Detrow reported, he took part in an exercise in which he had to paint symbols reflecting his identity. He drew an American flag, Chicago’s Sears Tower, the Augustinian emblem, a Christmas tree … and the White Sox logo.

He attended a handful of games every year with Ed Schmit, a friend from when both worked at a Chicago Catholic school, and when the White Sox made the 2005 World Series, Schmit called Prevost immediately. After Leo’s election, news outlets dug up photos of them together at Game 1, which made the pontiff chuckle — but not just for the reasons you might think.
“You know,” he has told people, “I was also at Game 2.”

He has made no promises about visiting a potential 2026 World Series game, but he is doing his part to help the White Sox get there: On the eve of the playoffs, team owner Jerry Reinsdorf was going through his mail when he noticed a large envelope, postmarked Vatican City.

“It is my hope that the White Sox will continue to foster bonds of friendship and solidarity among people, and thus bear hopeful witness to the possibility of living and working together in peace,” Leo wrote. “With these sentiments, I willingly invoke the Almighty’s abundant blessings upon you and your loved ones.”
“Imagine a Jewish kid from Brooklyn getting a letter from the pope,” Reinsdorf told reporters. “I’m going to convert.”
“By the way,” said Brooks Boyer, the White Sox’s head of marketing and a lifelong Catholic, “the Vatican has the coolest letterhead you could imagine.”

If the White Sox win the World Series, Boyer joked, maybe they will top the traditional White House visit with a trip to the Vatican. If they do, perhaps Leo will show them around the papal archives, where he stores many of the gifts he has received, including many of the contents of that care package.
But not all of them, said McCarthy. A few of those gifts went straight into the pope’s personal apartment, where Bobby can see them anytime he wants.
Anthony Faiola in Rome contributed to this report.

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/us/executions-dea.headline: Executions, After Christa Pike, Are on the Minds of a Divided Public

paragraphs.text: Within the span of eight days, the country has learned of a failed execution and a successful execution, and has been promised a livestreamed execution by military firing squad before year’s end.

The most severe form of criminal punishment — there are roughly 2,000 people on death row nationwide — execution has taken center stage in a nation already split politically and culturally, amplifying divisions just weeks before a pivotal midterm election.

Death penalty opponents have seized upon the blundered attempt to kill Christa Pike in Tennessee last week to push for an end to the death penalty. Conversely, the nation’s top military official said on Thursday that the United States would carry out the government’s first public execution since 1936.

The announcement from the Pentagon chief, Pete Hegseth, and its timing, exemplify the salient place that the death penalty has taken in the nation’s polarized political landscape in President Trump’s second term.

On the day Mr. Trump returned to office, he urged prosecutors across the country to pursue and carry out capital punishment. In 2025, states executed more people than they had since 2009, largely driven by a sharp jump in Florida under Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican.

The failed execution of Ms. Pike — who survived two doses of pentobarbital that may have been injected improperly — has galvanized death penalty opponents, who have denounced what they see as a grisly example of capital punishment’s faults.

And the two events together have brought the issue of the death penalty — something that has for decades taken place in hidden rooms inside mostly rural prisons — back into the forefront of Americans’ minds.

“What we’re seeing is the brutality of the institution of the death penalty coming back into public focus,” said Mark Osler, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas in Minneapolis who has studied the death penalty. “Tennessee didn’t intend to do that; the federal government does.”
“Given that there has been a rise in executions,” he added, “it’s a good time to have that debate.”

Nearly 1,700 people have been executed in the past 50 years, including Jamaal Howard, 46, who was put to death on Wednesday in Texas, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, with a peak of 98 killed in 1999. Mr. Howard had been convicted of murdering Vickie Swartout, 42, during a 2000 robbery. Tennessee had sought to execute Ms. Pike for her 1995 killing of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

While 27 states retain the death penalty, fewer than half of those have carried out an execution in the past five years. Virginia abolished the penalty in 2021, and Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, said in June that he wanted his state to do so as well.

In modern times, lethal injection has been used far more than any other method, though states have turned to alternative methods — both new and old — in recent years. Several have authorized the firing squad, and two, Alabama and Louisiana, have used the novel method of asphyxiation via nitrogen.

Public opinion polls have shown support for the death penalty steadily declining in recent decades, though a majority of Americans still support it. One poll from this past summer found that two-thirds were in favor.

Still, the specter of livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former Army major who was convicted of murdering 13 people — mostly soldiers — and wounding dozens more at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, has upset many who might otherwise support his killing.

“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, wrote on social media. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Mr. Hasan, now 56, was motivated by his radical views of Islam to carry out the killings in retaliation for America’s wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. He was wounded by responding police officers and is now paralyzed from the waist down, raising the possibility that he could be transported in a wheelchair to his execution, which is scheduled for Dec. 3. Mr. Hegseth said Mr. Hasan would be killed at Fort Hood around the same time of day — early afternoon — that he committed the crimes.

The reactions to the announcement fell largely along ideological lines — Republicans are much more likely to support capital punishment — but were far from uniform, underscoring the complexity of the issue.

Some Roman Catholic leaders condemned the execution plans. The Catholic Church has long opposed the death penalty as part of its theological commitment to humans across their life spans, though recently U.S. bishops have prioritized ending abortion and defending immigrants.
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, the president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, called the planned livestream “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death” and warned it would harm the country.
“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” he said.

Vice President JD Vance, an atheist turned Catholic, said on Friday that he would not watch the execution if it was livestreamed and also cast doubt on that idea, saying, “I don’t know if that’s actually going to happen.”
But in a sign of the continued sharp divide that the Trump movement has carved in American Christianity, an energetic cohort of right-wing Christians defended the livestream on biblical grounds.

Josh Howerton, the pastor of Lakepointe Church, an evangelical congregation with locations in and around Dallas, argued on social media that executions in the Bible were carried out publicly as deterrents.
“I do not think you can say it’s unbiblical or automatically wrong,” he said of public executions, noting passages that described public stonings.
The prospect of a public execution was raised prominently around the turn of the century, when some proposed televising the killing of Timothy McVeigh.

Mr. McVeigh, convicted of carrying out the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995 that killed 168 people, himself had urged as much in a letter to The Oklahoman newspaper in which he argued for “equal access” to his execution: “A reasonable solution seems obvious: hold a true ‘public’ execution — allow a public broadcast.”
