In the end, he was executed by lethal injection at an Indiana prison in 2001, with a couple of dozen people watching his death in person and about 232 more — including survivors and their relatives — viewing on closed-circuit television from Oklahoma City.
Notably, Mr. Hasan has said he wants to be killed for his crimes, saying he sees an opportunity for martyrdom, though he does not appear to expect the firing squad or a public death.
“I’m paraplegic and could be in jail for the rest of my life,” he told a military panel in 2010. “However, if I died by lethal injection I would still be a martyr.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/us/politics/trump.headline: Economic Pain and an Unpopular Trump Put G.O.P. on its Heels With Three Weeks to Go

paragraphs.text: Three weeks from Election Day, deep frustration over an economy that feels unworkable for Americans at most every level, from farmers to truckers to consumers, has expanded the map of competitive electoral contests into areas that seemed safely Republican just a couple of months ago.

Sustained high prices are putting at risk some of the constituencies, states and congressional districts that President Trump and Republicans won decisively in 2024. The widespread discontent has prompted candidates, parties and major G.O.P. fund-raising groups to shift their messages and ad spending in crucial races to try to move voters in the final days of the midterm campaign.

With control of the House, Senate and the vast majority of the country’s governor’s offices and legislatures at stake, Republicans are examining their own deteriorating internal polling, along with their experiences with voters, and say they are reassessing their odds and triaging the map.

On Friday, for example, the leading Senate Republican super PAC began to plunge another $30 million into advertising in Texas to try to save the state’s Senate seat for Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general.

Several races that are likely to determine the overall outcome on Election Day — the Maine and Michigan Senate elections, for example — remain tight. Control of the chamber could easily boil down to one or two of these razor-thin contests.

Still, Republican baggage is piling up, regionally and nationally. Mr. Trump is facing backlash to mass deportations in South Texas and South Florida. His party is bracing for anger at expanding data centers in states including Ohio and Michigan. In big farming states, record diesel prices have arrived just in time for harvest season. In colder northern states, spiking heating oil costs loom for families.

“When you’ve got a sitting president whose job approval rating is in the high 30s,” said Colin Reed, a veteran Republican strategist, “it makes it really difficult for any Republican candidate to compete and win.”

The White House is racing for stopgap solutions. Mr. Trump announced $90 payouts for millions of seniors on Medicare, and on Friday began sending $500 rebate checks he had promised for some Affordable Care Act customers. He has also promised a $5,000 check for every adult U.S. citizen if his party retains control of Congress. This week, in Nebraska — a typically solidly Republican state — Mr. Trump announced an executive order to loosen restrictions on the use of tax-free diesel on the roads.
On Friday, Mr. Trump said he would allow Russian diesel imports after years of sanctions, in an attempt to lower prices.
Mr. Trump’s unpopularity over his handling of the economy — one of his biggest strengths when he ran two years ago — is driving Republican troubles in a nationalized political environment.

The party still holds structural advantages over Democrats, including a Senate map with more contests in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024; redrawn congressional maps that made more seats favorable to the G.O.P.; and a wide financial lead, bolstered in part by Mr. Trump’s own powerful super PAC, MAGA Inc. In past elections, particularly when Mr. Trump has been on the ballot, some polls have underestimated his popularity.
Those advantages have provided little comfort to Republicans who see their candidates faltering in increasingly red corners of the nation.

The leading House Republican super PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund, all but ceded the first Republican-held seat of the election this week, moving money out of a district in Nebraska where Representative Don Bacon is retiring. Mr. Bacon occupies the most Democratic-leaning seat of any Republican in the House.
In an interview, Mr. Bacon said he had urged party officials not to abandon the seat just yet.
“I wish they could have shown a little more patience,” he said. “The No. 1 issue is the president is not popular in the district.”

Republicans also recently pulled money from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican, is retiring. They redirected cash to Kansas and South Carolina, which remain a stretch for Democrats but would have seemed out of reach earlier this year. The top super PAC backing Senate Democrats, Senate Majority PAC, is reserving $5 million in ad time in Kansas.

“There are states right now in play that I would not have imagined being in play,” former President Barack Obama said at a fund-raiser for Democratic Senate nominees in Virginia on Wednesday, rattling off states such as Texas, Kansas and Nebraska.
“We could end up losing all of them by two points,” he added, according to excerpts released by his office, warning against Democratic complacency. “But we have a chance.”

Republicans, privately and publicly, are concerned about an enthusiasm gap. Culture war issues, such as transgender athletes’ rights, are still in heavy rotation in Republican ads. But polls show voters are focused squarely on their deep unhappiness with the direction of an economy that Mr. Trump had promised to fix.

“Angry people vote and satisfied people don’t,” Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, warned a crowd at a diner this week in Nazareth, Pa. He said Republicans had successfully closed the border from unauthorized immigrants, but the achievement had pushed the issue out of mind.

Mr. Johnson, typically an optimist, later in the week mused to Fox News aloud about what he might do if his party were to lose the majority this fall. “If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor,” he said.

Mr. Trump has traveled in red states, including three times to Texas over the past month, with another visit by Vice President JD Vance planned for next week. They hope to get Trump supporters who typically vote only in presidential elections to also vote in the midterms. The president has repeatedly urged them to act as though his name were on the ballot.
The challenge with that plan, said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, is that many of those voters vote on the economy.

“The lower-income, blue-collar voters that Donald Trump brought to his winning coalition for Republicans is the demographic group of voters who are being impacted most by the higher energy costs,” Mr. Shumaker said.
Recent New York Times/Siena University polls of red states show Democrats also doing well with younger voters, older voters, independent voters and Latino voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024.

Still, Republicans could flip the Kansas governorship, which Democrats have held for eight years. And Democrats face unexpectedly competitive statewide races in Minnesota, which has not elected a Republican in a statewide election since 2006, when Gov. Tim Pawlenty won re-election.
Mr. Pawlenty said the state has offset some of the tough national political environment for Republicans in part because voters there blame a spate of fraud scandals on Democrats.
“Democrats are trying to make the election a referendum on President Trump while the Republicans are trying to make it a referendum on fraud,” Mr. Pawlenty said in an email.

Democrats in states like North Carolina vividly remember past elections where they expected to win or win comfortably only to lose or win by razor-thin margins. Republicans remember them, too. Austin Barbour, a Republican strategist based in Mississippi, invoked a quote made famous by his uncle, Haley Barbour, a former Republican National Committee chairman, to describe the political climate: “It’s never as bad as it seems or as good as it seems.”

The younger Mr. Barbour said he believed Republicans would ultimately prevail in states that are historically Republican, in part because of “the level of far-left candidates that the Democrats are nominating.”
But cries about looming socialism are proving a tough sell when voters are unhappy now.

Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister who is trying to flip an Iowa congressional seat, said a farmer told her it would cost $16,000 more this year to harvest his crop because of higher diesel costs. That was after dealing with tariffs in the farm market and higher costs for fertilizer, which made spring planting more expensive.

“I was at the Labor Day parade, and I had a union member say to me, ‘My parents told me if you vote for Republicans, your life will get better,’” she recounted. “And he said, ‘It isn’t getting better: We’ve got dirty water; we’ve got cancer; we’ve got higher costs. I’m voting all Democrat this year.’”
On Friday, the Cook Political Report moved Mr. Nunn’s seat to “lean Democratic.”

Ms. Trone Garriott said the evidence that Iowa Democrats are doing well is not merely anecdotal: Representative Zach Nunn, the two-term Republican she is trying to unseat, voted in Congress last month to end the Iran war or seek congressional authorization to continue it — after having campaigned with Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, just a month earlier.

Jim Runestad, a state senator and the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said it was smart for former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, and other Republican candidates to distance themselves from the president. Mr. Rogers has supported a one-year moratorium on data center developments in Michigan and called for an end to the Iran war and to what he has called the “tariff war.”
“You shouldn’t walk in lock step,” Mr. Runestad said. “In an off-year election when the president of your party is in office,” he added, “there is always a headwind.”
The next three weeks will determine whether seeking that distance this late in the campaign season will be enough.

State Representative Carrie Rheingans, a progressive Michigan Democrat, has been campaigning across the state for Democrats including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s Senate nominee. In past election years, she said, Trump voters “wanted somebody to come in and make things different because it wasn’t working.” Now, they have been let down again, she said.
That dejection created an opening for the left. “The voters are just tired of big corporations,” she said. “They’re either price-gouging us, or they’re monopolies.”
Vince Bjorling, a retired doctor from Scottsbluff, Neb., said he planned to vote for the Democratic nominee for governor and independent candidates for House and Senate.

Mr. Bjorling, a former Republican who said he left the party early in the Trump era, said he had volunteered for a independent House campaign and had encountered “a lot of people out there who are very, very angry with the policies that the president has put forward, and also our representatives basically falling in line.”
“The tariffs were a big problem, because that created affordability problems,” he said. “The war in Iran was miscalculated and misguided, and now has led to even more affordability issues.”
Republicans “can’t run on the issues,” he said, “and they can’t run on their record.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/10/school.headline: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/10/school.author: Angelique Chrisafis

paragraphs.text: On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.

“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”

The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.

“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”

The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.

Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.

Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.

“We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”

The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.

Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.

In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.

Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.

“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”

The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.

Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.

“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.

Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.

Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.

Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”.

She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”
Students’ names have been changed

npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5920376/lee-kra.headline: The Met puts a modern artist front and center (and there's some Jackson Pollock, too)
npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5920376/lee-kra.author: Anastasia Tsioulcas

paragraphs.text: There's a new blockbuster show at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Past Continuous features two artists: Jackson Pollock, with many of his instantly recognizable "drip" paintings, and Lee Krasner, an artist often overshadowed by Pollock, who was her husband. But in this major exhibition, Krasner is finally getting her due — and on her own terms.

This gargantuan show is replete with Pollock's greatest hits, the giant, frozen dances of paint splashed on canvas that have become iconic. But this exhibition of more than 120 works (74 from Krasner, and 48 from Pollock) reveals Krasner as an Abstract Expressionist titan, too.
One of the first works that catches your eye is a 1955 Krasner collage.

"Collage was very catalytic for her at these crucial moments in her life," said Brinda Kumar, one of the two Met curators who put together this exhibition. "She was literally sometimes tearing up older bodies of work to create a new chapter."

This work is 1955's Bald Eagle, a riotous mix of browns, blacks, fuchsia, and orange, with a claw-like slash of yellow. And right in the middle is a cutout whose shape evokes the head of a bald eagle — and that's the name that Krasner gave to this collage.

Pollock's rejects were the source material for Bald Eagle, according to Kumar. "Krasner has very intentionally and deliberately cut up discarded Pollock works from this era in the 1950s, where you can see his distinctive drip still evident," she said.
When you put Krasner's collages next to Pollock's drip paintings, we see something new in the juxtaposition, said another Met curator, David Breslin.

"But that doesn't mean that the individual parts forgo their histories or their pasts," Breslin said. "We see that almost as a metaphor for couples in relationships as well. You form a unit, yet you also have all the things in your head, in your mind, in your heart that are your own, that don't change."

And sure enough, just past these collages, a visitor will see one of Pollock's classic drip paintings — 1952's Convergence, with neon orange and electric yellow so bright and bold that they foreshadow 1980s subway graffiti. The curators have put Convergence on a freestanding wall near windows, with daylight shining through — evoking the energy of a contemporary gallery.

The unspoken challenge of this show is to invite comparisons between wife-and-husband artists. In popular imagination, Pollock is often the troubled genius and hero, and Krasner is sidelined as a helpmate. She knew what people thought — but she didn't care.
In a 1978 interview on a television program called Inside New York's Art World, the interviewer asked Krasner what she was doing while Pollock was becoming so famous.

"I was working all the time," Krasner replied. "I doubt our relationship could have existed at all if I weren't working. In terms of what other people think, I can't do anything about that. You know, that's not my preoccupation anyway. As long as I was able to work, I went about my business."
That's true, but Krasner was also very savvy about her market value as a female artist, said curator Brinda Kumar.
"She was very cognizant of the gender dynamics and the gender politics. His career was the one that was more successful at the time."

To that end, she made certain calculations. They made their home in Springs, N.Y., a small fishing community on the far side of Long Island — a location Krasner chose specifically to get Pollock away from the business and booze of Manhattan. Pollock used a barn on the property to work on his enormous canvases, while Krasner painted first in the kitchen and then in a small, upstairs bedroom.
Charting her own course

Lee Krasner was all about reinvention — both artistic and personal. Born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn, she was the child of Orthodox Jewish parents who came from a shtetl in what is now Ukraine. Nobody in her family knew anything about art.

She gave herself a series of new names: first Lenore, then Lee Krasner. She sculpted a new life as a young, bold artist. And she became a quintessential networker who knew everybody in New York's art scene.

Journalist Mary Gabriel has written extensively about Krasner, including in her 2018 book Ninth Street Women: Lee Krasner, Elaine de Kooning, Grace Hartigan, Joan Mitchell, and Helen Frankenthaler: Five Painters and the Movement that Changed Modern Art. Gabriel says that unlike her husband, Krasner kept reinventing her style.

"Krasner was so fascinating because she changed, not even by the decade. Every few years, she tries something new," Gabriel said. "She was always searching, which in a way is the most, I think, honest way to be an artist, because art is about discovery."

These include what Krasner called her "Little Images" — densely populated paintings from the late 1940s of nearly hieroglyphic looking symbols, all jostling for space on small canvases — as well as immense works she created, especially after Pollock died in a car crash in 1956. Pollock was plagued by alcoholism and depression, and he cheated on her; his girlfriend of the time was one of the passengers in the crash.

Krasner continued to be financially savvy as well. After Pollock's death, she more than tripled the price of one of his most famous works, Autumn Rhythm (Number 30), to sell it to the Met — a sum that not just set the pace for Pollock's market value, but for a tide of modern artists.
For this show, Autumn Rhythm was moved off its traditional museum wall to a freestanding display, Kumar noted.

"It is almost architectural in a way, because it's set against this slate grey color," she said. "The swirling blacks get animated in a whole new way, and the familiar teals and the familiar whites surge with a new energy."

Krasner seized upon her own new energy in the years after Pollock's death. She took over the barn studio that had been her husband's — and made giant, joyful work, brimming with life and lushness, as curator David Breslin noted.

"You see this incredible painting that's almost 17 feet wide called The Seasons, that has these forms and bodies, eyes and body parts and these things that look like vegetation sprawling out of it," Breslin said. "So she makes, almost in a contradictory way, some of the brightest, most vibrant paintings the year after his death."
And in some way, this whole show is all about Lee Krasner finally being able to claim her own space. Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous runs at the Met until Jan. 31.

npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5993688/16-cozy.headline: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list
npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5993688/16-cozy.author: Malaka Gharib

paragraphs.text: Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.

But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest.
Eat warming foods

Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook, shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup: a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more."

Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days.

Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta.
Make time for introspection

Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person? Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them."
If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health.

Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean?

"Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions.)
Create cozy vibes at home

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste, says interior designer Elaine Griffin.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen.

Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design.

Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month. "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you.
Do something indulgent for yourself

Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit, she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds.

Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing."
Create a home theater. Devika Girish, co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine, explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home.

Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies.
Recharge your energy
Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto, likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house."

If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks, says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity. If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes.

"It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain.
Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours.

"Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta.
Deepen your connections
Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move.

Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering. Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon.
Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor.

These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari, a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots.

Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions, shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you.

Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says.
Your turn: What are some creative ways you celebrate the fall season?
Email us at lifekit@npr.org with your response and full name, and we may feature your story on NPR.
This digital story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.
We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter.

persuasion.community/p/owen-zidar-eric-z.headline: Why America’s Real Wealth Isn’t in Silicon Valley
persuasion.community/p/owen-zidar-eric-z.author: Yascha Mounk

paragraphs.text: Owen Zidar is a Professor of Economics and Public Affairs at Princeton University.
Eric Zwick is the Joel F. Gemunder Professor of Economics and Finance at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.

In this week’s conversation, Yascha Mounk, Owen Zidar, and Eric Zwick discuss why the real concentration of American wealth lies with small business owners rather than tech billionaires, and whether entrepreneurship remains a viable path to upward mobility.
This transcript has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity.

Yascha Mounk: When we talk about the rich people in America, we think about Elon Musk, and you know, Sam Altman perhaps nowadays, and Mark Zuckerberg, and perhaps the Waltons and so on and so forth. But that is not where the real wealth lies in America, you argue. How is that the case?

Eric Zwick: We open the book with a very glamorous wedding. It’s a sixty million dollar wedding where the father of the bride and the parents of the bride flew all their guests by private jet to Paris. They rented out Versailles. They had Adam Levine sing the first dance. It was called the wedding of the century, and it was more expensive than Jeff Bezos’s recent wedding to Lauren Sanchez, at least per estimates from social media.

So you might have thought the road to wealth, how they got the money to have that wedding, was through Silicon Valley or through Wall Street—basically tech or finance, because that’s the typical path to prosperity that I think people have in their minds when you ask who’s really rich in America. Turns out that wealth came from a third generation car dealership. So the story of our book is a microcosmic version of that story, which is that there’s a tremendous amount of wealth that’s both more abundant than these Forbes 400 stories of tech and finance that we hear so much about, and also closer to home for many Americans than they think. Those are the everywhere millionaires that we write and talk about in the book.

Mounk: Give us some numbers on that. In your book, you take people with a net wealth of more than about five million dollars—how many of those are there in the United States? And when you put all of their wealth together, how does that compare to the wealth of, you know, the Forbes 400, the Forbes list of the wealthiest billionaires and trillionaires?

Owen Zidar: There are three million everywhere millionaires in the United States. Those are private business owners who have at least five million dollars in net worth. And if you add up their collective net worth, it’s thirteen times the total wealth of the richest four hundred people in the most recent year that we can measure, which is 2022.

Mounk: Help me understand that. You’re saying it’s business owners who have more than five million. What about a whole other category of people who are partners in law firms, on Wall Street? I was really struck—you’re political scientists, I’m a political scientist for my sins. At some point I tried to escape and did an internship at McKinsey, which obviously I didn’t tell anybody about at the time. The project that I was on that summer, for part of it, was for a pretty shitty software company that was basically fading. But the top salesperson each year would make more than a million dollars in commissions. This is not Google. This was not a software company you’ve heard of. It was not a software company that was thriving. And the top salesperson made a million a year. So presumably, do you exclude those kinds of people from that statistic? What role do they play?

Zwick: In the wealth data, when you think about how many people have more than five million in net worth—from the Survey of Consumer Finances we can get a good estimate of that—there are about five million households with that figure. Of that group, three million are private business owners, so the majority are. If you move further up the threshold, from five million to twenty-five million, then you see those working professionals who have accumulated substantial savings but maybe don’t own a stake in a company—they disappear. So private business ownership becomes more and more important the further up you go. At the $25 million, the $50 million, the $100 million threshold, you get to a point where pretty much they’re all private business owners.

There is a class of private business owner that we call a skilled service business owner, which your law firm partner would fall into. That’s an important element of the story of the rise of these everywhere millionaires—the skilled services companies where they own a stake in the upside. If it’s a boutique law firm, maybe there’s something more entrepreneurial about that than being a partner at Kirkland & Ellis. So we could have a nuanced conversation about how to interpret the behavior of those people. It’s relevant for some of the other arguments we make in the book about whether it’s labor versus financial capital that’s driving the rise of income inequality, but it is important to distinguish them for some of the conversation.

Mounk: Tell us a little bit more about where these people make the money and how they make the money. The lead example you give is an intergenerational car dealership. In a way you can say that seems like it’s inherited wealth—presumably the car dealership may have continued to expand over the generations, and in order to be able to pay for such an expensive wedding, the person running it at the moment must be doing a pretty good job. What share of these businesses are relatively new businesses? And by and large, are these people with fancy degrees from Ivy League universities? Are these people who studied marketing at the local community college? Are these working class people who started off as plumbers and then decided to take a risk and do their own plumbing company? What kind of composition does this group have, and how does that reinforce or complicate our picture of what kind of person rises to this quite remarkable wealth in America today?

Zidar: That’s a great question. In terms of inheritance, we estimate about a quarter of people in this group inherited their business. So the typical person either founded it or acquired it. And it’s a broad swath of people. The example you gave of a plumber working for ten years and then running a plumbing company is much more common. There are a lot of mundane businesses—ranging from a guy who started as a repo man repossessing cars to running one of the largest repossession companies in the country. There are some pretty large industries, like auto dealers, beverage distribution, realtors, contractors. There’s a guy who sold his business for two billion dollars in Phoenix for servicing garage doors. So it can be pretty mundane. Not all of them went to college, and especially not to advanced degrees. I think the typical one did go to college, has a college degree, but it’s often not a fancy school, because that’s just a smaller number of people. And most of them do not have advanced MBAs or other things, but the skilled services—the lawyers and that group—that subset do have advanced degrees.

Mounk: How should we think about this? I mean, one response to this is America is awesome, right? It’s a country with enormous opportunities. Even though we talk a lot about the downsides of a meritocracy, and you have to make it to Harvard in order to enter the most prestigious institutions in the country—much of which is true for a certain set of institutions and a certain set of career aspirations—here are these millions of people. You start out as plumbers, or servicing car garage doors, or saving up a little bit of money, investing in some business, being very good at running it, who are able to become richer than 99.99% of humans in the history of the world. What’s not to love? And hopefully some of these businesses actually do good jobs, right?

On the other hand, you might think that this amount of concentration of wealth, even if it’s not the Forbes 400 but the everyday millionaires, can have negative downstream social consequences. Perhaps sometimes they’re able to make money because they’re exploiting relationships with governments, closing off business opportunities to other people. Are you two cheers, one cheer, fifty-fifty, glass half full, glass half empty? How do we think about this?
Zwick: We were told, when we were having an earlier pitch about this book, that this is a unique time in history where being optimistic is also provocative.
Mounk: People hate nothing more than optimism. It provokes people to the bone.

Zwick: It’s amazing, right? So we’re having a little bit of fun with that, because we’re not trying to shy away from the part of the story that is kind of optimistic. There’s a part of the story where you think about the American dream—we’ll define that as people who start out with their parents in the bottom quintile of income and rise to the top quintile, achieving that kind of upward economic mobility. Going that way through an Ivy League school is a very, very rare outcome. It’s just a really small number of people who go that way, and it’s not a huge force multiplier in terms of the relative rate at which people achieve the American dream versus the base rate.

If you look at starting a business or being an entrepreneur, it’s almost an order of magnitude more common, because it’s much more accessible as a path, and it seems to be a force multiplier in the sense that if you’re up there, you’re much more likely to have been an entrepreneur than the base rate in the population. So this kind of risk-taking—starting out with relatively little, and not necessarily taking the credentialed labor market approach, the 1600 on the SAT path—seems to be a pretty important way to achieve upward mobility. And that’s something we should celebrate when people get there in ways that aren’t doing damage to society. But we should ask what are the precise ways in which they got there. That’s where there’s more nuance in the story, too.
