There are certain industries where folks at the top get really rich through maybe getting there but then erecting barriers behind them to entry or competition, so they achieve some local monopoly power. Some examples of industries we try to profile in the book would be that car dealer example, would be beer distributors. We talked about doctors and dentists, and the guilds that try to restrict what nurse practitioners and oral hygienists can do, which makes it harder to get those services and makes them more expensive. And then we get into tax policy, where we see the fingerprints of these “everywhere millionaires” littered across the tax code in ways that we find counterproductive and important for our fiscal position. So the optimism shades into realism, and it reveals problems that I think people are trying to solve, but maybe not understanding the problem as well as they should.

Mounk: One of my proudest achievements is that I was denounced in a public press release or letter or whatever by the president of the American Optometric Association for saying that you should not have to have a doctor’s prescription to get contacts, which you don’t have to in most European countries. I think some everyday millionaires took that as a threat to their ability to throw lavish weddings for their children, so they got quite upset.

But your book is very interesting to a lay reader, but it’s also a scholarly book. Tell me a little bit about the numbers here. When I’m thinking of this group of people who have over five million dollars of net worth, most of whom are business owners—how many of them grew up with a silver spoon in their mouth? How many of them worked their way up from the bottom of society in some kind of meaningful way? How many of them fall into the large middle category?

Zidar: There are different categories of how they did it. We have the set of people who started businesses, and the set of people who inherited. And it’s easier to track the people who founded a business. We have, underlying the book, the best data that anyone’s put together on entrepreneurship in America in the twenty-first century, where we have ten million entrepreneurs and can link many of them to where they came from to answer your question. The typical one did not come from a rich family—they’re often poor and middle class. Now, that’s not to say that richer kids don’t have many advantages for starting businesses—they start successful businesses at a much higher rate. But the key point is that there are so many more middle class and poor kids that even though rich kids have an advantage, once you have a large population of people, you get more numerous outcomes, even though their rate of starting one is lower than a rich kid’s.

Mounk: To make this plastic for the audience—let’s imagine that, well, by definition, 10% of people are in the top 10%. Let’s say they have twice the chance of the average to start a successful business. That’s an unfair advantage, right? We might think that’s a waste of talent and potential. We wish that everybody had the same opportunity to start a business. But even if that’s the case, then 20% of successful businesses are going to have been started by people in the top 10%. So they don’t end up taking up the majority of those successful businesses, even if they’re disproportionately likely to have done so, even if they got a leg up from having grown up in affluence.

Zwick: I can offer some specific numbers on that. That top 10% group, we think, accounts for about a third of star entrepreneurs, which we define as being in the top decile of firm performance after a few years—which is a good predictor of where you’re going to be in a decade, as a measure of star performance. And then we call the middle class, which is from the 33rd percentile of parent income up to the 90th percentile—I don’t know what your preferred definition of middle class is, but I think that’s a decently acceptable one—that’s about half, or a little bit more than half, of those star founders, coming from a group that’s about sixty percent of the population.

That gives you a sense that the relative odds from that top 10% group, compared to the bottom third group, are about six times the rate at which they become star founders. So there’s quite a lot of inequality in terms of the rate of success, which suggests that rich families are providing something to their kids. Is it financial resources? Is it occupational networks? Is it education? These are some of the questions we try to tackle and engage with, because they are founding successful companies at much higher rates than we think the underlying distribution of talent looks like.

Mounk: What about the middle group relative to the bottom group? The sort of stereotypical image of the American dream from—I was going to say the last century, but perhaps the previous century—is you start off washing dishes in a restaurant and you become a millionaire. Are people who are born in the bottom third just without a chance of making it into that group, or do they actually do pretty well too?
Zwick: About less than twenty percent of people from that bottom third become star founders. But there’s still a lot of them in that population.
Mounk: Well, obviously a lot less than twenty percent become star founders in general, presumably, but I take it you mean of the total population of star founders.

That’s a lot less depressing than you’d think, which is to say that their batting average is still more than fifty percent of the batting average of the population as a whole, if the bottom thirty-three percent end up representing twenty percent of star founders.

I have a reaction sometimes to Raj Chetty’s data where, obviously, the social origin of your parents influences your social origin, and some of his stats I’m like, yeah, that looks really bad, and some of his stats I’m like, that looks pretty good—that’s better than I’d expect. Now, obviously, we’d love to have equality totally, et cetera, I’m not saying normatively this is great, but I would bet that if I gave a multiple choice test to my very smart students and said, do you think that the bottom thirty-three percent of the income distribution has children that represent fifty, twenty, ten, five, or one percent of star founders, they would end up choosing something below twenty percent.

Zidar: I agree with you. One of the fun things about the book is that we could talk to some of these people and we include their stories. One is Dick Portillo, who grew up in the housing projects in Chicago and ended up not going to college and selling a hot dog business for a billion dollars. And then there’s another one named Saad Khan who, almost exactly like the situation you described, is an immigrant—was washing dishes, had five hundred dollars in his pocket when he came to the country to go to UIUC, ended up working at a car bumper company and becoming an owner of such a company. Toyota was an early client, and that really helped his business, and he ended up buying the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Mounk: Once you’ve talked about the social origins in all these different groups—what do they do with their money? We’ve talked about lavish weddings and so on, but what actually is the social impact of having this very large group of very affluent people? Here again, I could imagine telling a positive story where they become the sponsors of a local Little League team, very civically minded, engaged in their communities, the kind of pillars of why smaller towns—that aren’t where Wall Street is, that aren’t where the Hollywood studios are, that aren’t where Anthropic and OpenAI are located—still are able to provide amenities and have a society that holds together.

On the other hand, you could also imagine a very negative story where they use that money, first of all, to entrench their economic interests, to make sure that nobody can get contact lenses if they haven’t been to an eye doctor in the last two years. But even beyond that, to try and give their children a leg up in turn. I think there’s an interesting echo between your book and a book by Richard Reeves called Dream Hoarders—both some similarities and some differences of emphasis. Richard Reeves looks at a slightly broader group, the top 20 percent of society, and says, yes, if you’re Mark Zuckerberg, you can probably buy your kids’ way into Harvard, and that’s unfair. But when you look at why it is that the average social origin of people at Harvard is very high, that’s not Mark Zuckerberg—there aren’t that many billionaires, they don’t take up that many spots.

It is people growing up in super zip codes around Manhattan, around Washington, D.C., who have relatively ordinary jobs, make a good income, send their kids to very good schools, invest hugely in creating those opportunities for them. That’s the hoarding of opportunities—that’s actually what makes American society less mobile than it would be. So how does your argument relate to that argument?

Zwick: On your last point, I think we are suggesting that this credentialed path up through the Ivy League, those very scarce seats at those top schools, is way overweighted by this top twenty percent group when they’re thinking about how to make sure that their children have opportunities to at least become economically prosperous. That’s almost a status good more than it is a guarantee of economic success. That obsession is probably a little bit counterproductive, but it generates all kinds of weird, perverse behaviors that we see in the Varsity Blues scandal, or in some of Richard Reeves’s descriptions of that group.

Mounk: I don’t know how much of a sense you have of this, you probably don’t have statistics on it—but some of the members of this group may have aspirations of educational climbing, where they feel like if my kid goes to Harvard, that really is a feather in my cap. A lot of them may feel like, no, I want them to stay in state and get a sensible education, I want them to go and study business at the close-by campus of a state university or something like that.

Zwick: We say that they’re everywhere because, especially off the coasts, you really do find them in most cities and towns across the country. And in these places, you don’t see the same emphasis on a small number of elite schools as the goal for their kids—it’s not “Yale or die” or whatever. I think that’s an interesting observation, just thinking about what these kids end up doing. They do kind of aspire for their kids to take over the business, which is itself a challenge, because it’s hard to get your kids to be as excited about distributing garbage trucks as you maybe were. But they often stay closer to home, the kids of a lot of these everywhere millionaires, which is a different picture, but maybe not one that a lot of your listeners or folks who live in coastal markets have as much exposure to. Maybe you have some thoughts on the consumption habits, especially the first generation, this life cycle—we do spend a lot of time on that.

Zidar: It’s hard to systematically measure how people are spending their money, because one fact about the wealthy is that wealthy people don’t answer surveys. So we’ve pieced together things from real estate data, private jet data, super yacht data. And one thing that’s kind of striking is that you see inherited family firms—second and third generation folks—much more readily in this kind of high consumption, private jet and super yacht data. For some of the first generation people we talk to, often they’re rolling up their sleeves and working pretty hard initially, reinvesting a lot of their money in the business, and then as they get older you start to see more consumption. So it’s, as Eric was saying, a life cycle question of when this consumption is happening. But there are several decades when it does not look like they’re flying around on private jets.

Mounk: That’s interesting. You talked about the aspiration for the children to take over. I’m thinking about one of my favorite businesses in the United States, Absolute Bagels, up on Morningside Heights in New York. I’d thought about it previously in the context of cultural appropriation, because it was founded by Jewish refugees or immigrants to the United States, and became a very popular business. I assume it was quite financially successful—I don’t know how much money you rake in selling boatloads of bagels to people on a Sunday morning, I don’t know whether they would make the five million dollar net worth mark or not. But at some point their children decided that they didn’t want to take over the business and became, I believe, a lawyer or a doctor—or perhaps that’s just a cliché I made up in my mind. And instead the mostly Thai employees of this bagel shop decided to buy out the owners and have been running the company since. So that’s an interesting trajectory.

By and large, do the owners of these businesses aspire for their children to take them over? And by and large, do the children of these businesses take them over? Or do they say, I stand to inherit a good amount of money from mommy and daddy, and there’s no need for me to go around making sure that my crews are repairing garage doors in the right way?

Zidar: Eric likes to say private equity is the child that many of these founders never had, because if they don’t want to have their kids checking on garage doors, they can sell it to private equity. I do think there’s a lot of complexity, and we explore that in part of the book—for these family-run firms, it can sometimes tear families apart if some people want to treat it like a serious business and other people want to treat it like a bank account. That creates enormous tension, and some founders want to avoid that. So it’s not always the case that they want this to stay in the family, and there’s a huge appetite among private equity firms, and also people graduating top business schools, to buy profitable businesses and take the reins rather than starting something from scratch.

Mounk: Tell us a little bit about this private equity part of it, because I think that’s something that has really developed over the course of the last few years, or at least decades. I think most listeners, when they think private equity, imagine billion dollar deals in which a company, maybe a household name, is being taken over by private equity, and in the worst version of it, sold for scraps, has a bunch of debt loaded onto it, and the PE firm somehow makes money off it and nobody else does. I think that’s often a kind of unfair caricature. But it is true that historically, when you go back thirty, forty years, the average private equity deal was quite sizable. And what you’re alluding to is that we increasingly have had private equity firms entering into these comparatively much smaller businesses—partially with PE firms that specialize in this, and partially, as you’ve pointed out, some people who’ve gone to business school think, I know how to run a business, I don’t want to build one up from scratch, that’s a risky proposition, I don’t want to go and work for Procter & Gamble as the deputy head of strategy. Why don’t I get together some money and buy out one of those businesses, professionalize it, especially if the owner is a little bit older and hasn’t kept up over the years, hasn’t brought the business fully online, hasn’t used the latest technology, and then I can make a killing that way. So tell us about that trend, that transformation, and how it’s changing the nature of these kinds of businesses.

Zwick: We think one way of understanding the ubiquity of the everywhere millionaire phenomenon is to think about how it’s changed different institutions in society. In this chapter, we go through this transformation of private equity, which initially started, like you said, targeting large public companies where the private equity investors perceived inefficiency—your listeners might interpret that correctly as there being high-cost workers there that they want to replace with low-cost offshore workers, and doing some other things to cut costs, but without growing the business very much. That was the first generation, with a lot of debt that made it very costly, maybe for those businesses to even survive.

As that became very competitive, the returns came down in private equity in that very large part of the market, and the private equity firms looked around: where is there lots of profit, where is there a lot of growth, where are there ways to apply some of our strategies elsewhere? There are tens, if not hundreds of thousands, of mid-market businesses that are private, often first generation founders, that have grown into very successful operating businesses, but where they don’t have natural successors—the kids don’t want to take over, or aren’t there, the workers don’t want to buy it out, or maybe aren’t willing to pay anything close to what the private equity firm will, like a kid who wants to take over but also pay you for the right to do so.

So private equity has emerged in the middle market. It’s still maybe 10 to 15 percent of all employment that’s in private equity-owned companies, or something like that—it’s not the dominant ownership structure in the American economy, but it’s much more common here than in a lot of other countries, as a sort of escape valve for these businesses which might otherwise shut down if there’s nobody to take over. In these middle market cases, there’s more opportunity, maybe, to grow the business regionally or product-wise, or to professionalize aspects of it that the family hadn’t professionalized, where it’s a little bit less ugly in terms of implementation.

Although sometimes you might find the inputs are being cut on in ways that you can’t really tell—buying the cheaper salt instead of the nice Morton salt, or something like that. So you do worry sometimes that when private equity takes over, the quality of the product degrades. I think of that as a double-edged sword that creates an opportunity for a new entrant to come in and make better bagels. I was very excited to see H&H Bagels in my neighborhood, and less excited when I learned that it was because of some financial exit that maybe made it less likely that the bagels were going to be as good as the original H&H back in New York.

Mounk: How should we think about the influence of private equity here in general? I think one of the interesting things about your book is that it cross-cuts ideologically in interesting ways. You’re a social scientist just presenting this information, but in each aspect of it I find myself a little bit torn. Again, the temptation is to say this used to be honest local businesses started up by some hopefully charismatic and perhaps even charming person who worked their way up or whatever—they took a risk, they started these businesses, and now they’re being sold off to these faceless PE guys coming in from Manhattan, and they don’t care about the local community, they don’t care about the quality of a product, they just want to turn a quick buck.

On the other hand, you could say, well, actually, a lot of the time these companies are going to get bought because people see a real opportunity to grow it in some kind of way. In certain cases, that may be financed in a way that actually is free riding on various weird aspects of a regulatory framework. But a lot of the time it may be that, hey, you’re serving this area, but actually this other area would love your services. If you’re really good at providing the services, if the company has something really to offer, the company’s going to make more money and the customers in that new area are going to be happy, right? If it’s professionalizing the service—somebody set up the shop in a particular kind of way, and perhaps they have a website now, but all of a sudden you’d have a phone app and so on—well, perhaps that just makes a business better and makes customers more satisfied and so on. I assume it’s a double-edged sword. How do you puzzle through the positive and the negative ramifications of the PE revolution?

Zidar: One of the things we try to do in the book is just describe the economy as it actually is. You see many of these aspects, both of which are true. There are many cases—we’re talking about three million everywhere millionaires, and there are many industries, and there’s nuance. We’re not trying to sell a particular agenda. We’re trying to describe the wealth in America, and you see cases of both of these things. I think that’s part of the difficulty some people have digesting news, because if it doesn’t fit in a three word slogan, some political party might not run with it. But both of those features are true features of American life and private equity today.

Zwick: We have the Outback Steakhouse case, which I think is a very salient example of private equity coming in, buying a business that people kind of love the brand. I don’t know if you’ve ever been to an Outback Steakhouse, it’s probably not quite your vibe.

Mounk: I have not. At some point I need to go on a tour of fast casual restaurants, I guess. Outback Steakhouse is like at the upper end of fast casual or something like that. At some point I need to do a five-day tour where every day I eat at Chili’s, Outback Steakhouse. I’ve never been to an Olive Garden. I really can’t call myself an American until I’ve done that.

Zwick: I like to think of myself as sort of—what is the best thing on the menu at this place? And you might actually enjoy that. There are things at each of these places where you can kind of enjoy it, but it is slumming a bit. I sort of grew up in that world and kind of quite enjoyed it, and I still get back to it and have a bit of childhood memories tied to it. In that case, when the private equity company took the firm, they brought in some consultants because it was actually Bain Capital, and they brought in Bain consultants to value-engineer the menu. Instead of Swiss cheese from Switzerland, we’re going to have generic cheese. Instead of having the salad dressing made in-house so it’s fresh, we’re going to ship it in jugs. They did those kinds of hard-to-observe cost cutting things at the margin that might improve the profit margin of the business, but maybe at the expense of customers, not just at the expense of workers. We tell that story and talk about it, so people understand here’s what private equity is doing.

Then we tell the story of a different company where it was sort of a salumi manufacturer, a multi-generational business, but the next generation wasn’t really sure what to do with it or wasn’t sure about carrying it on. In this case, there was an opportunity to go national and to put it on shelves through distribution networks in places like Costco or other types of big stores that this family, which was sort of a regional business, wasn’t able to do. They didn’t necessarily sacrifice the product in that case, because the product was actually about a high quality salumi—a whole muscle salumi, not the chunks from the meatpacking kind of salumi that you’d associate with Upton Sinclair. I think they tried to preserve that aspect of it and just grow it. That’s a more positive angle. What is private equity doing there? They’re bringing a lot of capital externally. It might have taken the family fifty years to grow the business in the way that private equity is going to try and do in five to ten. Both can be true.

Mounk: Well, obviously there’s going to be enormous heterogeneity here, both in terms of individuals involved and in terms of the communities involved, but is there a way to describe the relationship between the everyday millionaire and the community in which they sit? One of the interesting things about the billionaires we imagine is they’ve kind of deracinated—they might sit in Silicon Valley or whatever, they fly around with a private jet, they probably grew up somewhere, went to college somewhere else, did the business somewhere else. There’s this idea of a homeless, elite overclass, and I think that’s actually not even true of the very richest people in the world, but it is somewhat true of the very richest people in the world.

Presumably for the most part here, we’re talking about people who have pretty strong local roots, many of whom I imagine still live in the communities they grew up in, certainly have been living in that same community for decades. By and large, we’re not talking about them living in Manhattan, despite my example of Absolute Bagels, or living in LA—they’re living all over the country. So they’re really deeply anchored in those communities, they’re in a position to do a lot of good for those communities. They also might be sort of local notables in ways that might be negative—they might lord it over those local communities in all kinds of ways. What can we say about what that looks like in day-to-day social practice?

Zidar: I think that’s exactly right. If you look at auto dealers, for example, auto dealers bring in about twenty percent of state sales taxes. They are very much rooted in place—it’s not like you’re moving an auto dealership from this place to that place. They are in town, they’re often sponsoring Little League teams, and they also have, along with other small business owners, a large amount of trust. Small business is one of the most trusted institutions in America, way higher than Congress and other institutions. That’s a very powerful force, and I think some of that reflects some of the good aspects you were talking about. But one of the things that we try to highlight in the third part of the book is that, like all successful people, many of them try to bend the rules to their own benefit. There are tremendous advantages that auto dealers have enjoyed, and I think some of those things are things that we can shine a light on.

Mounk: The most important of which—I believe you’ll know the details much better than I do—is that in most states you cannot sell a car directly to a customer. You have to have a physical dealership. I can’t just set up a website in which I sell cars. Tesla, for example, can’t set up a website where it sells cars directly in many states. You have to have these physical dealerships.

Zidar: Yes, that’s right. There are also other things like servicing a car. If you have a dealership and say you have a Jeep, and Jeep has some recall on some part of the car, it’s very much in the dealer’s interest to bring those back, service them there, and they’re paid quite handsomely for those warranties. It can be the type of thing where they’re charging a thousand dollars, or they get a thousand dollars for every repair, but it only costs them five hundred bucks. So it’s in their incentive to just bring in as many as they can. That proprietary relationship means other competitors can’t bid down the price, and it’s quite expensive. Similarly you see that for financing—it’s often pretty hard for people, and they end up signing up for all sorts of things when they try to buy a car. Car prices are quite high in America right now, and we’re in an era of people struggling with the cost of living, and I think this is the type of stuff that actually would help address affordability in America.

Zwick: One of the things we’re wanting to do is paint this picture of the political influence of this group of people, and to put them on the map. There’s never one millionaire—there’s several in every congressional district. They’re not geographically concentrated in the same way that tech and finance as an industry, through agglomeration, are concentrated, or these billionaires who are stateless, as you say. They don’t have the same local power as this group of people who are so rooted in their communities, both in terms of employment and in terms of where their businesses are. They have natural fundraising advantages when they’re running for office.

One of the things we were so struck by was their overrepresentation in public office relative to the general population. In Congress, we estimated that about a quarter of members are private business owners. If you add law firm partners, you could get closer to 40 to 50 percent, depending on how you want to characterize some of those law firm partners. The representation at the state and local level is maybe even a bit higher in terms of its skew towards business owners. It cuts across political parties, though they tend to be more Republican. We think recognizing the natural advantages they have in running for office, what their worldviews are, what they bring to office in terms of choosing policy priorities, implementing policies that directly benefit them, or that just reflect their worldview—I think that is something that really is eye-opening for people when they think about political power in the country, because we’re so indexed on the oligarchs right now as a national conversation on political power, especially on the left, I would say. We call these people the middle-garchs, because it’s like the oligarchs in the middle market, or the Mittelstand, I guess, is your German example of that, although I think that’s a different category of people with different historical relevance. But I think that’s an important part of the book that we want to talk about.

Mounk: One kind of provocative way to put that, to sharpen the point, is that we think of the Gilded Age as the era in which the Rockefellers and the railway barons and so on dominated American life. A lot of people on the left want to say that we’re now in a second Gilded Age—that the people who are really dominating the country are the tech billionaires and perhaps a few others: Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg and all of those kinds of people. I take it that you’re saying that is really the wrong way of thinking about this moment—that, yes, they have a lot of wealth and they’re politically influential, and I don’t think you would argue we shouldn’t be thinking about them, but a much higher share of the wealth is dominated by these other people.

How does that change our characterization of this political moment? What follows if we think that this is the second Gilded Age? In what way does that misdescribe the world? In what way do we understand the world in a more helpful way if we follow your characterization?

Zidar: One concrete way to take this on is to think about the main legislative accomplishment of the Trump administration, the One Big Beautiful Bill. If you look at what it did, Elon Musk was a bit of a loser in that bill—clean energy was gutted, electric vehicle credits were not favored—and the more mundane private business owners got a twenty percent deduction preserved that made their tax rate seven percentage points lower than everybody else’s. Auto dealers got a new deduction for no reason, kind of like the mortgage interest deduction. These things added up, this plus some estate tax relief, to about a trillion dollars of tax cuts that no one talks about. The legislative action is very much a broader thing, and we want to broaden the aperture.

I totally agree that if you look at the news as of just yesterday, or even I think it was this morning, you had every AI executive at a press conference with the Speaker of the House and Donald Trump. But one of the points that we want to make is that even the Speaker of the House, funnily enough, lives in the house of an auto dealer, and there’s this broader influence if you take a step back and think about wealth and power in America. I think that helps point to some solutions that you might not get if you think it’s only a handful of people. For example, if you want to think about broadening opportunities or increasing the tax base, the tax base is much bigger when you think about fifty trillion dollars of this group rather than five trillion dollars of a small handful of billionaires.

In the rest of this conversation, Yascha, Owen, and Eric discuss the policy implications of everywhere millionaires, how artificial intelligence may affect these businesses, and whether Owen and Eric were ever tempted to pack in academia to become millionaires. This part of the conversation is reserved for paying subscribers…

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/10/h.headline: Here’s why your pay raise still leaves you feeling broke
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/10/h.author: Michelle Singletary

paragraphs.text: “I hate payday.”
Who dislikes the day they get paid for all their work?
Yet over the years, as I’ve sat across the table from individuals and couples trying to stretch their income, I’ve heard variations of that same disheartening line.
“I hate it because all my money is gone as soon as it hits my bank account,” one guy told me during a financial meeting in which I was trying to help him and his wife balance their budget.
The feeling he described is the reality for millions of households: mounting debt payments make it hard to save for emergencies, invest for retirement or achieve other financial goals.

You expect necessities — housing, transportation and food — to take up much of your pay. But non-mortgage debt (credit cards, auto loans and student loans) is steadily consuming an increasing share of what remains.

A new report reveals that, for the average worker since late 2022, debt payments have risen 14.8 percent, compared with 1.7 percent real income growth, meaning the debt people are servicing has grown eight times faster than real take-home pay, according to the Century Foundation, a progressive think tank, and Protect Borrowers, an advocacy group focused on consumer debt.

About 80 percent of working-age adults carry consumer debt, with required monthly payments claiming roughly 10 percent of after-tax household income, up from 8.9 percent at the end of 2022. Credit cards and auto loans drive nearly all of this burden, accounting for 44 percent and 40 percent of monthly debt obligations, respectively.

For a single earner, real monthly take-home pay has risen by an average of $109 since late 2022, while required monthly debt payments have increased by $57. This means 52 cents of every dollar in wage gains was absorbed by non-mortgage debt service before it could be spent on basic necessities or used to build a savings cushion.

In a dual-earner household where both partners experienced the average increase in debt payments, their combined monthly debt obligations rose by $114, outpacing their total household real income gain of $109. As a result, 100 percent (and then some) of the household’s net income gain was wiped out by rising debt obligations.

“For the average family, it really feels like we’re on the precipice of a cliff where they’re trying to manage their finances with this kind of Jenga of different types of debt,” Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the Century Foundation, said in an interview. “The rest of the economy is humming along almost without them buoyed by AI stocks.”
Without adequately considering the liabilities side of a household’s budget, “conventional measures of real earnings increasingly understate workers’ financial insecurity,” the report notes.
With the midterm elections less than a month away, affordability is on the minds of many voters. The analysis raises an important question: Is your wage growth largely an illusion?
To emphasize the drag debt has on household finances, the two organizations propose a new economic metric: Real Income Net of Debt (RIND).
The goal is to force policymakers to confront the extent to which debt is precariously propping up American households, Margetta Morgan said.

I’ve often heard critics characterize consumer debt as the result of reckless or unnecessary spending. But the data disputes that narrative. The reality is many households are turning to debt to afford the basics, such as groceries and gas.

“There are these stereotypes that debt is some kind of frivolous spending,” Margetta Morgan said. “It is absolutely unfair. What we see time and again is people making pretty rational choices ... People are putting their basic expenses onto credit cards.”

When government safety nets pull back, families have no choice but to borrow to bridge the gap. Millions of Americans, including more than a million children, have lost access to federal food assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a progressive policy organization.

At the same time, about one-third of Americans — roughly 82 million people — say they have had to make financial sacrifices, cutting back on essentials like food and utilities to cover health care expenses, according to findings from the West Health-Gallup Affordability Index.
“Families are increasingly relying on consumer debt to build their own safety nets,” Margetta Morgan said.
Auto loans are also straining family budgets. A monthly car payment that includes a comma is the new normal for an increasing number of borrowers.

A record 21.2 percent of new-car buyers took out $1,000-plus monthly loans in the third quarter of 2026, borrowing an average of $44,664, according to recent data from Edmunds, a car-shopping website. The average new-car payment rose to $787, up from $756 a year earlier.
Used-car shoppers aren’t escaping the squeeze either. The average payment was $582 on $30,703 in debt, pushing a record 6.5 percent of used-car buyers into four-figure monthly payments.

Debt taken on for basic necessities disproportionately impacts working-class families, the report said. Monthly credit card and auto payments are surprisingly similar across income tiers, but lower-income earners pay far higher interest rates for less valuable goods.
“It is much more expensive to be poor in this country, and as a result, it’s also much harder to climb out of that kind of mountain of debt,” Margetta Morgan said.

For millions of working families, student debt adds another layer of burden. Student loans currently account for just 7.5 percent of total consumer debt payments, a share that could rise as more borrowers face higher monthly payments due to recent policy changes, according to findings from the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers.

This burden is even heavier when systemic inequities are factored in. Among prime borrowers with top-tier credit scores, Black workers spend 13.6 percent of their take-home income on consumer debt service, compared to 8.4 percent for White workers.

“Black workers have to achieve a higher level of postsecondary education to get the same wages as a White worker,” Margetta Morgan said. “Right from the get-go, you’re adding to your debt burden even just to get the wages that other workers would get.”
Traditional economic metrics measure affordability by looking at wages and prices. But that leaves out the hidden siphon draining family budgets every month: debt.
Workers are losing ground as prices outstrip paychecks. When required debt service is factored in, net earnings drop even further.

Wages, inflation and debt form an economic trio that provides a fuller picture of a household’s financial well-being. Taken together, these factors explain why families feel broke in an economy that looks good on paper. The affordability crisis isn’t a hoax or a phony talking point. It’s real people looking at their bank accounts and realizing the math simply isn’t mathing.

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/magazine/mirjana-.headline: She’s Been to Gaza. She Met With the Iranians. Now She Has a Warning.

paragraphs.text: Are we already in the middle of a new world war without realizing it? That’s the provocative question I wanted to explore when I sat down with someone in the rare position to know: Mirjana Spoljaric, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The I.C.R.C. is a secretive organization that is not well known outside war zones. Unlike the American Red Cross, which deals with blood drives and American disaster relief, the I.C.R.C. is the independent and neutral guardian of the Geneva Conventions, a series of international agreements created in the wake of World War II that laid out the rules of war. In her role, Spoljaric travels to all sides of active war zones — Gaza, Ukraine, Iran — meeting with the heads of governments and armed groups alike. She rarely gives interviews because of the politically fraught and confidential nature of her work, but she sat down with me just after the most recent U.N. General Assembly because she is deeply worried about not only the growing number of conflicts in the world but also how complex they have become.

She is also speaking out because she believes that her entreaties to global leaders when it comes to the rules of war are increasingly falling on deaf ears. (We spoke before Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the government would be live-streaming a public execution — another sign that the old rules and norms are eroding.) Many world leaders “simply don’t care anymore,” she told me. “And this lack of empathy, this lack of anger, is what I find most dangerous at the moment.”

I covered wars for a big part of my career as a journalist, and the world feels more dangerous and volatile than I can ever remember. How do you see things? I see it the same way, because the statistics prove it. We now count twice as many conflicts as 15 years ago. We are at 130 international and noninternational armed conflicts that we classify in our system. That’s the highest number since the Second World War. So I think it’s time we stop admiring the problem and start acting against this.

In my own newspaper, there was a recent headline asking if World War III had already begun, and I want to speak more deeply about why those fears about a global conflict are taking root. But first, you rarely give interviews. Why are you sitting down with me now? Because I want more people to understand that we live in a decade of war. And because we live in a decade of war, we have to understand the significance and importance of the rules of war and why they need to be respected. These treaties were created precisely for times like the ones we live in. People need to understand the importance of this.

Why do you think they don’t? We hear more and more leaders say that the rules of war don’t apply anymore, and that there can’t be rules because of the pursuit of total victory. But that is not possible. In history, there has never been total victory; there has only been death and destruction, over and above what was necessary.

Is there such a thing as a necessary war? As far as I’m concerned, no. But philosophers and politicians have argued for thousands of years that war is necessary. The point is that war has always been considered as something in the pursuit of a political objective. It’s a means to an end. Today you get the feeling that war becomes the means to an end itself, and wars continue because people want to stay in power. They have created an environment where war becomes the condition under which they can continue ruling, and that’s very dangerous. You ask me whether we are approaching a third world war. Honestly, history will judge that. History books will tell us whether today we were already in the beginning, or maybe already in the middle of such a situation. The I.C.R.C. didn’t know that we were in the Second World War when it was happening.

You are one of the few people in the world who regularly travels to both sides of armed conflicts. Can you tell me where you’ve been since you took over as the head of the I.C.R.C. in 2022? I’ve been to Gaza more than once during military operations. My organization facilitated the release and return of the hostages from Gaza and the Palestinian detainees back to Gaza. I was in Ukraine. I was in Myanmar. I was recently in Iran, in Iraq. I travel to the Middle East often, but I also travel to Africa. I was in Sudan, I was in Mali. I have to go see for myself what it looks like. I need to understand what civilians endure in conflict because I’m speaking to the holders of power. I wouldn’t be credible if I didn’t know what it means to be subject to this level of violence.

Your organization is one of the few that has been allowed inside and continues to work in Gaza. International journalists, most other international organizations haven’t been given access by the Israeli government. Can you describe what you have seen? I never go to any place of conflict without people telling me that they want to stop, without people telling me that they don’t understand why this is happening. I see children without parents. I see children without arms and legs. How senseless does the world feel to you when you’re confronting these things? When you then go to the power holders and they tell you that there’s nothing that they can do, you just don’t understand. I often don’t understand what I see in connection to what I hear.

Millions of Palestinians in Gaza are now forced to live on only around 30 percent of the territory. Over 80 percent of buildings in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged. In a 2025 interview with the BBC, you called Gaza worse than hell on earth, and you described people stripped of their human dignity. Have the rules of war been followed there? What I said about Gaza is still valid today. What happened to Gaza and in Gaza to Palestinians and Israelis supersedes every legal, moral and humane standard. There are so many people complicit in what happened there and continues to happen. The worst now is the fact that people are deprived of human dignity. The perception created that if there’s enough food, that’s good enough — for some people it’s good enough to just barely survive in rubble, and for other people it is only good enough if they can return to normalcy and bring their children back to a normal school. It’s applying two standards. And this will backfire. We cannot assume that for certain people certain things are sufficient when that doesn’t apply to everybody else. You can see that by how we measure humanitarian needs in Europe in comparison to South Sudan or Somalia. Intuitively and because we can’t prevent it, we continue applying two standards.

That some human lives are more valuable than others? Yeah. I always fear that if you allow double standards, it can happen to you. You never know when you’ll find yourself all of a sudden on the other side of the line. It happened in the Second World War to the Jewish people, but it’s happened to a lot more people than we nowadays keep in mind.

I want to stay with Gaza for one more moment before we broaden out. Did the I.C.R.C. have access to the Israeli hostages while they were in captivity? Because there were horrific stories of their conditions, and one of your main roles is to make sure that detainees and prisoners are treated well. [Shakes head no] Visiting hostages is much more complicated than bringing them back. And in my opinion, they should have come back unconditionally as of Day 1. But that’s not the reality in which we operate, and so we have to work with the tools that we have. You know, there’s nothing more complex, and to a certain extent also more brutal, than hostage taking. We know that also because our own colleagues find themselves more often than they should in such situations, and we know how important it is to negotiate them out as quickly as possible. So the objective always has to be to bring the hostages back. And the longer it takes, the more complicated it becomes. I personally think that pressure should have come earlier in the negotiations. We could have saved more lives. And this was the subject of our conversations. I traveled twice to Qatar to meet with the leadership of Hamas, to sit with Ismail Haniyeh at the time. I sat with Prime Minister Netanyahu myself. These were tough discussions, and trust me, we are very frank in these meetings. This is why these meetings have to always remain confidential.

Israel has also not allowed you access to detainees inside of Israel. How have they explained that to you, and how do you then respond? Prior to Oct. 7, the I.C.R.C. has had access for decades to detainees held by Israel, and we’ve organized tens of thousands, if not more, family visits, and that’s important. Access to prisons in situations of war is extremely challenging and complicated to achieve. And at a certain point in the conflict, parties decide that for security reasons they don’t want to give us access. That’s the most common argument. But it doesn’t matter what the reason is. According to the Geneva Conventions, which all these states have ratified, they have a legal obligation to give us access, and in my opinion also a moral obligation, because we need to inform the families about the whereabouts of or the fate of their relatives. You capture a soldier, this person is detained, but a soldier is not, per se, a criminal. And no matter how you classify these situations, torture is never allowed. Never. That is clear, and this is what we discuss with those who don’t give us access.

But there’s a different reason for me to be able to go, irrespective of my legal mandate. Detention is the place where you lose your identity. When there’s no possibility to notify the families and to receive information about them, detention becomes the place of utmost deprivation of yourself. And we’ve seen more often than not that people detained under horrible conditions over extended periods of time forget who they are. When I recently visited a detention facility in Iraq, the detainees told me their biggest challenge is information. What is always most important for everyone is to have information about what month it is, what day it is, where their families are, where their children are, whether the children are safe. You’re talking to human beings.

This is a bit of a basic question, but why does it matter how you treat your enemy? Of course it matters! Because you’re dehumanizing yourself if you torture. If you tell your soldiers, “Go and kill women and children, go rape them, looting is allowed, it’s our strategy,” these people dehumanize themselves. They will never be able to return to a normal life. I listen to so many interviews of former soldiers. All of them say that what haunts them is this child that was left in the street because they weren’t allowed to turn around and collect it. That they saw it bleeding to death. It remains with you. You debase yourself. This is why soldiers have all these problems when they return. I refuse to believe that the core human essence is bad. We are good people, we want to live with people we love, we want to have children that thrive, we want to be able to build a house and know that our grandchildren will be better off than us. This is a very normal human motivation. Our motivation is not to live in rubble. How could it be?

I want to learn a little bit more about you. You are Swiss Croatian, you studied philosophy and you worked primarily in international development and peacemaking for most of your career. Why did you want to take on a job about war? Do you have memories of the war in Croatia? My first memory of war was everybody telling me about the Second World War and how they endured it. My father was born in the middle, and when he was 5 years old he had to work in the field for 12 hours in the sun for a glass of milk. He said his whole childhood was marked by the memory of being hungry. And my mother was equally traumatized. She said that every time a child died of a disease in her neighborhood, she thought that the parents were lucky, and probably happy, because there was one less child to feed. Can you imagine thinking as a little girl that somebody’s happy about losing a child because you don’t have enough food for everyone? These are the stories that marked me probably more profoundly than anything else. And then came the Yugoslavia wars and my direct exposure to the impact of conflict. I cannot imagine how anybody could say we need this war. I’m not naïve. I’m surrounded by harsh interlocutors in a harsh environment. But I still think that if you keep the people in mind, if you at all times remember that it could happen to you, it could happen to your children, you will think twice before you start the war.

You are the first woman to be president of the I.C.R.C. Do you think gender matters in how you’re dealing with conflict? When I came into office, everybody was asking, “How is it being the first woman president of the I.C.R.C. after 160 years of male dominance?” And it’s not only at the top; it’s across the institution, because it’s an organization that was created in war, for wars. Then I went to northern Mali, and for the first time an I.C.R.C. president could sit with the women in a tent, because social norms prevented my predecessors from doing the same. I felt so shaken throughout the night when I realized what is happening to women in conflict and how brutal it is, because you have an overlap of many things affecting women and depriving them of even the minimum protection that any human being should have. And that night I realized it is different when it’s a woman. If there would never be a woman at the head of these organizations, we wouldn’t be as conscious of what it means for 50 percent of the world’s population.

You’ve seen many horrible things as part of your job. You deal, as you said, in a very harsh environment. How do you protect yourself from the relentlessness and awfulness? I mean, I’ve seen you get a little emotional thinking about it. In German, we say, “I was built close to water.” I’m very emotional. I try to be hard, but it doesn’t work. Maybe it’s good that I’m emotional, maybe it’s good that I get angry when I see bad things or unjust things, because it keeps me going, it keeps that feeling alive that you have to do something.

I was thinking about the I.C.R.C. and the difficulty of staying neutral in this era — this idea of having to speak to both sides and not taking sides. There have been many accusations that the I.C.R.C. hides behind its neutrality to mask inaction. The Holocaust is a moment where the I.C.R.C. failed catastrophically to prevent or to even acknowledge the extermination of the Jews. I know your background is in philosophy. What does it mean to be neutral in the face of extreme suffering? Is there an inherent tension in that? When I started my studies, I had my thoughts. I could get impatient with the stubborn insistence on neutrality and confidentiality. I very, very quickly changed my mind when I became president myself. Having accepted this unique opportunity, I had to learn quickly and acknowledge that we wouldn’t be able to do what we do without this strict insistence on neutrality, not in the context of prisoners of war in Russia and in Ukraine, and definitely we wouldn’t have been able to bring back the hostages from Gaza. You’ve seen the pictures of our colleagues unarmed among thousands, if not tens of thousands, of armed men, surrounded by rubble from which there was no escape. We had to negotiate the terms with everyone. Nobody would have trusted us to be able to do this highly complex operation if we hadn’t defended our neutrality over 160 years. You tweak it once, you become political, and that’s it. I know it makes so many people angry, but that’s the essence of our mission.

In that context, I want to ask you about Iran. You’ve spoken with the Iranians about the negotiations [with the United States]. I understand that you cannot divulge the nature of those discussions, but I am wondering how much you can say about how this conflict may or may not be resolved. I followed the nuclear talks between 2013 and 2015 under President Obama. It became clear to me at the time how complex these negotiations were. It’s much more complicated today in comparison. The first challenge is to establish trust. We have created a world where war is not a means of last resort. It happens at any moment in a process, which leads to a situation where parties always keep that possibility in mind and always keep a high readiness and preparedness to return to conflict. That in itself is not helpful, because these negotiations will take a long time and will require a lot of compromise. But on top of this, we have created a situation that is much more complex because of the overlapping of conflicts. Today’s conflicts are not limited to a given situation. They are turning into systems.
Explain what you mean exactly. You have countries aligning over continents. You have shifts in military cooperation. You have shifts in interests and economic goals.

So Iran’s relationship with Russia, Russia’s relationship with China, the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia and Yemen with the Houthis —— And then you have the nonstate armed groups that are connected with other nonstate armed groups — ideological groups, or radicalized groups, however you want to name them, they share ideologies, they share common objectives, they align, they realign, they trade their arms, they ensure the availability of technology and cheap weapons across many countries and thousands of kilometers. So if the situation escalates in Yemen, you can be sure that it won’t remain contained to that territory for long. You already have two very important sea straits affected. So you have a lack of trust. You have asymmetric warfare that allows these conflicts to continue for an extended period of time. And on top of this, there’s a total absence of economic growth and a fast loss of development gains that have been essential for the welfare of the people in many countries of the world. Take Iraq: Over the last 10 years, the country has been recovering from very large conflicts that have had a heavy impact on society and the economy. These gains are being undone. Countries don’t have the fiscal space anymore to cope with the fallout created by continued warfare. The convergence of these trends is extremely dangerous. And now, what do we need? We need political will. We need negotiations. We need powerful politicians to have the power to negotiate.

In his recent speech at the U.N. General Assembly, President Trump threatened the annihilation of Iran by U.S. forces, speaking of this idea of trust and using war as a method of negotiation. He’s used language like that quite a bit, but it was notable to me because he made that statement at a body explicitly created to stop wars, which is the United Nations. What do you think that kind of language says about America’s understanding and commitment to these very complex, in-depth negotiations that you say are needed? You know, I started my career as a diplomat about 25 years ago in New York. And ever since, I’ve been observing eroding language. Certain things said back then would have triggered points of order. People would have left the room. There would have been outrage. I remember when Hugo Chavez spoke at the General Assembly and what reactions this triggered.

When he talked about President Bush and the smell of sulfur, implying that he was the devil. Exactly. This is a gradual erosion. But there are things being said that in certain situations could even lead to war crimes, because depending on who you are and what the situation looks like, it could entice people to do things that would actually amount to war crimes. This is why hate speech and this brutal language is so dangerous. But I’m not accusing a specific person today, because this erosion has been happening for far too long, and I’ve been alert for many years now. Every politician that uses any term that points at there being no rules and no red lines sends this signal to any person in the world that bears a weapon. You have to be conscious that as a holder of power, you have far bigger reach. Many more people hear: Oh, there are no red lines. I have weapons. I can use them.

One of the things that struck me about why we’re in such a period of global conflict is that it’s relatively easy to get into wars but increasingly hard to get out of them. So they drag on and accumulate. Are we losing our capacity to resolve conflicts? Definitely. If you don’t negotiate over 10 years, you lose the practice. It’s like being a heart surgeon. You don’t stop operating and then come back and they give you the instruments and you resume. I spoke once with a senior representative of the A.N.C. [African National Congress] in South Africa who told me: “Our adversaries never had to negotiate anything. They didn’t know how to do it, so we had to train them first before we could sit at the negotiation table.”

Undergirding this whole discussion and your call for leaders to pick up the phone is the breakdown of many democracies and the institutions that hold them together. The weakness that we’re seeing in upholding liberal democracy means that international organizations are also weak. Are you worried about the complete breakdown of the post-World War II order? Of course I am. Because that order made it possible for Europe to stay out of a third world war, to stay out of the levels of destruction that we have seen. Europe is also the leader of bad wars. I feel very bad saying that, but we have to acknowledge that European or Western history is not one of peace and security. But coming out of that rubble, there were a few people who had the foresight and courage to establish an international system that is in no way perfect but for a long time prevented the worst. I mean, everything that is written in the Geneva Conventions today is still as valid. If you had to rewrite them, you would come back with the same principles because they’re so intuitive and logical. In any society, religion, culture, nobody will tell you it’s correct to torture a child.

To come back to this idea that perhaps we might already be in this third global war without us knowing: What can we do? Let’s go back to that time when we believed in peace. Why is it so wrong to start a global movement around the notion of world peace? It’s possible. When I talk to my children, peace is not something completely away and absent for them. This is how they imagine their future. I think we have to listen to them. We have to start retreating from an overfocus on weapons, weapons systems, defense technologies. But we also have to recreate a positive narrative about humanity, about peace, about coming together and working together and living together. We have to come back to recognizing that humanity is what holds us together and is something we need to protect as a priority today, because we are debasing almost everything.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/10/10.headline: He called himself the ‘most violent drunk in baseball.’ Then he found redemption.
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/10/10.author: Paul Duggan

paragraphs.text: In the 1960s and early ’70s, Sam McDowell, a six-time all-star pitcher with the Cleveland Indians, was “the biggest, most hopeless and most violent drunk in baseball,” as he said years later. His legacy was one of self-destruction, an elite major leaguer who drank himself out of the game, squandering his potential for greatness.

Then he found redemption. Five years after leaving baseball in an alcoholic haze, he finally quit drinking in 1980. Eventually he returned to the sport as a certified sobriety counselor, aiding active and former players for three decades, and he was credited with saving lives. He even got a World Series ring, in 1993, when he was an addiction consultant to the champion Toronto Blue Jays.

“I vowed … to help athletes with all my heart and soul,” he wrote in a 2022 memoir. “I had experienced the pain of losing a great career, and I would be damned if I would allow another player to throw away his if I could do anything about it.”

Mr. McDowell, who died Oct. 5 at 84, earned the nickname “Sudden Sam” for how quickly his scorching fastballs zipped past hitters. With the Indians (now the Guardians), he led the American League in strikeouts five times in six years, notched a 20-win season and, in 1970, finished third in voting for a Cy Young Award, given to the league’s top pitcher.

His death, at home in The Villages, Florida, was confirmed by his son, Timothy McDowell. In addition to his son, survivors include his wife, the former Eva Simova; a daughter, Deborah Liebling; two siblings; two grandsons; and a great-granddaughter.

At 6-foot-5 and 190 pounds, Mr. McDowell had a fluid, deceptive left-handed delivery. Long after Mr. McDowell’s playing days, The Washington Post’s Shirley Povich wrote that Sudden Sam, when at his best, had been “in many ways a valid counterpart to the National League’s pride, Sandy Koufax,” arguably the greatest pitcher of his generation.
By his own account, though, Mr. McDowell devoted more effort to planning his drinking bouts and breaking curfew on the road than he did to honing his craft.

In most of his 11 seasons with Cleveland, his admitted philandering and booze-soaked carousing — which occasionally resulted in bar fights and arrests — angered team officials, who saw superior talent being wasted. Despite Mr. McDowell’s stellar strikeout totals, he could be as out of control on the field as he was off it: He led the majors in walks five times in seven years, and in three of those seasons, he also led the American League in wild pitches.
“My arm was that of a man among boys,” he wrote. “My head and heart were those of a boy among men. My immaturity was battling my talent. … And my talent was losing.”

Mr. McDowell was traded to the San Francisco Giants in 1971, then had brief stints with the New York Yankees and Pittsburgh Pirates before being released for good in 1975. Struggling financially, a father of two with his first marriage in ruins, he spent the remainder of the decade binge drinking and posting new stats: By his reckoning, he was arrested seven times for public drunkenness or disorderly conduct from 1976 to 1980, the year he sobered up.

After a month in a rehab facility, and after working as a volunteer aide to a psychiatrist specializing in substance abuse, Mr. McDowell got an associate’s degree in sports psychology and addictions from the University of Pittsburgh. He later opened a counseling service for athletes and became a consultant to seven big league franchises.

In 1987, he joined the newly formed Baseball Assistance Team, set up by then-Commissioner Peter Ueberroth to help current and retired players facing financial or mental health crises. In his memoir, “The Saga of Sudden Sam,” written with Martin Gitlin, Mr. McDowell described the epiphany of self-awareness he experienced in recovery and the pleasure he took in guiding others out of the despair he’d once known.

Cases involving alcohol or drug abuse, emotional anguish or family strife “were turned over to me before my retirement” in 2016, he wrote, adding: “It was my job to find a solution. … I was responsible for talking players through nineteen live suicide threats and others in which the athletes were considered suicidal.”
He told the Miami Herald in 1983, “I’ve been lucky, because I believe very seriously in my heart that this had to be, that my calling in life is what I am right now.”

Mr. McDowell said that after the sitcom “Cheers” debuted in 1982, starring Ted Danson as bar owner Sam “Mayday” Malone, a skirt-chasing former big league pitcher and recovering alcoholic, he heard from a friend of his with inside knowledge that the show’s writers had loosely based the character on him. The supposed connection is a long-held popular belief, but the Athletic this week quoted a “Cheers” co-creator as saying that, while the writers admired Mr. McDowell, he was not their inspiration.
“I would say I’m better with women than he was,” Mr. McDowell once quipped to the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review.

Born Sept. 21, 1942, in Pittsburgh, Samuel Edward Thomas McDowell was a self-described “joyless boy,” one of six siblings in a household often beset by money problems. His father, who worked in a steel mill, drank heavily, he said, and his mother became an alcoholic in middle age.

“I simply plodded along as the black sheep of the family,” chronically lying and misbehaving and always craving attention, he recalled. As he later figured out, “The mixture was one part narcissism, one part depression, one part low self-esteem,” all of which festered as he got older, accelerating his descent into addiction.

As a teenager, he was a standout multisport athlete, but his parents barely acknowledged it. “Their philosophy was that praise weakened rather than strengthened offspring,” he said. Yet baseball scouts took notice. After graduating from high school in 1960 and fielding contract offers from more than a dozen big league teams, Mr. McDowell signed with Cleveland for a $75,000 bonus. Three years later, amid early performance struggles as a professional, his mental health woes deepened.
“I was gripped by a sense of hopelessness,” he wrote on the opening page of his memoir, describing the moments leading up to a suicide attempt in the offseason.

In 1964, his breakout season, Mr. McDowell finished with 11 wins, six losses and a solid 2.70 earned run average, and the following year he made his first all-star team. By 1971, though, General Manager Gabe Paul “had grown weary of and frustrated with my drunken escapades and bailing me out of jail.” Sudden Sam, then 29, was traded away, marking the beginning of the end of his days on the mound. Overall, in a career spanning a decade and a half, he compiled a won-loss record of 141-134 with a 3.17 ERA in 425 appearances.
“Baseball couldn’t take me anymore,” he once told the Post-Standard newspaper of Syracuse, New York, “I couldn’t take me anymore.”
Nor could his family in Pittsburgh. It was there, in April 1980, after he passed out drunk on his mother’s kitchen floor, that he resolved to confront his demons.

“The final crossroads had been reached,” he recalled. “Did I want to live or die? I wanted to live. But did I want to live desperately enough to act?” Within a few weeks, he was bound for the Gateway Rehabilitation Center and all the happiness ahead of him: a clear mind and sense of purpose, a new marriage and healthier relationships with his son and daughter, and a rewarding second act as a counselor, a resurrection that made him proud, he said.
“Life is a journey, and mine at one time was stormier than most,” Mr. McDowell wrote in 2022. “But now I sail in peaceful waters. It feels wonderful.”

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/us/elections/oreg.headline: Could the Oregon Governor’s Race Be a Republican Hope?

paragraphs.text: National Republicans, facing stiff headwinds in some of the most conservative parts of the country, see a ray of hope in an unlikely state: Oregon.

With Oregon’s ballots set to hit the mail next week, Gov. Tina Kotek’s quest for re-election in one of the country’s most consistently liberal states is at risk of being derailed by a conservative, anti-abortion Republican, State Senator Christine Drazan.

Conservatives are not exactly surging statewide in the land of protest frogs and craft beer. But Ms. Kotek, a first-term Democratic governor, has managed to become almost as unpopular among her constituents as President Trump, whom they denounce routinely on the streets.

“If this were just a straight-up question, ‘Do you want Tina Kotek to have another four years or not?’ she would get destroyed,” said John Horvick, senior vice president at DHM Research, a polling firm in Portland, Ore.

Oregonians haven’t elected a Republican governor since 1982, and Ms. Kotek would seem well positioned to continue that streak. She went toe-to-toe with Mr. Trump last fall over his efforts to deploy National Guard troops to Portland amid immigration demonstrations and she has already defeated Ms. Drazan once.

Yet polls show this race between Ms. Kotek and Ms. Drazan essentially tied. A recent statewide poll conducted by Mr. Horvick’s firm for Oregon Public Broadcasting found that 60 percent of potential voters viewed Ms. Kotek unfavorably, versus 63 percent for the president.

The situation in Oregon has echoes in another blue state: Minnesota. There, the Democratic lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, is struggling for a clear lead in her Senate race against a Republican newcomer, Michele Tafoya, and the progressive attorney general, Keith Ellison, is in danger of losing his re-election.

In both states, the pivotal issues are local, not national — a lingering social welfare fraud scandal in Minnesota and a sense in Oregon that the state’s post-pandemic malaise is not lifting, even as the cost of living goes up.
There’s also a political truth that Democrats risk forgetting even in a potential blue-wave year: Performance matters.
Ms. Kotek ran four years ago pledging to reduce homelessness, supercharge housing production and improve public schools, but the progress has been far slower than promised.

Ms. Kotek pushed through changes to ease construction of affordable homes, and housing starts have begun rising after falling early in her term. Still, they are nowhere near her goal of 36,000 houses a year, and the homeless population is substantially higher than when she took office.

In 2024, the most recent data available, Oregon’s fourth graders posted the fourth worst performance in reading in the country. This year, just 42 percent of third graders scored as proficient at reading and writing.
“Tina Kotek told Oregonians that she would solve the problems and challenges facing our state,” Ms. Drazan said at their first debate earlier this month. “She hasn’t.”

Priscilla Southwell, a political science professor emeritus at the University of Oregon, said she thinks Ms. Kotek “has actually done a good job with what she’s been handed.” But, she added, Oregon “is more purple than people may realize, and these are hard economic times.”

Some progressives have joined the criticism chorus, frustrated by the business-friendly recommendations from a bipartisan “prosperity council” she convened to tackle economic issues and her 2025 calls to reduce a tax on high earners that funds one county’s universal preschool program.

In a second term, Ms. Kotek has promised to bring Oregon schools up to the national average for instructional time, expand child care and affordable housing, create a new state commerce department to spur economic growth, and halt new data centers until the state passes its own standards. Her campaign pitch unwittingly echoes Vice President JD Vance’s: Just give her “more time.”
“I’m not satisfied, either,” Ms. Kotek said at the recent debate.

When it comes to Ms. Drazan, Ms. Kotek has been mostly focused on the president. One ad deemed the Republican his “right hand.” At the debate, the governor mentioned him so many times Ms. Drazan accused her of helping at-home viewers play a drinking game.

In the State Legislature, Ms. Drazan sponsored bills to bar transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams and to end Oregon’s pioneering universal vote-by-mail system. She opposes abortion, though she has said she would not challenge Oregon’s statutory abortion protections, which are among the strongest in the country.

Last fall, as Mr. Trump’s attempt to deploy federalized National Guard troops to Portland prompted demonstrations and a court challenge, Ms. Drazan accused state and local leaders of allowing “violent mobs and domestic terrorists” threaten federal agents. She’s banking on Oregonians, particularly suburban and rural voters, being tired of the homeless camps and empty storefronts in Portland lingering six years after the pandemic.
The candidates agree that Oregonians are hurting financially. Ms. Kotek has emphasized decisions made in Washington. Ms. Drazan points to the State Capitol.

The two candidates have a rivalry that stretches back before the 2022 campaign, when Ms. Kotek won 47 percent to 44 percent of votes. That lent a personal edge to the frowns, head shakes and mutual accusations of dishonesty that peppered their first debate.

As the State House Republican leader, Ms. Drazan used walkouts and other procedural tactics to block or slow Ms. Kotek’s legislative agenda. In 2021, Ms. Drazan accused Ms. Kotek of reneging on a deal to give Republicans equal representation on a redistricting committee in exchange for ending their delaying tactics.

History suggests Democrats and independents will “come home” to Ms. Kotek. Polls around this time four years ago also suggested a closer race than the final result., and a new poll from The Oregonian shows movement toward the governor and a slight Kotek lead. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report still says the race leans Democratic in a state where Republicans make up just 24 percent of the electorate.

Ms. Kotek also has a substantial financial advantage — her campaign has $3.4 million to spend, compared with nearly $2 million for Ms. Drazan’s. And Ms. Drazan has yet to receive any contributions from the one person in Oregon who could close that gap: Phil Knight, the Nike co-founder and frequent Republican donor.

The story of the science of dementia began on an autumn day in 1891, when a 71-year-old man was admitted to the psychiatric hospital at the University of Prague. The man, referred to as August H. in his medical file, had periods of freezing up mentally, sometimes fainting and not coming to for several minutes. More recently, he had been prone to fits of rage, and even threatened his wife with a knife, shouting that he was going to kill her.

The case caught the attention of the director of the clinic, Arnold Pick. After August H. died, Pick’s team examined his brain, dividing it into sections and weighing them and checking for abnormalities. The brain seemed essentially normal except for signs of decay, or atrophy, in one self-contained place: the left temporal lobe.

This was quite likely the first recorded moment that a scientist, staring at a piece of brain tissue, saw dementia as a problem to be understood and solved, rather than a natural, unavoidable part of aging. Until then, almost everyone, including Pick himself, had taken it as an article of faith that dementia, or senility, was a generalized condition, the sign of a brain in overall decline. But after seeing August H.’s brain, Pick began to search for and document other dementia cases in which the problem wasn’t aging, but this specific part of the brain that was starting to lose function and misfire.
His observations might have fallen into obscurity had they not come to the attention of one of his counterparts in Germany — Alois Alzheimer.

Pick’s clinic, in Prague, existed far from Germany’s well-known neurology centers. But Alzheimer was plugged in to a community of cutting-edge researchers in Frankfurt and, later, Munich, specialists in microscopy and histology who could analyze sections of a brain under a microscope by staining the samples on glass slides.

While Pick’s consequential patient was August H., Alzheimer’s was a woman named Auguste D. She arrived at the Frankfurt hospital where Alzheimer worked in 1901, when she was only 51 years old. Out of nowhere, it seemed, she had flown into fits of jealousy toward her husband, then suffered a rapid loss of memory. She got lost in her own apartment, carried things back and forth incessantly and then hid them, and became convinced someone was trying to kill her. After she died in 1906, Alzheimer found something strange in her brain cells, which he examined under a microscope.
