Instead of buying thousands of GPUs, early-stage startups with limited capital can borrow them for hours at a time for less through clouds. And for companies with heavy-duty computing needs, Oracle's new route might be more attractive than building whole data centers. OpenAI committed to spending over $300 billion with Oracle over five years, but it hasn't mentioned anything about bringing in GPUs.
OpenAI declined to comment.

The method might make sense for companies that have the capital to purchase AI chips but don't have enough power, data center space or skilled labor. Like its hyperscaler peers, Oracle works hard to secure all three in healthy quantities.
Tactical deals
Another emerging option is to cut large deals with firms that have truckloads of GPUs for rent.
SpaceX arranged to turn over excess capacity in separate deals with hyperscaler Google and open-source startup Reflection.

In April, SpaceX agreed to provide Cursor with GPUs and then bought the AI coding startup outright for $60 billion. And in May, SpaceX landed a deal to rent GPUs to Anthropic for $1.25 billion each month through mid-2029. That's more than what most startups can afford.
For SpaceX, though, the numbers work out nicely.
"The current economics have translated into a less than one-year payback on our new capital deployments for compute," Bret Johnsen, the company's finance chief, told analysts in August.
It's not only SpaceX. In July CNBC reported that Meta was working to form a cloud unit that could sell AI computing power.
Going old school
Meanwhile, companies continue to install GPU-filled servers in on-premises data centers the old-school way as CEOs work to balance capability with cost control.

Revenue nearly doubled in the enterprise and small and medium business parts of hardware maker Lenovo's Infrastructure Solutions Group during the June quarter. "We're seeing more and more enterprises now starting to say, 'How do I bring AI into my four walls?'" said Vlad Rozanovich, a senior vice president.
The hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March, according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes.
Collaboration software maker Dropbox relies on GPUs in its data centers, CEO Ashraf Alkarmi said.
"If we want to do a lot more, I think our supply chain connections will still be beneficial and a structural advantage," he said.
Everpure, which sells data center storage hardware and software, has acquired its own GPUs, to run open-weight AI models for the company's software engineers, said CEO Charlie Giancarlo.
"In a very dynamic pricing environment, it's always good to have multiple sources that you can go to," he said.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: 15 most extreme Method acting performances: Jeremy Strong to Jared Leto
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Laura Zornosa

paragraphs.text: The one consensus about Method acting is that it’s controversial. Other than that, everything’s up for debate: What is Method acting, exactly? Do actors and audiences love it or hate it? And, perhaps most importantly, who can afford to practice the technique?

Method acting is a technique in which an actor embodies a character absolutely, usually both on- and off-camera, for months at a time (and sometimes, as in the curious case of Austin Butler’s Elvis accent, beyond the project itself).

Some actors, like those in the list below — including Daniel Day-Lewis, Christian Bale and Robert De Niro — swear by it. But others — like Brian Cox, Toni Collette and Robert Pattinson — eschew the practice. (Collette called it “total bulls—” and “utter wankery,” and Jennifer Lawrence said working with a Method actor would make her nervous.)

Female actors — like Charlize Theron, Kristen Stewart, Natalie Portman, Anya Taylor-Joy and Ellen Burstyn — have pointed out that it’s a luxury they can’t afford. (“I don’t think that children or partners would be very understanding of, you know, me making everyone call me ‘Jackie Kennedy’ all the time,” Portman said about portraying the first lady.) And Black actors — like Brian Tyree Henry and Omari Hardwick — have said they wouldn’t be able to do it safely. (“I’ve never gone full Method,” Hardwick said. “I don’t want to be pulled over while ‘driving while Method.’ … I’ll get in trouble for that. That’s scarier.”)
Jeremy Strong — who plays Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning” — recently defended his commitment to Method acting. Here are some of the most extreme Method acting performances of all time.
Jeremy Strong (again)

Strong is known for his unrelenting adherence to Method acting, especially on the set of “Succession.” (“The result that Jeremy gets is always pretty tremendous,” his TV dad Cox told the New Yorker in 2021. “I just worry about what he does to himself. I worry about the crises he puts himself through in order to prepare. … It’s a particularly American disease, I think, this inability to separate yourself off while you’re doing the job.”)

This tendency held true on the set of “The Social Reckoning” too. “He showed up walking like Mark, talking like Mark,” director Aaron Sorkin told Entertainment Weekly. “I heard crew members on set call him Mark. I never heard him use his own voice until after I called ‘cut’ on his last shot.”
“I’ll be honest, I think this isn’t just the way he likes to do it,” Sorkin added. “I think it’s the only way he knows how to do it.”
Andrew Garfield
Then there are those who argue that the Method is misunderstood — first by actors, and subsequently by public perception.

“I’m kind of bothered by this idea that ‘Method acting is f— bulls—,’” Andrew Garfield said on the “WTF With Marc Maron” podcast in 2022. “No, I don’t think you know what Method acting is if you’re calling it bulls—, or you just worked with someone who claims to be a Method actor who isn’t actually acting the Method at all. It’s also very private. I don’t want people to see the f— pipes of my toilet. I don’t want them to see how I’m making the sausage.”

Garfield employed the Method in Martin Scorsese’s 2016 historical drama “Silence,” in which he played a 17th-century Portuguese Jesuit missionary who goes to Japan. He studied Catholicism with Jesuit priest James Martin, partook in the 31-day Ignatian Spiritual Exercises and denied himself food and sex.
Al Pacino

On that same podcast, Garfield praised two actors known for applying the Method well and seemingly with respect — to the craft and those around them: Al Pacino, especially in “Dog Day Afternoon,” and Robert De Niro, most notably in “The Mission.”

In “Dog Day Afternoon,” Pacino played Sonny Wortzik (based on John Wojtowicz), a first-time crook whose attempt to rob First Brooklyn Savings Bank goes awry and devolves into a hostage situation. Pacino backed out of the role three times before committing (though he later won a BAFTA Award for the performance).
Producer Martin Bregman attributed this hesitancy to Pacino’s Method acting, saying this might have been a world the actor didn’t want to explore, as “no major star had ever played a gay.”

“Scarface” drug kingpin Tony Montana is also considered the pinnacle of Pacino’s Method acting. “I’ve never been that committed to a role,” he said, also on “WTF With Marc Maron.” “I mean, I was there. I said, ‘I am this guy.’”
Robert De Niro

In “The Mission,” De Niro stars as Captain Rodrigo Mendoza, a mercenary, slave trader and guest of the Spanish governor of 18th-century Paraguay. Jeremy Irons co-stars as Jesuit priest Father Gabriel, who challenges Mendoza to undergo penance.
De Niro channeled real-life tension with Irons — who he didn’t want cast for the role — into on-screen animosity between the two characters.

And then there’s “Taxi Driver” — for which he got a real New York City cab license and drove 15 hours a day for a month — and “Raging Bull” — when he trained with the boxer he portrays, Jake LaMotta, for over 1,000 rounds — making him a quintessential Method actor.
Lady Gaga

There are also counterexamples of the limitations Method acting often places on women and actors of color. (Theron told The Times in 2020, “I can’t do the Method thing. I did it once, for ‘Devil’s Advocate,’ and I was just exhausted. It was really hard to go to those deep, dark places because I was so tired.”)

Lady Gaga, though, lived as Italian socialite Patrizia Reggiani for a year and a half while working on “House of Gucci.” She spoke with a thick Italian accent for nine months, both on- and off-camera.

“I was either in my hotel room, living and speaking as Reggiani, or I was on set, living and speaking as her,” Gaga told British Vogue. “I remember I went out into Italy one day with a hat on to take a walk. I hadn’t taken a walk in about two months and I panicked. I thought I was on a movie set.”
Jared Leto
Jared Leto also starred in “House of Gucci,” as Paolo Gucci, who aspires to be a designer, despite his apparent lack of talent.
“He works in a very similar fashion,” director Ridley Scott told Vulture. “Once he goes in, it’s like he’s immersed, and he doesn’t come out and breathe for air until he’s finished.”

Leto is infamous for his extreme and controversial approach to the Method. As the Joker in “Suicide Squad,” he sent bizarre “gifts” — a live rat, a dead pig, bullets, anal beads and used condoms — to co-stars Will Smith and Margot Robbie to create a dynamic of “surprise and spontaneity.”

“Leto’s Joker is the latest evidence that the prestige of method acting has dimmed,” essayist Angelica Jade Bastién wrote in the Atlantic, “thanks to the technique’s overuse by those seeking award-season glory or a reputation boost, as well as its history of being shaped by destructive ideas of masculinity.”
Joaquin Phoenix

The Joker seems to elicit intense psychological commitment like moths to a ghastly green flame. Joaquin Phoenix didn’t quite go Method to play him in “Joker” and “Joker: Folie à Deux,” but he shed 52 pounds for the role.

“And, as it turns out, that then affects your psychology,” Phoenix told the Daily Beast. “You start to go mad when you lose that amount of weight in that amount of time.” (Heath Ledger walked that same fine line for “The Dark Knight.”)

For his role in “The Master,” as Freddie Quell, a World War II Navy veteran struggling to adjust to a postwar society, Phoenix forced himself to talk out of one side of his mouth by asking the dentist to fasten metal brackets to his teeth.
Jamie Foxx

Taylor Hackford, the director of “Ray” — a biopic about Ray Charles — asked Jamie Foxx, who starred as the blind soul musician, to have his eyes glued shut. This was not Foxx’s idea (perhaps a key tenet of the Method), but he agreed to it.

“Imagine having your eyes glued shut for 14 hours a day,” Foxx, who won an Oscar for his performance, told the New York Times. “That’s your jail sentence.” For the first two weeks of filming, the actor suffered panic attacks, until he eventually got used to the claustrophobic sensation.

Years later, on the set of “Django Unchained,” Foxx and co-star Leonardo DiCaprio discussed embracing Method acting to help both of them better handle the disturbing material. (DiCaprio plays the ruthless owner of a plantation where Foxx’s character’s wife is enslaved.)
Leonardo DiCaprio

The film for which DiCaprio finally won an Oscar (after four previous lead actor nominations, plus one for supporting actor) was also his most Method approach. As fur trapper Hugh Glass in “The Revenant,” DiCaprio crawled inside of a prop horse carcass, ate raw bison liver (despite being a vegetarian) and endured freezing temperatures, his icy breath fogging up the camera lens.

Like Phoenix, DiCaprio might not be a traditional Method actor, but he comes quite close. In 2016, after his “Revenant” nom, Agnieszka Holland — who directed DiCaprio in “Total Eclipse,” before he filmed “Romeo + Juliet” — reflected on his technique.

She said he has never been a classic American Method actor, instead relying on personal experience. “But he’s doing some trick which is pretty mysterious to everyone watching — frankly even for the director,” she told the BBC. “Look at him on screen and, for the moment of the shot, he really becomes the character.”
Montgomery Clift

And then there are the true, original Hollywood Method actors. Montgomery Clift, Marlon Brando and James Dean are considered to have christened the technique in the 1950s. Even Clift, though, expressed reservations about the term when asked about it — “Method acting,” as it turns out, is a contentious phrase.

Method acting began with Russian/Soviet theatermaker Konstantin Stanislavski in the 1930s. From there, acting coach and actor Lee Strasberg — who co-founded the Group Theater — largely coined “the Method” in America. Group members Stella Adler and Sanford Meisner eventually left and rejected parts of Strasberg’s technique. All three of them approached the Method slightly differently, and became prominent acting teachers.

Clift was among the first actors invited to study in the Actors Studio with Strasberg and Elia Kazan. His role as George Eastman, the poor nephew of a rich industrialist, in “A Place in the Sun” is considered a landmark Method acting performance.
Marlon Brando

Clift and Brando were both contemporaries and, at times, acting rivals. But Brando was so moved by Clift’s performance in “A Place in the Sun” that he voted for him to win the 1952 Academy Award for lead actor — Clift, meanwhile, voted for Brando to win for his role as Stanley Kowalski in “A Streetcar Named Desire” the same year. (Humphrey Bogart ended up victorious for his role as Charlie Allnut in “The African Queen.”)

“A Streetcar Named Desire” — both the original 1947 Broadway production and the 1951 film adaptation — was directed by Actors Studio co-founder Kazan. Brando also starred in both versions, and, though his performance was temperamental, Kazan said: “Marlon was living on stage. … A performance miracle was in the making. What was there to do but be grateful?”
James Dean

James Dean only got the chance to star in three films — “East of Eden,” “Rebel Without a Cause” and “Giant” — before he died at 24, and the latter two were released after his death. Prior to all three, though, he also studied at the Actors Studio under Strasberg.

In “East of Eden,” also directed by Kazan, Dean played the wayward young man Cal Trask, who competes against his (favored) twin brother (played by Richard Davalos) for the affection of their pious father. Dean had a turbulent relationship with his own dad, and his mom died when he was 9. (The Trask brothers’ mother is ostensibly dead too.)

“One of the things that made [Dean] noticed,” actor Martin Landau told PBS, “was his vulnerability. He understood a mother he didn’t have. … ‘East of Eden’ was like a chance to meet his mother again, if one accepts that.”
Daniel Day-Lewis

Daniel Day-Lewis is perhaps the closest contemporary follower in Clift, Brando and Dean‘s footsteps. He has won a record three Academy Awards for lead actor, including in 1990 for his iconic performance as Irish writer and painter Christy Brown in “My Left Foot.” (Day-Lewis beat out Tom Cruise in “Born on the Fourth of July,” Morgan Freeman in “Driving Miss Daisy” and Robin Williams in “Dead Poets Society.”)

Brown, who was born with severe cerebral palsy, could not walk or talk, was wheelchair-bound and only had control of his left foot, which he used to paint and write. Day-Lewis refused to stand between takes, remaining in his wheelchair, and made production assistants feed him by hand. He is now renowned for his Method acting, grueling process and devotion to his roles.
Christian Bale

Another Method actor who rejects the label, Christian Bale is oft-associated with extreme physical transformations and intense focus onset, including in “American Psycho” as serial killer Patrick Bateman and in “The Machinist” as sleepless industrial worker Trevor Reznik.

Bale lost more than 50 pounds in four months to play the machinist, paranoid and deluded after being unable to sleep for a year. Bale’s daily diet consisted of black coffee, an apple and a tin of tuna.

But in 2011, Bale told the Mirror: “At the end of the day, I’m faking it. Pure imagination. I never took any classes, I just go, ‘I better wing this one and make it up!’ Everybody talks about the process too much. The interesting thing about a movie is the movie.”
He also shed or gained substantial weight for his roles in “The Fighter,” which earned him an Oscar; “American Hustle”; “Vice”; and “Ford v Ferrari.”
Austin Butler

Eight months after “Elvis” hit theaters in June 2022, Austin Butler — who starred as the King of Rock and Roll — said he would finally drop Presley’s deep Southern twang. (That came after fans noticed the Elvis accent creeping in during his Golden Globes acceptance speech, “Saturday Night Live” monologue and “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” appearance.)

“It’s funny to me because I don’t even think about it,” Butler told The Times after his Oscar nomination for the role. “I guess after three years of doing everything that I could to focus on this one goal of trying to bring life to Elvis in this film, I think that there’s certain muscular habits that must pop up.”

Once again, though, Butler wouldn’t use the term to describe himself. “I never have used the word ‘Method,’” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “I think that word gets thrown around a lot. It’s a very misunderstood thing that isn’t really what I do. … It’s more that I just like to immerse myself.”

npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5996652/glp1-fd.headline: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5996652/glp1-fd.author: Yuki Noguchi

paragraphs.text: Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.

In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."

The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION, for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.

Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.

More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.
Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.
His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.
In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.

The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.

When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it. The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.
A partial database

The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events. It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.

In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.

Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.
The legal challenge

That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.

It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."

Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."
NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)

Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."
Uncertainty in reporting

Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.

That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.
He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.
"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."
Calls to poison control
The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.

Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.
"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.
These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.
But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed
"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.
NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/10/peru-e.headline: Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/10/peru-e.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.
The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.
The candidate from the leftwing Ahora Nación party won 229 out of a total of 663 votes in elections on 4 October, according to the national office of electoral processes.
His closest rival, the far-right candidate Gaspar Osorio, received 204 votes.
Flores, who works in freight transportation, had belonged to Popular Force, the party of Peru’s rightwing president, Keiko Fujimori, until 2025, according to electoral authorities.
Despite the name being associated with Germany’s Nazi leader Adolf Hitler, several candidates with the name have won elections in Peru.
In 2021, the doctor Hitler Saavedra Casternoque was elected to parliament for the centrist party Somos Peru.
In 2018, Hitler Alba Sánchez was voted in as mayor of the Andean district of Yungar, saying during his campaign that he was “the good Hitler”.

That moment in a movie theater when the lights go down is such a sacred threshold. When the chattering and fidgeting fade and the crowd goes silent, there’s a feeling of shared anticipation, like we’re all embarking on an exciting trip.

That experience was amplified last week when I was in an audience of more than 1,000 people for a screening of the new documentary “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.” The film features Winter, the dazzlingly talented 24-year-old singer-songwriter and frontman of the band Geese, alone at the piano and singing. The performance was, as my colleague Lindsay Zoladz wrote, “utterly magical.” But equally magical for me was the experience of seeing a movie with that many people, in this case at Lincoln Center during the New York Film Festival. A bunch of strangers agreeing to be silent and focused on a screen as a communal activity — so rare in an age when we’re so frequently staring at our own personal screens.

Fall always lures me to the theater, a combination of the awards-season deluge of exciting films and a formative adolescent memory of emerging from a matinee of “Stand by Me” and noticing the changing October light. As I do each year, I’ve made a list of what I want to see, a sort of cinematic advent calendar. October alone could sate even the most insatiable cinephile.

This weekend, one could do a technology double feature, with Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” his follow-up to the 2010 Facebook thriller “The Social Network,” and the four-hour documentary “Musk,” about the world’s richest man. I’m also interested in the Romanian director Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as a conservative couple who are accused of abusing their children. Our critic Alissa Wilkinson told me it’s great and “provocative on purpose.”

If you’d prefer not to be provoked, or provoked in a different way, next weekend brings the arrival of a new adaptation of “Sense and Sensibility,” starring Daisy Edgar-Jones. There are also two exciting nonfiction films coming Oct. 16: “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” about a 1972 party at Duke Ellington’s apartment that reunited leading lights of the Harlem Renaissance, and “You Can See Everything,” the buzzy, three-hour documentary about the founder of the fraudulent blood-testing company Theranos, from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

On Oct. 23, “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” opens, a thriller starring John Turturro as an aging thief who gets mixed up with a dangerous crime family. “Small New York films don’t always get made anymore,” Alissa noted, praising this one’s fidelity to the geography of the city. There’s also Taika Waititi’s “Klara and the Sun,” based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel, whose trailer is creepily compelling. It’s about an A.I. companion, played by Jenna Ortega.

If you prefer your fantasies more fantastical, “Wicker” stars Olivia Colman as a medieval fisherwoman who commissions a local basket-maker to weave her a husband. The husband is played by Alexander Skarsgard; as soon as I learned this, I could not conceive of anyone more perfect to play a person made from woven plant fibers.
And there are more films to look forward to later in the year — “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall” opens on Nov. 20.
HURRICANE ISAIAS

The storm’s eye came ashore about 8:30 p.m. Central time on Friday near Destin, Fla., lashing the Gulf Coast with heavy rains and howling winds that toppled trees and flooded highways. Follow our live coverage here.

It landed with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour as a Category 2 hurricane, but dropped quickly over the next half-hour to a Category 1, with winds of 85 m.p.h. By early this morning, it had downgraded further to a post-tropical cyclone. At one point on Friday, the storm had reached Category 3 status. Read about the science behind its rapid intensification.

Isaias is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, which has been relatively quiet partly because of a powerful El Niño. And it is the first hurricane in two years to strike the mainland United States.
More on the storm:
• Beach towns on the Alabama coast typically spend early October preparing for the season’s biggest event: the National Shrimp Festival. This year, the hurricane “ruined all of that.”
• See how sky-high weather balloons helped meteorologists understand the storm.
• As Isaias approached, forecasters were confronted with a striking split in their data: The traditional models said one thing, and experimental A.I. models said another.
THE LATEST NEWS
• Republicans are suddenly racing to defend a Senate seat in Kansas, where polls show Democrats with a real chance for the first time in nearly a century.
• More Democrats are confident there will be a blue wave in November. But history shows that such waves can produce notably different outcomes.
• President Trump has attacked the integrity of U.S. elections on more than 70 percent of the days since he returned to office. See how he does it.
• President Trump said he had reached an agreement with Vladimir Putin of Russia to immediately import Russian diesel into the U.S., despite a Russian ban on fuel exports.
• He also said the White House would investigate Lisa Cook, a governor at the Federal Reserve, on accusations that she committed mortgage fraud.
• Vice President JD Vance said he would not watch the Pentagon’s planned execution of the 2009 Fort Hood shooter and cast doubt on whether the plan would go forward at all.
• Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator, was named the next White House press secretary.
• Millions of people with private Medicare coverage are being forced to change their insurance for next year and will face higher premiums.
• Trump has started sending $500 “refund” checks, along with a signed letter taking credit for the payments, to Americans enrolled in Obamacare.
Around the World

• Investigators in the United Arab Emirates said that the co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai flight had intended to carry out a Sept. 11-inspired suicide mission by crashing into an Israeli airport.

• Leaders of the Gen Z protest movement in India said they were detained in New Delhi. Demonstrators across the country had been met with walls of security forces as they tried to agitate against changes to the voter rolls.
• Houthi attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s capital, killed three people.
• Israel denounced the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a human rights lawyer who chaired a commission that found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
• The New York Police Department released body-camera footage from officers who arrived on the scene after an ICE agent shot a man in his car Thursday. Watch it here.
• Mike Ditka, the Super Bowl-winning, sideline-shouting coach of the Chicago Bears — known to many as “Da Coach” — died at 86.
• The F.B.I. arrested a man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of carrying out the computer hack that stole sensitive information about thousands of the agency’s employees.
GAME OF THE WEEK

Chicago White Sox vs. Cleveland Guardians, Game 5: There’s probably no Major League Baseball team having more fun than the White Sox. They have one player who swears that ice cream cones are good luck, another who wears a wizard hat in the dugout, and the whole team dances before games. It’s strange, but apparently effective: No other team in baseball history has emerged as a playoff contender after three straight 100-loss seasons. (The South Side squad really was the laughingstock of baseball a few short years ago.)

Now, the White Sox are on the road for a do-or-die American League division series game against the Cleveland Guardians, whose offense proved dominant earlier this week. The winner will head to the semifinals; the loser will be done for the year. First pitch is tonight at 8 p.m. Eastern. — Matthew Cullen
THE WEEK IN CULTURE
Film and TV

• The Tom Cruise film “Digger” bombed at the box office. David Gelles, host of our climate newsletter, says it should nonetheless be recognized for its go-for-broke attempt to dramatize the catastrophic effects of climate change. Sign up to get Climate Forward delivered to your inbox.
• “Fjord,” which won the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival and opened in the United States this weekend, is morally ambiguous. Some viewers don’t like that.
• Hear Aaron Sorkin explain how he evolved Mark Zuckerberg’s character in “The Social Reckoning,” the sort-of sequel to “The Social Network.”
• Karol G, the Medellín-born singer, became the first Latin woman to headline Coachella. On the latest episode of Popcast, she discusses her fame and Spanish-language music.
• A North Carolina man was sentenced to 18 months in prison for using A.I. to defraud streaming platforms and musicians of millions of dollars in royalties.
RECIPE OF THE WEEK
One-Pan Roasted Vegetables and Polenta

Yewande Komolafe lets the oven do most of the work in her colorful one-pan roasted vegetables and polenta. To make it, she bakes cornmeal, brussels sprouts and sweet potatoes together until the polenta is thick and porridge-like and the vegetables are thoroughly tender. Then she runs it all under the broiler to crisp and brown the edges. A little fresh lemon juice right at the end adds brightness, while some crumbled goat cheese lends a creamy tang. It’s a cozy early autumn meal.
REAL ESTATE
The Hunt: Even after stretching their budget, a family couldn’t buy their Southern California home from their landlord, so they moved to New York’s Hudson Valley. What did they find? Play our game.
What you get for $900,000: A Tudor Revival in Salt Lake City, a farmhouse in Woodbury, Conn., and a Craftsman in Denver. Which would you choose?
LIVING
Repurposed: Two architects transformed a Cold War-era radio tower that once served as the set for a zombie movie into a unique home. Go inside.
“Looks messy, helps frogs”: A backyard pond can promote biodiversity, especially during the winter. Learn how.
ADVICE FROM WIRECUTTER
Make a cheap but fun Halloween costume
You don’t need to spend a fortune to whip up a fun, easy Halloween costume. Start with stuff you already own.

My colleague easily made a Kermit the Frog meme costume with a green T-shirt, a glass mug and felt triangles. A tube of red lipstick smudged around the mouth could turn you into a vampire. Finally, there’s a whole genre of fun “attach a thing to a shirt” costumes. A few colorful balloons on a tee, and suddenly you’re a bunch of grapes or a gumball machine.

If you do buy something, make it something you can use it for non-costume purposes in the future. While we’re on Halloween: We found some great, non-junky decor that’ll charm and spook for years to come. — Annemarie Conte

Thanks for spending part of your weekend with The Times. — Melissa

theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/10/good.headline: Even Good Friends Can Be Bad Texters

paragraphs.text: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

“Forgive the bad texters,” Julie Beck wrote in a recent Atlantic essay. Beck is one of them: She routinely leaves messages unanswered for days or even weeks, not because she doesn’t care but because she gets distracted, is burned-out, or simply forgets. Yet in a world where everyone is expected to be constantly reachable, a delayed reply can easily be mistaken for indifference.

Texting has made staying in touch easier than ever, but it has also turned communication into a near-constant obligation. A third of Americans report feeling overwhelmed by the number of texts they need to respond to, Beck writes. People have felt guilty about unanswered correspondence for centuries, but technology has escalated both those expectations and the anxiety that comes with meeting them.

Being a good texter, Beck suggests, isn’t the same as being a good friend. Someone who takes days to reply might still be the first to show up when you need them. So the next time a friend leaves you on read, consider giving them the benefit of the doubt. And if you’re the one with a growing pile of unanswered messages, maybe give yourself a little grace too.

My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “About ten years ago, I saw a Joro spider for the first time. They are an invasive species from Asia. Since that time, they have become ubiquitous in my area,” Nancy C. from Marietta, Georgia, writes. “Last year I began to notice how incredibly beautiful the adult female spiders are. Their abdomens have a gorgeous, intricate design that looks like a colorful maze. I realized that for years, I had been walking by such sublime beauty, and I hadn’t even recognized it.”
We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.
— Rafaela

cnbc.com/2026/10/10/from-bjs-to-lululemo.headline: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
cnbc.com/2026/10/10/from-bjs-to-lululemo.author: Ryan Baker

paragraphs.text: Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets.

As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs.

In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs. In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%.

Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make.
Shrink to grow

When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems.

"If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly."
Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns.

Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue.

"Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price."
Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power.

Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years.
"Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer."
Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand.
Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level.
"It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel.
He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026.

Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June.
Inventory management
For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices.
Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business.

"When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel.

BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.

"That is sourcing sales growth as well and sort of giving us the formula where we can cut SKUs, and see sales go up, and see margin dollars go up," Eddy said on the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August.

In June 2025, Dollar General said the elimination of 1,000 SKUs from the previous year opened up more shelf space for its best-selling products and added to its top line. By March 2026, the company said, it had reduced up to 1,500 SKUs, providing benefits to the overall supply chain.

"Being more productive there means getting product to the shelf faster and being there for the consumer with the right amount of items and products that she's looking for as quickly as we possibly can," Dollar General CEO Todd Vasos said in the company's fiscal 2026 second-quarter earnings call in August. "As we go forward, the team is looking at continued SKU rationalization, albeit probably more surgical in nature."
Getting it right
Successfully slashing products from shelves is difficult in practice.
Box stores risk losing customers to competitors that offer the products they scrapped. BJ's, for instance, acknowledged that a previous attempt to cut SKUs was unsuccessful.

"We just cut SKUs which cut sales, and then we added some SKUs back and so really what we're doing now is removing unnecessary choice," Eddy said on the company's earnings call in August. "Think about in traditional soda, we don't carry cans and one-liters and two-liters of the same product anymore."
Meanwhile, publicly traded brands that acknowledge sales need to decline in order for the business to grow still have answers to investors in the near term.

"It's hard for a company ever to say we need to shrink anything, but it's dramatically harder to say we need to shrink revenues," said Siegel. "Frequently we find that brands hit a peak, a healthy peak, extend past the peak by forcing it and then find their way back down pretty harshly."

npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5982500/opinion.headline: Opinion: Can I keep the baseball I caught?
npr.org/2026/10/10/nx-s1-5982500/opinion.author: Scott Simon

paragraphs.text: This week, an ethical question, of all things, intruded into the baseball playoffs.

Tuesday night, Dodgers versus Braves, in Atlanta. A young man in a Dodger jersey caught a foul ball in the stands. As so often happens these days, someone seated nearby captured it on video, and then felt compelled to instruct the man, "Give it to the kid! Give it to the kid!"
And indeed there was a small boy, maybe preschool-aged, a few rows back in a Braves jersey.

But the Dodgers fan looked into the man's camera and told what turned out to be millions of viewers on social media, "I'm sorry, I can't! I'm not giving it to the kid! I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid!"
Some commenters denounced the man for keeping the ball. Some others have inveighed against the little boy for looking disappointed.
Before we criticize anyone's ethics, we ought to ask ourselves: what would we do if a baseball fell into our hands at a playoff game? Keep it, or give it to the nearest child?

Because I am a father, I'm pretty certain I would give it to a child. But also because I'm a father, I know that within a few days, the ball so tenderly bequeathed might have rolled, abandoned, under a bed, surrounded by lost socks and forgotten Labubus.
Also, a foul ball hit by almost any player would be a nice souvenir. But what if it had been a home run struck by, say, Shohei Ohtani? That ball could be as much of an investment as a Picasso!
We sought ethical advice from Nancy Sherman, a Professor of Philosophy at Georgetown University, who told us, "Manners are not morals."

The professor said she was mostly alarmed by the public shaming of both man and boy, who, after all, were not aware that their instinctive, personal reactions would soon be turned into some kind of moral exercise for the digital age.
"The young guy who caught the ball says, 'I'm sorry…I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid'"… says Professor Sherman. "I think that's a healthy, honest response."
So the next time you go to a game - if a fly ball seems to be arcing your way, you might pause before you reach for it to ask yourself, "Do I really want this ethical dilemma?"

theatlantic.com/culture/2026/10/megyn-ke.headline: Does Megyn Kelly Actually Believe What She’s Saying?

paragraphs.text: Do you remember Megyn Kelly? I once walked past her in a Chicago O’Hare bathroom in 2016, shortly after Donald Trump had won his first presidential election, and was momentarily stopped in my tracks by both her nuclear-grade charisma and her pixie cut. For a woman to have short hair on Fox News, where Kelly was a star anchor at the time, seemed as seditious to the network’s established order as reading Judith Butler or Karl Marx live on air. But this was a moment during which Kelly seemed to be leaning into the role of crusader for women—speaking out about being sexually harassed by the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and so inflaming Trump with her rigorous questioning during one debate that he later insinuated on CNN that she must have had her period.

All of which makes it so disconcerting, 10 years later, to see Kelly now, on her daily SiriusXM and YouTube show, cursing and sneering with long barrel curls and the gusto of someone hosting not a discussion of polling data but a Two Minutes Hate. “I’m just gonna be honest, she’s not the most attractive gal,” Kelly said on Monday, discussing the anonymous woman who has filed a lawsuit detailing her alleged gang rape at Cornell University. (The men named in the lawsuit have denied any wrongdoing.) “She’s extremely”—here Kelly screwed up her face in disgust—“beefy in, like, her arms and her legs. She has a whole video online talking about her cankles. And she possibly enjoyed being admired. This is how women make these mistakes. Admired, wanted—some women even foolishly say loved—by these guys at Cornell. This is probably a first for her. She’s probably thrilled to be so admired because she clearly didn’t grow up the incredibly beautiful one.”
[Sophie Gilbert: Is college getting less safe for women?]

We’ve seen some drastic heel turns in the media over the past few decades, but none quite as morally appalling as a former self-described advocate for female empowerment suggesting that a woman in this situation might have craved the attention because no one would have wanted to have sex with her otherwise. (Not to mention the contentions that the woman Kelly seems to be referring to, whose name has been leaked by some commentators, is not actually Jane Doe, based on her age and the fact that she would have been too young at the time to attend college.) Normally, I have a pretty strong constitution for this kind of bad-faith rage bait. But Kelly’s display this week of what I can describe only as performative hysteria has been hard to watch. Less than a minute into her show on Monday, she invoked the Salem witch trials. Twenty-three minutes in came her first pronounced use of the word fuck (I counted seven in total). That the whole performance was interspersed with ad reads for supplements and a tiny avatar of Kelly pointing giddily at the “Subscribe” button just added to the cognitive dissonance. It felt like watching morning television in Gilead.

I’ve been stuck all week on the question of how much of Kelly’s performance these days is attention-seeking behavior for the YouTube algorithm and how much is reflective of what she actually believes. Kelly, 55, grew up outside of Albany, where she also went to law school, becoming an editor at the Albany Law Review. She was an attorney for almost a decade, but has said that watching live newscasts on 9/11 inspired her to change careers and become a TV reporter. She was hired full-time at Fox News in 2004. Before long—according to her allegations—Ailes began making inappropriate comments, such as how sexy he imagined her bras must be. In January 2006, Kelly claimed, Ailes tried to kiss her; after his third attempt, she said she got up and walked out of his office. (Ailes denied Kelly’s allegations; he died in 2017.) Three months later, Kelly made a name for herself with her skeptical coverage of the Duke lacrosse team’s alleged gang rape of an erotic dancer. (The woman in question eventually admitted to fabricating the assault.)

All of this matters, I think, because it communicates to what extent Kelly’s apparent worldview—where she herself can face sexual harassment due to patriarchal power structures that protect and even reward abusive men, but other women are likely lying—has been shaped by her rise and fall on TV news. In 2016, she declined in an interview with NPR to call herself a feminist. (She dislikes the label, she said, as though it’s just a branding issue.) Her 2016 book, Settle for More, was published just a week after Trump won the presidential election, and became a No. 1 New York Times best seller. Reviews were lukewarm, perhaps because of the news environment: “For all the disgust that she claims to feel for the misogyny and male entitlement” that seemed to be ramping back up in the national culture, Isaac Chotiner wrote in Slate, “and for all the personal harm it caused her, our bleak future is one in which Megyn Kelly is likely to find herself right at home.”

But things took a downward turn when Kelly left the Fox fold. In 2017 she was poached by NBC News, which offered her an annual salary reported to be more than $20 million to host a daytime talk show, Megyn Kelly Today, and a Sunday-night news magazine, which was criticized for softball interviews with Vladimir Putin and Alex Jones and ultimately canceled. Megyn Kelly Today didn’t fare much better—Kelly, with her flinty self-possession, was criticized for being too chilly for daytime TV. During her first week, she awkwardly grilled Jane Fonda about whether she’d had plastic surgery while Fonda was promoting a movie next to her co-star Robert Redford. (“We really want to talk about that?” Fonda responded, after an agonizing few seconds of icy silence.) In October 2018, Megyn Kelly Today was canceled when Kelly defended blackface in a segment on Halloween costumes. Soon, she was dropped by her agency, CAA. A few months later, her NBC contract expired.

This moment seems to have influenced Kelly’s current persona. Public humiliation is hard for anyone to endure, but for someone with a renegade streak (“I’ve never been a ‘pc’ kind of person,” she reportedly wrote in her apology email to NBC staffers after her blackface comments), seeing so many people celebrating her failure must have been immensely painful. By the time The Megyn Kelly Show launched as a podcast in September 2020, mid-pandemic, Kelly was snidely describing her guests as lefties, complaining about the assault allegations against the Supreme Court justice Brett Kavanaugh, and raging at the “dishonesty” of the press covering Trump.

The pivot, whatever its reason, seems to have done what it was supposed to. Kelly has more than 4 million YouTube subscribers and The Megyn Kelly Show is one of the top podcasts in the country. Because Kelly is half-Italian and half-Irish, she told Semafor in 2024, “if you choose to watch the show, you will definitely glean something from the hand gestures and facial expressions that you might not pick up from listening alone.”

Having watched Kelly all week, I can attest to this. Although she injects real poison in her voice to rage against, say, the singer Olivia Rodrigo for expressing support for Cornell’s Jane Doe, she accompanies this with the shrugs and waves of a waiter trying to describe tonight’s special of veal parmigiana. “Olivia, in sum, you don’t know what the fuck you’re talking about,” she said. “Shut up and stick to singing. I liked you better when you were in front of a microphone singing your weird little depressing songs. Shut UP. You don’t know what you’re talking about.”

You can sense she’s imagining clips being spliced for TikTok and Instagram, and tailoring her delivery to provoke maximum indignation. As a rant, it feels much too phony—and cynical, given how fury seems to be the sole emotion that can build an audience in 2026, and the fact that Rodrigo is one of the most popular women alive. (“The only reliable way to reach mainstream or even moderate recognition against all the noise,” Rebecca Jennings wrote earlier this year in New York magazine, “is to either carpet-bomb social media with clips or to enrage wide swaths of the public.”)

But in moments, Kelly does seem to slip out of character. Although she seems perfectly happy excoriating Jane Doe, Kelly draws the line at revealing her name. “I know her name,” she said on Monday. “It’s been well publicized online. But no one in the mainstream media has said it. And as you know I’m seriously considering just saying it. And the reason I haven’t is because I don’t want to do anything to hurt this young woman, to get her hurt, or to add to the pain I’m sure she’s feeling.” Her voice is surprisingly gentle. Her hands stay down in her lap. Could it be that this woman who herself had to hire armed guards for her family after being personally targeted by Trump actually feels for someone caught in a similar nightmare? Is all this spewed-out ire and provocation really just about a reward as soul-rotting as clicks and followers? I don’t think Megyn Kelly will ever tell us, but I have my suspicions.

Somehow, America has yet to reach peak protein. Perhaps we never will. Even after David bars have gone viral for being bricks of essentially pure protein and Starbucks has rolled out lattes topped with “protein cold foam,” new and somehow weirder protein-laced products keep hitting shelves. You can now buy protein Honey Nut Cheerios, protein popcorn and PopCorners, protein sodas, protein ranch dressing, and protein chips. (Doritos launched a nacho-cheese-flavored version with 10 grams of protein per one-ounce serving.)

In an era of GLP-1 drugs and peptide stacks and Oura rings and self-optimization, of wellness influencers and looks-maxxers, everybody seems to be doing everything they can to eat as much protein as possible. The magical macronutrient will supposedly make you more muscular, or more toned, or thinner—or something, really anything, just better. Amid the protein frenzy, regular food seemingly doesn’t cut it anymore. Why order a simple flat white when you can instead sip a Dunkin’ Nutty Pumpkin Iced Protein Latte?
[Read: America has entered late-stage protein]

Into the fray, I would suggest a humble alternative: Have some yogurt. Calorie for calorie, Greek yogurt has more protein than Chipotle’s High Protein Low Calorie Bowl, Kraft’s new PowerMac, or yes, a Dunkin’ Nutty Pumpkin Iced Protein Latte. So do some traditional yogurts, as well as other fermented options in the dairy aisle such as skyr and kefir. And that’s if you opt for the full-fat, luscious kind (which I recommend). Nonfat Greek yogurt, which is lower in calories, is roughly as protein-dense as a David bar—with the added benefits of having just two ingredients (milk, culture) and not tasting like plastic.

Yogurt is not only full of protein but also good for your bones, your digestion, and your immune system. Yogurt is an ingredient: Eat it plain or bake with it, use it as the base of a sauce or dip, throw it in a marinade or soup. Sure, some yogurts have added sugars, but so does a Starbucks Iced Banana Protein Cream Matcha. And as far as health fads go, yogurt is typically probiotic. All things considered, yogurt may be the easiest protein of all.
[Read: Let’s not fool ourselves about yogurt]

In spite of everything it has going for it, yogurt has not been the face of the protein craze. Perhaps that’s because yogurt is not splashy or technologically innovative or referred to by a trademarked proper noun. A David bar may taste different and have distinct packaging from an RxBar or a Jacob protein bar made with beef tallow, but all plain yogurt is the same. Though some companies have released “protein-enhanced” yogurt (whatever that means), for the most part yogurt is not optimized by corporate food scientists and focus groups in the way that today’s protein-branded products are. Yogurt has been optimized in the sense that humans have consumed it for thousands of years.

Imagine wellness influencers suggesting that you dollop yogurt into a bowl and sprinkle berries on top without measuring anything. There wouldn’t be any regimen to adopt or wellness plan to pay for. There wouldn’t be any special trademarked protein products for influencers to hawk: The company behind the David bar, for instance, has sponsored Andrew Huberman and, until recently, Peter Attia was its chief science officer. The homemade parfait would all be rather mundane and boring compared with Attia’s rotation of four protein powders or the bodybuilder Chris Bumstead’s breakfast filet mignon. It wouldn’t get any views.

Protein is not just a health fad; it is a business. So is everything else in the world of wellness. Indeed, there’s something about many of these setups—which proffer the perfect low-calorie, high-protein snack to pick up on your way to work every morning; a biometric wristband to wear every night; supplements to consume every day for the rest of your life; a weight-loss drug you will inject every week—that keeps people coming back for more, giving their attention and money and energy to the endless pursuit of betterment.

Health and more broadly self-improvement are, obviously, admirable pursuits. Protein can be a way to achieve either. But obsessing over hitting those goals can become unhealthy, as most obsessions are. Have some yogurt, or don’t. You’ll probably be fine.

cnbc.com/2026/10/10/buffetts-trips-down-.headline: Buffett's 'trips down YouTube rabbit hole' revealed
cnbc.com/2026/10/10/buffetts-trips-down-.author: Alex Crippen

paragraphs.text: (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Buffett's 'nightly trips down the YouTube rabbit hole' revealed

Warren Buffett watches CNBC in the morning, but nearly every evening he "can't get enough" of watching YouTube clips while sitting on a recliner in front of an "enormous" television in his Omaha home.

A Wall Street Journal article this week quotes friends as saying he's "hardly ever" looking at anything related to investing or finance, although he is a "fan of Berkshire Hathaway's own content" and "proud of how it performs on the video platform."

Instead, it's things like "Glenn Close clips ... commercials from the 1950s ... Paul Anka videos ... speeches by complete unknowns ... show tunes, railroads, the big-band era, Nebraska and early Frank Sinatra performances from the 1930s."
He will also go down some "random rabbit holes."
For example, Buffett might "come into his office, gushing about a moving amateur rendition of 'My Way.'"
Sharon Osberg, the three-time world bridge champion who has taught Buffett and Bill Gates the finer points of the game, is also Buffett's "frequent viewing companion," says the WSJ.
She reports "Warren's range is broad. It can be the silliest things," like a "really good documentary on Roy Cohn" or "the Uzbekistan version of America's got talent."
Osberg says Buffett has also been watching clips featuring his late friend and business partner, Charlie Munger, including a 2017 appearance at the University of Michigan.
"You feel the bond between the two of them as he watches Charlie. It's really quite something."
The WSJ knocks down the idea Buffett's YouTube habit had anything to do with Berkshire's big investment in Alphabet, the platform's corporate parent.
"He just really likes watching the clips, friends say."
He's not alone.

The article notes that while Buffett, now 96 years old, is notoriously slow to adopt new technologies, in this instance his move to YouTube is in line with an ongoing shift from streaming to video clips that has made the platform the most-watched video provider on TVs in the U.S.
Lennar position edges higher
Berkshire Hathaway added another $192.6 million to its bet on homebuilder Lennar late last week.

In an SEC filing Monday, Berkshire reports buying 2.4 million shares of Lennar Class A at an average price of $79.65 and 15 thousand shares of Lennar Class B at an average price of $78.33 on Thursday, October 1 and Friday, October 2.
Since Berkshire's stake topped 10% in mid-September, it's been required by an SEC rule to disclose additional purchases within two business days.
There's been no filing so far this week, so it appears there wasn't any new buying through at least Tuesday.
In total, Berkshire has added $595.3 million of Lennar shares on 11 trading days since September 17.
At today's closing prices, its disclosed 12.2% stake of 29 million shares is valued at $2.2 billion.
At the end of last year, it owned just 7.2 million shares, then worth $742 million.
Over that period, LEN has dropped more than 25% as rising interest rates have made homes less affordable.
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET
Some links may require a subscription:
HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
'It's share of mind that counts' (1997)
Warren Buffett talks about the importance of how consumers think about a company.
AUDIENCE MEMBER: Could you explain a little more about what you call the "mind of the consumer" and the "nature of the product?" ...

WARREN BUFFETT: You know, what you really — when you get into consumer products, you're really interested in finding out — or thinking about — what is in the mind of how many people throughout the world about a product now, and what is likely to be in their mind five or ten or 20 years from now?
Now, virtually every person on the globe — maybe, well, let's get it down to 75 percent of the people on the globe — have some notion in their mind about Coca-Cola.
They have — the word "Coca-Cola" means something to them. You know, RC Cola doesn't mean anything to virtually anyone in the world, you know.
It does to the guy who owns RC, you know, but — and the bottler.
But everybody has something in their mind about Coca-Cola. And overwhelmingly, it's favorable. It's associated with pleasant experiences.

Now, part of that is by design. I mean, it is where you are happy. It is at Disneyland, at Disney World. And it's at ballparks. And it's every place that you're likely to have a smile on your face, including the Berkshire Hathaway meeting, I might add. (Laughter)
And that position in the mind is pretty firmly established. And it's established in close to 200 countries around the world with people.
A year from now, it will be established in more minds. And it will have a slightly, slightly, slightly different overall position. In ten years from now, the position can move just a little bit more.
It's share of mind. It's not share of market. It's share of mind that counts.

Disney, same way. Disney means something to billions of people. And if you're a parent of a couple of young children and you got 50 videos in front of you that you can buy, you're not going to sit down and preview an hour and a half of each video before deciding what one to stick in front of your kids.

You know, you have got something in your mind about Disney. And you don't have it about the ABC Video Company. Or you don't even have it about other — you don't have it about 20th Century. You know, you don't have it about Paramount.

So that name, to billions of people, including lots of people outside this country, it has a meaning. And that meaning overwhelmingly is favorable. It's reinforced by the other activities of the company.
And just think of what somebody would pay if they could actually buy that share of mind, you know, of billions of people around the world. You can't do it.
You can't do it by a billion-dollar advertising budget or a $3 billion advertising budget or hiring 20,000 super salesmen.
