nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/republica.headline: Republicans Have the Money. Democrats Have the Momentum.

paragraphs.text: From the midterm elections to advances in artificial intelligence, there’s no dearth of political news this week. The Opinion contributor Robert Siegel joins the contributing writer E.J. Dionne Jr. and the columnist Carlos Lozada to discuss the role money plays in political campaigns, how the Democrats should proceed in November and whether A.I. has the ability to feel emotions.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.
The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Robert Siegel: This week on our plate: Democrats appear to be doing very well in the midterm elections. What are they selling, and why are people buying? And it’s hard for A.I. developers to figure out how to deal with their models morally. And now comes the question: Are the models capable of making moral decisions on their own? Can they learn morals? Can they feel hurt?
But first, the midterms, and one stunning measure of what’s happening this year.

Records for campaign funding and spending are being shattered. In August, The Times published a list of megadonors — just 20 of them — although some of them are pairs of people, whose combined contributions to various federal races is $1.2 billion. Most of them are Republican donors. Democrats are bracing for a big G.O.P. spending blitz in the last month. Considering all this, the Democrats are doing pretty well in the polls, and that raises the question: How important is money in politics? Do we overestimate that importance? Carlos?

Carlos Lozada: I have conflicting views on money in politics. First of all, it is extremely important. Money buys you name recognition. It may preclude you from running at all if you are someone who lacks the ability to raise sufficient funds. And money buys access to politicians, right? The views of donors inevitably get more attention in Washington. If either of you are “Star Trek” fans, it’s like Spock’s line, “The needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few.” It’s the other way around in Washington, when it comes to money, you know? The preferences of the few outweigh the needs of the many. So money can tilt the playing field, but it doesn’t guarantee that you win the game, right? If it did, Jeb Bush would have been the 2016 Republican nominee, not Donald Trump. Michael Bloomberg would have been the 2020 Democratic nominee.
Siegel: Hillary Clinton would have been the winner of the presidential election.

Lozada: And we’d be somewhere, reaching the halfway point of the Kamala Harris-Tim Walz administration right now. So money can help you amplify a message. It doesn’t substitute for a message. If you don’t have one that resonates with voters, money doesn’t fix the problem. It might even expose that problem even more. The last thing I’ll say on it is, there can be diminishing returns to, say, ad spending. There comes a point of just saturation, where I think voters have had enough and kind of tune it out. I was in Ohio a couple of weeks ago, and my God, was it hard to watch television when I’m just trying to watch a college football game, guys. And every commercial is an attack ad; and after a while, you just sort of start tuning out.
Siegel: Yeah. E.J.?

E.J. Dionne Jr.: I’m glad you started with the few, not the many, buying interest. I think that we should take a step back and say that the Supreme Court, beginning with Citizens United, really destroyed all the guardrails that we had on big money in politics. My friend and mentor in many ways Robert G. Kaiser, famous editor of The Washington Post, wrote a book back in 2009, called “So Damn Much Money,” about the influence of money in politics. And if he did a sequel, it would be “So Damn Much More Money.”

An analysis released just this past Wednesday, by Americans for Tax Fairness, found that 170 billionaire families had spent over $1.7 billion to influence the election. There’s just something wrong here. Among pure democracies, they don’t do it like this, and that influence matters. But as Carlos says, does it always matter?

I think historically what people said is you can be outspent two to three to one. As long as you’re in the game, you can compete. These elections are going to test that further, but I think we’re reminded that no matter how much advertising you put up, the product has to be something people want to buy. And what Republicans so far seem to be up against is a lot of people just resisting the product. Sabrina Tavernise had a great piece in The Times this week, where she quoted a former Republican state representative who gave, I think, the simplest answer to what’s going on. He said, “People are tired. The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.” And that exhaustion may yet overcome all this money, but I think it is going to tighten some of these races. We shouldn’t deny that it has some impact.
Siegel: But Carlos, with all respect to Mr. Spock and his formulation, have we simply become desensitized to a massively corrupt relationship between money and politics?

Lozada: I think that money in politics can be especially dangerous when you have a set of politicians, or an administration that has shown itself to be especially susceptible to the desire to enrich itself while in office. There’s also this amazing story that, I believe, ran just this week in The Wall Street Journal, about Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.
Siegel: Wasn’t she also with the governor of California before that?

Lozada: Prior. Yeah. You know, politics is a family business. And The Journal got hold of all these text messages between Guilfoyle and a Trump donor, where she’s essentially begging him to pay off her American Express bill.

Lozada: And the line is: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” They really have all the receipts. And what you see is — aside from her messages where she’s telling him, “Do not say we have any arrangement. What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing” — there’s one moment when the donor responds and he says: “I have paid you $300,000 over the years. As of this memo, I have not received one favor. I am not naïve or a sucker. I need results.” And that captures so clearly, so blatantly, the quid pro quo expectations — why people donate money. “I need results.”

Siegel: Moving on. E.J., we talked the other week about how the midterms are likely to affect the Republicans in 2028. Let’s talk about the Democrats right now. Going by the polls, which admittedly can be very hazardous, Democrats are leading in states where they didn’t seem to have a chance. They’re competitive in places where they had been an endangered species. What are the Democrats selling so well, exactly?

Dionne: Well, as I mentioned, I think that the thing they’re selling most is a backlash against Trump, prices, and a war in Iran that is deeply unpopular, because it’s still not clear why we fought it.
Siegel: They’re selling who they are not.

Dionne: Well, right. And so, they are selling the thing you sell first in a midterm election, which is: You don’t like that guy in the White House; buy us. But I think, underlying here, there are a couple of big lessons. You’re seeing a lot of more moderate Democrats challenging in states, Kansas notably, where they haven’t elected someone in a long time. And so you’d say that’s an argument for moderation. But you’re also seeing an awful lot of Democrats, including moderate Democrats, running against concentrated economic power, big corporations, the power of billionaires and what and how that affects people’s lives.

And so, I’ve been thinking a lot about: The lesson of this election is what we need to move beyond. And our conversation partner for a long time, David Brooks, once made fun of me for being a beyond-ist, saying we need to move beyond this or that. Well, I’m a double beyond-ist in this election. I’m doubling down, I guess. Because I think, on the one hand, the Democrats need to move beyond the left-right fight in the party and say: Look, in order to win in a lot of places, you cannot be a left-wing Democrat. The word “socialist” doesn’t sell everywhere. And that a certain amount of care and moderation and understanding of who your constituents are is really important.

However, the left is right when it says that there is a lot of disaffection with the economy and about this inequality. The party has to find someone who can pull these messages together. But the other beyond is, I think the country so wants to get beyond this division, wants to get beyond where we are now, where we’re not solving any problems. And I think somebody who can move the country past this, who can plausibly make that argument. You’re seeing that in the campaign of James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas — both talk about trying to bring people together. And so, I think this double message comes out of this election and gives Democrats a potential road to not only a victorious message, but actually a substantively decent message.
Siegel: What do you think, Carlos?

Lozada: When I hear questions about the Democrats — Will the Democrats win back the Senate? How will the Democrats do? My question is always: Which Democrats are we talking about? Like, what version of the party? If there is a resounding Democratic victory next month, what version of the party will claim that victory?

What version will be able to use it as a governing mandate? Will it be the progressive wing, the D.S.A.-inflected wing, or will it be, as you mentioned, the Hamiltons in Kansas and Talaricos in Texas? That’s the key question leading into 2028, but also into your question of, what is it that they’re selling, because different people are selling different things. I think, regardless of how it turns out, and of which part of the party claims that mantle, there’s such a thing as overreading your victory. I think we’re seeing that with Trump right now. Donald Trump took his victory in 2024 to mean he could do whatever he wanted on immigration, on tariffs, foreign policy — and that has backfired massively.

Would a Democratic victory really mean an endorsement of Democratic priorities, or is it — as E.J. mentioned at the beginning — a repudiation of Donald Trump? Midterms are always a repudiation, or often a repudiation, of the party in power. Of course, people who win like to say elections have consequences, right? That was the famous Barack Obama line. But my corollary to that would be: Elections often have bizarre, unexpected consequences, even when you win. Just go back to 2022. People were thinking there might be a red wave. The opposite of today. And when there wasn’t — when the Democrats performed better than expected — that was read as some kind of victory for Joe Biden, for his agenda. It may have encouraged him to run again, despite worries over his age. And we all know how that turned out. So in some ways, I think you never really know exactly what an election means and what it’s going to lead to.

Dionne: You know, I think this is really important, and elections can be like Scripture. They can be read in many different ways, and people, partisans in various arguments, always read them as confirming whatever it was they thought going in. You saw that a lot in 2024: Why did Trump prevail? But Carlos’s comment on the nature of Democratic Party requires the obligatory reference to Will Rogers: “I’m not a member of an organized political party; I’m a Democrat.”

And the fact is that the Democratic Party is a very big coalition that is very hard to hold together — which is something each faction of the party has to remember. And so I think it’s a difficult line they have to walk, because the country really does seem to want substantial change from where we are. But that does not mean that the country has gone all ideological in one direction. Now, how do you square that circle?

Siegel: I do think what you said earlier is actually quite important; that there are people whom we call moderates, who are running in a way that during the Reagan and Bush presidencies, I think, was branded by Republicans as class warfare. If you keep on complaining about what the billionaires have got and how much rich people are getting away with, that’s divisive. It isn’t good for the country. And it seems that the line, the definition of moderation the way I hear it, has changed a bit to include some complaint about inequality in American life.

Dionne: One hundred percent. Although I think there was always class warfare on both sides, the Republicans wage class warfare against the educated class, and the Democrats did it against the moneyed class — and it was a clash of those two forms of class warfare. But absolutely right: You could argue that reality has moved to the left to some degree. And even some conservative economists I know acknowledge that rising inequality over the last 30 years is a fact and an important problem in the country. And so you have a lot of, yes, moderate Democrats speaking in class terms. Why? And I think, by the way, tech has brought that into relief because the tech folks are so wealthy, and have accumulated so much wealth, that this is an issue that sort of transcends ideology now. But you’re right. Class warfare, or at least an awareness of class inequality, is much more embedded in the conversation than it used to be.

Lozada: Yeah. Two thoughts on that: First, one of the things that has happened since that Reagan-Bush era attacks on class warfare by the Democrats is that you’ve had reality intervene in the form of the Great Recession. And that really, I think, crystallized for a lot of people what had been going on for a long time, which was the increase in inequality in both wealth and income in the United States. And so I think that, in a sense, has become a more mainstream concern that once would have been classified as a more extreme concern. The other thing I’ll say about that is that, in some ways, this is also a more palatable rebranding of the Democratic Party, away from what, say, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez would refer to as “Woke 1.” The culture war issues, on gender, on identity, on race. A.O.C. generated some headlines recently, when she said, “Woke 1 was crazy,” right? And this, I think, is Woke 2.

This is the far more focused attention on issues of economics, of class, of inequality, affordability that, in a sense, is a remaking of the party on issues that, because of that reality that has changed, seem much more palatable to the broad swath of voters.
Dionne: Of course, for the people who would recognize this, I don’t think it’s woke. I think it’s something that old Franklin Roosevelt and Harry Truman would recognize. And ——
Lozada: They were super woke, E.J.
Siegel: Long dormant.
Lozada: Reawakened.

Dionne: What all wings of the party actually agree on is that if Democrats don’t do better among working-class voters, they’re going to have a long-term problem. And so they argue about how to do it, but they all agree that they need bigger margins among the working class, not only to win, but to be able to govern.

Siegel: And just very briefly, a short-answer question: Is there some Democrat who stands out to you right now as looking like the person most likely to benefit from the results next month and become the party’s standard-bearer in 2028?

Dionne: My short answer is no. I don’t think it’s clear, at least to me. And I ask almost every Democrat I run into, “Who do you think is the person?” And more than at any time since I’ve been doing this, which is a long time, I don’t think I’ve ever heard so much uncertainty about who that person is. But if you ask the question: Who did himself the most good in this cycle so far? It’s probably Jon Ossoff. I think Ossoff has gotten attention and energy with his very focused attacks on corruption, and how he’s linked corruption to economic discontent. Assuming he wins by the margins people expect, I think he will emerge, certainly, as one of the big winners out of this election.

Siegel: From the very genuine intelligence of the two of you, onto artificial intelligence. And we are indebted to Times reporter Elizabeth Dias for a very thought-provoking piece on the interactions between the A.I. company Anthropic, in particular one of its founders, Christopher Olah, with religious thinkers representing many religious and philosophical traditions.

The questions they addressed are posed by what Anthropic technologists have come to see in the models that they have created. And just to give one example: Dias describes Olah as saying — and this isn’t a direct quotation of him, but her writing — But Mr. Olah believes that “if there is a chance the models experience suffering, the responsible thing is to avoid causing them harm.”
Carlos, you were especially struck by this story of people trying to implant morality into A.I. models, and first trying to figure out what morality is, exactly.

Lozada: This gets to the heart of the debate over what makes us human, what makes us distinct. It’s an extraordinary story, and it really does get into this question: Does this technology possess a consciousness of its own?

When people debate these issues, the term of art that is often used is “alignment,” right? Which, like every euphemism, is just terrific. It sounds kind of benign and neutral. If we just instill core human values into artificial intelligence, then things will be fine. We’ll be aligned. And whenever A.I. does something that looks dangerous or worrisome, it’s a misalignment incident. That’s how it’s described. The results from imperfect training. My question is: Aligned with what? Who has decided what the agreed-upon consensus is on human values and human behavior, and therefore what should be instilled in these programs? I don’t think we can leave that to agreements between the White House and tech companies — like the agreement that they signed just a few days ago. Anthropic is the company at the heart of the story, and Anthropic published a constitution for Claude, for its main A.I. program.
Siegel: Written by the in-house philosopher.
The company’s chief philosopher.

Lozada: Yes. And it embeds all these principles of safety and ethics and helpfulness for Claude. And if you read it, it treats Claude as this near-sentient being. It offers Claude advice on how to behave. It talks about its character and its nature. It expresses hope that Claude will genuinely care — that’s a quote about behaving in a way that is safe. I mean, I hope so too, right? I share this hope, but I think treating A.I. this way, hoping that it’ll care about our safety, is not a reassuring strategy. It’s an abdication of responsibility, and I think it’s kind of a corporate dodge.

Siegel: You mean, the more we acknowledge some separateness, that there’s a discrete entity that happens to be an A.I. model, the more we distance ourselves, its inventors, from responsibility for what it does.
Lozada: One me. That’s the answer.

Dionne: Everyone should read that story. It is a magnificent piece of work, and it drove me back to Genesis, where God says to Adam, “You are free to eat from any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will surely die.”

And I thought, oh my goodness, is A.I. the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? Now, for scientific rationalists out there: I am not saying that Genesis predicted A.I., but it does remind you, and this story did — this very scary thing about whether human beings are creating a technology with almost godlike qualities. Because what’s really striking about A.I. is it’s unlike other machines. Machines could replace aspects of human action, human labor. But this technology is gobbling up all human knowledge, all the work done by human beings over a long period of time. Philosophy, theology, novels — it’s all going into these models with the idea that they literally are superhuman. And that’s very scary. And the notion that these beings, these agents have consciousness — first of all, playing to type, maybe they should form a union. But this terrible error of thinking that an algorithm can have consciousness, that an algorithm can be a human being.

Both Carlos and I were talking about Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical. There were so many great lines in there about what it means to be human. Perhaps because I make many errors, I particularly like this line. He said, “For an algorithm, an error is a flaw to be corrected; for a person, however, an error can be a catalyst for profound change.” Insisting on a line between human beings and this technology, I think, is so important going forward.

Siegel: I’m glad that you raised the papal encyclical, in which Pope Leo XIV, who has a mathematics degree, is unusually well-suited for this debate. And he was much more concerned about the workers who would lose their jobs because of this technology, and with it, their dignity. Speaking up for the dignity of work doesn’t seem to be fitting, jibing easily, with Anthropic and the others.

Lozada: It’s interesting. Pope Leo XIV came of age in his formation, in kind of the post-Second Vatican Council, Catholic Church. He learned about liberation theology. And if you read his encyclical, which is called “Magnifica Humanitas” — magnificent humanity, right?
It is imbued in that kind of culture of the social doctrine of the church. And part of that is why he comes out swinging against this whole idea of alignment. \

He worries that what he calls “technocratic thinking” is going to dominate, because technology takes on the characteristics of those who devise it, who finance it, who regulate it. He also really, really dislikes the idea of anthropomorphizing technology. He says that the A.I. do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, nor do they have a moral conscience.

And yet, the Claude Constitution attributes almost all those things to Claude. It says we can’t ignore the potential moral status of the A.I. models. They may have some functional version of emotions. So if you take personality and self-perception, emotion and agency, I wouldn’t be surprised if legal personhood is what follows. That seems to be the logic at play here.
Siegel: And again, the legal personality for the model is, once again, insulation for the designer of the model.

Dionne: The Supreme Court created a precedent when it declared “corporations are people,” so why not a bot? I think everything you said, Carlos — which is really profound — is why there is so much uneasiness that is beginning to seep into the election conversation that we had earlier, about this technology. And whenever someone is critical of a technology, they’re accused of being a Luddite. You know, progress is inevitable. You’ve got to embrace it. And I don’t think any of us wants to be a Luddite in that sense. And Pope Leo XIV, by the way, is not. In that encyclical, he talks about potential gains from this technology. But people are genuinely petrified about the social impact of this, because they know, as these companies are kind of admitting now, that they themselves don’t fully understand what they are creating; that they may lose control of what they are creating.

And so, the desire to slow down and maybe think a little about what we’re doing, I think permeates the public reaction to this. And maybe this is one good thing. I think some of this backlash — or even better said, just quiet concern — does transcend the ideological categories in the country right now. And I’m reluctant to predict this because such predictions never turn out. This may be an occasion for us to sit down and forget our labels for a little bit and say, “What are we doing here?”

Lozada: I think part of the backlash to data centers — that is, a bipartisan backlash — is a tangible way to oppose something that, in some ways, feels so intangible and so difficult to understand. The debate over consciousness reminds me of this terrific novel from the ’50s, “A Canticle for Leibowitz.” Have you read it?
Dionne: Oh, what a wonderful book.

Lozada: Walter Miller Jr., I believe, is the writer. And it’s all about this tension between technology and politics and faith. But there’s a great moment when a skeptic and an abbot are talking, and the skeptic talks about his uncertainty over whether he even has a soul. And the abbot says: No, no, no — wait a second, doctor. You don’t have a soul. You are a soul. You have a body temporarily.
And the skeptic is like: Oh, that’s just semantic confusion. And the abbot is like: Yes, it probably is, but which one of us is confused here?
I think we’re in that moment right now, where we’re trying to discern body, soul, faith, reason.
Dionne: You are the soul of thoughtfulness, and I am so glad you raised that book because I had not thought of it until you said it — how relevant that is to this conversation.

Siegel: I just wanted to note, I was especially struck by the remark of a rabbi — Navon, an Orthodox rabbi or scholar who was part of this discussion that Anthropic organized — and he didn’t believe that the models had consciousness. But he told Anthropic: If you do believe that, then you’re advocating slavery. You want to create beings whom you regard as having soul or consciousness and human attributes and abuse them, abuse their labor.
It’s been a wonderful discussion. And as we end every discussion, I’d like to ask both of you — E.J., starting with you — some source of joy in your life recently.

Dionne: You know, Robert, when we started doing this 13 months ago, my joy was the fact that our daughter Julia had married a wonderful person, named Devin Stein, and they are still happily married. And I am now going full circle because my joy this week is that, at the beginning of the month, our son James got married to Kate Applegate, an absolutely wonderful woman we love, at a great ceremony where her parents, her brother Gray, joined our family, and it was really spectacular. And at the risk of being mushy for the tough-minded, smart readers, I want to say that what you can’t replicate is seeing your own three kids love each other so much, and to have your family grow in this way, really in such a spirit of love. And it was just a great event.
Siegel: Carlos?

Lozada: Congratulations. That sounds wonderful. I love that that’s where you went, E.J., because I’m also going to share something that is about family and about these big transition moments. It’s joy tinged with a little bit of sadness because our oldest son has gone off to college. And this is the first of our kids to do that. And he is so happy to be there, jumping into dorm life and his classes. And we’re the ones left with his empty room. So I’m sad at his absence, but I’m so happy for him. And at the same time, it’s a reminder that, really, parenting from the first moment you hold your child is about preparing them to leave you. And also, even with the tinge of sadness, I feel joyful at the new stage that our own relationship is going to embark upon, because as he really comes into his own as an adult, our relationship will evolve as well.
Dionne: These are perfect because my story says the joy doesn’t stop when these big transitions happen.

Siegel: Well, for me, this time I just wanted to add, in addition to some very nice time with family, also a very interesting play that my wife and I went to see called “The Score,” which the Shakespeare Theater Company in Washington, D.C., has brought over from London. And it’s an imagining of what went on when Johann Sebastian Bach met with Frederick the Great. Frederick the Great, who ruled with an iron fist, but presumably had at least some hand made of something more pliant, because he played the flute, and extremely well. And it’s a play about the authority of art and musical genius versus the authority of political strength and political power. And I found it a very fascinating and joyful day at the theater, and look forward to more.

Lozada: I went to see that as well last Friday. And of course, the lead is the great Brian Cox. Best known to many of this generation for playing Logan Roy in “Succession.” I found it a similarly captivating experience.
Dionne: I know what I have to do soon. Thank you.
Siegel: Carlos Lozada and E.J. Dionne, thanks again so much. Great to see you guys.
Dionne: Thank you.
Lozada: Thanks, Robert.
Thoughts? Email us at theopinions@nytimes.com.

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Presidents have long made bombastic pledges to voters in last-minute electoral appeals.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Now, that playbook is in full force ahead of November's midterm election, as President Donald Trump crisscrosses the country touting promised multibillion-dollar megaprojects in battleground states and credits his tariff agenda with ushering in a golden age of domestic manufacturing.

But pledges for a steel plant in Iowa, an aluminum smelter in Oklahoma and a long-sought gas pipeline in Alaska face significant questions, leaving it unclear whether the projects will fully materialize or amount to anything more than a midterm mirage.

And while Trump bets big on the long term — drawing on decades as a real estate developer and employing a tactic used by other incumbents ahead of Election Day — the risk is that the splashy pledges will ring hollow with voters more squarely focused on day-to-day costs and immediate pocketbook concerns.

The smelter destined for Inola, Oklahoma, underscores the skepticism. Chicago-based Century Aluminum Co. and Dubai's state-owned Emirates Global Aluminium PJSC say it would be the first new US plant in almost a half-century to process aluminum derived from raw material. Trump, during a campaign swing last week, said it would be "the largest aluminum factory, perhaps, in the world."

But even in deep-red Oklahoma, the project faces opposition from residents, and Inola's Board of Trustees imposed a moratorium to block the initiative. Century and EGA haven't reached a final investment decision, as they solicit proposals for engineering design services and seek to clear permitting hurdles. The joint venture in a statement said it was disappointed by the town's extended moratorium and called a proposed aluminum production ban premature.

Yet Century also has documented numerous risks that could paralyze the project, acknowledging in its 2025 annual report that even with support from the Energy Department, developers need "substantial additional financing" to make the project a reality.

Some of the planned projects already are aided by state and federal taxpayer dollars. Consider the $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, a state with a closely fought Senate race and three GOP House districts that could flip.

The plant stands to benefit from the support of the US Export-Import Bank, which helped finance a new Minnesota mine to supply the facility — the first of its kind to open in more than five decades. And last week, Iowa Republican Governor Kim Reynolds signed legislation unlocking as much as $1.4 billion in tax incentives for the steel mill.
Flanked by Iowa Republicans, Trump described the facility as an outgrowth of his trade policies, insisting that "everyone's building their plant here because they don't want to pay tariffs."

Although Trump claims his policies are bringing production back to the US, each of the projects requires "some special government assistance to happen," said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the American Action Forum. "It's not like the economics are so good everywhere that people are building stuff."
Questions also have been raised about the history of bankruptcies and restructurings involving units of Essar Group, the Indian conglomerate developing the steel complex.

An Essar unit that sought to develop a taconite mine in Minnesota filed for Chapter 11 protection in 2016 and a steel venture in Canada obtained creditor protection a year earlier. Minnesota also clawed back leases from Essar-backed Mesabi Metallics after it said the company failed to meet financing commitments. Mesabi has separately challenged a rival over what it alleges is anti-competitive behavior, with a trial set for next year.

Essar emphasized its strong commitment to invest in the US, vowing in an emailed statement that its proposed steel mill "will be completed successfully" and benefit both Iowa and Minnesota. "As of now, everything is on track for the project to be completed, making it the largest green field steel plant investment in America through this $18 billion investment," the company said.

A White House official said the Iowa project is well-capitalized and noted Essar's past successes, including commissioning ports, running electric generation and operating an iron pellet facility in India.

Alaska also has garnered heightened attention for massive building plans. Last week, Trump announced a $54 billion South Korean investment toward a long-stalled project to export liquefied natural gas from the state. "We make great deals," he said.

The venture to transport natural gas from Alaska's North Slope and liquefy it for export has been decades in the making, held up by its price tag and the technical challenges of building a pipeline across the state. Trump cast the Korean commitment as ironclad and hailed the help of Senator Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican in a tough reelection contest.
Hours later, South Korea cried foul. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said the country's investment in the LNG venture would hinge on commercial viability.

It was a stunning rebuke from a US ally — one that's pledged $350 billion in investment in exchange for lower tariffs on exports. And it drew pushback from Trump, who threatened that if the Koreans walked away, he'd hit their goods with higher levies.

"President Trump began carrying out an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda on day one, which has been and continues to deliver tangible wins for the American people," said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers. "He has a proven record of securing historic investment, creating high-paying jobs, and bringing manufacturing back to the United States."

Americans, meanwhile, are expressing acute concern about high costs of living, making affordability the election's dominant issue. While Trump frequently touts stock-market gains, booming 401(k) accounts, a surge in overall employment and fresh investment pledges, other indicators show a less rosy economy.

Elevated inflation prompted the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates last month and fuel costs have soared amid wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Mortgage rates are at the highest level of Trump's second term. Unemployment remains historically low but ticked up last month, and wage growth has been weaker than economists expected.

"They are scrambling for ways to show they have a strong economic agenda, so they're running around saying, 'Jobs are coming, jobs are coming,'" said Sameera Fazili, National Economic Council deputy director under former President Joe Biden. "Unfortunately for them that is not what is top-of-mind for voters this election season."

Trump isn't unique in seeking electoral momentum by showcasing landmark projects. Ahead of the 2022 midterms, Biden celebrated the groundbreaking of an Intel Corp. facility in Ohio. Construction is ongoing but Intel has pushed back its timeline.

Trump, too, has done this before. Ahead of the 2018 midterms, he celebrated Foxconn Technology Group's plans for a $10 billion plant in Wisconsin, boasting it would be "the eighth wonder of the world" and create 15,000 jobs. Foxconn eventually slashed its investment commitment by roughly 90% and ultimately employed only a fraction of the planned workforce.

A White House official pointed to several project announcements from Trump's first term that have been developed, including an LG Electronics Inc. factory in Tennessee and a Samsung Electronics Co. facility in South Carolina.
Trump has acknowledged the long timelines such projects face. It's not clear if the electorate will be patient.
"I want you to remember me in four or five years when this country's rocketing," Trump said at his September midterm convention. "Remember, I'm the one that got it started."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: One Year After $19 Billion Crash, Crypto Faces a New Reality
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: David Pan

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A year ago, crypto was riding a wave of White House support, Wall Street enthusiasm and expectations of a new golden age. Then came October's historic crash, wiping out a record $19 billion in leveraged bets in a single day, setting off an industry-wide retrenchment and exposing the fragility of a market structure supposedly coming of age.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Twelve months later, market bellwether Bitcoin remains more than 30% below its record high. Attempts at a sustained rally have repeatedly faltered and traders have been slow to rebuild the leveraged positions that once powered crypto's biggest booms.

Total open interest in Bitcoin-linked perpetual futures — a gauge of traders' appetite for leveraged bets — stood at about $45 billion a year ago, according to CryptoQuant data. It more than halved in the six months after the crash. Bitcoin's recent rally above $80,000 restored some confidence, but open interest in the world's biggest token remains well off its peak.

Still, the malaise hasn't stopped banks and major trading firms from experimenting with digital assets. More important than whether leverage returns is whether the market itself has become more resilient, said Julia Zhou, president at crypto market maker Caladan.

"More than $19 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated within 24 hours, but the bigger issue was how quickly available liquidity disappeared when the market needed it most," Zhou said. Today, while traders understand the risks better, "the market remains highly fragmented, and liquidity can still deteriorate rapidly," she added.
The case for a stronger market today is that leverage is lower, exchanges offer less-correlated assets and some venues have beefed up liquidation systems.

Meanwhile, investors haven't lost their taste for gambling, but have turned to new frontiers. Prediction markets are drawing crowds, and perpetual futures or "perps" — long a staple of crypto trading — are being used to place leveraged bets on stocks, commodities and other real-world assets. Put another way, some of the very machinery that helped turn crypto into a speculative phenomenon is finding uses well beyond the tokens it was designed to trade: Wall Street is forging ahead with stablecoins, tokenization and the financial infrastructure built on blockchain technology.

Open interest in perpetual futures for real-world assets, virtually non-existent a year ago, today stands at more than $17 billion, according to DefiLlama data. Much of that has been driven by Hyperliquid, the offshore crypto exchange, which was an early mover in tying perps to stocks and commodities.

The shift "tells a growth story of people that want yield and settlement on rails that never close, not from people chasing a narrative or a buzzy memecoin," said Adam McCarthy, head of research at trading firm LO:TECH.

The never-ending quest for higher returns helped make Bitcoin the world's best-performing financial asset since its inception 17 years ago. For long-time crypto-market participants, the increased institutionalization of the sector and corresponding rise of fresh alternatives from perpetual futures to sports betting are seen as an inflection point.

In a report released this week, QCP Capital said it expected Bitcoin to be stuck in a range of $80,000 to $90,000 in the fourth quarter. The structural case for crypto remains intact, but flows alone aren't enough without a dominant catalyst, the firm wrote.

A year out, the market looks fundamentally different, Galaxy Digital said in a report Friday. Despite the failure of US crypto regulation in September, federal regulators are moving ahead with plans to strengthen trading with guidelines over the use of collateral and margin.

All that means an industry born of disruptive idealism and defined by speculative excess is becoming more closely integrated with the financial establishment it once sought to displace. And with artificial intelligence commanding much of the market's imagination, crypto faces a different future from the one envisioned in its early boom years: less a rebellion against Wall Street than another corner of it.

"For the most part, the market that crashed on 10/10 doesn't really exist anymore," wrote Lucas Tcheyan, vice president of research at Galaxy Digital. "The one that replaced it is just starting to get priced in."

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/coal-r.headline: Coal’s Revival Is Creating Divisions in Canada’s Energy Heartland
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/coal-r.author: Iain Boekhoff, Michael McKee and Arielle Schwartz

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- At the top of Grassy Mountain, some 6,700 feet above sea level, seams of coal are baked into the mountainside, visible through mining in this stretch of the Rocky Mountains in southwestern Alberta from the early to mid-1900s. This and other former mines dot the picturesque mountain towns on the eastern side of the continental divide, the industry having moved out of the region decades ago after plummeting prices and demand made mining here unprofitable.
Most Read from Bloomberg

But Grassy still has more coal to give — much more. It's now the center of a yearslong battle pitting nearby towns' economic interests against environmental worries from downstream communities and ranchers. And this time, it's being driven not by demand to heat homes in Canada, but to feed steelmakers in China, Japan, South Korea, India and other Asian countries.

Nearly 60 years after this site closed, locals are once again pinning their hopes for an economic revival on this windswept mountainside. Northback Holdings Corp., a division of Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting Pty., is working to reopen the former mine.

This is Hancock's second attempt after an earlier application was rejected by a joint federal and provincial review panel in 2021 over concerns about the impact on the nearby water ecosystem. Northback Chief Executive Officer Brad Johnston believes the company can address the deficiencies in its first application and go further in restoring the mountain, including much of the unreclaimed former mine site.

Hancock has spent more than a decade and over C$150 million ($105 million) on a project that faces stiff opposition and is still at least four years from opening. It's promising to scale back its original plans by around 40% to produce 2.5 million metric tons a year instead of 4 million, boost reclamation efforts during the course of mining, build a water treatment plant and stick around for years after production ceases.
The company is persistent because its forecasts show an undersupply in the global market within the next decade and pricing levels far beyond what it costs to extract the coal.

The proposal and others like it have struck a nerve in Alberta, a region traditionally friendly toward resource development, both in terms of public support and government policy. Country music star Corb Lund led a petition campaign this year to stop coal mining in the eastern slopes of the Rockies, attempting to force a provincial vote on the issue this month, unsuccessfully. A recent survey found a majority of the public would have supported his position in a referendum.

The fight over the project also reveals a little-known fact about Canadian coal. Within the country, it has been on a long decline, as governments moved to reduce coal used for power production. But at the country's western ports, coal is still king of commodity volumes. About 39.9 million metric tons were exported from Vancouver last year, compared to 30 million tons of petroleum products.

While the province of British Columbia now accounts for the majority of coal production, Alberta has seen a number of proposals in recent years and the province recently approved an expansion of the Vista Coal Mine in Hinton, near Jasper National Park, that will make it the largest thermal coal mine in North America.
About 70% of the world's steel supply depends on metallurgical coal and Canada is the fifth-largest global supplier, accounting for roughly C$9 billion in exports.

Northback isn't the only such new proposal in the Rockies. Northwest of Calgary, Valory Resources Inc. is pitching Blackstone, an underground metallurgical mine in Clearwater County, and another one called Mine 14 near the town of Grande Cache.

In BC, Conuma Resources Ltd. reopened a mine near Tumbler Ridge in 2024 and a sister project was included in the province's recent deal book marketed to global investors. Glencore Plc is also seeking to expand its Fording River site to maintain the mine's 10 million metric tons of annual production.

Johnston, who took over as Northback's CEO in July, says any coal mined at Grassy Mountain will all be for export off the west coast of Canada, largely out of the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert. The company's projections, he says, show it can be profitable over the course of its projected 25-year lifespan due to strong Asian demand for steel-making coal, listing Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Malaysia and India as possible customers.
The type of coal here is also high-quality enough for European steel producers. "The world wants this coal, it needs it," he says.

The proposal would be a major employer for the five historic mining communities near Grassy Mountain. He cites the roughly 400 full-time jobs needed to operate it and the C$2.2 billion in government revenue the mine will generate over its lifetime, according to a report prepared for the company by EY.

The company has already been sponsoring local organizations and has hired locals for its preparatory work, including a First Nations security contractor. Johnston says he is aiming to file another application in the coming months, with a potential target of opening in late 2030 if it receives regulatory approval.

He acknowledges the company's first application did not sufficiently deal with concerns over its environmental impact. A joint federal-provincial review panel found the project was "not in the public interest" and would harm the nearby population of westslope cutthroat trout. He believes their new proposal is improved enough to meet regulatory hurdles, but knows there's widespread opposition to coal.

"There are some people that are opposed to what we do, no matter how well we do it, or whatever systems of controls we propose to put into place," he says. The company is always willing to answer questions about environmental management, he says, and local support "doesn't come unconditionally, and their expectation is that we're going to provide jobs and economic benefit, but we're going to do so in an environmentally responsible way.

There's been more public backing in Canada for energy projects since US President Donald Trump's administration began pressuring the country on trade, says Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute. That attention has largely been around oil and gas, and hasn't necessarily translated to coal.

"I think most people, even in Canada, don't appreciate that metallurgical coal is our biggest export by volume out of the Port of Vancouver and the Port of Prince Rupert, and that by revenue, after gold, it's usually our top-producing mineral product," she says.

She points out the towns closest to the proposed mine are largely in favor and people further away are opposed. In Crowsnest Pass, the municipality nearest Grassy Mountain, more than 70% voted to support the mine in a 2024 plebiscite. But municipal councils downstream, including in Lethbridge, Alberta's fourth-largest city, have been staunchly opposed.

While Prime Minister Mark Carney's federal government has been encouraging "nation building" projects to spur economic activity and build stronger interprovincial connections, the coal in western Canada won't be going to the steel factories of southern Ontario and Quebec. The cost to ship by rail across the country makes it too expensive for the steel factories to use.

Instead, demand is driven by Asian countries and interest in Canada as a conscientious steward in producing coal. "If you are a Japan or a Korea, you may be willing actually to pay a premium for that better environmentally and socially responsible product," Exner-Pirot says.

Steel is "ubiquitous" in products ranging from batteries to large-scale energy infrastructure, said Ian Lange, a professor at the Colorado School of Mines. Demand for steel and therefore metallurgical coal can be a proxy for economic activity around the world. Alberta is one of the most attractive places for natural resource extraction given its friendly regulatory environment and ease of getting to Pacific ports, he says, and miners have been making greater efforts to ensure environmental protection.
But he says "it's really hard to say with certainty that this won't be a problem 30, 40 years down the line."

The environmental pushback to increased mining in the Rockies can point to substantial levies against operators in recent years. Coal mines in BC faced C$60 million in federal fines in 2021 for water contamination breaches, and another C$16 million in fines from the province in 2023. And as recently as this past July, Glencore-owned Elk Valley Operations Ltd. was fined an additional C$269,000 as part of a larger C$3.6 million ruling over delaying construction of water treatment facilities and 171 water quality breaches related to selenium.

Concerns over water quality extend south of the border. A 2024 study from the US Geological Survey found evidence of selenium pollution as far as 350 miles away from Elk Valley's mine along the Columbia River and contamination in other cross-border waterways.

Lund is a fourth-generation Albertan, his family settling in the early 1900s on ranch land they still own near the Montana border. He spearheaded a petition to have a referendum on banning some new coal mining that garnered more than 170,000 signatures earlier this year, though the question did not get put on the ballot for voting day on Oct. 19.

He says he was drawn into the issue after rancher friends of his worried about the potential impacts on downstream water from selenium and other contamination. The amount of water used and the air quality are other concerns.

"As far as I can tell, it's a bad deal and it's going to ruin our water and our ranch land, and there's nothing in it for Albertans," he said. "And I think it's a foreign billionaire coming here to take our coal and make all the money and leave us with the mess."

His family's land isn't threatened by the mine reopening, but his residence in Lethbridge is served by the watershed from around Grassy Mountain. He says he's seen the issue resonate across political lines in the largely conservative, pro-resource development province. Many Albertans view the Rocky Mountains as "the soul of the province, and that includes a good chunk of the conservative base who are hunters and fishermen and ranchers and irrigating farmers," Lund says. "So it's not just a left-right issue. It's very close to a lot of people's hearts here."

He's "been in this fight for almost seven years now, and we've outlasted two premiers" as well as "multiple CEOs from the coal companies" and they will do everything they can to stop new mining in the nearby Rockies.

Lucas Michalsky, a cattle rancher about 20 minutes east of Grassy Mountain, has a different take on the mine's impact. "We are the forgotten corner of Alberta," says Michalsky, whose family worked in nearby coal mines after moving from Poland in the early 1900s.

The Grassy Mountain proposal has already brought more hope to local residents about the prospect of higher-quality jobs. "Northback has put in tens of millions of dollars," into the area, he says. "All the people that are against coal haven't put a dime into our community."

Some local residents work in Glencore's coal mines across the BC border, or see their children move to work in northern Alberta's oil sands. The draw for Michalsky is seeing his kids close to home where they might "have a job as a millwright or a welder or an electrician at Northback, and come home every night so they can run cattle."

He believes the environmental impact is overstated by opponents, who are largely not from the immediate towns that will benefit from the mine. "This is a blue-collar community. It always has been. And we've lost our logging. We've lost our oil and gas. Mining is the only thing we have left, because we never really had much of the first two."

marketwatch.com/story/i-have-no-children.headline: 'I have no children': My aunt gave me $50,000 for a down payment. Now she wants me to leave my home to her two children.

paragraphs.text: 'The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close.'
"I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about." (Photo subject is a model.)

Eleven years ago, my aunt gave me $50,000 toward my house, and I'm still grateful. I was 44, newly divorced and buying my first home on my own. I had about $65,000 saved but was short on the down payment for a three-bedroom in a neighborhood I liked. My aunt had money in a savings account earning next to nothing, and she said she'd rather see it go toward a home. She called it a gift and never asked me to sign anything.

The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close. Since then I've put in about $90,000 more: a new roof, kitchen appliances, plumbing work and new windows. The house is worth around $650,000 now, though that isn't cash in my pocket, and I still owe about $180,000. My aunt is 78 and has two adult children, a son,52, and a daughter, 49.

I barely know them. We see each other at Thanksgiving and Christmas; I send cards and birthday texts, and that's about it. My aunt has been a big part of my life. She helped me through the divorce, sat with me when my father was dying and stayed with me for a week after my surgery a few years ago. She has never held the $50,000 over me until now. At dinner last month, she asked me to change my will so the house goes to her two children when I die.

She said it isn't unreasonable and wanted me to consider her offer. She doesn't need the money herself. She just wants her kids to eventually benefit from what she gave me. I told her I'd always understood the money as a gift to me, not an investment in the house or an early inheritance for her children. She had a poker face, but I could tell she did not like my response. I don't want to punish her for being generous. But I'm not comfortable with that request.

I don't want to leave a house worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to two people I barely know. I have no children, and I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about. I haven't thought of the house as a bargaining chip, just as the biggest thing I own. My aunt says I'm being too literal and that family isn't supposed to keep score. Now I feel gaslighted!
Am I being selfish for refusing to leave the house, or a good part of it, to my aunt's children?
Related: After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?
You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.
The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan.
You are not being selfish. You have agency over your own life and finances. You are not being gaslighted. You are feeling pressured.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan and that, to split hairs, is being used as the bargaining chip. You can acknowledge that without agreeing to change your will. If you want to offer something, a modest bequest to her children is a proportionate option. Your aunt may not have meant to have come across so aggressively. Sometimes, people can feel embarrassed in the moment.

If you are uncomfortable about leaving her children any money, don't do it. It's far better to be uncomfortable with your aunt's request and her response to your answer than it is to be uncomfortable with giving money to people you barely know. It's your house - and you can leave it to whom you want to.

What now? Let's assume that $50,000 would be worth $216,000 in 30 years with compounding. You could leave each of her children $108,000, which is more than generous, and reimburses them for the money your aunt gave you out, with interest, assuming that the down payment reduced their inheritance. That's a suggestion, not a request.

You have poured $90,000 into this home to renovate, which has added value; you have worked hard over the last 11 years to pay off the principal and the interest; and you have taken pride in knowing that you have created a home that you can be proud of. Millions of housebuyers get help with a down payment, although it varies by generation.
Homebuyers frequently receive financial help

Four in 10 homeowners received financial help with a down payment on their current home, including nearly 80% of Generation Z homeowners, 56% of millennials and 35% of Generation X (which happens to be your cohort), according to a recent LendingTree survey. The percentage was much lower (12%) for baby boomers.

However, arguably it was easier to buy a house 30 years ago, as the price-to-income ratio has narrowed significantly. Depending on the study, the typical home costs up to seven times the median annual salary today versus just four times the median annual salary 30 years ago. That would explain why fewer baby boomers needed a leg up from parents/family members.
Your aunt definitely overstepped the mark.

Your aunt, for better or for worse, bided her time. You are now in your 50s and never had children of your own, and she has your home in her crosshairs. Yes, she has been a kind and supportive aunt, attending your graduation and helping you get your foot on the property ladder. In many ways, she has been like another mother to you.

If she were your mother, I could see a similar scenario playing out where she would suggest that you support the family cause and leave your house to your brother. But you have no children, and you have already decided to remember your brother in your will, and yet your aunt decided to proffer a version of that request. As an aunt, it doesn't quite land in the same way.
Children often ask the same of their parents

Lest we forget, these pages are rife with adult children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews making similar requests of their elders, asking what will happen to their estate after they're gone, and giving helpful suggestions about what should happen to the estate - which, surprise, surprise! - always seem to favor the one asking the question.

Asking the question is certainly a brazen, if not entirely unusual, state of affairs in families, especially if she considers herself a de facto guardian. However, she definitely overstepped the mark by indicating that leaving the home to her two adult children is the "decent" thing to do. That's a lot more prescriptive than just asking a question.

You don't have to feel ashamed about accepting her gift. Without your aunt's gift, you may never have been able to buy a home or it would have taken you many years. Yes, you are one of the millions of homebuyers receive assistance in the form of a down payment, mortgage payments and/or acting as a guarantor - so her generosity means you are not alone

What do you tell your aunt? You can tell her that you appreciate her help with the down payment, and you will give some thought, but that your estate plans are private. You don't have to answer to anyone. If she persists, you may wish to make it clear that being single and without children does not mean that you have to abide by other people's wishes.
Ultimately, it was a gift, and you can do what you want.
Related: 'We lived within our means': I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably. Why don't you tell people that?

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkgjrpmr47vo.headline: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkgjrpmr47vo.author: George Wright

paragraphs.text: Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".

The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.
"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.

Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.
Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".
He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmlyle97pqd7o.headline: Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers say
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmlyle97pqd7o.author: Grace Eliza Goodwin

paragraphs.text: US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.
The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.
She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.
Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition in hospital.
Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.
Her case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
