Lucas is a senior writer at TechCrunch, where he covers artificial intelligence, consumer tech, and startups. He previously covered AI and cybersecurity at Gizmodo. You can contact Lucas by emailing [email protected].

phys.org/news/2026-10-stability-distingu.headline: New stability rules distinguish quantum phases of matter that an older method wrongly groups together
phys.org/news/2026-10-stability-distingu.author: Daniel Inafuku

paragraphs.text: edited by Sadie Harley, reviewed by Robert Egan

Most of us recognize basic phases of matter and their properties: solids maintain their shape, liquids flow freely with constant volume, and gases expand to fill their container. Quantum phases, on the other hand, are much harder to categorize, overturning traditional notions of what a phase even is and forcing physicists to rethink their definitions.

Even so, physicists have made substantial advances in classifying quantum phases for isolated systems. Yet categorizing those for open, nonequilibrium systems—those that freely interact with their environment—has presented numerous technical challenges, hindering our understanding of fundamentally new quantum behaviors and their implementation in quantum-computing applications.

Now, in a new paper published in Physical Review X, Illinois physicists at the Anthony J. Leggett Institute for Condensed Matter Theory have developed a framework for classifying nonequilibrium quantum phases of matter, generalizing principles governing closed systems. Their work overcomes the shortcomings of current classification schemes, enabling scientists to distinguish between a wider range of quantum phenomena than ever before.
How do we classify phases?

Ordinary phases of matter are generally classified by their symmetries. Liquids, for instance, look roughly the same from any direction and have a high degree of symmetry, whereas crystalline solids possess symmetries only along well-defined axes, a difference showing that they're distinct phases.
This classification paradigm, pioneered by Lev Landau in the 1930s, has extraordinary explanatory power, describing everything from solids, liquids and gases to magnets and even superconductors.

Since the 1980s, however, physicists have realized that many phases can't be explained by symmetry alone. They also require topology, a branch of mathematics that studies fundamental, global properties of shapes while ignoring their local, small-scale details. To give an oft-cited example, although seemingly different, a coffee cup can be mathematically "massaged," or continuously deformed, into a doughnut like clay, showing that they're globally identical and belong to the same class of shapes.

Each class is characterized by so-called topological invariants, special numbers such as the number of holes a shape possesses, that don't change under continuous deformations. On the other hand, making a new, distinct topological shape requires a discontinuous change such as tearing—a banned operation in topology.

Like the topological shapes they correspond to, topological phases are distinguished by their invariants too, maintaining their order when locally perturbed by external interactions. Physically, they arise when temperatures are brought so low that quantum fluctuations, once masked by thermal jostling, emerge to produce system-wide quantum entanglement.

In these phases, information gets stored nonlocally so that it's "smeared out" across the entire system. Particle-like excitations called anyons that don't fall into the familiar boson-fermion paradigm can also arise, a phenomenon that physicists are only just beginning to understand. And because of their resilience, topological phases could form the basis for new quantum-computing technologies, which are notoriously vulnerable to environmental noise.

How are these phases classified? Phases in closed quantum systems, those isolated from their environment, are typically described using tractable quantum states called pure states. Classifying pure-state phases conventionally rests on the structure of their gapped Hamiltonians, mathematical objects that encode their states' energies and impose energy gaps between the states.

Illinois physics professor Jong Yeon Lee emphasized, "The most important idea in defining a phase of matter is that it should be stable. It should be defined in such a way that if you perturb the state slightly, it still stays in the same phase.

"For pure states, this notion is well defined: two states belong to the same phase if their local parent Hamiltonians can be connected without closing the energy gap, while an unavoidable gap closing signals a phase transition."

Sadly, pure states are often idealizations. In the real world, they interact with their environment and degrade, or decohere, turning into unpredictable statistical messes called mixed states. And unlike pure states, out-of-equilibrium mixed states don't have Hamiltonians, so classifying their phases using the conventional approach doesn't work.
Another way in: Bootstrapping

Luckily, there's another classification scheme: entanglement bootstrapping. In this procedure, one concocts stability criteria that define fixed points, quantities of a system that look the same at different length scales. Physicists hunt for a system's fixed points by zooming out to large length scales, or coarse-graining, to observe how the system's parameters change.

"As you coarse-grain further and further," Lee elaborated, "each point in the phase diagram converges to a fixed point. We can think of phases of matter as perturbations away from these fixed points."

Such points are indicators of stability, serving as anchors for defining phases. Once identified, one can move away from fixed points and look for regions of stable quantum states, which can be collectively defined as phases.

This bootstrapping procedure—identifying fixed points through stability criteria, then defining phases as sets of stable quantum states around fixed points—has found much success in classifying pure-state phases.

Naturally, Lee's team wondered whether the same bootstrap approach could be extended to mixed states, an effort that gained momentum when Illinois physics postdoctoral fellow Bowen Shi joined Lee's group.

"The entanglement-bootstrap program provides a complementary way of looking at the same physics," Lee asserted. "But instead of starting from a Hamiltonian, it asks how much topological order we can reconstruct directly from the entanglement structure of a given quantum state.
"This philosophy is especially useful for our mixed-state problem, suggesting that we can identify a small set of information-theoretic properties that play a similar role as the Hamiltonian."
Stability criteria & topological data

To find fixed points for mixed-state phases, the first step in bootstrapping, the researchers looked for ways to eliminate correlations, which suppress stability, and incorporate the right topological ingredients that such phases require. They devised three conditions to capture these ideas.

The first condition, M0, ensures stability by requiring that any two physically separated regions of matter, A and C, don't affect each other much ((b) in the diagram). Otherwise, perturbations could use the regions' long-range correlations to propagate throughout the system, destabilizing the phase, similar to how a car crash on a highway can propagate from car to car, causing a pileup if they're too jam-packed.

Another condition, P0, demands that if the information encoded in a local region C is lost or corrupted, its surrounding neighborhood B can recover this lost information ((a) in the diagram). This condition accounts for the notion that topological information is stored nonlocally, independent of local details, so that the information is spread across the system E through long-range entanglement.
Finally, condition M1 imposes mathematical technicalities on quantum states to ensure they're tractable enough to talk about the right topological physics.

These three conditions hold at all length scales and together define fixed points, so that any quantum state satisfying all three simultaneously is stable. Moreover, Lee added, "If we limit our scheme to pure states, then our three conditions become equivalent to those used in pure-state bootstrapping. So our framework includes pure-state classification as well."
The researchers also derived several important quantities, collectively known as topological data, to distinguish and characterize different fixed points.
Not only do these data provide measures of the topological information contained in the fixed points, but they're also topological invariants, providing a way to label phases once they're defined.
Defining mixed-state phases

To finally define whole phases as part of bootstrapping's second step and move away from fixed points, the researchers allowed their stability criteria to relax. States near fixed points can't be expected to be as stable as the fixed points themselves, but they should be stable enough. That is, the stability conditions need not hold exactly, just approximately.

With this in mind, the researchers made the following definition: if one can build an intermediate boundary between two mixed states at which the deviation from the stability criteria drops off exponentially fast as you coarse-grain, then the states belong to the same phase. Simply put, if two phases look the same when you zoom out—except for perhaps an exponentially small difference—then they're essentially the same phase.

To confirm this definition is satisfactory, the researchers implemented coarse-graining numerically, quantifying the degree to which the stability criteria deviate from the fixed points as one coarse-grains away from them. They discovered that the deviation indeed decays exponentially with coarse-graining, showing that the states are, in fact, stable enough to define phases.

Significantly, this definition for mixed-state phases is compatible with the topological data: as a result of topological invariance, if two mixed states have different values of a topological quantity, then they belong to different phases—a quick, surefire test to identify and label distinct phases without having to establish the stability criteria from scratch.
Comparing approaches

How does this scheme compare to others? The leading method for classifying mixed-state phases relies on the idea of a finite-depth local channel (FDLC), a kind of communication link between two quantum states. According to this approach, two states belong to the same phase if there exists an FDLC that maps one state to the other, and another FDLC that maps that state back to the first.

Upon closer inspection, however, this FDLC approach breaks down: In their paper, Lee's team gives an example of two states—a generic product state and the maximally dephased toric code—that physically belong to different phases even though the FDLC definition incorrectly says they should belong to the same phase.
"The FDLC approach doesn't necessarily preserve topological structure," Lee noted. "It seems researchers forgot this subtlety and naively extended this idea to describe mixed states."
Mixed-state bootstrapping, by contrast, correctly categorizes the product state and toric code into distinct phases, in exact agreement with what is observed physically.

Lee continued, "Our method diagnoses what goes wrong: The channel changes the underlying topological structure, violating one of our stability criteria. Instead, bootstrapping gives us intrinsic diagnostics rather than defining a phase solely through the existence of a particular preparation protocol."
On to new topological data, phases and transitions

With this new classification scheme, the researchers have faced major hurdles in frontier condensed matter theory, most notably the perennial inability to distinguish clearly different quantum phases that has hampered even the most inventive methods.

And they're not done yet. Lee's team is actively hunting for more topological data to complete their framework. Computing certain topological invariants exactly, for instance, isn't always easy or even possible. And whereas states having different values of a given invariant denote different phases, the converse is not true in general, so that states sharing the same value could still belong to different phases.
A comprehensive lineup of topological data would give physicists additional tools to constrain and better distinguish between phases.

Armed with this new method, Lee's team is looking to experimentally incorporate mixed-state topological order into actual devices. They're also exploring specific kinds of phases and phase transitions, particularly those near critical points, where different types of correlations blow up.

"What excites me most is that this work points toward a new way of defining phases of matter directly from how quantum information is organized in the state, both in and out of equilibrium," Lee said.

"At the same time, the present bootstrap framework is not yet universal—for example, it does not naturally capture fracton phases. I see that limitation as an important clue. Ultimately, I hope to develop a broader framework that can encompass these more exotic forms of quantum matter as well."
Tai-Hsuan Yang et al, Topological Mixed States: Phases of Matter from Axiomatic Approaches, Physical Review X (2026). DOI: 10.1103/3bpt-f9pd

marketwatch.com/story/elon-musk-is-now-r.headline: Elon Musk is now richer than any American ever - and it's not even close

paragraphs.text: Musk's trillioniare status means he's wealthier than his next three contemporaries combined - and also worth more than historical tycoons like John D. Rockefeller
Elon Musk's fortune eclipses that of any other American in history when tracked by how their wealth compares to U.S. GDP at the time.
Recent gains in shares of SpaceX and Tesla have pushed Elon Musk's net worth back beyond the trillion-dollar mark.

Musk's wealth has earned him the title of the world's first and only trillionaire - and the richest person in the history of America by certain measures, surpassing the wealth of industrialists like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie when looking relative to economic output.

As of Thursday, Musk's net worth was $1.02 trillion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The majority of Musk's wealth comes from his stakes in SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA), two companies with multi-trillion-dollar market capitalizations. Since the beginning of the month, shares of both companies have risen 6%.

Musk holds a 48.4% equity stake in SpaceX, which represents approximately 6.42 billion shares across common stock, options and unvested performance awards, according to an August SEC filing. Musk also owns 20% of Tesla, according to a June SEC filing. However, wealth calculations typically exclude the value of unvested performance shares. Musk also owns shares of his private companies Neuralink and the Boring Co.
These positions make Musk's net worth highly volatile. His wealth peaked at $1.32 trillion in June following SpaceX's IPO but then fell below $700 billion in August as those shares lost ground.
Despite these fluctuations, Musk has solidly established himself as the wealthiest person in the world, both now and compared to previous eras.

Musk's current net worth makes him richer than the world's next three wealthiest individuals - Google (GOOG) (GOOGL) co-founder Larry Page, Amazon.com (AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos and and Google co-founder Sergey Brin - combined.

Musk has spent the majority of the past five years in the top position since first overtaking Bezos in 2021. Musk's current trillionaire status is also a testament to how much the ceiling for wealth has expanded in the past few years. In 2020, Bezos became the first person to ever cross the $200 billion mark. In April 2025, Musk's net worth of $342 billion made him the wealthiest person in the world. In the 18 months since, Musk's net worth has nearly tripled.
Musk also remains peerless when compared to the richest Americans in history.

The industrialists of the 19th and 20th centuries made their fortunes on new markets like oil, steel and railroads. Today, the artificial-intelligence boom has drawn comparisons to the Industrial Revolution in terms of the transformative potential of the technology. While the economic impact of AI has yet to fully emerge, Musk has already surpassed the richest Americans in history in terms of his relative share of gross domestic output.

MarketWatch identified comparable historic figures from Forbes' 2007 list of the richest Americans of all time, then calculated each individual's peak net worth as a percentage of U.S. GDP at the time. Those historical GDP shares were then applied to today's economy.

U.S. GDP reached an annualized $32.56 trillion in the second quarter ending Sept. 30. That means Musk's fortune equates to roughly 3.1% of the entire national economy - a higher percentage than any American before him.

Measuring historic wealth by modern-day standards is challenging because the underlying economic conditions have changed drastically. Additionally, readers should note that historical net-worth estimates are often debated due to differences in record-keeping and varying valuation methods. With that being said, economists typically measure historic wealth as a share of GDP instead of adjusting by standard consumer price inflation.

For example, Standard Oil founder John D. Rockefeller has long been considered the richest American in history. Rockefeller was worth $900 million at his peak in 1913, according to biographer Ron Chernow. Adjusted for inflation, his fortune would be worth $30.4 billion today. But when compared to U.S. GDP in 1913 - which was $39.5 billion, according to Measuring Worth - Rockefeller's wealth comprised 2.3% of total national output, or the equivalent of roughly $742 billion in today's economy.

Andrew Carnegie is believed to have given away $350 million, or roughly 90% of his fortune, over his lifetime. But to pinpoint his net worth at a specific point in time, MarketWatch used the 1901 buyout of Carnegie Steel to J.P Morgan as a benchmark for his peak wealth. While the exact amount is debated, PBS claims Carnegie walked away from the transaction with $250 million, earning him the title of the richest man in the world at the time. The proceeds of the sale represented 1.1% of U.S. GDP at the time, or the equivalent of $355 billion today.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/10/pope.headline: Pope criticizes death penalty after Hegseth announces public execution
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/10/10/pope.author: Anthony Faiola

paragraphs.text: ROME — Pope Leo XIV waded into the debate over the death penalty Saturday, calling it “an attack” on human dignity a day after senior Church officials pointedly condemned the decision by the U.S. Defense Department to live-stream the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan.

On a day that capital punishment opponents have dubbed “World Day Against the Death Penalty,” Leo did not specifically reference the United States or Hasan, who on Dec. 3 is scheduled to die in the first known U.S. military execution by firing squad since 1945.

Writing on X, Leo reiterated his opposition, describing the death penalty as “inadmissible” and arguing that the “common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment.”
He ended with the hashtag #NoDeathPenalty.

Hasan, a former U.S. Army psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. In an unprecedented move, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said this week that Hasan’s execution by firing squad would be live-streamed for the public. President Donald Trump told reporters Friday that he had personally authorized the live stream.

Since a dustup in April, when Trump sharply criticized the first U.S.-born pope and Leo responded by saying he had “no fear” of the administration, the pontiff has sought to lower the tone of confrontation with the White House. Instead, he has left it to top proxies to more pointedly challenge specific administration policies the Church opposes while Leo takes to issuing broader, higher altitude statements.

That tactic appeared to be playing out again on the Pentagon’s decision to live-stream Hasan’s execution. Leo issued his broader comments after his No. 2 — Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state — on Friday delivered more stinging criticism of the Pentagon’s decision, calling it “unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.”

The debate over the death penalty has also heightened in the U.S. following the botched execution in Tennessee of Christa Pike, 50, who survived two doses of pentobarbital following a death sentence for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.

Leo has encouraged senior Church hierarchy in the U.S. to respond on U.S. domestic affairs. And also on Friday, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops — Oklahoma City Archbishop Paul Coakley — issued a statement decrying the planned live stream as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”
“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” Coakley said in a statement.

The Catholic Church has hardened its opposition to the death penalty in recent years, including under Pope Francis. Since becoming pope last year, Leo has repeatedly denounced capital punishment. Last year, he challenged those who describe themselves as “pro-life” in the U.S. for opposing abortion while still supporting the death penalty.
“Someone who says ‘I am against abortion’ but says ‘I am in favor of the death penalty’ is not really pro-life,” Leo said.

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/impeachme.headline: Trump Is Begging to Be Impeached

paragraphs.text: President Trump has been impeached twice.
The first time was in 2019, after he was caught trying to extort the Ukrainian government into manufacturing “evidence” to use against Joe Biden ahead of the 2020 presidential race.
The second time was after that race, in 2021, when he led an effort to overturn the election results on Jan. 6, culminating in a riot and assault on the U.S. Capitol.

Much of what Trump has done in his second term either meets or exceeds the threshold of his first impeachment. There is his corrupt profiteering off the presidency, his occupation of American cities with the National Guard, his use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection as a secret police, his attempts to seize the power of the purse, his abuse of the pardon power, his unlawful political retaliation against law firms and universities and his attacks on press freedom — all impeachable offenses.

No, he hasn’t done anything as singularly transgressive as Jan. 6. But in a real sense, the second Trump administration is no less than an authoritarian conspiracy against the constitutional order — a Jan. 6 by other means, including a whole-of-government effort to subvert the midterm elections and preclude any prospect for true democratic accountability.

In Federalist No. 65, Alexander Hamilton explained that impeachment covered those offenses that “are of a nature which may with peculiar propriety be denominated political, as they relate chiefly to injuries done immediately to the society itself.”
By that standard, the despotic and anti-republican character of Trump’s presidency is itself an impeachable offense, above and beyond any particular action.

But while there is fertile ground for a third impeachment, it is unclear whether Democrats are willing to make one happen. When asked, Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, has been noncommittal, saying that Democrats have neither “ruled anything in” nor “ruled anything out” with regards to a possible impeachment.

The former Chicago mayor Rahm Emanuel, who has been soft-launching a campaign for president for the last year, says that Democrats should avoid impeachment altogether. Asked on NBC’s “Meet the Press” if Democrats should impeach Trump, he said, “No, because it’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight, and it’s just going to be we return to the politics of fighting.” According to Axios, Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois has taken a similar stance: “Don’t be impeaching anybody,” she said. “Let’s just get back to work.”

Rather than devote time to an impeachment investigation and a subsequent trial, the idea is that Democrats would pass legislation and attempt to make good on the promise of a more affordable America. But while it is important that Congress get back into the habit of legislating, it seems naïve to the point of delusion to think that Democrats would have anything like a cooperative partner in the White House. If anything, the loss of a supine Republican majority and the prospect of any accountability is quite likely to push Trump to abuse power even further. Think of it as a game of chicken, in which he’s daring the Democratic majority to try to stop him.

We can already see inklings of this. He has basically threatened, for example, a post-election escalation of the war in Iran. It is not hard to imagine a future in which, cornered by defeat, Trump lashes out in ways that only underscore his threat to American democracy.

In that world, it is foolish to take impeachment — the Constitution’s main remedy for a rogue executive — off the table, even if the odds of removal are slim to none. Even in the absence of a conviction, the impeachment process is a valuable political tool. It underscores, for the public, the simple fact that the president is unfit to serve. And an extended impeachment investigation could uncover the kind of pervasive wrongdoing, even criminality, that could lead to real accountability for other figures in the administration.

If nothing else, impeachment would show voters that Democrats were not simply blowing smoke when they accused the president of lawless behavior. It should be said as well that a serious investigation would put pressure on the Republican Party, which would either have to distance itself from Trump or, more likely, bind itself even closer to an unpopular but vengeful and vindictive president. Ahead of the next presidential election, impeachment would put Republican hopefuls between a rock and a hard place.

Impeachment might be inconvenient to Democratic leaders and it might carry some political risk, but it is simply not tenable to allow the president to run roughshod over the rule of law and the constitutional order without meaningful, constitutional pushback. As flawed as it is, impeachment is the tool we have for that particular job.

Now Eating: Baked Spaghetti

I had leftover tomato sauce in the freezer, leftover mozzarella in the fridge and random boxes of leftover pasta in the pantry, and this recipe (from New York Times Cooking) is what I used to turn them into a meal. This is basically a variation on a baked ziti, and it is very easy to put together. Serve with a crisp green salad.
• Unsalted butter, for greasing the pan
• Kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal) and black pepper
• 1 pound spaghetti
• 2 tablespoons olive oil
• 1 large yellow onion, chopped
• 2 tablespoons minced garlic (about 5 cloves)
• 2 teaspoons chopped fresh thyme or rosemary, or 1 teaspoon dried
• 1 ½ teaspoons dried oregano, plus more for serving
• ¼ teaspoon red-pepper flakes, plus more to taste
• 1 pound ground beef (at least 85-percent lean)
• 1 (32- to 35-ounce) jar marinara sauce
• ½ cup fresh basil or parsley leaves, chopped, plus more for serving
• 1 cup/8 ounces ricotta cheese
• ¾ cup grated Parmesan
• 1 large egg
• 2 cups/8 ounces shredded low-moisture mozzarella

Heat the oven to 350 degrees and grease a 9-by-13-inch baking dish with butter. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the spaghetti and cook according to the package directions until 1 minute shy of al dente.

While the water comes to a boil, heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until tender, 6 to 8 minutes. Add the garlic, thyme, oregano, red-pepper flakes, 1 ½ teaspoons salt and a few grinds of black pepper, and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the beef and cook, breaking up the meat with a wooden spoon, until browned, about 5 minutes.
Turn off the heat and stir in the marinara sauce and basil. Drain the spaghetti, add it to the sauce and toss well.
In a small bowl, combine the ricotta, ½ cup of the Parmesan, the egg and ¼ teaspoon salt. Mix with a fork until smooth.

Transfer half the pasta and sauce to the prepared baking dish and smooth it into an even layer. Dollop the ricotta mixture onto the pasta in large spoonfuls, then sprinkle 1 cup of the mozzarella on top. Add the rest of the pasta and sauce to the pan, again smoothing it into an even layer.

Cover the pan with aluminum foil and bake for 40 minutes. Sprinkle the remaining 1 cup mozzarella and the remaining ¼ cup Parmesan on top, then bake, uncovered, until the mozzarella has melted, 5 to 10 minutes more.
Cool for 5 minutes, then serve with more chopped basil, a pinch of dried oregano and more red-pepper flakes, if desired. Slice the baked spaghetti into large squares and serve hot or warm.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-10/.headline: Postal worker charged with beating Sugar, the Pasadena white peacock
latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-10/.author: Ruben Vives

paragraphs.text: A U.S. Postal Service worker seen on video beating Pasadena’s beloved white peacock was charged with animal cruelty, according to authorities and court records.
Los Angeles County prosecutors identified the suspect in court records as Charanjit Singh.

The 48-year-old Rosemead resident was charged Thursday with a misdemeanor count of cruelty to animals, records show. It is the first time the mail carrier has been identified since the Aug. 18 incident.
Singh could not immediately be reached for comment.
The USPS, which is conducting an investigation into the incident, did not respond to a request for comment.
The criminal charge came a week after the Pasadena Humane Society announced that the rare white fowl had recovered from its injuries and was relocated to a private ranch in Northern California.

“After carefully considering what would be best for his long-term well-being,” the nonprofit said in a statement at the time, “our wildlife experts determined that relocation would offer him the best quality of life and help reduce the risk of future negative encounters given the significant public attention surrounding his case.”
The peacock made headlines two months ago when a resident found the injured bird in the 3700 block of Mohawk Street.
The peacock was well known in the neighborhood where it lived for years, and some residents had come to call him Sugar. The bird was also known for its disposition, especially toward men.
“When it came to males, he could be a little, well, aggressive,” Gina Davis, a Pasadena schoolteacher, told The Times in a previous interview.
She said the bird had chased off her husband and a neighbor. Davis said her husband named the bird Sugar.
“Because it was white, not because of his personality,” she said.

Davis said she checked her home security footage and was shocked to see what caused Sugar’s condition: A postal worker was caught on camera throwing a rock at the bird and later striking it with a club or stick.
Davis said the video showed the bird following the mail carrier to his truck.
“The peacock was just standing in front of his truck,” she said. “He got out of his truck and had a club or stick or something and hit it,” in the head or neck.
Pasadena Humane said it rushed the bird to its Wildlife Center, where vets found swelling but no broken bones.
The incident prompted an investigation by animal service investigators.
Singh is scheduled to be arraigned on Nov. 6.

fortune.com/2026/10/10/baby-boomer-vs-ge.headline: ‘Fantasy economics’: Baby boomer vs. Gen Z tensions hit France as pension costs drive debt crisis and education cuts that fuel student protests
fortune.com/2026/10/10/baby-boomer-vs-ge.author: Jason Ma

paragraphs.text: Bond market turmoil and the simultaneous mass student protests at French schools are not a coincidence and point to the generational tradeoffs made in government spending, according to Nobel laureate Paul Krugman.

In a Substack post on Thursday, the economics professor at the City University of New York’s Graduate Center acknowledged that the high debt and deficits driving up French bond yields lately are not unique to the eurozone’s second largest economy.
In fact, the U.S. is guilty of the same fiscal sins, especially as aging demographics push entitlement spending up faster than revenue comes in.
“But France does stand out, even among fiscally troubled nations, in one main way: its persistent inability to get realistic about retirement,” Krugman added.

That’s as France’s official French retirement age, when workers can collect full benefits, was just 62 in 2023, while the average actual age of retirement was lower than anywhere else in Western Europe at only 60.4 years.

Meanwhile, French students are taking to the streets to protest missing teachers, run-down classrooms, and buildings that aren’t equipped for rising temperatures. Protestors blame years of underinvestment in public education.

Krugman drew a straight line from France’s retirement largesse to the student unrest, highlighting the generational tensions over how to allocate public resources to baby boomers versus the country’s youth.

“Thus the fiscal pressure caused largely by France’s very generous government pension plan has led to cutbacks in other spending, notably on education,” he wrote. “France is effectively handing over large subsidies to older French at the expense of everyone else. Mass national student demonstrations should come as no surprise.”

Of course, U.S. debt is also on an unsustainable trajectory as spending on seniors jumps amid more baby boomer retirements. But even some Republicans have expressed openness to tax hikes to keep Social Security’s trust fund solvent.
For his part, French President Emmanuel Macron attempted to raise the retirement age to 64, but intense political pushback has stalled those efforts.

And the front-runner in France’s presidential election next year, far-right leader Marine Le Pen, has vowed to roll back the official retirement age to 62 and even previously suggested dropping it to as low as 60.

“This would be extremely expensive and is symptomatic of a general unwillingness on the part of France’s rising right to face reality,” Krugman said. “Again, this is hardly unique to France — think of all the false promises and claims Donald Trump has made. But for now, at least, financial markets believe that fantasy economics is an even bigger problem for France than for the rest of us.”

Indeed, markets are pricing in growing odds of a French debt default. Earlier this month, French 10-year bond yields jumped to the highest since 2002, and the premium over equivalent German yields widened to the most since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011.
Those metrics later eased, but France’s fundamentals remain troubling, with anemic GDP growth, a budget deficit estimated at about 5.4% of GDP, and rising debt-service costs as yields jump.
France’s debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to climb to 122% next year from 119% this year, and the government’s latest plan failed to halt the surge in bond yields as investors doubted its credibility.
Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry, global strategists at Macquarie, also drew a connection between the French debt crisis and the student protests.
In a note Wednesday, they warned that the longer the protest go on, the more likely it is that the government will cave and approve more spending, which would make the debt situation worse.
That would drive up yields on French bonds, making borrowing to fund that spending even more expensive—and thus worsen the problem that the rioters are complaining about.

“France is veering toward a full-blown civil crisis because of its political polarization, which heretofore had been manifested mainly in the political realm itself, and at the ballot box only,” they wrote. “And rather than being isolated events, we think a direct and self-reinforcing causal connection can be drawn between the rise in France’s debt yields and the street riots of the past few days.”

In less than three weeks’ time Israelis are scheduled to vote in national elections they widely view as the most consequential of their lives. The most common term used in the country these days to describe the salience of the upcoming election is “B’hirot Goraliot”—literally, fate-defining elections. According to a September survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute, 81% of Israelis regard the October 27 election as either “the most important in the country’s history” (40%) or “especially important” (41%).

Popular awareness that the stakes are high, however, has not translated into clear political choices. On the contrary. In its fragmentation, mercuriality, conspiracism, and cast of fantastical characters, contemporary Israeli politics makes Game of Thrones look like The Golden Girls. The political waters in which Israelis are swimming—domestically, in the Palestinian arena, in the region and the wider world—are all swirling.

This translates into chaotic electoral politics. In a country of ten million people, no fewer than thirty-eight parties—including The Pirates Party and a list dedicated to achieving national unity through marijuana consumption—are running for seats in Israel’s 120-member parliament, the Knesset. Even the most dedicated students of Israeli politics have abandoned all hope of remembering the names of its political parties; as they sprout in the morning, then merge, splinter, and defect in the afternoon, or evaporate by nightfall. In this electoral season there is even a character called “Winter,” and Winter is coming, but only if he passes the electoral threshold.

Of the thirty-eight parties in the race, somewhere between eleven and fourteen are expected to achieve the magic 3.25% threshold of valid ballots cast and make it into the Knesset—a minimum of four seats, which means roughly 172,000 votes. The outcome of the elections may well hinge on one or two small parties failing to clear the threshold by a few hundred votes.

But who will sit with whom in what kind of coalition government, under what conditions, and under whose leadership? The range of possible permutations is near infinite, yet some measure of order can be imposed on this shape-shifting mess using scenarios. Five such scenarios are structurally possible. Each needs to be taken seriously, none are inevitable, though some are more likely than others.

Before proceeding to outline each scenario specific to October 27, a word about what the existence of this degree of uncertainty means. Sometimes, to paraphrase George Orwell, the first duty of a sober observer is the restatement of the obvious. Functional democracies do not normally face five alternative outcomes less than three weeks before a crucial election. With rare exceptions, two-party systems produce binary results—either one party wins, or the other. In multi-party systems, like Israel, the range of the possible should extend to no more than a third scenario—the establishment of some form of coalition government. The fact that electoral politics in Israel now deviates from this bounded set of options indicates a degree of democratic volatility and fragility both novel and concerning. Only one scenario points to a path towards national recovery and repair after the terrible traumas of the past few years.
Scenario One: Disruption

The first scenario is one in which the election is postponed, interrupted, or contested so severely that its legitimacy is seriously questioned. This has never happened in seventy-eight years of modern Israeli statehood and would have been unthinkable even five years ago. After three years of a multifront war that is essentially ongoing—Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, the Houthis in Yemen, none of which are resolved—and amidst a combustible internal atmosphere, however, disruption is not a hypothetical and could come from multiple sources. Israelis certainly fear the prospect. An Israel Democracy Institute survey in July found that 72% of Jewish and 58.5% of Arab Israelis believe the integrity of elections is in danger, and that was before repeated warnings in recent days by security chiefs that Israel’s enemies are seeking to subvert the election or exploit it as an opportunity for an armed attack.

We should distinguish between two categories of disruption. The first, and less likely, is formal postponement or the prevention of viable elections due to internal or external violence. Israeli law does not contemplate the possibility of elections being cancelled and a military coup in Israel is outside the realm of credible scenarios. The law does, however, provide for the possible temporary postponement of elections in the event of an extraordinary national emergency that makes voting impossible. There is no exhaustive list for such circumstances, but it would certainly include a large-scale missile attack by Iran and/or its remaining proxies—Shi’a militias in Iraq, Hezbollah in Lebanon, or the Houthis in Yemen. It would also certainly include a surprise attack from a less predictable source, such as Syria, Sinai, or Turkey.

It is unclear whether the outbreak of a Third Intifada in the West Bank, rocket-fire from Gaza, the kidnapping of Israeli soldiers or civilians, large-scale rioting by protestors, or a high-level political assassination taking place shortly before or on elections day, would constitute grounds for postponement. The disruption would have to be widespread and debilitating enough to stymie the process in large parts of this small country. In any case, Israeli law sets strict limits on postponement. Delaying elections cannot be decreed. It requires the passage of Knesset legislation by a supermajority of two-thirds (80 members of Knesset) and the delay caused must be as brief as practicable—a condition that will be closely supervised by the courts.

Disruption may also come in the form of a breakdown of trust in the electoral process or the announced outcome, either as the result of active subversion or, more corrosively, a large proportion of the Israeli public coming to believe that the election was “stolen” by the opposing camp and is therefore illegitimate. The latter is more likely to come from the pro-Netanyahu right, which is less concerned about the risk of voter suppression among Arab Israelis than it is about preventing initiatives helping Israeli expats fly home to vote in the upcoming election.

Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud party has already petitioned Israel’s Central Elections Committee—the non-partisan national body responsible for conducting elections—to demand it blocks such initiatives, alleging that they constitute voter bribery. If the anti-Netanyahu camp wins by one or two Knesset seats, it is likely that at least some of his supporters will point to the expats and cry foul.

The Central Elections Committee is far better prepared to manage the threat of attempted subversion on the part of external actors than the more nebulous risk of internal conspiratorial mistrust. David Zini, head of the Shin Bet (Israel’s internal security agency), recently told legislators in closed session that Iran is the leading foreign actor seeking to interfere in the Israeli vote—with Russia, China, and Turkey also involved—and that candidates themselves may be targeted.

The raw material for an Israeli version of the January 6, 2021 assault on the U.S. Capitol is in place and may or may not be kindled on October 27. If it does, and trust in the essential integrity of elections is destroyed, Israel will find itself in a constitutional crisis that it has no agreed rules to resolve.
Scenario Two: Stalemate

The second scenario—inconceivable a year ago, improbable two months ago, but now perhaps the most likely—is stalemate: an outcome where neither bloc obtains the sixty-one seats needed to form the barest majority; no combination of parties manages to negotiate a coalition; or the anti-Netanyahu camp decides it is better off going to another round of elections than attempting to form a minority government.

Israelis are intimately familiar with this situation, having lived through it repeatedly in recent history, and many now believe it is about to happen again. A survey published by Haaretz on October 1, for example, saw 49% of respondents express the view that the elections will not be determinative and that the country will likely go to another round.

Israel held five rounds of national elections between April 2019 and November 2022. Of these, two ended up in stalemate, but for different reasons. The elections of April 2019 saw Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc nominally achieve a majority, but Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu party refused to join over the Haredi miliary draft issue, leading to another round of elections five months later. Those produced another stalemate, with neither Netanyahu’s nor Benny Gantz’s Blue and White bloc able to reach sixty-one. The Knesset promptly dissolved, forcing a third election in March 2020, just as the world plunged into the Covid pandemic.

Current opinion polls suggest a stalemate, with neither the perennial Netanyahu nor his maiden chief opponent, and Gantz’s erstwhile party member, Gadi Eizenkot, likely to secure more than 52-55 seats for their respective blocs. If the polls are correct, Eizenkot can rely on 54 seats—23 for his own Yashar party, 12 from Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s combined Beyahad party, 10 from Yair Golan’s The Democrats—remnants of the old, once hegemonic, Israeli Labor Party, plus left-secular-cosmopolitan Meretz—and 9 seats provided by the seasoned Avigdor Lieberman, still at the helm of Yisrael Beiteinu (more about him in scenario four).

Facing Eizenkot’s 54, under this scenario, will be Netanyahu’s 52-54: a diminished Likud with 20-21 seats, the Ashkenazi Haredi party United Torah Judaism (UTJ) with 8, the Sephardic Haredi party, Shas, with 7, and the three ultra-nationalist parties, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, 7-8, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist party, 6, and Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael party, 4. Neither bloc would be able to reach sixty-one, even if they include the only Arab party that would agree to sit in a Zionist coalition government, Ra’am, or in the unlikely event that every single one of the right-wing satellite parties currently hovering just above or below the electoral threshold make it through.

For Netanyahu, stalemate would represent a “win on points”; for Eizenkot, it would spell disaster. Under Israeli law, Netanyahu continues to serve as prime minister unless and until a new government, headed by an alternative PM, is sworn in by the Knesset. If he can force a stalemate, Netanyahu remains interim PM after October 27 and can then use all his skill to set the agenda, divide and rule, and take the country into another electoral round in April 2027 (then another and another still if he needs to) until he does to Eizenkot what he did to the now politically defunct Benny Gantz—grind him down to irrelevance.

Gadi Eizenkot has one shot to slay the dragon; if he does not win this round, he will be weaker in the next, as the anti-Bibi camp searches desperately for the next Benny, the next Gadi, to lead the charge against Bibi. Eizenkot, more politically savvy than Gantz, knows this full well, and will do everything in his power to avoid the stalemate trap. But there is another trap waiting for him in scenario five.
Scenario Three: A Netanyahu-bloc Victory

Under a third scenario, Netanyahu’s camp would win a majority to form a narrow but viable government. This could happen through a combination of several factors. First, voting rates in favor of the pro-Netanyahu camp will need to be substantially higher than for the anti-Netanyahu bloc. A low Arab-Israeli voting rate would reward the pro-Bibi camp by increasing the likelihood that small far-right parties manage to cross the electoral threshold.

Second, Netanyahu could eke out a victory if the existing members of his coalition, especially Likud, do dramatically better at the ballot box than most polls predict. Channel 14—roughly speaking, Israel’s version of Fox News—wishcasts exactly this, with Likud winning 31-32 seats, rather than the 20-22 recorded by other pollsters.

Third, the Netanyahu bloc could win if its existing members do substantially better than most polls predict and the two new right-wing satellite parties cross the electoral threshold and join a Netanyahu-led coalition. The most significant of these is Ofer Winter’s new far-right party, Amcha Yisrael, which could give Netanyahu the crucial 4-5 seats he requires to retain power. Similarly, Netanyahu could end up on top if, during coalition negotiations, yet another small satellite party, The Reservists, crosses the electoral threshold and breaks its promise not to sit in government with the ultraorthodox. Lastly, in the cauldron of post-elections coalition negotiations, Netanyahu might poach a party from the opposing camp, for example Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, or Naftali Bennett’s Beyahad. An outright Netanyahu victory remains a tall order, but it is far from inconceivable, and the momentum of the past few weeks is drifting exactly in this direction.

A Netanyahu bloc win, even if by a bare majority, would amount to a vote of confidence in the same government that orchestrated the attempted dismantlement of the rule of law in Israel and then presided over the country’s worst security disaster—a multilayered failure it has consistently refused to impartially investigate—which was followed by three years of unresolved war.

To the Israeli soft right this would be explicable in terms of Netanyahu’s grit and experience: After being punched in the face by Yahya Sinwar in the brutal terrorist invasion of October 7, 2023, the logic would be, Bibi got himself off the floor and, despite intense international pressure, proceeded to fight a determined multifront war against Israel’s mortal enemies, all of whom are now either gone (the Assad regime in Syria), broken (Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon), or diminished (Iran). The vote for Netanyahu, for this sizeable portion of Israeli society, would be justified because the war is not over and because they believe that none of the alternatives to Netanyahu—not Eizenkot, Bennett, or Lieberman, let alone Yair Lapid—would have withstood the pressures of the past three years.

Under this scenario, Netanyahu remains the default choice for the Israeli electorate—an electorate that has moved strongly to the right after October 7—not because they believe he is blameless for October 7, but because, when push comes to shove, they conclude that in the face of continued existential dangers no one is better qualified to navigate the ship. Netanyahu’s main campaign message is directed precisely at this narrative. Strewn across Israel are giant posters with his image next to a two-word caption: “Doesn’t Surrender.”

To the nationalist-religious camp, a Netanyahu victory would mean vindication and license wrapped in messianic cellophane. Like the son of the widow of Zarephath, whom the prophet Elijah brought back from the dead, Netanyahu is resurrected in an astonishing feat of political revival. The true sons of Israel are with him and have been handed a popular mandate to complete the judicial overhaul, sweep away the last remaining bastions of the liberal “deep state,” extend efforts to drive Palestinians out of Gaza, and annex Judea and Samaria.

For liberal Israelis, this outcome would signal that the Israel they were born and grew up in is no more; that the country’s DNA has irrevocably mutated to illiberalism and that—given the steady demographic tilt in favor of the nationalist-religious—they are unlikely to win another election ever again. If not now, when?

In retrospect, under this scenario, we would look back at the November 2022 election as the crucial tipping-point at which a certain Israel perished, and another was born. Viewed through this lens, October 2026 would be seen as the mere consolidation of the historic triumph of Israel’s religious right. Judaism has beaten secular Zionism; conservative Judea has vanquished liberal Israel.

For secular-liberal Israelis the loss would also mean diminished faith in the capacity of the state—a state they fight for and disproportionately fund through their taxes—to provide long-term physical and ontological security to their children. It would be read as a clear signal that the essential link between government performance and democratic accountability has been severed, and that, going forward, tribal identity politics would be so dominant that the fundamental corrective mechanisms of democracy no longer work in Israel.

Some liberal Israelis—the most cosmopolitan and mobile—will give up and leave, emigrating reluctantly into an increasingly antisemitic world. Some will take inspiration from Hungary and continue to struggle for a liberal-democratic Israel. Others will stay to defend their gradually shrinking enclaves; others still will try to moderate the transition to a religious-nationalist Israel or will join the successor regime.
Scenario Four: An Anti-Netanyahu Victory

A fourth scenario would see a narrow victory for the opposing bloc, which is united by one goal and one goal only—the removal of Netanyahu from power. The anti-Bibi camp, referred to as Gush Ha’Shinui (“the Change Bloc”) is composed of four core parties—Yashar, Beyahad, Yisrael Beiteinu, and The Democrats—the leaders of which, with the exception of Yair Golan of The Democrats, all see themselves as the most qualified to replace Netanyahu as PM.

Until a month ago polls suggested the combined strength of the four might just achieve the 61 seats required to form a narrow but viable majority or at least reach the 57-60 seats needed for a minority government propped up from outside with the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, who are desperate to dispatch Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich.

That is no longer the case, as the momentum has drifted away from the Change Bloc over the past weeks. The polls may be off, and we can envisage a reality in which the Change Bloc wins a bare majority through a combination of a dramatically high anti-Netanyahu voting rate (here again the Arab-Israeli voting rate may prove decisive) coupled with a low pro-Netanyahu one, as disappointed Likud voters stay at home on elections day. But if the latest polls are to be believed, even if the four core members of the Change Bloc bring in Ra’am—and all except The Democrats have vowed not to do so—they are unlikely to rise above 60 seats.

To comfortably clear 61, therefore, the Change Bloc would have to first hope that Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael and The Reservists cross the electoral threshold and then manage to persuade both that—in order to avoid a stalemate, and for the sake of establishing “a Zionist government” that would exclude the “anti-Zionist” Arab and Ultraorthodox parties—they have no choice but to join the Change Bloc. Israeli journalist Raviv Drucker has recently argued that Eizenkot may be able to bring Winter into his coalition by first trying to form a national unity government with Likud, and failing, so that Winter can justify his switching camps as being both reluctant and necessary to prevent Ra’am from being in government. Under such a scenario, Drucker observes, Amcha Yisrael and The Reservists would be able to demand senior cabinet positions, with Winter likely becoming Israel’s next minister of defense.

A less likely, but not entirely inconceivable, variation would have the Change Bloc poach a party currently solidly in the Netanyahu camp, possibly Shas, by bestowing lavish budgets and ministerial appointments upon it while violating their own campaign promises on key policy issues, such as a major compromise on the Haredi military draft.

The question of Haredi military service is worth lingering on for a moment as it stands at the core of the identity-based fissure between the contending camps and is by far the anti-Netanyahu bloc’s most salient argument for his replacement. The Haredi draft dispute pertains to the question of whether ultraorthodox men, long exempted from compulsory military service so they can study Torah full-time, must serve in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) like all other Jewish Israelis. The rapid demographic growth of the ultraorthodox—a population that grows by about 4% per year, the fastest rate among any population in the developed world—means that what in 1948 appeared to be a token concession by David Ben-Gurion to four hundred yeshiva students, now extends to tens of thousands of draft-age men. After two decades of failed attempts to legislate a consensual formula, in June 2024 the Israeli Supreme Court ruled unanimously that Haredi draft exemption has no legal basis and cannot continue. At the same time, the heavy burden imposed by the post-October 7 wars on the rest of Israeli society, particularly the reservists and their families, turned a simmering chronic grievance into an acute demand to sanction those who do not serve.

The IDF has since issued roughly 24,000 call-up orders, to which only about 1,200 Haredi recruits responded, while polling shows 85% of non-Haredi Jewish Israelis favor sanctioning those who refuse to share in the national defense burden. The pro-Netanyahu coalition depends on the ultraorthodox parties (United Torah Judaism and Shas) and has therefore tried to legislate the exemption back into law. Yet the pro-Netanyahu bloc itself is deeply divided on this issue, since Likud and religious-Zionist voters (Otzma Yehudit and the Religious Zionism party) serve in large numbers. In fact, the religious-Zionist community, which makes up roughly 10% of Israel’s population, has sacrificed disproportionally in the post-October 7 wars, with roughly one-third of all fallen soldiers coming from this community.

If anything can make right-leaning Israelis switch camps and side with the Change Bloc, it is the absolute knowledge that every single one of its leaders—particularly Eizenkot, who lost his son, Gal, in the December 2023 battle of Jabaliya in Gaza—is determined to increase Haredi service rates as part of a broader drive to integrate the ultraorthodox into modern Israeliness.

An outright victory for the anti-Netanyahu bloc remains a tall order, but not an impossibility, especially if it is Avigdor Lieberman who will emerge as PM under this scenario. It is Gadi Eizenkot’s Yashar party that is certain to be the largest opposition party. But this does not automatically mean Eizenkot will stand at the head of a Change Government. Israeli law provides that it is not the head of the largest political party, but the head of the party most likely to be able to form a stable government, that is invited by Israel’s president to attempt forming a coalition. In 2021, Naftali Bennett became prime minister at the head of a party with only six Knesset seats.

Something similar could happen with Lieberman this time. With his hawkish reputation, close personal ties to Ofer Winter (who reputedly despises Eizenkot), distance from the October 7 debacle, and decades of experience in senior roles—including minister of finance (2021-22), minister of defense (2016-2018), and deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs (2009-2012 and again in 2013-2015)—it is Lieberman, not Eizenkot or Bennett, who may prove to be the only enzyme capable of the alchemical feat of ousting Netanyahu.

Whether headed by Lieberman, Eizenkot, or Bennett, a narrow Change Bloc government that will see Netanyahu deposed and his current coalition partners sent into opposition will be greeted with relief by Israeli moderates as well as most international audiences. Yet unless it can be quickly enlarged—by poaching a few members of the opposition or bringing in another party—a narrow Change Government will be immediately vulnerable to internal fissures and the risk of defections. Unlike the pro-Netanyahu camp, there is no ideological glue holding an anti-Netanyahu coalition together, and the fate of a 2026 Change Government could easily replicate that of the 2021 Change Government, which disintegrated after a year.

In the longer term, the most demoralizing and dangerous outcome for the liberal camp in Israel may not be a stalemate that drags the country into another round of elections, but a fragile anti-Bibi victory that then produces a dysfunctional coalition paralyzed by endless bickering and is liable to crumble in the face of its first serious internal or security challenge.
Scenario Five: A Broad Centrist Coalition (with or without Netanyahu)

Which brings us to the final scenario: the dissolution, or at least temporary suspension or blurring, of the pro-Bibi/anti-Bibi firewall that defines all other scenarios, and the emergence of some form of broad centrist coalition.

At its broadest, such a coalition would extend from Ra’am—an Arab party whose number two is now Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish, proudly Zionist former police commissioner—and The Democrats, on the left, through Yashar, Beyahad, and The Reservists in the center, to Likud and Yisrael Beiteinu on the right. Based on current polling, such a coalition would command 82 Knesset seats, more than two-thirds of members—an enormous majority capable of passing any legislation it can agree on.

Even a somewhat more limited, but more ideologically aligned, center-right coalition composed of Yashar, Likud, Beyahad, Yisrael Beiteinu, Amcha Yisrael, and The Reservists—which would exclude the more divisive Democrats, Arab parties, and Jewish ultranationalists and ultraorthodox parties—would command some 70 seats. It would be a broad coalition capable of far-reaching reforms, including in politically sensitive areas such as military conscription, constitutional changes, and law enforcement vis-à-vis settler violence and organized crime in the Arab-Israeli community.

The temporary suspension of rivalry between antagonistic political camps is familiar to Israelis. In 1967, four days before the outbreak of the Six-Day War, Prime Minister Levi Eshkol (of the Mapai party, the predecessor of Labor) brought the Menachem Begin-led opposition Gahal bloc (precursor of Likud) into the government, uniting 111 members of Knesset in the face of an imminent existential threat. National unity governments built on Labor-Likud cooperation were also formed to save Israel from hyperinflation (1984-88) and manage the crisis presented by the collapse of the Oslo Process and outbreak of the Second Intifada (2000-2002).

What are the prospects of something similar taking shape in late 2026? The answer depends, first and foremost, on whether Israel faces either an extraordinary national emergency or an exceptional geopolitical opportunity sometime between October 28 and mid-December. War with Iran-Houthis or Turkey would constitute an example of the former, but so could the outbreak of a Third Intifada in the West Bank. The world of 2026 is, sadly, defined by the proliferation of known unknowns and unknown unknowns that could force even Netanyahu and Eizenkot together. Conversely, the imminent and credible prospect of a regional “deal of the century”—involving normalization with Saudi Arabia that is conditional on progress towards Palestinian self-determination—is an example of a positive game changer that could drive the Israeli center left and center right to temporarily unite.

Barring such a deus ex machina, the prospect of a broad centrist coalition increases dramatically if Netanyahu exits the political scene. This could happen for health reasons, by Netanyahu agreeing to a plea bargain in which he receives a preemptive presidential pardon for his criminal indictments, or through some force majeure. All three heads of the Change Bloc who are credible candidates for PM—Eizenkot, Bennett, and Lieberman—would be willing to make far-reaching concessions to a post-Netanyahu Likud, including offering his successor the prospect of a rotating premiership—a power-sharing arrangement in which two coalition leaders agree to split a government’s term, each serving as PM for part of it.

None of them, however, would be so naïve as to enter a rotation agreement with Netanyahu, who has repeatedly destroyed his opponents by making, and then breaking, rotation deals. Eizenkot in particular has had a front row seat to the undoing of his colleague, Benny Gantz, who broke his promise to his electorate and signed a rotation agreement with Netanyahu in the early months of the Covid crisis. The Netanyahu-Gantz “emergency government” was sworn in on 17 May 2020, with Netanyahu as PM and Gantz as “alternate prime minister” and defense minister, due to rotate into the premiership in November 2021. It never happened. Netanyahu let a budget vote fail and dissolved the Knesset in late December 2020, taking Israel to another round of elections in March 2021. Benny Gantz never recovered. The man who, in April 2019, stood at the helm of the mighty Blue and White party with 35 Knesset seats is now being urged by the Change Bloc to announce his withdrawal from the race; Blue and White is now utterly defunct, scoring 0% of the projected vote.

After seven years of political instability, toxic polarization, and war, Israel desperately needs a government broad enough to possess the legitimacy and stability necessary for the country to heal, reform, and rebuild. Assuming the elections scheduled for October 27 are not disrupted, a stalemate on October 28 may, just may, compel a torn and exhausted Israel to negotiate the formation of some kind of unity government.
As one wag put it after three Israeli passengers rescued Fly Dubai flight 1073 from being hijacked and crashed last month, it is Netflix that should take out a subscription on Israel.
Amichai Magen is the founding director of the Jan Koum Israel Studies Program at Stanford University’s Center on Democracy, Development, and the Rule of Law.
