npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-147632/at-least-.headline: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
npr.org/2026/10/10/g-s1-147632/at-least-.author: Bill Chappell

paragraphs.text: Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed.
Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.

One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.
"The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email.
Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

"We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence."

As of 11:50 a.m. ET Saturday, about 780,000 power customers remained without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the monitoring site Poweroutage.us. That figure had been closer to 900,000 earlier Saturday.

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.
The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to theNational Hurricane Center. It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.
Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county,"tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

But the storm's effects extended for hundreds of miles. By around 9:30 a.m. Saturday, the system sent a long band of powerful thunder storms up the center of Georgia. And as theFlorida Public Radio Emergency Network notes, forecasters warn that tornadoes could spin off of the system, causing further havoc far from the Gulf Coast.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cq1j42.headline: Pascal Gross: Has the Brighton midfielder been underrated all this time?
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cq1j42.author: Emlyn Begley, Emma Smith

paragraphs.text: Brighton midfielder Pascal Gross may be one of the best value-for-money signings in Premier League history.
In fact the 35-year-old has effectively cost the Seagulls minus £3m - and been involved in 86 Premier League goals over two spells.
Already in this campaign, Gross has been involved in seven Brighton goals in six games.
His latest provided the opener in his side's 2-0 win at Sunderland on Saturday, a slide-rule pass finding Maxim de Cuyper to slot home.
Gross became the oldest player to provide an assist in three successive Premier League games since a 38-year-old Ryan Giggs did so for Manchester United in February 2012.
In 2026, only Bruno Fernandes and Dominik Szoboszlai have created more chances than the German - and that includes the 18 months he was away from the Premier League.
Gross was Brighton's first Premier League signing in 2017 for a reported £3m from Ingolstadt.
He left for his boyhood club Borussia Dortmund in 2024 for £8m - but in a surprise move he returned to Albion in January for about £1.7m.
So has Gross been underrated all this time?
Former England midfielder, and BBC pundit, Danny Murphy doesn't think so.
"The Premier League is shown worldwide, and he has been a part of that for so many years during a time when Brighton have been a shining light," he said.
"You don't have to play for a big-six team to be appreciated in the Premier League. Gross is not under the radar, because people know how good he is."
How big an impact has Gross had?
A little-heralded German from relegated Ingolstadt, nobody could have anticipated the impact Gross, nor Albion, would go on to have.

"There's an argument Gross is pound-for-pound the best value player in the Premier League over the last 10 years, especially when you look at his goal involvements," said BBC Radio Sussex commentor Johnny Cantor.
"However, he also drives standards in training, sets a high bar and is a huge influence in the dressing room.

"Technically he is excellent, has superb delivery but also possesses an awareness, popping up in spaces all around the pitch. Managers have leaned on him, team-mates respect him, and fans of all generations adore him.
"He will surely be remembered as one of the best Albion players of the modern age."
Since joining Brighton, Gross is seventh for Premier League assists with 52 to go with his 34 goals in 253 league games.
All the more remarkable when you consider his journey with Brighton appeared over two years ago when he went home to join his beloved Borussia Dortmund.
Albion supporter Maz Mirzadeh said: "When he left for Dortmund, it was like going through a heartbreak and seeing an ex go back to their childhood sweetheart.
"He's outrageously good and massively underappreciated.

"If you watch him play, you would think someone's put him in slow-motion settings, but what he lacks in pace, he makes up in superior football IQ, technical brilliance and working harder than any other player on the pitch."
Follow Brighton & Hove Albion on BBC Sounds
Pre-match, post-match and topical Albion content
'Already one of the Brighton greats'
Gross played 66 times for Dortmund, scoring one goal and assisting 17 times, but on 2 January 2026, he came back to Brighton.
Aged 34 at the time, many wondered if it was more of a romantic career swansong.
"There may have been concerns that he may not have been able to recreate the impact of his first period at the Amex but that has been dispelled already," added Cantor.
Only Chelsea's Joao Pedro can better Gross' goal contributions this season in the top flight. Pedro has five goals and three assists, to his former Brighton team mate's three goals and four assists.
The midfielder - who retired from international football after the World Cup - has also played every single minute for Brighton in all competitions, nine games so far.
Former Liverpool and Fulham midfielder Murphy said: "He's an intelligent footballer, with a great football IQ.
"You can see that he has grown into that version of himself over the years. That happens in football - it happened to me - when you know what you can't do, as much as you know what you can do.

"So, you don't see him trying to beat people on the outside with his pace. Instead he loves a little chop, or a Cruyff turn to give himself space and time, or to play a quick first-time pass around the corners. That's why he always seems to be in space.
"His versatility tells you about his intelligence as well. He is able to play as a full-back, central midfield or, recently, as more of a 10. He is scoring and making goals.

"I am sure this won't be his last season with Brighton but, even if it was, he is already going to be remembered as one of the Brighton greats by their supporters for what he has given so far to the club, especially with him coming back and doing what he is doing. It is nothing short of remarkable."
This form led to Gross being the sixth oldest player to be named Premier League player of the month, for September.
Seagulls fan Mirzadeh added: "Even in his 'unc' era, he's showing the Premier League's elite how it's done.
"If he was called Pascal Silva and played for a top-six club he might get the recognition and respect he truly deserves."
Danny Murphy was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan
A version of this feature was published on 2 October 2026.

thehill.com/opinion/technology/6139168-a.headline: AI will make Americans dumber and poorer
thehill.com/opinion/technology/6139168-a.author: John Mac Ghlionn, opinion contributor

paragraphs.text: For decades, Hollywood warned us about killer robots marching through the streets, reducing humanity to piles of ash. But that scenario represents only one side of the rather scary story.

The alternative is that humans remain firmly in control of advanced technology. This is a more reassuring prospect for many, I imagine, but not for me. That’s because the age of AI risks creating a form of high-tech feudalism, in which people rent access to essential tools but never own them.

If that sounds alarmist, consider social media’s dry run from 2012 to 2023. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data revealed a sharp spike in teen depression during that decade, remarkably coinciding with the rise of algorithms that seemed to know everything about everyone. In 2021, internal documents leaked from Meta proved that company executives knew their design choices were harming the mental health of young users. Engineers kept the engagement loops running anyway.
The reason was simple: User attention translates into ad revenue, and more attention means more money. An entire generation grew up trading its sanity for likes, clicks and shares.

Things were bad, but they’re likely to get worse. Social media merely hijacked our attention. AI is coming for the rest of the operating system. Generative models construct synthetic realities and personalized companions that mirror human affection. Today, a teen can spend their entire waking hours talking to a custom conversational bot that remembers every secret and gradually replaces real human interaction. AI monopolizes human cognition and influences how people think and act. Users become entirely dependent on proprietary software for even the most basic tasks, including sending emails and texting a loved one.
As the machines get smarter, we get dumber. And the people building the machines profit handsomely from the madness.

OpenAI is now worth $852 billion. Microsoft committed more than $13 billion to secure commercial access to its underlying models. Anthropic, Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon spend tens of billions annually on computing infrastructure to maintain market domination. These entities operate to maximize shareholder value above all other priorities. Staff members who voice legitimate concerns are often ignored or shown the door. Wall Street demands exponential growth. Executives deliver that growth by locking users into addictive and exploitative ecosystems.

In 1998, major tobacco companies signed the Master Settlement Agreement after decades of knowingly selling addictive products to teenagers. In 2008, global investment banks crashed the mortgage market and collected taxpayer bailouts while millions lost their homes. History shows a consistent pattern of corporate actors pursuing immediate profits while shifting long-term societal costs onto the public. Why would anyone of sound mind expect that to change?

Tech executives ask the public to trust their internal ethics committees, even as many figures inside the industry voice deep concerns about where this technology could lead. These are the people building the systems themselves. They understand that a small number of companies could eventually control technologies capable of doing a vast share of the work humans do today. If that sounds like an exaggeration, consider the pace of progress. AI is advancing rapidly. It’s not unreasonable to imagine a future, perhaps within the next decade, when these systems outperform humans across virtually every task.

To compound matters, the days of the plucky little startup are coming to an end. The sheer cost of building powerful AI systems creates an almost insurmountable barrier to entry. Running an advanced model requires specialized data centers that consume hundreds of megawatts of power and billions of dollars in hardware. A normal American operating out of a garage doesn’t stand a chance. The centralized setup guarantees that a select group of tech executives will maintain absolute control over the digital infrastructure of modern civilization. Every search and every automated workflow will pass through servers owned by four or five mega-corporations.

That dominance over information creates an unprecedented source of influence on society. The word unprecedented matters. Comparisons to the Industrial Revolution or the internet are nonsensical. Neither put this much power over human knowledge and decision-making in the hands of so few private companies.
The dystopian scenario requires no Terminators, only compliant consumers paying monthly bills to let their friend Claude tell them what to say and how to say it.
John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/us/politics/trump.headline: More Than 500 Trees to Be Cut Down at D.C. Golf Club That Trump Wants to Redo

paragraphs.text: The National Park Service will begin cutting down more than 500 trees on Saturday at a public golf course in Washington, D.C., that President Trump is planning to replace with a “championship-level” course.

In a court filing on Friday, Kevin Griess, the superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, said the agency planned to cull hundreds of the trees on the course as part of the clearing operation. The work, scheduled to begin on Saturday, will start at a heavily overgrown area that he said is known as “Trash Island” near the center of the course. He said such work would take place whether or not Mr. Trump moved forward with his plan for an elite golf course at the site.

“In total, the N.P.S. estimates that up to 529 trees that do not contribute to the historic landscape will be removed as part of this tree management and cultural landscape rehabilitation project,” Mr. Griess wrote. “No healthy trees that are contributing features of the historical golf course (such as healthy, historic cherry trees) will be removed as part of this project.”

Facing a federal lawsuit over the proposed golf course renovation, the Trump administration notified a federal judge about the tree-clearing operation because the court requested updates if the administration planned to “conduct any imminent, significant construction or destructive activities of an irretrievable character at East Potomac Golf Course.”

Mr. Griess said the work was being done now because the Park Service had received a “temporary work force support consisting of approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities” to remove the trees.

The D.C. Preservation League filed a federal lawsuit over Mr. Trump’s plans to overhaul the golf course. The Trump administration denied in court that any plans were underway to break ground on the new course by Sept. 1, as Mr. Trump had promised in a post on Truth Social in June. The judge, Ana Reyes, has warned that she would intervene if plans were set in motion without the administration notifying her.

Historic preservationists say the latest tree-clearing work on the course goes beyond merely chopping down dying or damaged trees, and should trigger a new round of public input and reviews under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. The section requires that federal agencies take into account the effects of their actions on historic or cultural properties.

“The work is not routine maintenance, and therefore, for a designated property, they need to undertake Section 106,” Charles A. Birnbaum, president of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, said Saturday.

A top fund-raiser for Mr. Trump has been soliciting donors for the new golf course and a nearby National Garden of American Heroes that Mr. Trump is planning. The project will convert the existing 36-hole property into one that includes a larger 18-hole course that could host major tournaments.
Another of Mr. Trump’s major construction projects is already affecting the public golf course. Soil and debris from the East Wing demolition have been dumped on the site.

nytimes.com/2026/10/10/world/asia/delhi-.headline: Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi

paragraphs.text: The capital of the world’s largest democracy turned into a fortress Saturday, as an extraordinary show of force by Indian authorities met an equally extraordinary display of defiance by the country’s young.

Throughout the day, thousands of people, mostly in their 20s and 30s, tried to gather in Delhi to protest a sweeping revision of their country’s voter roll. Security forces hauled them away, sometimes grabbing them by their arms and legs, and stuffed them, often forcefully, into buses and vans.

Those detained banged on the doors of police vans. They shouted from the windows of buses. One police officer was seen grabbing a protester by the throat. By early evening, more than 2,000 people had been detained, according to a lawyers’ group providing legal aid to the detainees, though an exact number was impossible to ascertain.
The leaders of the Gen Z movement that called for the protest, the Cockroach Janta Party, said they, too, had been detained, including Abhijeet Dipke, one of the movement’s founders.

He shared a video of their encounter with police officers on Instagram. They were landing in Delhi on a flight from Mumbai after attending rallies in other cities earlier in the week, when police officers boarded the plane.
“You can see where the nation is heading. This is dictatorship,” he said. By Saturday evening, it was not known where they were being detained.

The Delhi police appeared to confirm that Mr. Dipke was in their custody. In a post on social media, they said they had offered “assistance” to help him travel home “on humanitarian grounds” after his grandmother’s death on Saturday.

The protest on Saturday followed a week of nationwide demonstrations demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of India’s election commission, a body that was long held in high regard but has come under intense public criticism because of the revision of the national voter roll. That eliminated 130 million names, and critics say it is an effort directed by the government to entrench Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s power.
The protests, while focused on the voter roll issue, signal growing frustration with the government of Mr. Modi, who has been in power for 12 years. Mr. Modi has not commented on the protests.

A member of Parliament from the governing Bharatiya Janata Party, Ravi Shankar Prasad, on Saturday evening issued a scathing attack on the protests. “Indian democracy has destroyed the quest for anarchy,” he said. “The country will be run from the Parliament and not from the streets.”

The measures taken by security officials to prevent protesters gathering were highly unusual in a country that has long prided itself as a vibrant democracy. The heavy-handedness drew comparisons to the 1970s, when the prime minister at the time, Indira Gandhi, suspended the Constitution and jailed opposition leaders.

By Friday, the police had ordered the cancellation of trains bound for the capital and closed 45 metro stations in the city. Videos circulated online of would-be protesters being pulled from trains bound for Delhi in various parts of the country. Some youth activists were placed under effective house arrest days ahead of the protest. Mobile internet was shut in the center of the city, where the protest was to be held.
By early morning, hours before the protest was scheduled to begin at 10 a.m., security officials were out in full force, brandishing batons and shooing away small clusters of protesters.

“Aren’t we children of this nation?” asked Nada Haseen, 22, who had come with several fellow university students to protest, only to be met by a blockade of yellow police barriers. “We are asking for our basic right, to vote.”

They were undeterred. Tanmay Koli, 20, rode a train for two days by himself to come to his nation’s capital. He found his way to a Sikh temple to sit for a while and eat. Then he headed out into the streets of New Delhi with two other young men, who, like him, had come by train from their own hometowns far away.

On Saturday, the three of them, strangers until just a few hours ago, sat together on a curb staring at barricades and a phalanx of security forces. They were nervous, they said, but they wanted to be here.
“They’re stealing votes,” Mr. Koli, said. He had come from Pune, a city to the south.
“Democracy is not safe,” said his new friend, a 28-year-old man who, fearing reprisal, gave only his first name, Om. He had traveled from Chandigarh, a city to the north.

Delhi police said Friday they had denied permission for the Cockroach Janta Party-led protest at Jantar Mantar, the 18th-century monument that is a designated protest site. Police said they had not asked for permission sufficiently early.

In Connaught Place, a shopping and restaurant hub, detained protesters in police vans rolled past a tricolor Indian flag, flying high behind them, and a statue of Gandhi’s spinning wheel, a symbol of India’s nonviolent independence movement.

A group of lawyers, dressed in their signature black and white garb, set out to march from the Supreme Court and a nearby district court, holding copies of the Indian Constitution; 400 of them were soon detained, according to Utkarsh Sinha, a lawyer who attended the demonstrations. From a Sikh house of worship near Jantar Mantar, a small group of protesters set off; several were plucked off by police, and many others sprinted away.

By midday, when it became abundantly clear that there would be no gathering at Jantar Mantar, another group, including by a prominent student activist named Neha Bora, began marching from a market nearly six miles away. She too was detained.
Throughout the afternoon, spontaneous protests erupted, some with a handful of people, others with hundreds.

All the detainees were taken away from the city center and held in various places, including a meeting hall and a stadium, before being taken to several police stations around the city, according to several of the detainees.
Lawyers groups fanned out across the city to help the detained at police stations. Others organized caravans of cars to retrieve detainees and bring them home. Some of them were also detained.

Ajinkya Shinde, a Cockroach Janta Party leader, issued a video message on behalf of the other leaders who had been detained. He urged people to continue protesting even if they were prevented from reaching the designated protest site, Jantar Mantar, “Wherever you are stopped, turn that place into Jantar Mantar.”

engadget.com/2279929/what-is-ray-tracing.headline: What Is Ray Tracing In Gaming And Does It Really Make A Difference?
engadget.com/2279929/what-is-ray-tracing.author: Dave Meikleham

paragraphs.text: Games look way more beautiful, but it comes at a high cost.

One of the main selling points of the current console generation is that Sony and Microsoft's machines can finally handle ray tracing (RT) at a decent level. Yet while the PS5 and Xbox Series X can provide moderate ray-traced experiences, the top end of the PC gaming food chain is on an entirely different level. High-end rigs offer the most advanced RT features with incredible fidelity. But what if you're on an aging or average PC? Is ray tracing really worth enabling?

It all comes down to the hardware you're using. If your GPU is more than five years old, any ray-traced games your PC is capable of running will likely perform poorly. Ray tracing is a luxury gaming feature that should only be turned on if you own a fairly high-end rig. And that's not even mentioning its flashier sibling: path tracing.
Is ray tracing worth it?

For your average PC gamer playing on a middling GPU, ray tracing will cost too many frames to make it worth enabling. That said, at time of writing, the Steam Hardware Survey ranks the extremely capable NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 as the graphics card with the highest usage share. We thus see dedicated PC players are embracing graphics cards more than capable of handling ray tracing. If your GPU is a couple of generations old, though, RT should be disabled.

But what is ray tracing exactly? In short, it's an advanced rendering technique that simulates realistic lighting effects, shadows and reflections more accurately than old-school rasterization methods. In older games that don't support ray tracing, screen-space reflections are used, which aren't very accurate. By contrast, modern titles that support RT can reflect offscreen objects and shadows by bouncing rays around the screen, before accurately calculating how the in-game world should be lit.

I've been enjoying ray tracing in some of the best PC games for years, and I absolutely adore the technology. There are a couple of major caveats, though. I'm fortunate to have access to an RTX 5090, and I often don't mind embracing NVIDIA's DLSS 4.5 Multi Frame Generation tech to boost my frame rates (at the admitted cost of increased input lag).

For folks gaming on an RTX 3060 or AMD Radeon RX 6600 XT, there's no way I can recommend ray tracing. Instead, focus on locking down a stable frame rate at your monitor's native resolution. After all, if you've never seen ray tracing in action, you're not going to miss it.
How much does ray tracing impact FPS?

"A whole lot," is the succinct answer. Though it depends on the specific game you're booting up, performance in many modern AAA PC titles will often plummet once you enable ray tracing features, unless you're rocking a seriously powerful rig. You can improve your fps for smoother gaming by turning on DLSS or embracing frame generation, sure. Yet if you're not into frame rate-boosting AI tech, ray tracing can be a performance killer.

A while back, TechSpot analyzed the impact of ray tracing across a whopping 36 different games. During the site's comprehensive testing, average FPS dropped between 20 to 40 percent when RT was on. That's a whole lot of frames to sacrifice for a fancy lighting technique many folks will struggle to notice in motion.

Some of the worst offenders, according to the report: Hogwarts Legacy saw a 45 percent dip in frame rates; for Alan Wake 2 the decrease is around 52 percent, and Hitman 3's average frame rate drops by an absurd 65 percent. I've played Agent 47's latest assassination adventure with RT cranked to the max, and as much I admire all of those geometrically correct rays bouncing off the chrome dome killer's head, that's a brutal performance hit.
Ray tracing vs. path tracing: what's the difference?

Permit me to indulge in a nerdy Star Wars analogy: if ray tracing is a talented Padawan, path tracing is a full-blown Jedi Master. Path tracing is still a type of RT, but a more advanced one. In the handful of PC games that deploy this incredibly pretty technique, the results are often jaw-dropping.

Path tracing — sometimes referred to as "full ray tracing" in certain titles — can calculate far more lighting sources than traditional RT. In games that don't support path tracing, RT is often combined with traditional rasterization methods, with ray tracing handling specific effects like reflections or shadows. Path tracing works differently. Compared to standard RT, it usually controls the entire look of a game, leading to a more consistently lit image.

I replayed the opening scene of Resident Evil Requiem for this feature and compared its High ray tracing preset to the full path tracing option (as you can see in the screenshot above). If you're reading this on your phone, you probably won't be able to spot the differences between the two techs. But they definitely exist.

Path tracing's multi-bounce global illumination is most clearly seen in the car's left headlight. Notice the slight red tinge being cast by the neon lights from a nearby, off-screen shop window. This is absent with ray tracing, where bounce lighting is more limited. If you squint, you can also see that path tracing handles the specular reflections on the car's windshield more effectively, exhibiting less aliasing compared to standard RT. Trust me, it's a lot easier to spot the difference when looking at an uncompressed 4K image.

As much as I admire path tracing in the likes of 007: First Light and Cyberpunk 2077, it's even more brutally taxing on frame rates than traditional ray tracing. With the latter title, enabling path tracing can be 50 percent more demanding than RT depending on the scene. Unless you're lucky enough to own an RTX 5090 or RTX 5080, you're best off steering well clear of the gorgeous but performance-punishing tech.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8r5l7n92jo.headline: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe8r5l7n92jo.author: Rorey Bosotti

paragraphs.text: US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.

Zelensky warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war in Ukraine, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking as he left the White House on Saturday, Trump said the Ukrainian president "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".
Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," he said.
"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.
The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.

His criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal was echoed by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism, saying suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA – up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.
Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.

A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" – but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".
In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.
Diesel production in the Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.
Trump had already called for new elections in Ukraine last December, external, saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.
Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

phys.org/news/2026-10-himalayan-zone.htm.headline: Nearly 300,000 at risk from Himalayan floods, as flood zone building accelerates
phys.org/news/2026-10-himalayan-zone.htm.author: Nature Publishing Group

paragraphs.text: edited by Lisa Lock, reviewed by Robert Egan

Nearly 300,000 people may live in areas at risk of flooding in the Nepalese, Indian and Chinese areas of the Himalayas. The results, from a study published in Scientific Reports, also indicate that the total area covered by buildings within potential flood zones increased by approximately 45% between 2016 and 2023.

Flooding in the Himalayas is typically caused by seasonal monsoons, extreme rainfall or rare but devastating debris flows or floods from glacial lakes (known as glacial lake outburst floods). Climate change is predicted to increase the severity of these events, while the steep, narrow valleys in mountainous areas can exacerbate flood heights and the subsequent effects. However, the number of people at risk from flooding in this area remains unclear.

C. Scott Watson and colleagues assessed changes in the potential exposure of buildings and people to flooding between 2016 and 2023 in areas up to 50 km (31 miles) downstream of 1,361 Himalayan lakes in Nepal and neighboring regions of India and China. They used five data sets validated against manually recorded data to estimate the total building footprint (the area covered by the bases of all existing buildings) in these areas.

The estimated footprint of buildings within 50 vertical meters (164 feet) of a river channel—used as a proxy for exposure to potential flooding—increased by 45.75%, from 12.38 to 18.04 km2 (4.78 to 6.97 square miles). In areas at a high risk of glacial lake outburst floods, the footprint increased by 77.78%, from 0.72 to 1.28 km2 (0.28 to 0.49 square miles).

The authors then used the calculated building footprint to estimate that, in 2026, approximately 293,800 people (18% of the population in the study area) may live in buildings exposed to potential flooding. This includes an estimated 108,500 people in Nepal, of whom 22,800 live within 10 vertical meters (33 feet) of a river channel. The population living within the flood risk zones is projected to increase by 17,900 (6%) between 2015 and 2030.

The authors caution that the estimates of both total building footprint and population growth are highly uncertain. They highlight the need for more accurate building databases to better calculate risk.
C. Scott Watson et al, Increasing exposure to potential flooding in high-mountain catchments, Scientific Reports (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-70268-0
Journal information: Scientific Reports

latimes.com/lifestyle/image/story/2026-1.headline: What is luxury now? 5 fashion buyers share their personal luxuries
latimes.com/lifestyle/image/story/2026-1.author: Viv Chen

paragraphs.text: Does our cultural understanding of luxury need a reset?

That’s the question that drove my conversations with five luxury buyers behind some of the most original concept stores in Los Angeles, New York and San Francisco. Because buyers are responsible for deciding what actually gets sold on the shop floor (you can think of them as professional treasure hunters, art curators and merchants all in one), I was interested in their personal ideas of luxury.

It was quickly established what luxury was not. It’s not defined by a high price tag or a designer label. Everyone I spoke to described a personal luxury that was grounded in their lived experiences. Knitting with cashmere yarn, driving a vintage car down Sunset Boulevard, people-watching in Paris. It was about how beauty shows up in their real lives, not online.

The inimitable André Leon Talley once described American fashion as a “famine of beauty.” In 2026, it’s tempting to say the same about luxury. But it’s still there, for anyone who is willing to experience it.
McMullen (San Francisco)

McMullen has been bringing luxury fashion to the Bay Area for nearly two decades. The shop opened in Oakland in 2007, moved to Presidio Heights in San Francisco in 2024 and its new flagship store on Maiden Lane opened in September.

The owner was drawn to San Francisco for its intersection of creativity, technology and entrepreneurship. She designed the stores to feel like discovery spaces, where established houses sit alongside emerging designers, and every piece has a point of view. In a city that is not particularly known for its fashion scene, McMullen is a rare hub where designers like Amy Smilovic and Henrik Vibskov will host pop-ups and events when they’re in town.

As a veteran buyer, McMullen believes that luxury comes from intention, not price point or a label. She looks for exceptional craftsmanship, originality and pieces that create an emotional response. Her taste and eye for beauty has been cultivated through lived experiences, like exploring Mexico City’s La Lagunilla antique market, or sifting through the beauty shelves of a Parisian pharmacy.
“Style is how a woman moves through the world,” she muses.

McMullen’s luxury: “Paris. I spend a lot of time there, and it’s a city that continues to reveal itself to me no matter how often I return. My pleasure is having the time to experience it beyond work, walking without a destination, returning to places I love, discovering a new gallery or restaurant, and simply observing how people live and dress. There’s an ease and beauty in the everyday that always stays with me and continues to shape the way I see the world.”
Maxfield L.A. (Los Angeles)
Founded by Tommy Perse in 1969, Maxfield was the first retail concept store in America of its kind, bringing together design-forward objects and unusual products alongside clothing.

Today, Sarah Stewart and Anthony Cataldo keep the spirit of Perse’s original idea alive in the West Hollywood store. Here, you can find rarities you can’t find online — like 18th century memento jewelry, a Transylvanian vampire-slaying kit or a vintage Paris-exclusive Chanel handbag.

The world of Maxfield begins before you even step in the store. In the parking lot, there’s a Jean Prouvé structure — a rare architectural piece that functions as a “luxury mic drop” because “no one else in the world has a Prouvé structure outside of France,” says Stewart. That alone draws in a certain kind of “if you know, you know ” design enthusiast into the store.

On any given Saturday, you could spot a Grammy- or Oscar-winning performer, a celebrity stylist, Beverly Hills ladies and kids who just came over from the Chrome Hearts store. It’s a perfect spot for people-watching in L.A.

For Cataldo, luxury is quality you can feel, both in the craftsmanship and the emotion it elicits. “It’s that feeling of, wow, this is luxurious and I really look forward to having this for the rest of my life,” he explains. Stewart adds that luxury comes from authenticity, which — in this day and age — means something “created by and touched by human hands.”

Stewart’s luxury: “Unexpected encounters with art. I remember going into Kenzo’s tea house in Paris after someone had rented it to show a collection. In the back room, where the models were changing their clothes, was a lithograpgh by Francis Bacon. When you see something like that in your regular working life, it reminds you of how much beauty there is in the world.”

Cataldo’s luxury: “Driving around L.A. in my old Mercedes. Everything about the car is manual, so when the traffic dies down and the sun’s about to go down, you hear the popping of the door and the rattle of the key; it’s all buildup to a moment where you roll the top down and then you’re driving down Sunset Boulevard. The sensory of it all, the lights, the smell, the air. I feel like I’m in an old Hollywood film.”
Outline (Brooklyn)

“Our store is a place for real life,” Margaret Austin says. Outline, the shop she co-founded in 2022 with Julia Edelman and Hannah Rieke, was opened in response to several of her favorite stores shuttering during the pandemic. The idea was to open a womenswear boutique that felt personal, with a brand mix that could offer women special pieces to wear for their everyday lives.

The assortment ranges from fashion-girl staples like Margiela Tabis to brands with niche devoted followings, like Dosa, Colleen Allen and Auralee. The clientele is just as varied: artists and owners of creative businesses, visitors to New York, busy working mothers, bankers and lawyers — all of whom appreciate craftsmanship and quality fabrics.

Three years later, in 2025, Outline made the choice to indefinitely retire its e-commerce site in favor of a catalog printed twice a year. Avoiding the internet as much as possible — “it’s hard,” she admits — is how Austin cultivates her perspective as a buyer. She’s interested in what real women are thinking and doing in their lives, and wants the clothes at Outline to be pieces they will actually want to wear.
Ultimately, she believes luxury is “something that cuts no corners.”
Austin’s luxury: “I’m a knitter and so I love to treat myself (and the people I knit for) to really special yarn (for example cashmere or something hand-dyed in an amazing color).”
Mohawk General Store (Los Angeles)

Mohawk General Store opened in 2008 in a tiny space in Echo Park, just months before the Great Recession hit. For Carney, the shop began almost as a personal project — something to focus on while she awaited her green card. With her husband, Kevin Carney, the two envisioned a space that contained everything they loved: fashion, design, home, lifestyle, art, vintage, high and low.

You can still see that vision today, where sumptuous leather Lemaire flats and technicolor Pleats Please tops sit alongside frilly silk scrunchies and incense from Kyoto. “We have a really interesting and sophisticated mix of clients,” Carney notes. There are the longtime locals who have been shopping there since the early days, plus a mix of creative types like directors, writers, chefs, models, stylists, designers and actors. Lately, she’s noticed more mother-daughter duos.

She defines luxury as “the freedom to dress in a way that is true to your values.” It should encompass quality, integrity, beauty and function. For inspiration, Carney looks to old films, documentaries, travel and art encountered in person rather than online. She also believes that dialogue with clients is integral to honing a sharp perspective, season after season.

Carney’s luxury: “Efficiency and productivity are deemed so important these days. I have recently discovered the joy of doing nothing and going offline for certain periods of time. The days when I am able to unplug and just be able to do anything or nothing are some of the most enjoyable.”

thehill.com/policy/international/6140669.headline: Pope Leo decries death penalty as Hegseth’s public execution plan sparks backlash
thehill.com/policy/international/6140669.author: Sarah Davis

paragraphs.text: Pope Leo XIV on Saturday called capital punishment “inadmissible” on World Day Against the Death Penalty, amid the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the December execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan in Texas.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” the pontiff wrote on social media.

“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” he continued.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the public would be able to view the convicted terrorist’s Dec. 3 execution by firing squad. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted in the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, which killed 13 people and injured 32 others.
While the pontiff did not directly comment on Hasan’s case, other Catholic leaders and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle denounced the livestream plans directly.
Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin told reporters Friday that the plans were unacceptable, according to The Vatican News.

“It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this method in this day and age,” he said. “I do not know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle. However guilty the person may be, there are other ways.”
The president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, Archbishop Paul Croakley, urged the Pentagon to reconsider the public execution.
“In no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in an interview with Vatican News.
The Hill has reached out to the Pentagon for comment regarding the pontiff’s criticism.

fortune.com/2026/10/10/anthropic-claude-.headline: After Anthropic’s Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case, police say ‘cases involve real victims, grieving families’
fortune.com/2026/10/10/anthropic-claude-.author: Mae Anderson, The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said.

It’s the latest example of AI models acting in unintended ways and manipulating government and other websites during tests. In a report Friday, Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission.
The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said.
Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site.

Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police.
There are rising concerns about AI companies’ unchecked AI agentsmeddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation.
In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models.

“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the Philadelphia Police Department said in a statement. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”

Anthropic said in its report that most of the reported behaviors are forms of what it calls “persistence” — “in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping.”
The company said it was modifying its training to “reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.”
Anthropic said it briefed the White House on cases that involved U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, and notified each agency involved.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/10/nine-kille.headline: Nine killed in shooting in US state of Pennsylvania, including two children
aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/10/nine-kille.author: AFP and AP

paragraphs.text: The shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania happened on Friday, according to state officials.
Nine people were killed Friday in a shooting in the US state of Pennsylvania, according to Governor Josh Shapiro. Police said the suspected shooter was among the nine dead.
Local media reported that two children were also among those killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, which is 188 kilometres (117 miles) north of Pittsburgh.
Recommended Stories
Police in the city of Erie were called Friday around 5:00pm local time (21:00 GMT) to reports of shots fired and discovered two women dead in the street, the Erie News Now outlet said.
The attacker barricaded himself inside the home as police surrounded the building and ordered him to exit.
More gunshots were heard during the standoff, Erie News Now reported.

When police eventually entered the building, they found several more victims around the home, including the two children. The deceased attacker had an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, the outlet said, citing police.
Erie News Now said that police officers who responded to the scene were being offered counselling over the horrifying incident.

“I have not seen anything like this in my 28-plus years,” Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah told a local news station on Saturday. “I’m not sure that the city of Erie has ever seen the loss of life and the devastation that we just witnessed.”
Lorah declined to provide more details but said the circumstances of the shooting were “deeply disturbing”.
Shapiro said Saturday he offered his administration’s “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin.
Mass shootings occur frequently in the United States, where guns vastly outnumber the population and efforts to increase firearm restrictions face steep political and legal hurdles.

bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/articles/cmn4ez.headline: Singapore Grand Prix: Max Verstappen builds major momentum as 'no-one very happy' at McLaren after bad day at office
bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/articles/cmn4ez.author: Andrew Benson

paragraphs.text: Max Verstappen is too far behind, and Kimi Antonelli too far ahead, to consider that Red Bull's revival might create any real jeopardy in the championship fight - but the Dutchman is certainly building some major momentum as the Formula 1 season moves into its closing stages.
Verstappen finished Saturday in Singapore with pole position for the grand prix to add to the sprint-race victory he had completed in tricky wet conditions earlier in the day.
And that gives him a great opportunity to complete a second grand prix victory within a week if he can convert on Sunday.
Verstappen has two eager Ferrari drivers right behind him, after Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both felt that they had just missed out on a pole position that was possible.
He also has concerns about Red Bull's inconsistent starts - he lost the lead off the line both in Malaysia last weekend and in the sprint.

If he does drop back at the start in Singapore, it is the sort of track where overtaking is at a premium and he will not find it as easy to get back in front as he did on his way to his first victory of the season.
And he is, as one would expect, not getting ahead of himself.
"It was a good qualifying," Verstappen said. "It was always very close and we got ahead when it mattered and we are very happy with that.

"All weekend the car has been in a good window and that makes it a lot easier to find your rhythm. Incredibly happy to start first. Still a long race ahead, a lot of things can go wrong but we have done everything up until now well so hopefully we can continue that tomorrow.
"It's been a really positive last few races and we want to keep that momentum going."

Verstappen's maiden win of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend came after a run of three podium finishes in Italy, Spain and Azerbaijan, the last of which might very well have been a first victory had he not had problems in qualifying that left him eighth on the grid when he could have been on the front row.
His upturn in form has come as a result of steady work from Red Bull in improving their car and getting it into a position where he feels he can predict its behaviour and therefore push to the limit.
When a Red Bull is in that spot, Verstappen can be close to unbeatable.

He proved that in his remarkable comeback last year, when he gave McLaren and Lando Norris nightmares with a quite brilliant second half of the season that saw him eat into a 100-point deficit to the championship lead and ultimately miss out on taking a fifth title by just two points.
This year, Verstappen's deficit to Antonelli is even bigger than that.

He is 129 points behind the Mercedes driver with only 175 still remaining, assuming the two end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi do actually take place in the context of the war in the Middle East.

It would take some kind of miracle - involving not only a non-stop stream of wins for Verstappen and a highly unlikely run of poor form and bad luck for Antonelli - for him to turn that around. So the prospect can be realistically dismissed.
But he certainly looks as if he will be a contender at the front for the remainder of the season.
If that is not a major concern for Antonelli, it certainly is for McLaren.

They had their own purple patch in the summer, when Lando Norris took consecutive wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, and would have won in Madrid had it not been for the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car.

But the world champions have slipped from competitiveness in recent races, and before the Singapore Grand Prix they lie in third place in the constructors' championship, only 11 points ahead of Red Bull.
Saturday in Singapore was a bad day at the office for McLaren.
Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were heading for fourth and fifth places in the sprint when Norris made a dive down the inside of his team-mate at Turn Five on the final lap.
This is not a common overtaking spot and from a McLaren point of view it was a move with no reward, only risk.
The move might have made sense if it had come earlier in the race and enabled Norris to challenge Leclerc, struggling in front of them, for third.
But on the last lap, Norris was not going to have a go at Leclerc even if he had got through - the only remaining overtaking place was at the end of the following straight into Turn Seven.
If the McLaren drivers swapped places, it would make no difference to the team in terms of a collective points haul, but if it went wrong, the cost could be high.

And so it did. Norris was in a position to make a legitimate move, but they came together, pirouetted in tandem, Piastri into the barriers and out of the race and Norris slipping down to eighth. Nine points had become one.
The stewards took no action, feeling that "both drivers had contributed to the incident".
Piastri had explained in the hearing that he did not expect Norris to try a move there, and attempted to leave space when he saw him.

Norris argued that his his car was in a position that, according to the rules, entitled him to make an overtaking attempt, so expected to be left space and had braked and gone over the kerb when he realised he was not going to get as much as he expected.

He said: "There are two sides, one is what the stewards say and that's a fair reasoning, no-one's to blame. But I did apologise because it was still me attacking, as I had the right to do. If I just sat there and was boring like I should be, nothing would have happened. So really it's still my fault but I deserved to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it."

Norris added: "As you probably expect, no-one's very happy. I'm not happy, Oscar isn't happy. None of us wanted it to go that way. There was things both of us could have done better and, yeah, we spoke about it and we moved on."
Sunday, 11 October at 13:00 BST
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app
Team principal Andrea Stella is a measured man who chooses his words carefully, but his displeasure was clear.

"It was a very long, tiring and challenging day," he said. "Very simply, it is unacceptable that two McLarens ever come together on track. This is a fundamental principle of how we go racing, and something both drivers are very well aware of.

"As always, we discuss these incidents as a team in a constructive and productive way as there is always something to learn and take forward to emerge stronger. These are not conversations we need to have in public, but we have reminded our drivers that the interests of the team must always come first, and that did not happen today."

The context for the collision comes after two seasons where Norris and Piastri have had a number of incidents that created tensions, especially in their title battle last season. Lessons do not appear to have been learned in the way Stella might have expected.
Stella said he was "disappointed" more than anything, pointing out that this was far from the first conversation he had had with the drivers on the need to put the team's interests first.
"We as a team need to reflect as to how we make sure that these situations do not happen any more," he said.
"It is serious. It is serious because the damage for the team is material. We are in a close fight in the championship.

"We had the ambition to challenge Ferrari and this is a problem in the challenge for the second position, and we have an ambition to finish ahead of Red Bull, and this is a problem to finish ahead of Red Bull.

"And it is also serious because we come from a few seasons in which we have reflected together, team and drivers, as to how we approach racing together and how we make sure that the interest of the team is protected.

"It is serious, but at the same time we approach it with a very constructive mindset because there is only one outcome, that the team will be more united and the team will be stronger in the way we pursue our quest, which is the drivers' and the team's quest, together."

paragraphs.text: , South Yorkshire Police said in a statement. The Yorkshire Ambulance Service said it dispatched two ambulances, an air ambulance and a doctor to attend the scene. The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers.

Visitors to several zoos and wildlife parks around the world have tried to enter tiger enclosures. A woman was caught in 2024 jumping over a fence and taunting a tiger at the Cohanzick Zoo in New Jersey. In 2016, a zookeeper was fatally attacked by a Malayan tiger at a Florida zoo when she entered the enclosure for the tigers' night house, a medical examiner's investigation found.

Several years earlier, in 2012, a man jumped from an area near the monorail in the Bronx Zoo over two fences, including an electrified one, in one bound to get into the tiger enclosure, police said. He was severely injured in what appeared to be a suicide attempt, police said.

engadget.com/2283091/anthropic-says-its-.headline: Anthropic Says Its AI Agents Tried To Break Into Government Websites
engadget.com/2283091/anthropic-says-its-.author: Mariella Moon

paragraphs.text: The company didn’t name them, but the affected agencies were ‘at the federal, state and local levels.’

Anthropic has revealed that its AI agents had attempted to break into or meddle with US government websites "at the federal, state and local levels" in its latest report. The company didn't name specific agencies and organizations in the report to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems at their request. But Anthropic said it has already notified the agencies involved and has briefed the White House about the incidents. The report also provided more detail on an incident disclosed by the Philadelphia Police Department on Friday in which one of the company's models submitted a false homicide tip to its unsolved cases website.

That instance involved Claude Haiku 4.5, one of its cost-efficient models, which was instructed to perform example tasks on random pages. It found a page referencing an unsolved homicide case with a tip form. As you may have guessed, Claude filled out the form and submitted a tip. It said: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to The New York Times that Anthropic recently notified its office about the submission. It said the tip was dated July 18 and that it was flagged as spam, so the department at least didn't waste resources investigating it.

In another instance, Anthropic made Claude Mythos 5, its cybersecurity-focused model, identify a location shown in a photo. Claude tried to access a government property map to triangulate its guesses, because it could not click links on web pages like a person could. It found access tokens instead and sent inquiry requests straight to the map's server to gain access to its data. Mythos 5 also requested an access token from a state agency website to pull data for a statistics task without paying a fee that visitors were supposed to pay.

Anthropic discovered these events upon reviewing transcripts of its evaluations. It started looking through them in July, after OpenAI had admitted that its agents escaped their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face without prompting. OpenAI also confirmed in September that its agents had meddled with government websites, particularly those operated by the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

In the Remediation section of its report, Anthropic said it has "taken several preventative measures" after discovering the unintended model actions. "Some of the public evaluations we no longer run; others we have moved to their offline versions, or rebuilt them so that their tasks do not reach live websites," the report states. "We've also made broader changes. We have updated the guardrails on some of our internet access tools, such as the web fetch tool, to heavily restrict what the model can do with them." Anthropic also says it's "built tooling to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described" in the report, among other measures.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/10/pope-says-.headline: Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution
aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/10/pope-says-.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Pope Leo XIV has declared that the death penalty is “inadmissible” while his home country, the United States, announces plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

Marking World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, the pope reiterated the Catholic Church’s teaching on capital punishment, writing on X that it was “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person”.
Recommended Stories
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” his post said.

“Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” added the leader of the Catholic Church.
The American Pope’s comments come days after US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan on December 3 will be livestreamed.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009.
Pope Leo did not specifically refer to the planned execution, or last month’s botched execution attempt on Christa Pike, who survived two doses of the lethal injection in Tennessee.
But his post came hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, told Vatican News that the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution was “unacceptable”.
It was Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, in 2018 who first amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances.

Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church did not exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.”

The planned livestream of Hasan’s execution has sparked outrage across the US political divide. Republican representative Austin Scott said he supported executing Hassan but that “livestreaming executions is what Jihadists do. America is better than that.”

Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice”, but that public executions are “the kind of thing that Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?”

On Thursday, a Pentagon official confirmed the plans, but on Friday, Vice President JD Vance, who is a practising Catholic, expressed doubt on whether the livestream would be going ahead, telling reporters that if it is, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

sports.yahoo.com/articles/dont-feel-fear.headline: 'I don't feel fear': Fulham boss Arbeloa hits back as pressure mounts

paragraphs.text: Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa hit back at his critics after a 2-1 defeat against Ipswich on Saturday extended their winless run in the Premier League to six matches.
Former Real Madrid manager Arbeloa was denied his first win in the English top-flight in painful fashion as Fulham conceded twice in the final moments at Portman Road.
Ryan Sessegnon's 55th-minute strike for Fulham was cancelled out by Abdoul Ouattara's long-range rocket in the 88th minute before Dara O'Shea headed home in stoppage-time.
Fulham are mired in the relegation zone as questions mount about Arbeloa's ability to save his club from a relegation battle.
"I never worry about my position. I don't feel fear. You cannot be a coach if you feel it," he said.
"You have to work, take the decision and you need to show confidence to your players.
"It's not about my position, it is about Fulham's position. That is the most important thing. Obviously it is just six games, but it is true we need points."
It is four league losses in six games this season for Arbeloa, whose team have conceded after 75 minutes in matches with Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Manchester United and now Ipswich.
Although Arbeloa had a brief spell at Real last season following Xabi Alonso's sacking, the former Liverpool defender has never managed in the Premier League before.
His only managerial experience prior to Real came with the Spanish club's second team.
But the 43-year-old pointed to his impressive playing career with Real, Liverpool and Spain as proof he is equipped to handle the heart.
"Me? No, maybe you don't know me but I played for the best team in world. I have coached the best team in the world," he said.
"Maybe you don't know, but just to let you know, that pressure is part of my life since I was a kid.
"So, it is normal in football. It is normal for players, it is normal for coaches and everybody that is around a team. I think pressure is something that is important for me and I like it."
